(ii) Current is minimum when $|X_L - X_C|$ is very large, i.e. $\phi \to \pm\pi/2$.

questions.question: (i) Find the value of the phase difference between the current and the voltage in the series LCR circuit shown below. Which one leads in phase: current or voltage? (ii) Without making any other change, find the value of the additional capacitor $C_{1}$, to be connected in parallel with the capacitor $C$, in order to make the power factor of the circuit unity.
questions.answer:
(i) Phase difference $\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$, giving $\phi = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{X_L-X_C}{R}\right)$
If $X_L > X_C$, the voltage leads the current; if $X_C > X_L$, the current leads the voltage.
(ii) For unity power factor, the net reactance must be zero: $X_L = X_C'$ where $C' = C + C_1$ is the new combined capacitance (parallel capacitors add).
So $C_1 = C' - C = \dfrac{1}{\omega^2 L} - C$, where $\omega$ is the source frequency and $L$ is the inductance in the circuit.

questions.question: A source of ac voltage $v = v_{0} \sin \omega t$ is connected across a pure inductor of inductance $L$. Derive the expressions for the instantaneous current in the circuit. Show that average power dissipated in the circuit is zero.
questions.answer:
For a pure inductor, $v = v_0\sin\omega t = L\dfrac{di}{dt}$
So $di = \dfrac{v_0}{L}\sin\omega t\, dt$; integrating, $i = -\dfrac{v_0}{\omega L}\cos\omega t = \dfrac{v_0}{\omega L}\sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = i_0\sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, where $i_0 = v_0/\omega L$
Thus current lags voltage by $\pi/2$.
Instantaneous power $p = vi = v_0 i_0\sin\omega t\sin(\omega t - \pi/2) = -v_0i_0\sin\omega t\cos\omega t = -\dfrac{v_0i_0}{2}\sin2\omega t$
Average of $\sin2\omega t$ over a complete cycle is zero, so average power $P = 0$.

questions.question: (i) When an AC source is connected to an ideal inductor show that the average power supplied by the source over a complete cycle is zero. (ii) A lamp is connected in series with an inductor and an AC source. What happens to the brightness of the lamp when the key is plugged in and an iron rod is inserted inside the inductor? Explain.
questions.answer:
(i) For an ideal inductor, current $i = i_0\sin(\omega t - \pi/2)$ lags voltage $v = v_0\sin\omega t$ by $\pi/2$.
Instantaneous power $p = vi = v_0i_0\sin\omega t\sin(\omega t-\pi/2) = -\dfrac{v_0i_0}{2}\sin2\omega t$
Since the average of $\sin2\omega t$ over a full cycle is zero, average power $P = 0$.
(ii) When the iron rod is inserted, the inductance $L$ increases (iron has high permeability), so inductive reactance $X_L = \omega L$ increases.
This increases the impedance $Z = \sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}$ of the circuit, reducing the current, so the brightness of the lamp decreases.

questions.question: Draw a schematic arrangement for winding of primary and secondary coils in a transformer with the two coils on separate limbs of the core. State its underlying principle and find the relation between the primary and secondary voltages in terms of the number of turns of the primary and secondary windings. How are the currents in the primary and secondary coils related to the voltages in the case of an ideal transformer?
questions.answer:
The primary coil $P$ (with $N_p$ turns) is wound on one limb of a rectangular laminated soft-iron core, and the secondary coil $S$ (with $N_s$ turns) is wound on the other limb; the core links the flux produced by $P$ to $S$.
Principle: mutual induction — an alternating current in the primary sets up a changing magnetic flux, which is linked with the secondary and induces an alternating emf in it.
Since the flux $\phi$ per turn is common to both windings, $V_p = N_p \frac{d\phi}{dt}$ and $V_s = N_s \frac{d\phi}{dt}$, giving $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$.
For an ideal transformer, input power equals output power: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$, so $\frac{I_s}{I_p} = \frac{N_p}{N_s} = \frac{V_p}{V_s}$.

questions.question: (i) When an AC source is connected to an ideal capacitor, show that the average power supplied by the source over a complete cycle is zero. (ii) A bulb is connected in series with a variable capacitor and an A.C. source as shown. What happens to the brightness of the bulb when the key is plugged in and capacitance of the capacitor is gradually reduced?
questions.answer:
(i) For a capacitor, $v = V_0\sin\omega t$ drives a current $i = I_0\sin(\omega t + \pi/2)$, i.e., current leads voltage by $\pi/2$.
Instantaneous power $P = vi = V_0 I_0 \sin\omega t\cos\omega t = \frac{V_0 I_0}{2}\sin 2\omega t$.
Over a complete cycle $\sin 2\omega t$ averages to zero, so $P_{avg} = 0$; the capacitor only stores and returns energy without dissipating any.
(ii) As $C$ is reduced, $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}$ increases, so impedance $Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2}$ increases and current $I=V/Z$ decreases; the brightness of the bulb therefore decreases.

questions.question: A capacitor of unknown capacitance, a resistor of $100 \Omega$ and an inductor of self inductance $L = (4/\pi^{2})$ henry are connected in series to an ac source of $200$ V and $50$ Hz. Calculate the value of the capacitance and impedance of the circuit when the current is in phase with the voltage. Calculate the power dissipated in the circuit.
questions.answer:
$X_L = \omega L = 2\pi(50)\left(\frac{4}{\pi^2}\right) = \frac{400}{\pi}\,\Omega \approx 127.3\,\Omega$
Current is in phase with voltage when the circuit is at resonance, i.e., $X_C = X_L$.
$C = \frac{1}{\omega X_C} = \frac{1}{2\pi(50)\left(\frac{400}{\pi}\right)} = \frac{1}{40000} = 2.5\times10^{-5}\,\text{F} = 25\,\mu\text{F}$
At resonance $Z = R = 100\,\Omega$.
Power dissipated $P = \frac{V^2}{Z} = \frac{(200)^2}{100} = 400\,\text{W}$

questions.question: A series LCR circuit is connected across an a.c. source of variable angular frequency ’ $\omega$’. Plot a graph showing variation of current ’ $i$’ as a function of ’ $\omega$’ for two resistances $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ ($R_{1} > R_{2}$). Answer the following questions using this graph: (a) In which case is the resonance sharper and why? (b) In which case is the power dissipation more and why?
questions.answer:
The current $i$ rises from a small value at low $\omega$, peaks at the same resonant frequency $\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$ for both resistances, and falls off at high $\omega$; the curve for $R_2$ shows a taller, narrower peak than that for $R_1$, since $R_1>R_2$.
(a) The resonance is sharper for $R_2$. The sharpness is measured by the quality factor $Q=\frac{\omega_0 L}{R}$ (or bandwidth $\Delta\omega = R/L$); a smaller resistance gives a larger $Q$ (smaller bandwidth), making the peak sharper.
(b) At resonance $Z=R$, so $P_{avg}=\frac{V_{rms}^2}{R}$; since $R_2<R_1$, power dissipation is greater in the circuit with $R_2$.

questions.question: An inductor L of inductance $X_{L}$ is connected in series with a bulb B and an ac source. How would brightness of the bulb change when (i) number of turns in the inductor is reduced, (ii) an iron rod is inserted in the inductor and (iii) a capacitor of reactance $X_{C} = X_{L}$ is inserted in series in the circuit. Justify your answer in each case.
questions.answer:
(i) Reducing the number of turns decreases the inductance $L$, so $X_L=\omega L$ decreases; impedance decreases, current increases, and the bulb glows brighter.
(ii) Inserting an iron rod increases the permeability and hence $L$, so $X_L$ increases; impedance increases, current decreases, and the bulb becomes dimmer.
(iii) With $X_C=X_L$, the inductive and capacitive reactances (which act in opposite phase) cancel exactly, so the net impedance $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}=R$ (bulb resistance only); this is the resonance condition, current becomes maximum, and the bulb glows with maximum brightness.

questions.question: A voltage $V = V_{0} \sin \omega t$ is applied to a series LCR circuit. Derive the expression for the average power dissipated over a cycle. Under what condition is (i) no power dissipated even though the current flows through the circuit, (ii) maximum power dissipated in the circuit?
questions.answer:
Let $v=V_0\sin\omega t$ and $i=I_0\sin(\omega t-\phi)$, where $\tan\phi=\frac{X_L-X_C}{R}$.
Instantaneous power $P=vi=V_0I_0\sin\omega t\sin(\omega t-\phi)=V_0I_0[\sin^2\omega t\cos\phi-\sin\omega t\cos\omega t\sin\phi]$
Averaging over a full cycle, $\langle\sin^2\omega t\rangle=\tfrac12$ and $\langle\sin\omega t\cos\omega t\rangle=0$, so
$P_{avg}=\frac{V_0I_0}{2}\cos\phi = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi$, where $\cos\phi=R/Z$ is the power factor.
(i) No power is dissipated when $\cos\phi=0$ ($\phi=\pi/2$), i.e., in a purely inductive or purely capacitive circuit ($R=0$); the current is then called the wattless current.
(ii) Maximum power is dissipated when $\cos\phi=1$ ($\phi=0$), which occurs at resonance ($X_L=X_C$, $Z=R$), giving $P_{max}=\frac{V_{rms}^2}{R}$.

questions.question: In a series LCR circuit connected to an ac source of variable frequency and voltage $v = v_{m} \sin \omega t$, draw a plot showing the variation of current $(I)$ with angular frequency $(\omega)$ for two different values of resistance $R_{1}$ and $R_{2} (R_{1} > R_{2})$. Write the condition under which the phenomenon of resonance occurs. For which value of the resistance out of the two curves, a sharper resonance is produced? Define Q-factor of the circuit and give its significance.
questions.answer:
At resonance $X_L = X_C$, i.e. $\omega_0 L = \dfrac{1}{\omega_0 C}$, giving $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$; at this frequency $Z_{min}=R$ and the current is maximum, in phase with the applied voltage.
The $I$-$\omega$ graph is a peaked curve for each resistance value, both curves peaking at the same $\omega_0$; the curve for $R_2$ rises to a taller, narrower peak than that for $R_1$.
Since $R_1 > R_2$, sharper resonance is produced for the curve with $R_2$.
Q-factor is defined as $Q = \dfrac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \dfrac{1}{\omega_0 CR} = \dfrac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}$, where $\Delta\omega$ is the bandwidth; it measures the sharpness of resonance and equals the voltage magnification (ratio of voltage across $L$ or $C$ to the applied voltage) at resonance.

questions.question: A series LCR circuit is connected to an ac source. Using the phasor diagram, derive the expression for the impedance of the circuit. Plot a graph to show the variation of current with frequency of the source, explaining the nature of its variation.
questions.answer:
The same current $I=I_m\sin\omega t$ flows through $R$, $L$ and $C$.
$V_R=IR$ is in phase with $I$; $V_L=IX_L$ leads $I$ by $90°$; $V_C=IX_C$ lags $I$ by $90°$.
On the phasor diagram $V_R$ is drawn along $I$, $V_L$ at $+90°$ and $V_C$ at $-90°$ to $I$; being antiparallel, their resultant is $(V_L-V_C)$, perpendicular to $V_R$.
By the parallelogram law, $V=\sqrt{V_R^2+(V_L-V_C)^2}=I\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$
so the impedance is $Z=\dfrac{V}{I}=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$, with $X_L=\omega L$, $X_C=\dfrac{1}{\omega C}$.
Graph: current $I=V_m/Z$ is small at low and high $\omega$ (since $X_C$ or $X_L$ dominate), rising to a single maximum $I_m=V_m/R$ at $\omega=\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$ (resonance).

questions.question: The figure shows a series LCR circuit with $L = 5.0$ H, $C = 80 \mu$ F, $R = 40 \Omega$ connected to a variable frequency $240$ V source. Calculate (i) The angular frequency of the source which drives the circuit at resonance. (ii) The current at the resonating frequency. (iii) The rms potential drop across the capacitor at resonance.
questions.answer:
(i) $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5\times80\times10^{-6}}} = 50$ rad/s
(ii) At resonance $Z=R$, so $I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{240}{40} = 6$ A
(iii) $V_C = I\times X_C = \dfrac{I}{\omega_0 C} = \dfrac{6}{50\times80\times10^{-6}} = 1500$ V

questions.question: A series LCR circuit with $L = 4.0$ H, $C = 100 \mu$ F and $R = 60 \Omega$ is connected to a variable frequency $240$ V source as shown. Calculate: (i) the angular frequency of the source which drives the circuit at resonance; (ii) the current at the resonating frequency; (iii) the rms potential drop across the inductor at resonance.
questions.answer:
(i) $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{4\times100\times10^{-6}}} = 50$ rad/s
(ii) At resonance $Z=R$, so $I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{240}{60} = 4$ A
(iii) $V_L = I\times\omega_0 L = 4\times50\times4 = 800$ V

questions.question: An inductor $200 mH$, capacitor $500 \mu F$, resistor $10 \Omega$ are connected in series with a $100 V$, variable frequency a.c. source. Calculate the (i) frequency at which the power factor of the source is unity (ii) current amplitude at this frequency (iii) Q-factor
questions.answer:
(i) Power factor is unity at resonance: $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.2\times500\times10^{-6}}} = 100$ rad/s, so $f_0 = \dfrac{\omega_0}{2\pi} \approx 15.9$ Hz
(ii) At resonance $Z=R$, and with $V_{rms}=100$ V, $V_m = 100\sqrt{2}$ V, so $I_m = \dfrac{V_m}{R} = \dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{10} \approx 14.1$ A
(iii) $Q = \dfrac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \dfrac{100\times0.2}{10} = 2$

questions.question: Given below are two electric circuits $A$ and $B$. Calculate the ratio of power factor of the circuit $B$ to the power factor of circuit $A$.
questions.answer:
The power factor of a series circuit is $\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}}$, where $Z$ is found from the $R$, $X_L=\omega L$ and $X_C=1/\omega C$ values shown for that circuit.
Compute $Z_A$ from the elements of circuit $A$ and $Z_B$ from the elements of circuit $B$, giving $\cos\phi_A = R_A/Z_A$ and $\cos\phi_B = R_B/Z_B$.
The required ratio is $\dfrac{\cos\phi_B}{\cos\phi_A} = \dfrac{R_B Z_A}{R_A Z_B}$; if both circuits have equal resistance and equal magnitude of net reactance, $Z_A=Z_B$ and $R_A=R_B$, so the ratio equals $1$.

questions.question: In a series R-C circuit, $R = 30 \Omega$, $C = 0.25 \mu F$, $V = 100 V$ and $\omega = 10,000$ radian/second. Find the current in the circuit and calculate the voltage across the resistor and the capacitor. Is the algebraic sum of these voltages more than the source voltage? If yes, resolve the paradox.
questions.answer:
Capacitive reactance: $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{10^4 \times 0.25\times10^{-6}} = 400\ \Omega$
Impedance: $Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2}=\sqrt{30^2+400^2}\approx 401\ \Omega$
Current: $I=\dfrac{V}{Z}=\dfrac{100}{401}\approx 0.25$ A
Voltage across R: $V_R=IR\approx 0.25\times30\approx 7.5$ V
Voltage across C: $V_C=IX_C\approx 0.25\times400\approx 99.7$ V
Algebraic sum $V_R+V_C\approx 107.2$ V, which is more than the source voltage $100$ V.
This is not a real paradox: $V_R$ (in phase with $I$) and $V_C$ (lagging $I$ by $90°$) are out of phase with each other, so they cannot be added algebraically.
They must be added as phasors: $V=\sqrt{V_R^2+V_C^2}=\sqrt{7.5^2+99.7^2}\approx 100$ V, which correctly equals the source voltage.

questions.question: The teachers of Geeta’s school took the students on a study trip to a power generating station, located nearly $200$ km away from the city. The teacher explained that electrical energy is transmitted over such a long distance to their city, in the form of alternating current (ac) raised to a high voltage. At the receiving end in the city, the voltage is reduced to operate the devices. As a result, the power loss is reduced. Geeta listened to the teacher and asked questions about how the ac is converted to a higher or lower voltage. (a) Name the device used to change the alternating voltage to a higher or lower value. State one cause for power dissipation in this device. (b) Explain with an example, how power loss is reduced if the energy is transmitted over long distances as an alternating current rather than a direct current. (c) Write two values each shown by the teachers and Geeta.
questions.answer:
(i) The device is a transformer. Power is dissipated in it mainly due to $I^2R$ heating (copper loss) in its resistive windings.
(ii) In transmission, power $P=VI$, so for a given power the current $I$ can be greatly reduced by stepping up the voltage with a transformer. Since line power loss is $I^2R_{line}$, halving the current (by doubling voltage) reduces the loss to one-fourth. This voltage step-up/step-down is easily done with transformers only for alternating current, because transformers work on the principle of mutual induction, which requires a changing (alternating) flux; direct current cannot be stepped up or down this way, so ac transmission gives much lower power loss than dc for the same power delivered.
(iii) Teacher: knowledge, willingness to educate/patience. Geeta: curiosity, eagerness to learn.

questions.question: Shiv had a high tension tower erected on his farm land. He kept complaining to the authorities to remove it since it occupied a large portion of his land. His uncle, who was a teacher, explained to him the need for erecting these towers for efficient transmission of power. As Shiv got convinced and realized its significance, he stopped complaining. Based on the above paragraph, answer the following questions: (a) Why is it necessary to transport power at high voltages? (b) ’A low power factor implies large power loss’. Explain. (c) Write the two values displayed by Shiv and his Uncle.
questions.answer:
(a) At high voltage, the current required to transmit a given power $P=VI$ is small. Since line power loss is $I^2R$, a small current keeps this loss low, so power is transported at high voltage to minimise energy wasted as heat in the transmission wires.
(b) Power delivered is $P=VI\cos\phi$, so for a low power factor $\cos\phi$, a larger current $I$ is needed to deliver the same power $P$ at a given voltage $V$. Since line loss is $I^2R$, this larger current causes greater power loss in the transmission lines; hence a low power factor implies large power loss.
(c) Shiv: open-mindedness, cooperation, willingness to accept reason. Uncle: patience, knowledge, guidance.

questions.question: During a thunderstorm the ’live’ wire of the transmission line fell down on the ground. A group of boys passing through noticed it and some of them wanted to place the wire by the side. As they were approaching the wire and trying to lift it, Hari noticed it and immediately pushed them away to prevent them from touching the wire. Two of them got hurt in the process. Hari took them to a doctor to get medical aid. Based on the above paragraph, answer the following: (a) Write two values which Hari displayed during the incident. (b) Why is it that a bird can sit over a suspended ’live’ wire without any harm whereas touching it on the ground can give a fatal shock? (c) The electric power from a power plant is set up to a very high voltage before transmitting it to distant consumers. Write the reason for it.
questions.answer:
(a) Hari displayed presence of mind, courage/alertness, and a sense of responsibility and care for others (helping the injured boys get medical aid).
(b) A bird sitting on a live wire touches the wire at only one point (both its feet are at nearly the same high potential), so there is negligible potential difference across its body and no closed path for current through it, hence no shock. A person touching the live wire while standing on the ground provides a path from the high potential wire to the zero-potential earth; the large potential difference drives a large current through the body to the ground, causing a fatal shock.
(c) Transmitting power at very high voltage keeps the current low for a given power ($P=VI$), which reduces the $I^2R$ power loss in the long transmission lines.

questions.question: (a) A series combination of $L$, $C$ and $R$ is connected to an a.c. source. Using a phasor diagram, derive an expression for the impedance of the circuit and phase difference between $V$ and $I$.
questions.answer:
Let the current in the series LCR circuit be $I=I_0\sin\omega t$, taken as the reference phasor.
Voltage across $R$: $V_R=IR$, in phase with $I$.
Voltage across $L$: $V_L=IX_L$, leading $I$ by $90°$.
Voltage across $C$: $V_C=IX_C$, lagging $I$ by $90°$.
In the phasor diagram, $V_R$ is drawn along $I$, $V_L$ perpendicular to $I$ on the leading side, and $V_C$ perpendicular to $I$ on the opposite (lagging) side, so the net reactive phasor is $(V_L-V_C)$, at right angles to $V_R$.
The resultant applied voltage is the vector sum: $V=\sqrt{V_R^2+(V_L-V_C)^2}=I\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$
Comparing with $V=IZ$, the impedance is $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$
The phase angle $\phi$ between $V$ and $I$ is given by $\tan\phi=\dfrac{V_L-V_C}{V_R}=\dfrac{X_L-X_C}{R}$, so $\phi=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{X_L-X_C}{R}\right)$.

questions.question: (b) Under what conditions: (i) the impedance of the circuit is minimum? (ii) wattless current flows in the circuit?
questions.answer:
(i) The impedance $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$ is minimum when $X_L=X_C$, i.e. at resonance ($\omega L=\dfrac{1}{\omega C}$); its minimum value is $Z=R$.
(ii) A wattless current flows when the average power $P=VI\cos\phi=0$, which requires $\cos\phi=0$, i.e. the phase difference between $V$ and $I$ is $90°$. This occurs in an ideal circuit containing only $L$ or only $C$ (no resistance), where current flows but no net power is dissipated.

questions.question: (i) A light bulb and an open coil inductor are connected in series across an ac source of variable frequency. How will the glow of the bulb be affected when: (I) an iron bar is inserted inside the coil, and (II) the frequency of the source is decreased? Justify your answers. Assume that in each above case other factors remain unchanged.
questions.answer:
(I) Inserting an iron bar (ferromagnetic core) into the coil increases its permeability, so the self-inductance $L$ of the coil increases.
Since inductive reactance $X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L$, $X_L$ increases, so the impedance $Z = \sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}$ of the R-L series circuit increases.
Current $I = V_{rms}/Z$ decreases, so the bulb glows dimmer.
(II) Decreasing the frequency $f$ of the source decreases $X_L = 2\pi f L$, since $X_L \propto f$.
Hence impedance $Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}$ decreases, current increases, and the bulb glows brighter.

questions.question: (ii) An ac voltage $V = 280 \sin(100\pi t)$ volt is connected across a series LCR circuit in which $\sqrt{} R = 400 \Omega$, $L = \frac{5}{\pi}$ H and $C = \frac{1}{\pi}\mu$ F. Taking $2 = 1$· $4$, calculate: (I) impedance of the circuit. (II) rms value of current that flows in the circuit. (III) power factor of the circuit.
questions.answer:
(I) Impedance:
$\omega = 100\pi$ rad/s
$X_L = \omega L = 100\pi \times \frac{5}{\pi} = 500\,\Omega$
$X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{100\pi \times \frac{10^{-4}}{\pi}} = 100\,\Omega$
$Z = \sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2} = \sqrt{400^2+400^2} = 400\sqrt2 = 560\,\Omega$
(II) rms current:
$V_{rms} = \dfrac{V_m}{\sqrt2} = \dfrac{280}{1.4} = 200$ V
$I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z} = \dfrac{200}{560} = 0.357$ A
(III) Power factor:
$\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{400}{560} = 0.714$; the circuit is inductive since $X_L>X_C$.

questions.question: (a) (i) Define the terms (I) resonant frequency, and (II) power factor of a series LCR circuit. For what value of the power factor will the power dissipated in the circuit be maximum? (ii) An inductor of 5 H, a capacitor of 50 $\mu F$ and a resistor of 400 $\Omega$ are connected in series across an ac voltage $v = 140 \sin(100\pi t)$ V. Calculate: (I) impedance of the circuit, and (II) rms value of current that flows in the circuit. $\sqrt{}$ (Take $2 = 1$ · $4$) OR (b) (i) Draw a labelled diagram of a step-up transformer. Obtain the ratio of secondary voltage to primary voltage in terms of number of turns in the two coils. (ii) The number of turns in the primary and the secondary coil of an ideal transformer are 100 and 5000 respectively. If 3·3 kW power is supplied to the transformer at 220 V, find (I) current in the primary coil, and (II) output voltage.
questions.answer:
(a)(i)(I) Resonant frequency is the frequency of the ac source at which $X_L=X_C$, so the impedance of the series LCR circuit is minimum ($Z=R$) and the current is maximum: $\omega_0=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$.
(a)(i)(II) Power factor $\cos\phi = R/Z$ is the ratio of resistance to impedance (equivalently, ratio of true power to apparent power). Power dissipated is maximum when $\cos\phi=1$, i.e. $\phi=0$, which occurs at resonance ($Z=R$).
(a)(ii) $\omega=100\pi$ rad/s
$X_L=\omega L = 100\pi\times\frac{5}{\pi}=500\,\Omega$
$X_C=\dfrac{1}{\omega C}=\dfrac{1}{100\pi\times\frac{50}{\pi}\times10^{-6}}=200\,\Omega$
(I) $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}=\sqrt{400^2+300^2}=500\,\Omega$
(II) $V_{rms}=\dfrac{140}{1.4}=100$ V, $I_{rms}=\dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z}=\dfrac{100}{500}=0.2$ A

questions.question: (a) (i) Write the principle of working of an ac generator. Draw its labelled diagram and $[]$ explain its working. (ii) A resistor of $400 \Omega$, an inductor of $\frac{2}{\pi}$ H and a capacitor $[]$ of $\frac{50}{\pi}\mu$ F are joined in series across an ac source $v = 140 \sin(100\pi)t$ V. Find the rms voltages across these three circuit elements. The algebraic sum of these voltages is more than the rms voltage of source. Explain. OR (b) (i) Write the principle of working of a transformer. With the help of a labelled diagram, explain the working of a step-up transformer. (ii) An ideal transformer is designed to convert $50$ V into $250$ V. It draws $200$ W power from an ac source whose instantaneous voltage is given by $v_{i} = 20 \sin(100\pi)t$ V. Find: (I) rms value of input current. (II) expression for instantaneous output voltage. (III) expression for instantaneous output current.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Principle: an ac generator works on electromagnetic induction — rotating a coil with constant angular velocity in a uniform magnetic field changes the flux linked with it, inducing an alternating emf.
Diagram (labelled parts): field magnet (N-S poles) giving a uniform field, rectangular armature coil ABCD mounted on a rotating axle between the poles, two slip rings fixed to the coil ends, carbon brushes pressing on the slip rings connecting to the external circuit/load.
Working: as the coil rotates, flux $\phi=BA\cos\omega t$ changes, inducing emf $e=-\frac{d\phi}{dt}=NBA\omega\sin\omega t=e_0\sin\omega t$ (Faraday's law), which drives alternating current through the external circuit via the slip rings and brushes.
(a)(ii) $\omega=100\pi$, $X_L=100\pi\times\frac{2}{\pi}=200\,\Omega$, $X_C=\dfrac{1}{100\pi\times\frac{50}{\pi}\times10^{-6}}=200\,\Omega$
Since $X_L=X_C$, the circuit is at resonance, $Z=R=400\,\Omega$.
$V_{rms}=140/1.4=100$V, $I_{rms}=100/400=0.25$A
$V_R=IR=100$V, $V_L=IX_L=50$V, $V_C=IX_C=50$V; sum $=200$V $>100$V.
This is because $V_L$ and $V_C$ are not in phase with $V_R$ — $V_L$ leads current by $90°$ and $V_C$ lags by $90°$, so they are $180°$ out of phase with each other and cancel; only phasor addition is valid: $V=\sqrt{V_R^2+(V_L-V_C)^2}=\sqrt{100^2+0^2}=100$V, equal to the source voltage.

questions.question: (i) Mention the factors on which the resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit depends. Plot a graph showing variation of impedance of a series LCR circuit with the frequency of the applied a.c. source. (ii) With the help of a suitable diagram, explain the working of a step-up transformer. (iii) Write two causes of energy loss in a real transformer.
questions.answer:
(i) Resonant frequency $f_0=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$ depends only on the inductance $L$ and capacitance $C$; it is independent of resistance $R$.
Graph of impedance $Z$ vs frequency $f$: $Z$ is large at low $f$ (since $X_C=1/2\pi fC\to\infty$ as $f\to0$), falls as $f$ increases, reaches a minimum value $Z=R$ at the resonant frequency $f_0$, then rises again at high $f$ (since $X_L=2\pi fL\to\infty$) — a valley-shaped curve with its lowest point at $f_0$.
(ii) A step-up transformer works on mutual induction between two coils wound on a common laminated soft-iron core, with secondary turns $N_S$ greater than primary turns $N_P$. An alternating voltage applied to the primary sets up a changing flux in the core; this changing flux links the secondary and induces an emf in it, given by $V_S=V_P(N_S/N_P)$. Since $N_S>N_P$, $V_S>V_P$.
(iii) Copper loss ($I^2R$ heating in the resistance of the windings); iron loss due to hysteresis and eddy currents induced in the core.

questions.question: (i) You are given three circuit elements X, Y and Z. They are connected one by one across a given ac source. It is found that $V$ and $I$ are in phase for element X. $V$ leads $I$ by $(\frac{\pi}{2})(\frac{\pi}{2})$ for element Y while $I$ leads $V$ byfor element Z. Identify elements X, Y and Z. (ii) Establish the expression for impedance of circuit when elements X, Y and Z are connected in series to an ac source. Show the variation of current in the circuit with the frequency of the applied ac source. (iii) In a series LCR circuit, obtain the conditions under which (i) impedance is minimum and (ii) wattless current flows in the circuit.
questions.answer:
(i) X is a resistor $R$ (V and I in phase).
Y is a pure inductor $L$ (V leads I by $\pi/2$).
Z is a pure capacitor $C$ (I leads V by $\pi/2$).
(ii) Taking current $I$ as reference: $V_R=IR$ is in phase with $I$; $V_L=IX_L$ leads $I$ by $90°$; $V_C=IX_C$ lags $I$ by $90°$, opposite to $V_L$.
By phasor addition, $V=\sqrt{V_R^2+(V_L-V_C)^2}=I\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$
so $Z=\dfrac{V}{I}=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$, with $\tan\phi=\dfrac{X_L-X_C}{R}$.
Variation with frequency: current is small at very low and very high frequencies (large $Z$) and rises to a maximum at the resonant frequency $f_0=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$, giving a peaked resonance curve, sharper for smaller $R$.
(iii) Impedance is minimum when $X_L=X_C$ (i.e. $\omega L=1/\omega C$, resonance), giving $Z_{min}=R$.
Wattless current flows when average power dissipated is zero, i.e. $\cos\phi=0$ ($\phi=\pi/2$), which occurs in a purely reactive (zero-resistance) circuit where current is $90°$ out of phase with voltage.

questions.question: (i) Describe the construction and working of a transformer and hence obtain the relation $[]$ for $\frac{V_{s}}{V_{p}}$ in terms of number of turns of primary and secondary. (ii) Discuss four main causes of energy loss in a real transformer.
questions.answer:
(i) A transformer consists of a laminated soft-iron core on which two coils are wound: the primary with $N_p$ turns and the secondary with $N_s$ turns, both electrically insulated from each other and from the core but linked by the same magnetic flux.
When an alternating voltage $V_p$ is applied to the primary, it drives an alternating current that sets up an alternating flux $\phi$ in the core.
This same flux links the secondary (assuming no flux leakage) and induces an emf in it by mutual induction.
Induced emf per turn is the same in both windings, so $\frac{V_p}{N_p} = \frac{V_s}{N_s}$, giving $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$.
(ii) Causes of energy loss:
Copper loss: heat generated due to resistance of windings, $I^2R$.
Iron/hysteresis loss: energy lost as heat due to repeated magnetisation and demagnetisation of the core.
Eddy current loss: induced eddy currents in the core dissipate energy as heat; reduced by laminating the core.
Flux leakage: not all flux from primary links the secondary, reducing efficiency.

questions.question: With the help of a labelled diagram, explain the working of a step-up transformer. Give reasons to explain the following: (i) The core of the transformer is laminated. (ii) Thick copper wire is used in windings.
questions.answer:
A step-up transformer has a laminated iron core with a primary winding of $N_p$ turns and a secondary winding of $N_s$ turns, where $N_s > N_p$, both wound on the same core so they link the same alternating flux.
An alternating voltage $V_p$ applied to the primary sets up an alternating flux in the core, which induces an emf in the secondary given by $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$.
Since $N_s > N_p$, the output voltage $V_s$ is greater than the input voltage $V_p$, while the secondary current is correspondingly smaller, so that $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$ (ideal transformer).
(i) The core is laminated to reduce eddy currents: thin, insulated laminations break up the conducting path for induced eddy currents, increasing resistance and reducing eddy current (heat) losses, thereby improving efficiency.
(ii) Thick copper wire is used in the windings to keep the resistance of the coils low, which minimises $I^2R$ (copper) losses, especially important in the low-voltage, high-current winding.

questions.question: (a) Show that an ideal inductor does not dissipate power in an ac circuit. (b) The variation of inductive reactance ($X_{L}$) of an inductor with the frequency ($f$) of the ac source of $100$ V and variable frequency is shown in the fig. (i) Calculate the self-inductance of the inductor. (ii) When this inductor is used in series with a capacitor of unknown value and a resistor of $10 \Omega$ at $300 s^{-1}$, maximum power dissipation occurs in the circuit. Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor. OR (a) A conductor of length $l$ is rotated about one of its ends at a constant angular speed $\omega$ in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B$. Plot graphs to show variations of the emf induced across the ends of the conductor with (i) angular speed $\omega$ and (ii) length of the conductor $l$. (b) Two concentric circular loops of radius $1$ cm and $20$ cm are placed coaxially. (i) Find mutual inductance of the arrangement. (ii) If the current passed through the outer loop is changed at a rate of $5$ A/ms, find the emf induced in the inner loop. Assume the magnetic field on the inner loop to be uniform.
questions.answer:
(a) For an ideal inductor in an ac circuit, current lags voltage by $90°$: $v = v_0 \sin\omega t$, $i = i_0 \sin(\omega t - \pi/2)$.
Instantaneous power $P = vi = v_0 i_0 \sin\omega t \sin(\omega t - \pi/2) = -v_0 i_0 \sin\omega t \cos\omega t = -\frac{v_0 i_0}{2}\sin 2\omega t$.
Average power over a full cycle $\bar{P} = -\frac{v_0 i_0}{2}\langle \sin 2\omega t\rangle = 0$, since the average of $\sin 2\omega t$ over a cycle is zero.
Hence an ideal inductor dissipates no power; it only stores and returns energy.
(b) From the graph, $X_L$ increases linearly with $f$, reading $X_L = 200\,\Omega$ at $f = 100$ Hz, so slope $= 2\pi L = 2$, giving $L = \frac{1}{\pi} \approx 0.318$ H.
(ii) Maximum power dissipation occurs at resonance, so $\omega = 300$ rad/s satisfies $\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$.
$C = \frac{1}{L\omega^2} = \frac{1}{0.318 \times (300)^2} \approx 3.5 \times 10^{-5}$ F $= 35\,\mu$F.
OR
(a) Induced emf across the rotating rod is $e = \frac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$.
Variation with $\omega$ (for fixed $l$): a straight line through the origin (emf $\propto \omega$).
Variation with $l$ (for fixed $\omega$): an upward-opening parabola through the origin (emf $\propto l^2$).
(b) Mutual inductance of concentric coaxial loops (inner radius $r_1 = 1$ cm, outer $r_2 = 20$ cm, $r_1 \ll r_2$): $M = \frac{\mu_0 \pi r_1^2}{2 r_2} = \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times \pi \times (0.01)^2}{2 \times 0.2} \approx 9.87 \times 10^{-10}$ H.
(ii) $\varepsilon = M\frac{dI}{dt} = 9.87 \times 10^{-10} \times \frac{5}{10^{-3}} \approx 4.94 \times 10^{-6}$ V.

questions.question: In a series LCR circuit connected across an ac source of variable frequency, obtain the expression for its impedance and draw a plot showing its variation with frequency of the ac source.
questions.answer:
In a series LCR circuit with applied voltage $v = v_0\sin\omega t$, the resistor, inductor and capacitor carry the same current $i = i_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$, but their voltages differ in phase: $V_R$ in phase with $i$, $V_L$ leading $i$ by $90°$, $V_C$ lagging $i$ by $90°$.
Since $V_L$ and $V_C$ are antiphase, the net reactive voltage is $(V_{L0} - V_{C0})$, and by the phasor (voltage) triangle: $v_0^2 = V_{R0}^2 + (V_{L0} - V_{C0})^2 = i_0^2[R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2]$.
Hence impedance $Z = \frac{v_0}{i_0} = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$, where $X_L = \omega L$ and $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}$.
Variation with frequency: as $f$ increases from zero, $X_C$ decreases and $X_L$ increases, so $Z$ first decreases, reaches a minimum value $Z = R$ at the resonant frequency $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$ (where $X_L = X_C$), and then increases again — giving a U-shaped ($Z$ vs $f$) curve with its minimum at $f_0$.

questions.question: What is the phase difference between the voltages across inductor and the capacitor at resonance in the LCR circuit?
questions.answer:
In a series LCR circuit, the same current $i = i_0\sin\omega t$ flows through $L$ and $C$.
Voltage across the inductor leads the current by $90°$: $v_L = i_0 X_L \sin(\omega t + \pi/2)$.
Voltage across the capacitor lags the current by $90°$: $v_C = i_0 X_C \sin(\omega t - \pi/2)$.
This holds at all frequencies, including at resonance (where additionally $X_L = X_C$, so $v_L$ and $v_C$ have equal magnitude).
Therefore the phase difference between $v_L$ and $v_C$ is $\frac{\pi}{2} - \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \pi$, i.e. they are exactly out of phase ($180°$) — at every instant $v_L = -v_C$, so the two voltages cancel and the entire applied voltage appears across $R$.

questions.question: When an inductor is connected to a $200$ V dc voltage, a current of $1$ A flows through it. When the same inductor is connected to a $200$ V, $50$ Hz ac source, only $0.5$ A current flows. Explain, why? Also, calculate the self inductance of the inductor.
questions.answer:
With dc, there is no self-induced emf (since $\frac{dI}{dt} = 0$ in steady state), so only the coil's resistance $R$ limits the current: $R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{200}{1} = 200\,\Omega$.
With ac, the inductor additionally offers inductive reactance $X_L = \omega L$, so the effective opposition is impedance $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$, which is greater than $R$, reducing the current to $0.5$ A.
$Z = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{200}{0.5} = 400\,\Omega$.
$X_L = \sqrt{Z^2 - R^2} = \sqrt{400^2 - 200^2} = \sqrt{120000} \approx 346.4\,\Omega$.
$L = \frac{X_L}{2\pi f} = \frac{346.4}{2\pi \times 50} \approx 1.1$ H.

questions.question: Draw the diagram of a device which is used to decrease high ac voltage into a low ac voltage and state its working principle. Write four sources of energy loss in this device.
questions.answer:
A step-down transformer has a laminated soft-iron core on which a primary coil (more turns, $N_p$) and a secondary coil (fewer turns, $N_s < N_p$) are wound, insulated from each other and from the core.
Working principle: it works on mutual induction — an alternating current in the primary produces a changing magnetic flux in the core, which links the secondary and induces an alternating emf in it, given by $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$; since $N_s < N_p$, the output voltage is lower than the input.
Four sources of energy loss:
Copper loss — $I^2R$ heating in the resistance of the primary and secondary windings.
Iron (hysteresis) loss — energy dissipated in repeatedly magnetising and demagnetising the core.
Eddy current loss — induced eddy currents in the core dissipate heat (reduced by using a laminated core).
Flux leakage — not all the flux produced by the primary links the secondary, causing loss of output.

questions.question: A small town with a demand of $1200$ kW of electric power at $220$ V is situated $20$ km away from an electric plant generating power at $440$ V. The resistance of the two wire line carrying power is $0.5 \Omega$ per km. The town gets the power from the line through a $4000$- $220$ V step-down transformer at a sub-station in the town. Estimate the line power loss in the form of heat.
questions.answer:
The line supplies power at the transmission voltage of $4000$ V (input to the step-down transformer at the town).
Line current, $I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{1200 \times 10^{3}}{4000} = 300$ A.
Resistance of the two-wire line, $R = 0.5 \times 2 \times 20 = 20 \, \Omega$.
Line power loss, $P_{loss} = I^{2}R = (300)^{2} \times 20 = 9 \times 10^{4} \times 20 = 1.8 \times 10^{6}$ W $= 1800$ kW.
Thus the heat loss in the transmission line is $1800$ kW.

questions.question: (a) What do you understand by ’sharpness of resonance’ for a series LCR resonant circuit? How is it related with the quality factor ’Q’ of the circuit? Using the graphs given in the diagram, explain the factors which affect it. For which graph is the resistance (R) minimum? (b) A $2 \mu$ F capacitor, $100 \Omega$ resistor and $8$ H inductor are connected in series with an ac source. Find the frequency of the ac source for which the current drawn in the circuit is maximum. If the peak value of emf of the source is $200$ V, calculate the (i) maximum current, and (ii) inductive and capacitive reactance of the circuit at resonance. OR (a) Draw a schematic diagram of an ac generator. Explain its working and obtain the expression for the instantaneous value of the emf in terms of the magnetic field $B$, number of turns $N$ of the coil of area $A$ rotating with angular frequency $\omega$. Show how an alternating emf is generated by a loop of wire rotating in a magnetic field. (b) A circular coil of radius $10$ cm and $20$ turns is rotated about its vertical diameter with $-1 -2$ angular speed of $50$ rad sin a uniform horizontal magnetic field of $3.0 \times 10$ T. (i) Calculate the maximum and average emf induced in the coil. (ii) If the coil forms a closed loop of resistance $10 \Omega$, calculate the maximum current in the coil and the average power loss due to Joule heating.
questions.answer:
(a) Sharpness of resonance describes how rapidly the current falls as the frequency is moved away from the resonant frequency $\omega_r$; a sharper (narrower) resonance curve means the circuit responds strongly only over a small band of frequencies.
It is measured by the quality factor $Q = \frac{\omega_r L}{R} = \frac{1}{\omega_r C R} = \frac{\omega_r}{2\Delta\omega}$, where $2\Delta\omega$ is the bandwidth.
For fixed $L$ and $C$, smaller $R$ gives larger $Q$, hence a sharper, taller resonance peak; larger $R$ gives a flatter, broader curve.
So the graph with the tallest, narrowest peak corresponds to the minimum value of $R$.
(b) At resonance $\omega_r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{8 \times 2\times10^{-6}}} = 250$ rad/s, so $f_r = \frac{\omega_r}{2\pi} \approx 39.8$ Hz.
(i) $I_0 = \frac{E_0}{R} = \frac{200}{100} = 2$ A (since $Z = R$ at resonance).
(ii) $X_L = \omega_r L = 250 \times 8 = 2000\,\Omega$; $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega_r C} = \frac{1}{250 \times 2\times10^{-6}} = 2000\,\Omega$.

OR
(a) An ac generator has a rectangular coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ rotated with angular speed $\omega$ about an axis perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B$, between the poles of a magnet; slip rings and brushes connect the rotating coil to the external circuit.
As the coil rotates, flux through it $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$ changes, and by Faraday's law the induced emf is $e = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$, where $e_0 = NBA\omega$; this alternating emf drives a sinusoidal current through the external circuit.
(b) $A = \pi r^2 = \pi(0.1)^2 = 0.0314\,\text{m}^2$.
(i) $e_0 = NBA\omega = 20 \times 3\times10^{-2} \times 0.0314 \times 50 \approx 0.94$ V; average emf over half cycle $= \frac{2e_0}{\pi} \approx 0.6$ V.
(ii) $I_0 = \frac{e_0}{R} = \frac{0.94}{10} \approx 0.094$ A; average power loss $= \frac{I_0^2}{2}R \approx 0.044$ W.

questions.question: A device $X$ is connected across an ac source of voltage $V = V_{0} \sin \omega t$. The current through $(\frac{\pi}{2}) X$ is given as $I = I_{0} \sin\omega t +$. (a) Identify the device $X$ and write the expression for its reactance. (b) Draw graphs showing variation of voltage and current with time over one cycle of ac, for $X$. (c) How does the reactance of the device $X$ vary with frequency of the ac? Show this variation graphically. (d) Draw the phasor diagram for the device $X$.
questions.answer:
(a) Since the current leads the voltage by $\frac{\pi}{2}$, device $X$ is a pure capacitor. Its reactance is $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}$.
(b) Both $V$ and $I$ are sinusoidal of the same frequency; the current curve is shifted a quarter period earlier than the voltage curve (current peaks before voltage).
(c) $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}$, so $X_C$ decreases as frequency increases; the graph of $X_C$ versus $f$ is a rectangular hyperbola, falling steeply at low $f$ and approaching zero at high $f$.
(d) In the phasor diagram, the voltage phasor $V_0$ and current phasor $I_0$ rotate counter-clockwise with angular speed $\omega$; the current phasor $I_0$ is drawn $90^\circ$ ahead of the voltage phasor $V_0$.

questions.question: A device $X$ is connected to an ac source $V = V_{0} \sin \omega t$. The variation of voltage, current and power in one cycle is shown in the following graph: (a) Identify the device ’X’. (b) Which of the curves $A$, $B$ and $C$ represent the voltage, current and the power consumed in the circuit? Justify your answer. (c) How does its impedance vary with frequency of the ac source? Show graphically. (d) Obtain an expression for the current in the circuit and its phase relation with ac voltage.
questions.answer:
(a) Device $X$ is a pure inductor.
(b) The curve in phase with the source (zero phase difference between its peaks and the source's) represents the voltage $V$; the curve whose peaks are delayed by a quarter cycle relative to $V$ represents the current $I$, since in a pure inductor current lags voltage by $\frac{\pi}{2}$; the remaining curve, which oscillates at twice the source frequency and is symmetric about zero (equal positive and negative loops), represents the instantaneous power $P = VI$, whose average value over a full cycle is zero.
(c) Impedance of a pure inductor is $Z = X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L$, so $Z$ increases linearly with frequency; the graph of $Z$ versus $f$ is a straight line through the origin.
(d) $I = I_0\sin\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, where $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{\omega L}$; the current lags the applied voltage $V = V_0\sin\omega t$ by a phase angle of $\frac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.question: (i) Draw a labelled diagram of a step-down transformer. State the principle of its working. (ii) Express the turn ratio in terms of voltages. (iii) Find the ratio of primary and secondary currents in terms of turn ratio in an ideal transformer. (iv) How much current is drawn by the primary of a transformer connected to $220$ V supply when it delivers power to a $110$ V $-550$ W refrigerator? OR (a) Explain the meaning of the term mutual inductance. Consider two concentric circular coils, one of radius $r_{1}$ and the other of radius $r_{2} (r_{1} < r_{2})$ placed coaxially with centres coinciding with each other. Obtain the expression for the mutual inductance of the arrangement. (b) A rectangular coil of area $A$, having number of turns $N$ is rotated at $f$ revolutions per second in a uniform magnetic field $B$, the field being perpendicular to the coil. Prove that the maximum emf induced in the coil is $2\pi fNBA$.
questions.answer:
(i) A step-down transformer has a laminated iron core carrying a primary winding (many turns, $N_p$) connected to the input supply and a secondary winding (fewer turns, $N_s$) delivering the output; it works on the principle of mutual induction — an alternating current in the primary sets up a changing flux in the core, which induces an alternating emf in the secondary.
(ii) $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$.
(iii) For an ideal transformer, input power equals output power: $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$, so $\frac{I_p}{I_s} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$.
(iv) $I_p = \frac{P}{V_p} = \frac{550}{220} = 2.5$ A.

OR
(a) Mutual inductance is the property by which a changing current in one coil induces an emf in a neighbouring coil, $e_2 = -M\frac{dI_1}{dt}$.
For two coaxial coils of radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ ($r_1 < r_2$), current $I$ in the outer coil produces field at the centre $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2r_2}$, taken uniform over the smaller coil's area since $r_1 \ll r_2$.
Flux linked with inner coil, $\Phi_1 = B\pi r_1^2 = \frac{\mu_0 I \pi r_1^2}{2r_2}$, so $M = \frac{\Phi_1}{I} = \frac{\mu_0 \pi r_1^2}{2r_2}$.
(b) Flux through the rotating coil, $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$, where $\omega = 2\pi f$.
Induced emf, $e = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$.
Maximum emf occurs when $\sin\omega t = 1$: $e_{max} = NBA\omega = NBA(2\pi f) = 2\pi fNBA$.

questions.question: In a series $LCR$ circuit connected to an a.c. source of voltage $v = v_{m} \sin \omega t$, use phasor diagram to derive an expression for the current in the circuit. Hence obtain the expression for the power dissipated in the circuit. Show that power dissipated at resonance is maximum.
questions.answer:
In a series LCR circuit the same current $i = i_m\sin\omega t$ flows through $R$, $L$, $C$.
Voltage across $R$: $v_R=i_mR$, in phase with current.
Voltage across $L$: $v_L=i_mX_L$ ($X_L=\omega L$), leading current by $\pi/2$.
Voltage across $C$: $v_C=i_mX_C$ ($X_C=1/\omega C$), lagging current by $\pi/2$.
On the phasor diagram $v_L$ and $v_C$ are antiparallel, so the net phasor is $v_R$ (horizontal) and $(v_L-v_C)$ (vertical).
Resultant: $v_m=i_m\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}=i_mZ$, where $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$.
Hence $i=i_m\sin(\omega t-\phi)$, with $i_m=v_m/Z$ and $\tan\phi=(X_L-X_C)/R$.
Instantaneous power $p=vi$; averaged over a cycle, $P=\dfrac{v_mi_m}{2}\cos\phi=v_{rms}i_{rms}\cos\phi$.
At resonance $X_L=X_C$, so $Z=R$ is minimum, $\phi=0$, $\cos\phi=1$, and $i_m=v_m/R$ is maximum.
Since both current amplitude and power factor are maximum simultaneously, $P=v_{rms}i_{rms}$ is maximum at resonance.

questions.question: (a) Show that in an a.c. circuit containing a pure inductor, the voltage is ahead of current by $\pi/2$ in phase. (b) A horizontal straight wire of length $L$ extending from east to west is falling with speed $v$ at right angles to the horizontal component of Earth’s magnetic field $B$. (i) Write the expression for the instantaneous value of the e.m.f. induced in the wire. (ii) What is the direction of the e.m.f.? (iii) Which end of the wire is at the higher potential?
questions.answer:
(a) For a pure inductor $L$, $v=L\dfrac{di}{dt}$, so $\dfrac{di}{dt}=\dfrac{v_m}{L}\sin\omega t$.
Integrating, $i=-\dfrac{v_m}{\omega L}\cos\omega t=i_m\sin(\omega t-\pi/2)$, where $i_m=v_m/\omega L$.
Comparing $v=v_m\sin\omega t$ with $i=i_m\sin(\omega t-\pi/2)$, the current lags the voltage by $\pi/2$, i.e., voltage is ahead of current by $\pi/2$.
(b) (i) $e=BLv$.
(ii) By $\vec F=q(\vec v\times\vec B)$, the force on free positive charges in the wire acts from west to east, so this end of the wire acts as the positive terminal of the emf.
(iii) The east end of the wire is at the higher potential.

questions.question: (i) With the help of a labelled diagram, describe briefly the underlying principle and working of a step up transformer. (ii) Write any two sources of energy loss in a transformer. (iii) A step up transformer converts a low input voltage into a high output voltage. Does it violate law of conservation of energy? Explain.
questions.answer:
(i) Principle: mutual induction — a changing current in the primary produces a changing magnetic flux, which, linked through a common laminated soft-iron core, induces an emf in the secondary.
Construction: primary (with $N_p$ turns) and secondary ($N_s$ turns, $N_s>N_p$) coils are wound on the same core; primary connects to the input ac source, secondary to the load.
For an ideal transformer, $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}=\dfrac{I_p}{I_s}$, so with $N_s>N_p$, $V_s>V_p$, giving a stepped-up output voltage.
(ii) Copper loss ($I^2R$ heating in the windings) and core loss (hysteresis and eddy current losses in the iron core).
(iii) No, energy conservation is not violated. In an ideal transformer input power equals output power, $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$; as $V_s$ increases, $I_s$ decreases proportionately, so total power (and hence energy) is conserved, not created.

questions.question: Derive an expression for the impedance of a series LCR circuit connected to an AC supply of variable frequency. Plot a graph showing variation of current with the frequency of the applied voltage. Explain briefly how the phenomenon of resonance in the circuit can be used in the tuning mechanism of a radio or a TV set.
questions.answer:
Let $i=i_m\sin(\omega t-\phi)$ flow in the series LCR circuit driven by $v=v_m\sin\omega t$.
Phasor voltages: $v_R=i_mR$ in phase with $i$; $v_L=i_mX_L$ leading $i$ by $\pi/2$; $v_C=i_mX_C$ lagging $i$ by $\pi/2$, with $X_L=\omega L$, $X_C=1/\omega C$.
Since $v_L$, $v_C$ are opposite, resultant voltage $v_m=i_m\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$, so impedance $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$ and $i_m=v_m/Z$.
Graph: $i_m$ plotted against $\omega$ rises to a sharp peak at the resonant frequency $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$ (where $X_L=X_C$, $Z=R$ minimum) and falls off on either side; the peak is sharper for smaller $R$.
Tuning application: the tuning circuit of a radio/TV is an LCR circuit with variable capacitance $C$. Adjusting $C$ changes $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$; when $\omega_0$ matches the broadcast frequency of a desired station, the current (and signal response) for that frequency becomes maximum while signals of other frequencies remain weak, thus selecting that station.

questions.question: (a) An alternating voltage $v = v_{m} \sin \omega t$ applied to a series LCR circuit drives a current given by $i = i_{m} \sin(\omega t + \phi)$. Deduce an expression for the average power dissipated over a cycle. (b) For circuits used for transporting electric power, a low power factor implies large power loss in transmission. Explain. (c) Determine the current and quality factor at resonance for a series LCR circuit with $L = 1.00$ mH, $C = 1.00$ nF and $R = 100 \Omega$ connected to an a.c. source having peak voltage of 100 V.
questions.answer:
(a) Instantaneous power $p=vi=v_mi_m\sin\omega t\sin(\omega t+\phi)$.
Averaging over one cycle, the terms oscillating in time vanish, giving $P=\dfrac{v_mi_m}{2}\cos\phi=v_{rms}i_{rms}\cos\phi$, where $\cos\phi$ is the power factor.
(b) For a given power $P$ transmitted at voltage $V$, the current drawn is $I=P/(V\cos\phi)$. A low power factor means a larger $I$ is needed for the same $P$, and since line loss is $I^2R$, this loss increases sharply (varies as $1/\cos^2\phi$); hence low power factor causes large power loss in transmission.
(c) Resonant frequency: $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}=1/\sqrt{(1.00\times10^{-3})(1.00\times10^{-9})}=1.00\times10^{6}$ rad/s.
At resonance $Z=R$, so peak current $i_m=v_m/R=100/100=1$ A.
Quality factor: $Q=\dfrac{\omega_0L}{R}=\dfrac{(1.00\times10^6)(1.00\times10^{-3})}{100}=10$.

questions.question: A series LCR circuit is connected to an ac source having voltage $v = v_{m} \sin \omega t$. Derive the expression for the instantaneous current I and its phase relationship to the applied voltage. Obtain the condition for resonance to occur. Define ’power factor’. State the conditions under which it is (i) maximum and (ii) minimum.
questions.answer:
Let current $i=i_m\sin(\omega t-\phi)$ flow due to $v=v_m\sin\omega t$.
Phasor voltages: $v_R=i_mR$ (in phase with $i$), $v_L=i_mX_L$ (leads $i$ by $\pi/2$), $v_C=i_mX_C$ (lags $i$ by $\pi/2$).
Since $v_L$ and $v_C$ oppose, $v_m=i_m\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}=i_mZ$, so $i_m=v_m/Z$ and $\tan\phi=(X_L-X_C)/R$.
Thus $i=\dfrac{v_m}{Z}\sin(\omega t-\phi)$; current lags voltage if $X_L>X_C$, leads if $X_C>X_L$, and is in phase if $X_L=X_C$.
Resonance occurs when $X_L=X_C$, i.e., $\omega_0L=1/\omega_0C$, giving $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$; then $Z=R$ is minimum and current is maximum.
Power factor is defined as $\cos\phi=R/Z$, the ratio of true power to apparent power ($P=v_{rms}i_{rms}\cos\phi$).
(i) It is maximum ($\cos\phi=1$) when $\phi=0$, i.e., at resonance where $X_L=X_C$ and the circuit is purely resistive.
(ii) It is minimum ($\cos\phi=0$) when $\phi=\pi/2$, i.e., when $R=0$, a purely inductive or purely capacitive circuit.

questions.question: (a) Derive an expression for the average power consumed in a series LCR circuit connected to a.c. source in which the phase difference between the voltage and the current in the circuit is $\phi$. (b) Define the quality factor in an a.c. circuit. Why should the quality factor have high value in receiving circuits? Name the factors on which it depends.
questions.answer:
(a) Let the applied voltage be $e = e_0\sin\omega t$ and the resulting current $i = i_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$, where $\phi$ is the phase difference between voltage and current.
Instantaneous power: $p = ei = e_0 i_0 \sin\omega t\sin(\omega t-\phi) = e_0i_0[\sin^2\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t\sin\phi]$
Averaging over one complete cycle, $\langle\sin^2\omega t\rangle = 1/2$ and $\langle\sin\omega t\cos\omega t\rangle = 0$, so
$P = \frac{1}{2}e_0i_0\cos\phi = e_{rms}i_{rms}\cos\phi$
Here $\cos\phi$ is called the power factor of the circuit.
(b) The quality factor $Q$ measures the sharpness of resonance; it is defined as $Q = \dfrac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \dfrac{1}{\omega_0 CR} = \dfrac{1}{R}\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}}$, or equivalently as the ratio of voltage across $L$ (or $C$) to the voltage across $R$ at resonance.
A high $Q$ is desirable in receiving circuits because it gives a very sharp resonance curve, allowing the circuit to select a narrow band of frequencies (the desired station) and reject nearby frequencies effectively, i.e. good selectivity.
$Q$ depends on the values of $R$, $L$ and $C$ of the circuit.

questions.question: (a) Derive the relationship between the peak and the rms value of current in an a.c. circuit. (b) Describe briefly, with the help of a labelled diagram, working of a step-up transformer. (c) A step-up transformer converts a low voltage into high voltage. Does it not violate the principle of conservation of energy? Explain.
questions.answer:
(a) Let the alternating current be $i = i_0\sin\omega t$. The mean square current over one cycle is $\langle i^2\rangle = i_0^2\langle\sin^2\omega t\rangle = i_0^2/2$.
So $i_{rms} = \sqrt{\langle i^2\rangle} = \dfrac{i_0}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.707\,i_0$, and similarly $e_{rms} = e_0/\sqrt2$.
(b) A step-up transformer has a laminated soft-iron core with a primary winding of $N_p$ turns connected to the a.c. source and a secondary winding of $N_s$ turns ($N_s > N_p$) connected to the load. The changing current in the primary produces a changing magnetic flux in the core, which links the secondary and induces an alternating emf in it by mutual induction.
For an ideal transformer, $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = \dfrac{I_p}{I_s}$; since $N_s>N_p$, $V_s>V_p$ (voltage steps up) while $I_s<I_p$ (current steps down).
(c) No, energy conservation is not violated. In an ideal transformer, input power equals output power: $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$. As voltage increases, current decreases proportionally, so the power (and hence energy) delivered remains the same; only voltage and current are transformed, not energy.

questions.question: State the condition for resonance to occur in a series LCR a.c circuit and derive an expression for the resonant frequency. Draw a plot showing the variation of the peak current ($i_{m}$) with frequency of the a.c source used. Define the quality factor, Q of the circuit. Calculate the (i) impedance, (ii) wattless current of the given a.c circuit.
questions.answer:
Resonance in a series LCR circuit occurs when the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal, i.e. $X_L = X_C$, so that the current and voltage are in phase and impedance is minimum.
$\omega_0 L = \dfrac{1}{\omega_0 C} \Rightarrow \omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$, so the resonant frequency is $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.
Plot: $i_m$ versus $\omega$ (or $f$) rises from a low value, reaches a sharp maximum at $\omega_0$ (where $i_m = e_0/R$), and falls off on either side; the peak is sharper for smaller resistance $R$.
Quality factor: $Q = \dfrac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \dfrac{1}{\omega_0 CR}$, a measure of the sharpness of resonance.
For the given circuit:
(i) Impedance $Z = \sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$
(ii) Wattless (reactive) current $= i_{rms}\sin\phi$, where $\sin\phi = \dfrac{X_L-X_C}{Z}$, since this component does no net work over a cycle.

questions.question: Draw a labeled circuit arrangement showing the windings of primary and secondary coil in a transformer. Explain the underlying principle and working of a step-up transformer. Write any two major sources of energy loss in this device. How much current is drawn by the primary coil of a transformer which steps down $220 V$ to $22 V$ to operate a device with an impedance of $220 ohm$?
questions.answer:
Circuit arrangement: a laminated soft-iron core carries two windings — the primary of $N_p$ turns connected to the input a.c. source, and the secondary of $N_s$ turns connected to the load, both wound on the same core but electrically insulated from each other.
Principle: mutual induction — an alternating current in the primary sets up a changing magnetic flux in the core, which links the secondary and induces an alternating emf in it.
Working: for a step-up transformer, $N_s > N_p$, so $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}>1$, giving $V_s>V_p$, while the current decreases correspondingly ($I_s<I_p$), keeping power $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$ conserved.
Two major energy losses: (1) Copper loss — $I^2R$ heating in the windings; (2) Core loss — hysteresis and eddy current losses in the iron core.
Numerical: turns ratio $\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}=\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{22}{220}=\dfrac{1}{10}$
Secondary current $I_s = V_s/Z = 22/220 = 0.1$ A
Primary current $I_p = I_s\times\dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = 0.1\times\dfrac{1}{10} = 0.01$ A

questions.question: Explain the term ’inductive reactance’. Show graphically the variation of inductive reactance with frequency of the applied alternating voltage. An a.c. voltage $E = E_{0} \sin \omega t$ is applied across a pure inductor of inductance $L$. Show mathematically that the current flowing through it lags behind the applied voltage by a phase angle of $\pi/2$.
questions.answer:
Inductive reactance is the opposition offered by a pure inductor to the flow of alternating current, given by $X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L$; it is analogous to resistance but depends on frequency.
Graph: $X_L$ versus $f$ is a straight line passing through the origin, since $X_L \propto f$.
Let the applied voltage be $e = e_0\sin\omega t$ across a pure inductor $L$. Since there is no resistance, $e = L\dfrac{di}{dt}$, so $\dfrac{di}{dt} = \dfrac{e_0}{L}\sin\omega t$.
Integrating: $i = -\dfrac{e_0}{\omega L}\cos\omega t = \dfrac{e_0}{\omega L}\sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ (no constant of integration, as there is no steady/dc component).
Thus $i = i_0\sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, where $i_0 = e_0/\omega L = e_0/X_L$.
Comparing with $e = e_0\sin\omega t$, the current lags the voltage by a phase angle of $\pi/2$.

questions.question: The given circuit diagram shows a series LCR circuit connected to a variable frequency $230 V$ source: (a) Determine the source frequency which drives the circuit in resonance. (b) Obtain the impedance of the circuit and the amplitude of current at the resonating frequency. (c) Determine the rms potential drops across the three elements of the circuit. (d) How do you explain the observation that the algebraic sum of the voltages across the three elements obtained in (c) is greater than the supplied voltage?
questions.answer:
(a) Resonance occurs when $X_L = X_C$, giving resonant frequency $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$; substituting the given values of $L$ and $C$ gives the numerical value of $f_0$.
(b) At resonance the reactances cancel, so impedance is minimum and purely resistive: $Z = R$.
Current amplitude: $i_0 = \dfrac{V_0}{R} = \dfrac{\sqrt2\,V_{rms}}{R}$, using $V_{rms}=230$ V and the given $R$.
(c) rms voltage across each element: $V_R = i_{rms}R$, $V_L = i_{rms}X_L$, $V_C = i_{rms}X_C$, where $i_{rms}=i_0/\sqrt2$; at resonance $X_L=X_C$ so $V_L=V_C$.
(d) $V_L$ and $V_C$ are equal in magnitude but opposite in phase (differ by $\pi$), so they cancel each other in the phasor sum, while $V_R$ alone equals the applied voltage. The algebraic (arithmetic) sum $V_R+V_L+V_C$ exceeds the source voltage because it ignores these phase differences; only the phasor sum of the three voltages correctly equals the supplied rms voltage.

questions.question: The primary coil of an ideal step-up transformer has $100$ turns and the transformation ratio is also $100$. The input voltage and power are $220 V$ and $1100 W$ respectively. Calculate: (i) number of turns in the secondary (ii) the current in the primary (iii) voltage across the secondary (iv) the current in the secondary (v) power in the secondary
questions.answer:
(i) Turns ratio $\frac{N_s}{N_p}=100$ and $N_p=100$, so $N_s=100\times100=10000$
(ii) $I_p=\frac{P}{V_p}=\frac{1100}{220}=5$ A
(iii) $V_s=\frac{N_s}{N_p}\times V_p=100\times220=22000$ V
(iv) For an ideal transformer $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$, so $I_s=\frac{1100}{22000}=0.05$ A
(v) Since the transformer is ideal (no losses), power in secondary = power in primary $=1100$ W

questions.question: What is a choke coil? Why is it preferred to resistance in a.c. circuits? In figures (a), (b) and (c) are shown three a.c. circuits with equal currents. If the frequency of e.m.f. be increased, then what will be the effect on the currents flowing in them? Explain with reason.
questions.answer:
A choke coil is a coil of low ohmic resistance and high inductance, used in series in an a.c. circuit to reduce current without dissipating power.
It is preferred over a resistor because in a pure inductor the current lags the voltage by $90^\circ$, so the power factor $\cos\phi=0$ and the average power dissipated over a cycle, $P=V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi$, is zero; a resistor of the same current-limiting effect would continuously waste energy as $I^2R$ heat.
The reduction in current is achieved instead by the inductive reactance $X_L=\omega L$, which increases with frequency.
If frequency $f$ is increased: in a circuit containing only a resistor, current stays unchanged since $R$ is independent of $f$.
In the circuit containing the choke (inductor) in series, current decreases because $X_L=2\pi fL$ increases, raising impedance $Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}$.
In the circuit containing a capacitor in series, current increases because $X_C=\frac{1}{2\pi fC}$ decreases, lowering impedance $Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2}$.

questions.question: Two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the options below: (A) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A). (B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A). (C) Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false. (D) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false. Assertion (A): In Bohr model of hydrogen atom, the energy levels are discrete and quantised. Reason (R): In a hydrogen atom, the electrostatic force on the electron provides the necessary centripetal force to it to revolve around the nucleus. (A) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of (A). (B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of (A). (C) Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false. (D) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Both statements are true, but the quantisation of energy levels follows from Bohr's postulate of quantised angular momentum $L=\frac{nh}{2\pi}$, not directly from the Coulomb force providing centripetal force, so R does not explain A.

questions.question: The ’distance of closest approach’ of an alpha-particle is ’ $d$’ when it moves with a velocity $v$ head-on towards the target nucleus. If the velocity of alpha particle is halved, the new ’distance of closest approach’ will be: (A) $\frac{d}{2}$ (B) $2d$ (C) $\frac{d}{4}$ (D) $4d$
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
At closest approach all kinetic energy converts to potential energy, $\frac{1}{2}mv^2=\frac{kZe(2e)}{d}$, giving $d\propto\frac{1}{v^2}$; halving $v$ makes $d$ four times, i.e. $4d$.

questions.question: The distance-of-closest-approach for an alpha particle is ’ $d$’ when it moves head-on with speed $v$ towards a target nucleus. If the alpha particle is replaced by a proton moving with the same speed, the new distance-of-closest-approach will be: (A) $2d$ (B) $d$ (C) $\frac{d}{2}$ (D) $\frac{d}{4}$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
$d=\frac{2kZeq}{\frac{1}{2}mv^2}$; for the same speed a proton has half the charge but a quarter the mass of an alpha particle, so $d_{proton}=2d$.

questions.question: The ratio of the potential energy to the kinetic energy of an electron in $n$ th orbit of Bohr model of hydrogen atom is: (A) $-\frac{1}{2}$ (B) $\frac{1}{2}$ (C) $2$ (D) $-2$
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
In the Bohr model $KE=\frac{ke^2}{2r}$ and $PE=-\frac{ke^2}{r}$, so $\frac{PE}{KE}=-2$.

questions.question: In Bohr model of hydrogen atom, the electron makes a transition from $n = 5$ to $n = 1$ state. As a result, a photon of wavelength $\lambda$ is emitted in the process. The wavelength of the photon emitted when an electron makes a transition from energy level $n = 5$ to $n = 2$ will be: (A) $\frac{8}{7}\lambda$ (B) $\frac{24}{7}\lambda$ (C) $\frac{16}{7}\lambda$ (D) $\frac{32}{7}\lambda$
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
$E \propto \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$ and $\lambda \propto 1/E$, so $\lambda_{5\to2}/\lambda_{5\to1} = \frac{24/25}{21/100} = \frac{32}{7}$, giving $\lambda_{5\to2} = \frac{32}{7}\lambda$.

questions.question: In Bohr model of hydrogen atom, for large values of $n$, the distance between the consecutive orbits is proportional to: (A) $\sqrt{n}$ (B) $n$ (C) $n^{2}$ (D) $n^{3}$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Since $r_n = n^2 a_0$, $\Delta r = r_{n+1} - r_n \approx \frac{dr}{dn} = 2n a_0$ for large $n$, which is proportional to $n$.

questions.question: In Bohr model of hydrogen atom, the value of potential energy of an electron in $n$ th orbit varies with $n$ as: (A) $\frac{1}{n^{2}}$ (B) $\frac{1}{n}$ (C) $n$ (D) $n^{2}$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
$U_n = -\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r_n} = 2E_n \propto \frac{1}{n^2}$.

Option (B) is correct.
$h
u \propto \left( rac{1}{n_1^2}- rac{1}{n_2^2}ight)$, so $
u_{4	o2}/
u_{4	o1} =  rac{1/4-1/16}{1-1/16} =  rac{3/16}{15/16} =  rac{1}{5}$, giving frequency $
u/5$.

questions.question: According to Bohr model of hydrogen atom, the time period of an electron in its $n$ th orbit is proportional to: (A) $n$ (B) $n^{2}$ (C) $n^{3}$ (D) $n^{4}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
$T_n = 2\pi r_n / v_n$ with $r_n \propto n^2$ and $v_n \propto 1/n$, so $T_n \propto n^3$.

questions.question: In Bohr model of hydrogen atom, an electron is moving in an orbit, with total energy $-3$· $4$ eV. Its angular momentum will be: (A) $1$· $05 \times 10^{-34}$ J s (B) $6$· $63 \times 10^{-34}$ J s (C) $3$· $31 \times 10^{-34}$ J s (D) $2$· $1 \times 10^{-34}$ J s
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
$E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2}$ eV $= -3.4$ eV gives $n = 2$, so $L = \frac{nh}{2\pi} = \frac{2 \times 6.63\times10^{-34}}{2\pi} = 2.1\times10^{-34}$ J s.

questions.question: The ratio of the de Broglie wavelengths associated with the electron revolving in the first and third orbits in hydrogen atom is: (A) $2$ (B) $\frac{1}{3}$ (C) $3$ (D) $\frac{3}{2}$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Since $2\pi r_n = n\lambda_n$ and $r_n \propto n^2$, the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda_n \propto n$, so $\lambda_1/\lambda_3 = 1/3$.

questions.question: The energy of an electron in an orbit in hydrogen atom is $-3.4$ eV. Its angular momentum in the orbit will be: (A) $\frac{3h}{2\pi}$ (B) $\frac{2h}{\pi}$ (C) $\frac{h}{\pi}$ (D) $\frac{h}{2\pi}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
$E_n = -13.6/n^2$ eV gives $n=2$ for $E=-3.4$ eV, so angular momentum $= nh/2\pi = 2h/2\pi = h/\pi$.

questions.question: The energy of an electron revolving in the $n$ th orbit in Bohr model of hydrogen atom is proportional to: (A) $n^{2}$ (B) $n$ (C) $\frac{1}{n}$ (D) $\frac{1}{n^{2}}$
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
In the Bohr model, $E_n = -13.6/n^2$ eV, so $E_n \propto 1/n^2$.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The potential energy of an electron revolving in any stationary orbit in a hydrogen atom is positive. Reason (R): The total energy of a charged particle is always positive. (A) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A). (B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A). (C) Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false. (D) Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
The potential energy $U = -e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r$ is actually negative in every stationary orbit, and the total energy $E = -KE$ is also always negative for a bound electron, so both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.question: The energy of an electron in a hydrogen atom in ground state is $-13.6$ eV. Its energy in an orbit corresponding to quantum number n is $-0.544$ eV. The value of n is (A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 4 (D) 5
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
Using $E_n = -13.6/n^2$ eV, $n^2 = 13.6/0.544 = 25$, so $n = 5$.

questions.question: Assertion (A): In Bohr model of hydrogen atom, the angular momentum of an electron in $n^{th}$ orbit is proportional to the square root of its orbit radius $r_{n}$. Reason (R): According to Bohr model, electron can jump to its nearest orbits only. (A) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A). (B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A). (C) Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false. (D) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Since $L_n = nh/2\pi$ and $r_n \propto n^2$, $L_n \propto \sqrt{r_n}$ is true, but the electron in the Bohr model can jump to any orbit, not just the nearest one, so the Reason is false.

questions.question: A body acquires charge $8.0 \times 10^{-12}$ C. The mass of the body: (A) increases by $4.5 \times 10^{-7}$ kg (B) decreases by $1.0 \times 10^{-8}$ kg (C) decreases by $4.55 \times 10^{-23}$ kg (D) increases by $9.1 \times 10^{-23}$ kg
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Acquiring charge means losing $n = q/e = 8.0 \times 10^{-12}/1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 5 \times 10^{7}$ electrons, so the mass decreases by $n m_e = 5 \times 10^{7} \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} = 4.55 \times 10^{-23}$ kg.

questions.question: Case Study (Q30): A hydrogen atom consists of an electron revolving in a circular orbit of radius $r$ with certain velocity $v$ around a proton located at the nucleus of the atom. The electrostatic force of attraction between the revolving electron and the proton provides the requisite centripetal force to keep it in the orbit. According to Bohr’s model, an electron can revolve only in certain stable orbits. The angular momentum of the electron in these orbits is some integral multiple of $\frac{h}{2\pi}$, where $h$ is the Planck’s constant. Further, when an electron makes a transition from one orbit of higher energy to that of lower energy, a photon is emitted having energy equal to the difference between energies of the initial and final states. Assuming the mass and charge of an electron as $m$ and $e$ respectively, answer the following questions. (i) The expression for the speed of electron $[] v$ in terms of radius of the orbit ($r$) and physical constant $K =\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}$ is: $2$ (A) $\frac{Ke}{mr} 2$ (B) $\frac{\frac{Ke}{mr^{2}}}{2} r$ (C) $\frac{\frac{Ke}{mr}}{2} r$ (D) $\frac{Ke}{mr^{2}}$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Equating the Coulomb force to the centripetal force, $\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{Ke^2}{r^2}$, gives $v = e\sqrt{\frac{K}{mr}}$.

questions.question: (ii) The total energy of the atom in terms of $r$ and physical constant $K$ is: $2$ (A) $\frac{Ke}{r} 2$ (B) $-\frac{Ke}{2r} 2$ (C) $\frac{Ke}{2r} 2$ (D) $-\frac{3Ke}{2r}$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Total energy is half the potential energy (in magnitude), $E = KE + PE = \frac{Ke^2}{2r} - \frac{Ke^2}{r} = -\frac{Ke^2}{2r}$.

questions.question: (iii) A photon of wavelength $500$ nm is emitted when an electron makes a transition from one state to the other state in an atom. The change in the total energy of the electron and change in its kinetic energy in eV as per Bohr’s model, respectively will be: (A) $2.48, -2.48$ (B) $-1.24, 1.24$ (C) $-2.48, 2.48$ (D) $1.24, -1.24$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Photon energy $= \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{1240 \text{ eV nm}}{500 \text{ nm}} = 2.48$ eV, so $\Delta E = -2.48$ eV; since $KE = -E$ (virial theorem), $\Delta KE = +2.48$ eV.

questions.question: (iv) OR: An electron makes a transition from $-3.4$ eV state to the ground state in hydrogen atom. Its radius of orbit changes by: (radius of orbit of electron in ground state $= 0.53$ Å) (A) $0.53$ Å (B) $1.06$ Å (C) $1.59$ Å (D) $2.12$ Å
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
The $-3.4$ eV state is $n = 2$, whose radius is $n^2 r_1 = 4 \times 0.53 = 2.12$ Å, so the radius changes by $2.12 - 0.53 = 1.59$ Å.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Balmer series in hydrogen atom spectrum is formed when the electron jumps from higher energy state to the ground state. Reason (R): In Bohr’s model of hydrogen atom, the electron can jump between successive orbits only. (A) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A). (B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A). (C) Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false. (D) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
The Balmer series is formed by transitions to $n = 2$ (not the ground state), and an electron can jump directly between any two orbits, not just successive ones, so both statements are false.

questions.question: Assertion (A): In Rutherford’s alpha particle scattering experiment, the presence of only few alpha particles at angle of scattering $\pi$ led him to the discovery of nucleus. Reason (R): The size of nucleus is approximately $10^{-4}$ times the size of an atom and therefore only few alpha particles are rebounded. (A) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A). (B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A). (C) Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false. (D) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Both statements are true, and the small nuclear size ($\approx 10^{-4}$ times the atomic size) correctly explains why only a very small fraction of alpha particles suffer head-on collisions and rebound at $\theta = \pi$, leading Rutherford to conclude that the atom's positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

questions.question: Assertion (A): X-rays are produced when slow moving electrons are stopped by a metal target of high atomic number. Reason (R): X-rays consist of low-energy photons.
