It is related to current by $I = nAev_d$, where $n$ is the free electron density and $A$ is the cross-sectional area.

questions.question: A $10$ V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected across a $200$ V battery and a resistance of $38 \Omega$ as shown in the figure. Find the value of the current in circuit.
questions.answer:
The two batteries oppose each other, so the net emf drives current through the total resistance in the loop.
$I = \dfrac{200 - 10}{38 + 1} = \dfrac{190}{39} \approx 4.87$ A.

questions.question: The emf of a cell is always greater than its terminal voltage. Why? Give reason.
questions.answer:
This is because a cell has internal resistance $r$, and when current flows, some potential drops across it internally.
$V = E - Ir$, so the terminal voltage $V$ is always less than the emf $E$ whenever $I \neq 0$.

questions.question: Two conducting wires X and Y of same diameter but different materials are joined in series across a battery. If the number density of electrons in X is twice that in Y, find the ratio of drift velocity of electrons in the two wires.
questions.answer:
Since X and Y are in series, the current $I$ through both is the same, and the drift velocity is $v_d = I/(nAe)$.
With the same diameter (same $A$) and same $I$, $v_d \propto 1/n$, so $\dfrac{v_{dX}}{v_{dY}} = \dfrac{n_Y}{n_X} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.question: Two wires of equal length, one of copper and the other of manganin have the same resistance. Which wire is thicker?
questions.answer:
Since $R = \rho L/A$ and both wires have equal $L$ and equal $R$, the area $A \propto \rho$.
Manganin has a much higher resistivity than copper, so it must have a larger cross-sectional area to give the same resistance; hence the manganin wire is thicker.

questions.question: When electrons drift in a metal from lower to higher potential, does it mean that all the free electrons of the metal are moving in the same direction?
questions.answer:
No, all the free electrons do not move in the same direction.
They possess random thermal velocities in all directions; the applied field only superimposes a small net drift velocity $v_d = eE\tau/m$ opposite to $E$, which is common to all electrons, but their instantaneous individual motion remains largely random.

questions.question: A wire of resistance $8R$ is bent in the form of a circle. What is the effective resistance between the ends of a diameter AB?
questions.answer:
The effective resistance between A and B is $2R$.
The wire forms two semicircular arcs between A and B, each of resistance $4R$, connected in parallel, so $R_{AB} = \dfrac{4R \times 4R}{4R+4R} = 2R$.

questions.question: The plot of the variation of potential difference across a combination of three identical cells in series, versus current is as shown below. What is the emf of each cell?
questions.answer:
The emf of each cell is one-third of the V-axis intercept of the graph.
For three identical cells of emf $\varepsilon$ and internal resistance $r$ in series, $V = 3\varepsilon - I(3r)$, so at $I=0$ the intercept on the V-axis equals $3\varepsilon$, giving $\varepsilon = \dfrac{\text{intercept}}{3}$.

questions.question: Sketch a graph showing variation of resistivity of carbon with temperature.
questions.answer:
Carbon is a semiconductor, so its resistivity decreases as temperature increases.
The graph is a curve that falls steadily from a high value at low temperature and slopes downward continuously as temperature rises, since more charge carriers become available for conduction, unlike the nearly linear rise seen in metals.

questions.question: Define electrical conductivity of a conductor and give its S.I. unit.
questions.answer: Electrical conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity, $\sigma = \dfrac{1}{\rho}$, and its SI unit is siemens per metre ($\text{S m}^{-1}$), equivalent to $\Omega^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}$.

questions.question: What happens to the power dissipation if the value of electric current passing through a conductor of constant resistance is doubled?
questions.answer:
The power dissipation becomes four times the original value.
Since $P = I^2R$ and $R$ is constant, doubling $I$ gives $P' = (2I)^2R = 4I^2R = 4P$.

questions.question: What is the order of magnitude of drift velocity of electrons in a conductor? Deduce the relation between the current flowing through a conductor and drift velocity of electrons in it.
questions.answer:
The drift velocity of free electrons in a conductor is of the order of $10^{-4}$ m/s.
If $n$ is the free electron density and $A$ the area of cross-section, electrons drifting with velocity $v_d$ sweep out a volume $Av_d\,\Delta t$ in time $\Delta t$, containing $nAv_d\Delta t$ electrons.
Charge crossing this area in time $\Delta t$ is $\Delta Q = neAv_d\Delta t$, so the current is $I = \Delta Q/\Delta t = neAv_d$.

questions.question: A heating element using nichrome is connected to a $220$ V supply. Initially it draws a current of $2$· $9$ A. After some time, the current attains a steady value of $2$· $5$ A. Find the steady temperature of the heating element if the room temperature is $27^{^{\circ}}$ C. The temperature coefficient of resistance of nichrome is $1$· $7 \times 10^{-4 ^{\circ}}$ C $-1$.
questions.answer:
Resistance at room temperature: $R_1 = 220/2.9 = 75.86\,\Omega$; resistance at steady state: $R_2 = 220/2.5 = 88\,\Omega$.
Using $R_2 = R_1[1+\alpha(T-27)]$: $88 = 75.86[1+1.7\times10^{-4}(T-27)]$, giving $T-27 \approx 941^{\circ}$C.
So the steady temperature $T \approx 968^{\circ}$C.

questions.question: Calculate the temperature at which the resistance of a conductor becomes $20\%$ more than its resistance at $27^{^{\circ}}$ C. The value of the temperature coefficient of resistance of the material of conductor is $2$· $0 \times 10^{-4 ^{\circ}}$ C $-1$.

(a) Why is manganin used in wire-wound standard resistors? Calculate the temperature at which the resistance of a wire increases by $25\%$ of its resistance at room temperature $27$· $5^{^{\circ}}$ C. The temperature coefficient of resistance of the material of the wire is $0$· $004^{^{\circ}}$ C $-1$.
questions.answer:
(a) Manganin has an almost negligible temperature coefficient of resistance, so its resistance remains nearly constant with temperature changes, making it suitable for wire-wound standard resistors.
Using $R_2 = R_1[1+\alpha(T-27.5)]$ with $R_2 = 1.25R_1$: $0.25 = 0.004(T-27.5)$, so $T-27.5 = 62.5$, giving $T = 90^{\circ}$C.

questions.question: In the given figure, a steady current $I$ flows through the circuit when points $A$ and $C$ are connected by a wire of negligible resistance. Find the potential difference between points $B$ and $C$.
questions.answer:
Since $A$ and $C$ are joined by a wire of negligible resistance, they are at the same potential, and the steady current $I$ flows only through the arm(s) connecting $A$ to $C$ via $B$; any branch that does not lie on this closed conducting path (such as one containing a capacitor) carries no current, so there is no potential drop across resistors in that branch.
The potential difference between $B$ and $C$ is then given by Ohm's law, $V_{BC} = IR$, where $R$ is the resistance of the arm between $B$ and $C$ that actually carries the current $I$.

questions.question: A battery of emf $21$ V and internal resistance $3 \Omega$ is connected to a resistor. If the current in the circuit is $3$ A, find: (i) the resistance of the resistor. (ii) the terminal voltage of the battery.
questions.answer:
(i) Using $\varepsilon = I(R+r)$: $21 = 3(R+3)$, so $R+3 = 7$, giving $R = 4\,\Omega$.
(ii) Terminal voltage $V = \varepsilon - Ir = 21 - 3\times3 = 12$ V (also $V = IR = 3\times4 = 12$ V).

questions.question: An electric iron rated $2.2$ kW, $220$ V is operated at $110$ V supply. Find: (i) its resistance, and (ii) heat produced by it in 10 minutes.

A current of $4.0$ A flows through a wire of length $1$ m and cross-sectional area $1.0$ mm $2$, when potential difference of $2$ V is applied across its ends. Calculate the resistivity of the material of the wire.
questions.answer:
Resistance $R = V/I = 2/4.0 = 0.5$ $\Omega$.
Resistivity $\rho = RA/L = (0.5)(1.0 \times 10^{-6})/1 = 5 \times 10^{-7}$ $\Omega$ m.

questions.question: A battery of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ is connected to a rheostat. When a current of $2$ A is drawn from the battery, the potential difference across the rheostat is $5$ V. The potential difference becomes $4$ V when a current of $4$ A is drawn from the battery. Calculate the value of $E$ and $r$.
questions.answer:
Using $V = E - Ir$:
$5 = E - 2r$ and $4 = E - 4r$.
Subtracting: $1 = 2r \Rightarrow r = 0.5$ $\Omega$, and $E = 5 + 2(0.5) = 6$ V.

questions.question: Show that $\vec{E} = \rho\vec{j}$ leads to Ohm’s law. Write a condition in which the Ohm’s law is not valid for a material.
questions.answer:
Drift velocity $v_d = eE\tau/m$, so current density $j = nev_d = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}E$.
This gives $E = \left(\dfrac{m}{ne^2\tau}\right)j = \rho j$, where $\rho = m/(ne^2\tau)$ is a constant for a given material at constant temperature.
Since $E = V/l$ and $j = I/A$, this becomes $V = I(\rho l/A) = IR$, i.e., $V \propto I$, which is Ohm's law.
Ohm's law fails when $\rho$ (or $R$) itself depends on $V$ or $I$, e.g., in semiconductor diodes or when the temperature of the conductor changes appreciably with current.

questions.question: $n$ identical cells, each of e.m.f. $E$ and internal resistance $r$, are connected in series. Later on it was found out that two cells $X$ and $Y$ are connected in reverse polarities. Calculate the potential difference across the cell $X$.
questions.answer:
With two cells reversed, net emf of the loop $= (n-2)E - 2E = (n-4)E$, while total internal resistance remains $nr$ (resistance is unaffected by polarity).
Current in the circuit: $I = \dfrac{(n-4)E}{nr}$.
Since cell $X$ is reversed, it is being driven backward by the rest, so its terminal p.d. is $V_X = E + Ir = E + \dfrac{(n-4)E}{n} = \dfrac{2(n-2)E}{n}$.

questions.question: Two wires of the same material and the same radius have their lengths in the ratio 2: 3. They are connected in parallel to a battery which supplies a current of 15 A. Find the current through the wires.
questions.answer:
Same material and radius $\Rightarrow$ resistance $R \propto L$, so $R_1:R_2 = 2:3$.
In parallel, voltage is same, so $I \propto 1/R$, giving $I_1:I_2 = 3:2$.
Total current $15$ A splits in ratio $3:2$: $I_1 = 9$ A, $I_2 = 6$ A.

questions.question: In the circuit three ideal cells of e.m.f. V, V and 2V are connected to a resistor of resistance R, a capacitor of capacitance C and another resistor of resistance 2R as shown in figure. In the steady state find (i) the potential difference between P and Q and (ii) potential difference across capacitor C.
questions.answer:
In steady state the capacitor is fully charged, so no current flows in the branch containing $C$; current flows only through $R$ and $2R$ around the loop formed by the three cells.
Applying Kirchhoff's voltage law, the net emf drives current $I = \dfrac{2V+V-V}{R+2R} = \dfrac{2V}{3R}$ through the resistors.
(i) $V_P - V_Q = IR = \dfrac{2V}{3}$.
(ii) Since no current flows in the capacitor branch, there is no potential drop across any resistor in that branch, so the capacitor acquires the same potential difference as exists between $P$ and $Q$: $V_C = \dfrac{2V}{3}$.

questions.question: (a) In the given figure, three identical bulbs $P$, $Q$ and $S$ are connected to a battery. (i) Compare the brightness of bulbs $P$ and $Q$ with that of bulb $S$ when key $K$ is closed. (ii) Compare the brightness of the bulbs $S$ and $Q$ when the key $K$ is opened. Justify your answer in both cases. OR (b) Two cells of emf $10$ V each, two resistors of $20 \Omega$ and $10 \Omega$ and a bulb $B$ of $10 \Omega$ resistance are connected together as shown in the figure. Find the current that flows through the bulb.
questions.answer:
(a) (i) With $K$ closed, bulbs $P$ and $Q$ (in series, resistance $2R$) form one branch and $S$ (resistance $R$) forms a parallel branch across the same battery voltage.
Current in the $S$ branch, $I_S = \varepsilon/R$, is twice the current in the $P$-$Q$ branch, $I_{PQ} = \varepsilon/2R$, so $S$ glows brighter than $P$ and $Q$; since $P$ and $Q$ carry the same current, they are equally bright.
(ii) When $K$ (in series with $S$) is opened, the $S$ branch is broken so $S$ goes off completely, while $P$ and $Q$ continue to carry the same current $\varepsilon/2R$ as before, so $Q$ keeps glowing with unchanged brightness while $S$ does not glow at all.
OR
(b) The two cells (each $10$ V) with their series resistors $20\,\Omega$ and $10\,\Omega$ form two branches in parallel across the bulb $B$ ($10\,\Omega$).
Using Millman's theorem, $V_B = \dfrac{\frac{10}{20}+\frac{10}{10}}{\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{10}} = \dfrac{1.5}{0.25} = 6$ V.
Current through the bulb, $I = \dfrac{V_B}{10} = 0.6$ A.

questions.question: The resistance of a wire at $25^{^{\circ}}$ C is $10.0 \Omega$. When heated to $125^{^{\circ}}$ C, its resistance becomes $10.5 \Omega$. Find (i) the temperature coefficient of resistance of the wire, and (ii) the resistance of the wire at $425^{^{\circ}}$ C.
questions.answer:
Using $R_t = R_0(1+\alpha \Delta t)$: $10.5 = 10.0(1+\alpha \times 100)$, giving $\alpha = \dfrac{0.5}{10.0 \times 100} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \, ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$.
At $425^\circ$C, $\Delta t = 400^\circ$C from $25^\circ$C, so $R = 10.0(1+5\times10^{-4}\times 400) = 10.0 \times 1.2 = 12.0 \, \Omega$.

questions.question: A wire of resistance $X$ ohm is gradually stretched till its length becomes twice its original length. If its new resistance becomes $40 \Omega$, find the value of $X$.
questions.answer:
Since volume is conserved on stretching, $R \propto L^2$ (as $R = \rho L/A = \rho L^2/(AL) = \rho L^2/V$).
When length doubles, resistance becomes $4$ times: $R_{new} = 4X$.
So $4X = 40 \, \Omega$, giving $X = 10 \, \Omega$.

questions.question: Find the equivalent resistance between points $A$ and $B$ for the network shown in the figure.
questions.answer:
First check the network for a balanced Wheatstone-bridge arrangement, i.e., whether the products of resistances of opposite arms are equal ($R_1R_4 = R_2R_3$).
If balanced, no current flows through the bridge (galvanometer) arm, so it can be removed without affecting the currents in the rest of the network.
The circuit then reduces to two series combinations (using $R_{series} = R_1+R_2$) connected in parallel (using $\dfrac{1}{R_{parallel}} = \dfrac{1}{R_1}+\dfrac{1}{R_2}$), which combine to give the equivalent resistance $R_{AB}$ between $A$ and $B$.

questions.question: A cell of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ is connected to an external variable resistance $R$. Plot a graph showing the variation of terminal voltage $V$ of the cell as a function of current $I$, supplied by the cell. Explain how the emf of the cell and its internal resistance can be found from it.
questions.answer:
Since $V = E - Ir$, the graph of terminal voltage $V$ versus current $I$ is a straight line with a negative slope, starting from a maximum value on the $V$-axis and decreasing as $I$ increases.
The intercept of the line on the $V$-axis (where $I=0$) gives the emf $E$ of the cell.
The magnitude of the slope of the line, $\left|\dfrac{dV}{dI}\right| = r$, gives the internal resistance of the cell; equivalently, $r = \dfrac{E-V}{I}$ for any point on the graph.

questions.question: (a) What is the difference between ’velocity’ and ’drift velocity’ of electrons in a currentcarrying conductor. (b) A copper wire of uniform cross-sectional area carries a current of $3$· $4$ A. The drift velocity of conduction electrons is $0$· $2$ mm/s. If the number density of electrons in copper is $8$· $5 \times 10^{28}$ m $-3$, find the area of cross-section of the wire.
questions.answer:
(a) Velocity is the actual instantaneous speed of an electron due to random thermal motion; it is very large ($\sim 10^5$ m/s), randomly directed, and averages to zero net displacement in the absence of a field.
Drift velocity is the small net velocity ($\sim 10^{-4}$ m/s) acquired by electrons along the length of the conductor due to the applied electric field, and it is responsible for current flow.
(b) $I = nAev_d$
$A = \dfrac{I}{nev_d} = \dfrac{3.4}{8.5\times10^{28}\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.2\times10^{-3}} = 1.25\times10^{-6}$ m$^2$

questions.question: A cell of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ is connected across a resistor of variable resistance $R$. Show graphically the variation of (a) the terminal voltage across the cell, (b) the current supplied by the cell, with $R$ as it is increased from $0$ to the maximum value.
questions.answer:
(a) Terminal voltage $V = E - Ir = \dfrac{ER}{R+r}$: at $R=0$, $V=0$, and as $R$ increases, $V$ rises and asymptotically approaches $E$ as $R\to\infty$, giving a curve that starts at the origin and saturates at $E$.
(b) Current $I = \dfrac{E}{R+r}$: at $R=0$, $I$ has its maximum value $E/r$, and as $R$ increases, $I$ falls continuously and asymptotically approaches zero, giving a monotonically decreasing curve.

questions.question: Two wires made of the same material have the same length ($l$) but different cross-sectional areas $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$. They are connected together with a cell of voltage $V$. Find the ratio of the drift velocities of free electrons in the two wires when they are joined in (i) series, and (ii) parallel.
questions.answer:
(i) Series: the same current $I$ flows through both wires, and $v_d = \dfrac{I}{nAe}$, so $\dfrac{v_{d1}}{v_{d2}} = \dfrac{A_2}{A_1}$
(ii) Parallel: both wires (same length $l$) have the same voltage $V$ across them, so the electric field $E = V/l$ is the same in each; since $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$ depends only on $E$ (same material, same $\tau$), $\dfrac{v_{d1}}{v_{d2}} = 1$

questions.question: Calculate the value of the current passing through the battery in the given circuit diagram.
questions.answer:
The resistors are first combined into a single equivalent resistance $R_{eq}$ using the series rule $R_{eq}=R_1+R_2+\ldots$ for resistors in series and the parallel rule $\dfrac{1}{R_{eq}}=\dfrac{1}{R_1}+\dfrac{1}{R_2}+\ldots$ for resistors in parallel.
The current drawn from the battery is then found using $I=\dfrac{E}{R_{eq}+r}$, where $E$ is the emf and $r$ the internal resistance of the battery (or $I=E/R_{eq}$ if the battery is ideal).

questions.question: Find the temperature at which the resistance of a wire made of silver will be twice its resistance at $20^{^{\circ}}$ C. Take $20^{^{\circ}}$ C as the reference temperature and temperature coefficient of resistance of silver at $20^{^{\circ}}$ C $= 4.0 \times 10^{-3}$ K $-1$.

Two batteries of emfs $6$ V and $3$ V and internal resistances $0.8 \Omega$ and $0.2 \Omega$ respectively are connected in series to an external resistance $R$, as shown in figure. Find the value of $R$ so that the potential difference across the $6$ V battery be zero.
questions.answer:
For the terminal p.d. across the $6$ V battery to be zero: $E_1 - Ir_1 = 0 \Rightarrow I = \dfrac{E_1}{r_1} = \dfrac{6}{0.8} = 7.5$ A
For the series circuit: $I = \dfrac{E_1+E_2}{R+r_1+r_2}$
$7.5 = \dfrac{6+3}{R+0.8+0.2} = \dfrac{9}{R+1}$
$R+1 = 1.2 \Rightarrow R = 0.2\ \Omega$

questions.question: A uniform wire of length $L$ and area of cross-section $A$ has resistance $R$. The wire is uniformly stretched so that its length increases by $25\%$. Calculate the percentage increase in the resistance of the wire.
questions.answer:
$R = \rho L/A$ and volume $V = AL$ remains constant on stretching, so $R = \rho L^{2}/V$, i.e. $R \propto L^{2}$.
New length $L' = 1.25L$, so $R' = R(1.25)^{2} = 1.5625R$.
Percentage increase in resistance $= 56.25\%$.

questions.question: Define resistivity of a conductor. How does the resistivity of a conductor depend upon the following: (a) Number density of free electrons in the conductor (n) (b) Their relaxation time ($\tau$)
questions.answer:
Resistivity of a conductor is the resistance offered by a wire of unit length and unit cross-sectional area, $\rho = RA/L$, and it is a property of the material only.
It is given by $\rho = \dfrac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}$.
(a) $\rho \propto 1/n$, so resistivity decreases as the number density of free electrons increases.
(b) $\rho \propto 1/\tau$, so resistivity decreases as the relaxation time increases.

questions.question: (a) "The electron drift speed is only a few mm/s for currents in the range of a few amperes for a given conductor." How then is current established almost the instant a circuit is closed? Explain. (b) " $V = IR$ is a statement of Ohm’s Law" is not true. Explain.
questions.answer:
(a) On closing the circuit, the electric field is set up inside the conductor almost instantaneously (at a speed close to the speed of light), so free electrons all along the wire begin to drift together at nearly the same instant; hence current starts almost immediately even though the drift speed of any individual electron is only a few mm/s.
(b) $V = IR$ merely defines resistance as the ratio $V/I$ and holds for any conductor, ohmic or non-ohmic.
Ohm's law is the additional statement that this ratio $R$ is constant, independent of $V$ and $I$, i.e. current is directly proportional to voltage; this is true only for ohmic conductors at constant temperature.

questions.question: An electric field $\vec{E}$ is maintained in a wire of length ’ $l$’ and area of cross-section ’ $a$’. Derive the relation between the current density ’ $\sigma$’ in the wire and the electric field $\vec{E}$.
questions.answer:
The drift velocity acquired by free electrons is $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$, where $\tau$ is the relaxation time.
Current $I = neAv_d$, so current density $j = I/a = nev_d = \dfrac{ne^{2}\tau}{m}E$.
Thus $j = \sigma E$, where $\sigma = \dfrac{ne^{2}\tau}{m}$ is the conductivity of the material.

questions.question: What is meant by ’relaxation time’ of free electrons in a conductor? Show that the resistance of a conductor can be expressed by $R =\frac{ml}{ne^{2}\tau A}$, where symbols have their usual meanings.
questions.answer:
Relaxation time is the average time that elapses between two successive collisions of a free electron with the lattice ions in a conductor.
Drift velocity $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$, and current $I = neAv_d = \dfrac{ne^{2}A\tau}{m}E$.
Since $E = V/l$, $I = \dfrac{ne^{2}A\tau V}{ml}$, so $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{ml}{ne^{2}\tau A}$.

questions.question: Draw the circuit diagram of a Wheatstone bridge. Obtain the condition when no current flows through the galvanometer in it.
questions.answer:
The Wheatstone bridge has four resistances $P, Q, R, S$ forming a closed quadrilateral $ABCD$: $P$ between $A$-$B$, $Q$ between $B$-$C$, $R$ between $A$-$D$, $S$ between $D$-$C$; a battery is connected across $A$-$C$, and a galvanometer across the diagonal $B$-$D$.
Applying Kirchhoff's laws, at balance no current flows through the galvanometer, so $B$ and $D$ are at the same potential.
This gives the same current $I_1$ through $P$ and $Q$, and $I_2$ through $R$ and $S$, with $I_1P = I_2R$ and $I_1Q = I_2S$.
Dividing these, the balance condition is $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$.

questions.question: Two electric heaters have power ratings $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$, at voltage $V$. They are connected in series to a dc source of voltage $V$. Find the power consumed by the combination. Will they consume the same power if connected in parallel across the same source?
questions.answer:
In series, $R_{1}=V^{2}/P_{1}$ and $R_{2}=V^{2}/P_{2}$, so equivalent resistance $R=R_{1}+R_{2}$.
Power consumed, $P=\dfrac{V^{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}=\dfrac{P_{1}P_{2}}{P_{1}+P_{2}}$.
No, in parallel each heater gets the full voltage $V$ across it, so each consumes its own rated power; total power drawn is $P_{1}+P_{2}$, which is different from the series case.

questions.question: Two wires $A$ and $B$ of different metals have their lengths in ratio $1: 2$ and their radii in ratio $2: 1$ respectively. $I$- $V$ graphs for them is shown in the figure. Find the ratio of their (i) Resistances $(R_{A}/R_{B})$ and (ii) Resistivities $(\rho_{A}/\rho_{B})$
questions.answer:
From the graph, the slope of line $A$ is twice that of line $B$ (for the same $V$, $I_{A}=2I_{B}$), so $R_{B}=2R_{A}$, i.e. $R_{A}/R_{B}=1/2$.
Using $R=\rho l/A$ with $l_{A}/l_{B}=1/2$ and area ratio $A_{A}/A_{B}=(r_{A}/r_{B})^{2}=4$:
$\dfrac{\rho_{A}}{\rho_{B}}=\dfrac{R_{A}}{R_{B}}\times\dfrac{A_{A}}{A_{B}}\times\dfrac{l_{B}}{l_{A}}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times4\times2=4$.

questions.question: Find the temperature at which the resistance of a conductor increases by $25\%$ of its value at $27$ C. The temperature coefficient of resistance of the conductor is $2.0 \times 10^{-4}$ C $-1$.
questions.answer:
$R_{T}=R_{27}(1+\alpha\Delta T)$, and $R_{T}=1.25R_{27}$ gives $\Delta T=\dfrac{0.25}{\alpha}=\dfrac{0.25}{2.0\times10^{-4}}=1250\ ^\circ C$.
So $T=27+1250=1277\ ^\circ C$.

questions.question: Refer to the circuit diagram. Find the potential difference across resistance $R_{2}$.
questions.answer:
First find the equivalent resistance $R_{eq}$ of the circuit and the total current drawn from the source using $I=\dfrac{V}{R_{eq}}$.
If $R_{2}$ carries this current directly (series branch), the potential difference across it is $V_{2}=IR_{2}$; if $R_{2}$ is in parallel with another resistor, use the current-divider rule to get the current $I_{2}$ through it and then $V_{2}=I_{2}R_{2}$.

questions.question: Refer to the circuit diagram. What is the power dissipated in resistance $R_{2}$?
questions.answer:
Using Ohm's law and the series-parallel reduction of the circuit, find the current $I_{2}$ actually flowing through $R_{2}$.
The power dissipated in $R_{2}$ is then $P_{2}=I_{2}^{2}R_{2}=\dfrac{V_{2}^{2}}{R_{2}}$, where $V_{2}$ is the potential difference across $R_{2}$.

questions.question: Write two differences between the emf and terminal potential difference of a cell. What is the most important precaution that one should take while drawing current from a cell?
questions.answer:
(i) EMF is the potential difference between the terminals of a cell when no current is drawn (open circuit), while terminal p.d. is the potential difference when current flows through the circuit (closed circuit).
(ii) EMF is a fixed characteristic of the cell independent of current, whereas terminal p.d. depends on current drawn: $V=\varepsilon-Ir$, so $V<\varepsilon$ during discharge, due to the drop $Ir$ across internal resistance.
Precaution: never short-circuit the cell (draw very large current), as this makes $I$ very large and dissipates excessive heat inside the cell, damaging it.

questions.question: Two identical cells, each of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$, are connected with a load resistance $R$, first in series and then in parallel. Obtain the condition under which the current through $R$ is same in both cases.
questions.answer:
For series combination, current through $R$: $I_s = \dfrac{2E}{2r+R}$
For parallel combination, current through $R$: $I_p = \dfrac{2E}{r+2R}$
Equating $I_s = I_p$ gives $2r+R = r+2R$, i.e., $R = r$.
So the current through $R$ is the same in both cases when the load resistance equals the internal resistance of each cell.

questions.question: A cell of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ is connected to a variable resistance $R$. Draw plots showing the variation of (a) terminal voltage $V$ with $R$, and (b) $V$ with current $I$, in the circuit.
questions.answer:
(a) $V = E - Ir = \dfrac{ER}{R+r}$: as $R$ increases from zero, $V$ rises from $0$ and asymptotically approaches $E$ for large $R$, giving a curve that increases steeply at first and then flattens.
(b) $V = E - Ir$ is a straight line of negative slope $-r$, cutting the $V$-axis at $V=E$ (when $I=0$) and the $I$-axis at $I=E/r$ (when $V=0$).

questions.question: The potential difference applied across a given conductor is doubled. How will this affect (i) the mobility of electrons and (ii) the current density in the conductor? Justify your answers.
questions.answer:
(i) Mobility $\mu = e\tau/m$ depends only on the relaxation time $\tau$, which is fixed by the material and temperature, not by the applied potential difference; so mobility remains unchanged.
(ii) Current density $J = \sigma E = \sigma V/L$; since conductivity $\sigma$ is constant and $V$ is doubled, the field $E$ doubles, so $J$ also doubles.

questions.question: A potential difference (V) is applied across a conductor of length ’L’ and cross-sectional area ’A’. How will the drift velocity of electrons and the current density be affected if another identical conductor of the same material were connected in series with the first conductor? Justify your answers.
questions.answer:
On connecting an identical conductor in series, the total length becomes $2L$, and if the same $V$ is now applied across the combination, the field reduces to $E' = V/2L$, half the original value.
Since $v_d = \mu E$, the drift velocity becomes half: $v_d' = v_d/2$.
The total resistance doubles to $2R$, so the current $I' = V/2R = I/2$; as area $A$ is unchanged, current density $J = I/A$ also becomes half.

questions.question: Two conductors, made of the same material have equal lengths but different crosssectional areas $A_{1}$ and $A_{2} (A_{1} > A_{2})$. They are connected in parallel across a cell. Show that the drift velocities of electrons in two conductors are equal.
questions.answer:
Since the two conductors are in parallel across the same cell, the potential difference $V$ across each is identical, and as both have the same length $L$, the electric field $E = V/L$ inside each is also identical.
Drift velocity $v_d = \mu E = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$ depends only on $E$ and on material properties ($\tau$, same material), not on the cross-sectional area.
Hence $v_{d1} = v_{d2}$ even though $A_1 > A_2$.

questions.question: Define drift velocity of electrons in a conductor connected across a battery. Figure shows variation of the drift velocity $(v_{d})$ of electrons in two copper wires A and B of different lengths versus the potential difference $(V )$ applied across their ends. (i) What does the slope of the line represent? (ii) Which one of the two wires is longer?
questions.answer:
Drift velocity is the average velocity acquired by the free electrons of a conductor in the direction opposite to an applied electric field.
(i) Since $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m} = \dfrac{e\tau}{mL}V$, the slope of the $v_d$-$V$ graph equals $\dfrac{e\tau}{mL}$, which is inversely proportional to the length $L$ of the wire.
(ii) As the slope is proportional to $1/L$, the wire whose line has the smaller slope corresponds to the greater length; that wire is the longer one.

questions.question: Explain the principle of working of a meter bridge. Draw the circuit diagram for determination of an unknown resistance using it.
questions.answer:
A meter bridge works on the principle of the Wheatstone bridge: four resistances $P, Q, R, S$ arranged in a bridge are balanced when no current flows through the galvanometer, giving $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$.
Here the unknown resistance $X$ is in one gap and a known resistance $R$ in the other; a $1$ m resistance wire (with a jockey sliding on it) forms the other two arms, so at the null point $\dfrac{X}{R} = \dfrac{l}{100-l}$, where $l$ is the balancing length from the end near $X$.
Circuit: a battery, key and rheostat are connected across the wire $AB$; $X$ and $R$ form the two gaps of the bridge above the wire, with a galvanometer and jockey connected between their junction and the sliding contact on the wire.

questions.question: Define the term ’mobility’ of charge carriers in a current carrying conductor. Obtain the relation for mobility in terms of relaxation time. OR Define the term ’drift velocity’ of electrons in a current carrying conductor. Obtain the relationship between the current density and the drift velocity of electrons.
questions.answer:
Mobility $\mu$ is the magnitude of drift velocity acquired by a charge carrier per unit electric field applied: $\mu = \dfrac{v_d}{E}$.
Since $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$, we get $\mu = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}$, where $\tau$ is the relaxation time, $e$ the electronic charge and $m$ the electron mass.
OR
Drift velocity is the average velocity acquired by free electrons in a conductor under an applied electric field, superposed on their random thermal motion.
Current $I = neAv_d$, so current density $J = \dfrac{I}{A} = nev_d$, where $n$ is the free electron density and $e$ the electronic charge.

questions.question: A battery of emf $12$ V and internal resistance $4 \Omega$ is connected to an external resistance $R$. If the current in the resistance is $0.5$ A, calculate the value of (a) $R$, and (b) the terminal voltage of the battery.
questions.answer:
Using $\varepsilon = I(R+r)$: $12 = 0.5(R+4)$, so $R+4 = 24$, giving $R = 20\ \Omega$.
Terminal voltage $V = \varepsilon - Ir = 12 - 0.5 \times 4 = 10$ V.

questions.question: The number densities of free electrons in three conductors $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are in the ratio $4: 1: 8$, and their electrical conductivities are in the ratio $2: 1: 2$. For which conductor will the relaxation time of free electrons be (a) maximum, and (b) minimum?
questions.answer:
Since $\sigma = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}$, $\tau \propto \dfrac{\sigma}{n}$.
$\tau_X : \tau_Y : \tau_Z = \dfrac{2}{4} : \dfrac{1}{1} : \dfrac{2}{8} = 0.5 : 1 : 0.25$.
(a) Relaxation time is maximum for conductor $Y$.
(b) Relaxation time is minimum for conductor $Z$.

questions.question: A wire of length $L_{1}$ has a resistance $R_{1}$. It is gradually stretched till its length becomes $2L_{1}$. (a) Plot a graph showing variation of its resistance $R$ with its length $l$ during stretching. (b) What will be its resistance when its length becomes $2L_{1}$?
questions.answer:
Since volume $V = Al$ is constant on stretching, $R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A} = \dfrac{\rho l^2}{V}$, so $R \propto l^2$: the $R$-$l$ graph is a parabola curving upward as $l$ increases.
(b) When length becomes $2L_1$, $R_2 = R_1\left(\dfrac{2L_1}{L_1}\right)^2 = 4R_1$.

questions.question: A uniform wire is cut into three parts with their lengths in the ratio $2: 3: 6$. The ends of each of these three parts are connected across an ideal battery of $10$ V. If a current of $5$ A is drawn from the battery, find the initial resistance of the wire.
questions.answer:
Let the wire's total resistance be $R$; since length ratio is $2:3:6$ (total $11$ parts), the three pieces have resistances $\dfrac{2R}{11}, \dfrac{3R}{11}, \dfrac{6R}{11}$.
Each is connected across the same $10$ V battery, so total current $I = 10\left(\dfrac{11}{2R}+\dfrac{11}{3R}+\dfrac{11}{6R}\right) = \dfrac{10 \times 11}{R}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{6}\right) = \dfrac{110}{R}$.
Given $I = 5$ A: $\dfrac{110}{R} = 5$, so $R = 22\ \Omega$.

questions.question: Two bulbs are rated $(P_{1}, V )$ and $(P_{2}, V )$. If they are connected (i) in series and (ii) in parallel across a supply $V$, find the power dissipated in the two combinations in terms of $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$.
questions.answer:
Resistances of the bulbs are $R_1=V^2/P_1$ and $R_2=V^2/P_2$.
(i) In series, same current flows, so power dissipated $P_s=\dfrac{V^2}{R_1+R_2}=\dfrac{P_1P_2}{P_1+P_2}$.
(ii) In parallel, same voltage $V$ appears across each, so power dissipated $P_p=P_1+P_2$.

questions.question: A set of ’ $n$’ identical resistors, each of resistance ’ $R$’ when connected in series have an effective resistance ’ $X$’. When they are connected in parallel, their effective resistance becomes ’ $Y$ ’. Find out the product of $X$ and $Y$.
questions.answer:
In series, $X=nR$.
In parallel, $Y=\dfrac{R}{n}$.
So the product $XY=nR\times\dfrac{R}{n}=R^2$.

questions.question: A wire of resistance $R$, length $l$ and area of cross-section $A$, is cut into two parts, having their lengths in the ratio $1: 2$. The shorter wire is now stretched till its length becomes equal to that of the longer wire. If they are now connected in parallel, find the net resistance of the combination.
questions.answer:
The wire is cut in ratio $1:2$, so the pieces have resistance $R_1=R/3$ (length $l/3$) and $R_2=2R/3$ (length $2l/3$), since resistance is proportional to length for the same cross-section.
The shorter piece is stretched so its length becomes $2l/3$, i.e. doubled; since volume is conserved, resistance scales as (length)$^2$, giving $R_1'=R_1\times 2^2=4R/3$.
Parallel combination: $R_{net}=\dfrac{R_1'R_2}{R_1'+R_2}=\dfrac{(4R/3)(2R/3)}{4R/3+2R/3}=\dfrac{4R}{9}$.

questions.question: A wire of resistance $R$, length $l$ and uniform area of cross-section $A$ is stretched till its length becomes double. It is then cut into three pieces of equal length which are connected in parallel. Find the net resistance of the combination in terms of the resistance $R$.
questions.answer:
On stretching to double the length, volume is conserved, so resistance scales as (length)$^2$: new resistance $=R\times 2^2=4R$, with new length $2l$.
Cutting this into three equal pieces (each of length $2l/3$) gives each piece resistance $\dfrac{4R}{3}$.
Connecting three equal resistors of $4R/3$ in parallel: $R_{net}=\dfrac{4R/3}{3}=\dfrac{4R}{9}$.

questions.question: Two electric bulbs P and Q have their resistances in the ratio of $1: 2$. They are connected in series across a battery. Find the ratio of the power dissipation in these bulbs.
questions.answer:
In series, the same current $I$ flows through both bulbs.
Power dissipated $P=I^2R$, so $\dfrac{P_P}{P_Q}=\dfrac{R_P}{R_Q}=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.question: A 10 V cell of negligible internal resistance is connected in parallel across a battery of emf 200 V and internal resistance $38 \Omega$ as shown in the figure. Find the value of current in the circuit.
questions.answer:
Since the $10\ \text{V}$ cell has negligible internal resistance and is connected in parallel (opposing) with the $200\ \text{V}$ battery, current flows in the loop due to the net emf, limited only by the $38\ \Omega$ internal resistance of the $200\ \text{V}$ battery.
$I=\dfrac{200-10}{38}=\dfrac{190}{38}=5\ \text{A}$.

questions.question: A battery of emf $12$ V and internal resistance $2 \Omega$ is connected to a $4 \Omega$ resistor as shown in the figure. (a) Show that a voltmeter when placed across the cell and across the resistor, in turn, gives the same reading. (b) To record the voltage and the current in the circuit, why is voltmeter placed in parallel and ammeter in series in the circuit?
questions.answer:
(a) An ideal voltmeter draws negligible current, so circuit current $I = \varepsilon/(R+r) = 12/6 = 2$ A.
Voltmeter across the cell reads terminal voltage $V = \varepsilon - Ir = 12 - 2\times2 = 8$ V.
Voltmeter across $R$ reads $V = IR = 2\times4 = 8$ V, which is the same reading.
(b) A voltmeter has very high resistance, so connecting it in parallel draws almost no current and does not disturb the voltage being measured; an ammeter has very low resistance, so connecting it in series lets the full current pass through with negligible change, giving the true current.

questions.question: When $5$ V potential difference is applied across a wire of length $0.1$ m, the drift speed of electrons is $2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ m/s. If the electron density in the wire is $8 \times 10^{28}$ m $-3$, calculate the resistivity of the material of wire.
questions.answer:
Electric field $E = V/l = 5/0.1 = 50$ V/m.
Current density $J = nev_d$ and also $J = E/\rho$, so $\rho = E/(nev_d)$.
$\rho = 50/(8\times10^{28}\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times2.5\times10^{-4}) \approx 1.95\times10^{-5}\ \Omega$ m.

questions.question: In a meter bridge shown in the figure, the balance point is found to be 40 cm from end A. If a resistance of $10 \Omega$ is connected in series with R, balance point is obtained 60 cm from A. Calculate the values of R and S.
questions.answer:
First balance: $R/S = l_1/(100-l_1) = 40/60 = 2/3$.
After adding $10\ \Omega$ in series with $R$: $(R+10)/S = 60/40 = 3/2$.
Solving the two equations simultaneously gives $S = 12\ \Omega$ and $R = 8\ \Omega$.

questions.question: Use Kirchhoff’s rules to obtain conditions for the balance condition in a Wheatstone bridge.
questions.answer:
Let the bridge arms $P, Q, R, S$ carry currents $I_1, I_2, I_3, I_4$ with a galvanometer in arm $BD$; at balance $I_g = 0$.
Junction rule at $B$ and $D$ then gives $I_1 = I_3$ and $I_2 = I_4$.
Loop rule applied to loops $ABDA$ and $BCDB$ (with $I_g=0$) gives $I_1P = I_2Q$ and $I_1R = I_2S$.
Dividing these equations gives the balance condition $P/Q = R/S$.

questions.question: State Kirchhoff’s rules. Explain briefly how these rules are justified.
questions.answer:
Junction rule: at any junction, the algebraic sum of currents is zero, $\Sigma I = 0$, i.e., current entering equals current leaving.
Loop rule: around any closed loop, the algebraic sum of potential differences (including emfs) is zero, $\Sigma V = 0$.
The junction rule follows from conservation of charge, since charge cannot accumulate at a junction in steady state.
The loop rule follows from conservation of energy, since the electrostatic field is conservative and work done in a closed loop is zero.

questions.question: Estimate the average drift speed of conduction electrons in a copper wire of cross-sectional area $2.5\times10^{-7}$ m $2$ carrying a current of 2.7 A. Assume the density of conduction electrons to be $9 \times 10^{28}$ m $-3$.
questions.answer:
Drift speed $v_d = I/(nAe)$.
$v_d = 2.7/(9\times10^{28}\times2.5\times10^{-7}\times1.6\times10^{-19})$.
$v_d \approx 7.5\times10^{-4}$ m/s.

questions.question: A cell of emf ’E’ and internal resistance ’r’ is connected across a variable resistor ’R’. Plot a graph showing variation of terminal voltage ’V’ of the cell versus the current ’I’. Using the plot, show how the emf of the cell and its internal resistance can be determined.
questions.answer:
The relation $V = E - Ir$ is a straight line with $I$ on the x-axis and $V$ on the y-axis, having a negative slope.
The graph is a straight line that intercepts the V-axis (at $I=0$) at a value equal to the emf $E$ of the cell.
The magnitude of the slope of this line gives the internal resistance $r$ of the cell, i.e., $r = -\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}$.
As $R$ decreases, $I$ increases and $V$ decreases along this line.

questions.question: In the given circuit diagram, a voltmeter ’ $V$ ’ is connected across a lamp ’ $L$’. How would (i) the brightness of the lamp and (ii) voltmeter reading ’ $V$ ’ be affected, if the value of resistance ’ $R$’ is decreased? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
(i) The brightness of the lamp increases.
Decreasing $R$ reduces the total resistance of the series circuit, so the current $I$ through the lamp increases, and power dissipated $P = I^2R_L$ increases.
(ii) The voltmeter reading $V$ across the lamp increases.
Since the emf is fixed and the drop across $R$ decreases (as $R$ decreases), a larger share of the emf appears across the lamp, so $V$ across it rises.

questions.question: A cell of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ is connected to two external resistances $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ and a perfect ammeter. The current in the circuit is measured in four different situations: (i) without any external resistance in the circuit (ii) with resistance $R_{1}$ only (iii) with $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ in series combination (iv) with $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ in parallel combination The currents measured in the four cases are $0.42$ A, $1.05$ A, $1.4$ A and $4.2$ A, but not necessarily in that order. Identify the currents corresponding to the four cases mentioned above.
questions.answer:
(i) Without any external resistance, current $I = E/r$ is maximum, so this corresponds to $4.2$ A.
(iv) With $R_1$ and $R_2$ in parallel, the external resistance is least among the resistor combinations (since $R_1\|R_2 < R_1$ and $< R_1+R_2$), giving the next highest current, $1.4$ A.
(ii) With $R_1$ alone, the current is $1.05$ A.
(iii) With $R_1$ and $R_2$ in series, the external resistance is maximum, giving the least current, $0.42$ A.

questions.question: A conductor of length ’ $l$’ is connected to a dc source of potential ’ $V$ ’. If the length of the conductor is tripled by gradually stretching it, keeping ’ $V$ ’ constant, how will (i) drift speed of electrons and (ii) resistance of the conductor be affected? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
(i) Drift speed decreases to one-third of its original value.
Since $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m} = \dfrac{eV\tau}{mL}$, and $V$ is constant while $L$ becomes $3l$, $v_d$ becomes $v_d/3$.
(ii) Resistance increases to $9$ times its original value.
On stretching, volume is conserved so area becomes $A/3$; since $R = \rho L/A$, tripling $L$ and reducing $A$ to $A/3$ gives $R' = \rho(3l)/(A/3) = 9R$.

questions.question: In the given circuit, assuming point $A$ to be at zero potential, use Kirchhoff’s rules to determine the potential at point $B$.
questions.answer:
Apply Kirchhoff's junction rule at each node to relate the branch currents, and Kirchhoff's loop rule (sum of emf's = sum of $IR$ drops) around each closed loop to solve for the current $I$ in the branch joining $A$ and $B$.
Then, starting from $V_A = 0$ and moving along that branch to $B$, add the algebraic sum of emf's crossed (positive from $-$ to $+$ terminal) and subtract the $IR$ drops in the direction of current flow.
This gives $V_B = V_A + \sum \varepsilon - \sum IR$ evaluated along the path from $A$ to $B$, yielding the potential at $B$.

questions.question: In the metre bridge experiment, balance point was observed at $J$ with $AJ = l$. (i) The values of $R$ and $X$ were doubled and then interchanged. What would be the new position of balance point? (ii) If the galvanometer and battery are interchanged at the balance position, how will the balance point get affected?
questions.answer:
(i) The balance point shifts to the position $(100-l)\,\text{cm}$ from $A$.
Doubling both $R$ and $X$ leaves their ratio unchanged, but interchanging them inverts the ratio $R/X$ to $X/R$, and since originally $R/X = l/(100-l)$, the new balance satisfies $l'/(100-l') = (100-l)/l$, giving $l' = 100-l$.
(ii) The balance point remains unaffected.
By the symmetry (reciprocity) of the Wheatstone bridge network, interchanging the positions of the battery and the galvanometer does not change the balance condition, though it may change the sensitivity of detecting the balance.

questions.question: Derive an expression for drift velocity of free electrons in a conductor in terms of relaxation time.
questions.answer:
Consider a conductor with free electrons of charge $-e$ and mass $m$, in an electric field $E$.
Between two successive collisions, an electron acquires acceleration $a = eE/m$ in a direction opposite to $E$.
If $\tau$ is the average time between collisions (relaxation time), the average velocity gained is $v_d = a\tau$.
Thus the drift velocity is $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$.

questions.question: A cell of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ is connected across a variable resistor $R$. Plot a graph showing the variation of terminal potential $V$ with resistance $R$. Predict from the graph the condition under which $V$ becomes equal to $E$.
questions.answer:
The terminal potential difference is $V = E - Ir = \dfrac{ER}{R+r}$.
As $R$ increases from zero, $V$ increases from $0$ and rises steadily, approaching the value $E$ asymptotically (the $V$-$R$ curve flattens out near the line $V = E$ but never quite meets it for finite $R$).
From the graph, $V$ becomes equal to $E$ only when $R \to \infty$, i.e., when the circuit is open and no current is drawn from the cell.

questions.question: Calculate the current drawn from the battery in the given network.
questions.answer:
The resistors of the network are combined step by step using the series rule $R_s = R_1+R_2+\ldots$ and the parallel rule $\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{R_1}+\dfrac{1}{R_2}+\ldots$ until a single equivalent resistance $R_{eq}$ across the battery terminals is obtained.
The current drawn from the battery is then given by Ohm's law, $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R_{eq}+r}$, where $\varepsilon$ is the emf of the battery and $r$ its internal resistance (taken as zero if not specified).

questions.question: A wire of $15 \Omega$ resistance is gradually stretched to double its original length. It is then cut into two equal parts. These parts are then connected in parallel across a $3.0 V$ battery. Find the current drawn from the battery.
questions.answer:
On stretching to double the length, area becomes half, so new resistance $R' = R\left(\dfrac{l'}{l}\right)^2 = 15 \times 4 = 60\ \Omega$.
Cutting this into two equal parts gives two resistors of $30\ \Omega$ each.
Connected in parallel, $R_{eq} = \dfrac{30 \times 30}{30+30} = 15\ \Omega$.
Current drawn, $I = \dfrac{V}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{3.0}{15} = 0.2$ A.

questions.question: Two wires X, Y have the same resistivity, but their cross-sectional areas are in the ratio $2: 3$ and lengths in the ratio $1: 2$. They are first connected in series and then in parallel to a d.c source. Find out the ratio of the drift speeds of the electrons in the two wires for the two cases.
questions.answer:
Drift speed is given by $v_d = \dfrac{I}{nAe}$.
In series, the same current $I$ flows through both wires, so $v_d \propto \dfrac{1}{A}$, giving $\dfrac{v_{dX}}{v_{dY}} = \dfrac{A_Y}{A_X} = \dfrac{3}{2}$.
In parallel, both wires have the same potential difference $V$, and since $I = \dfrac{VA}{\rho l}$, we get $v_d = \dfrac{V}{\rho l n e}$, so $v_d \propto \dfrac{1}{l}$, giving $\dfrac{v_{dX}}{v_{dY}} = \dfrac{l_Y}{l_X} = \dfrac{2}{1}$.

questions.question: The following graph shows the variation of terminal potential difference $V$, across a combination of three cells in series to a resistor, versus the current, $i$: (i) Calculate the emf of each cell. (ii) For what current $I$, will the power dissipation of the circuit be maximum?
questions.answer:
(i) The graph follows $V = E_{total} - I r_{total}$, where $E_{total}$ is the sum of the emfs of the three cells in series.
The $y$-intercept (value of $V$ at $i=0$) gives $E_{total}$, and dividing this reading by $3$ gives the emf $E$ of each cell.
(ii) Power delivered to the external resistor is maximum when the external resistance equals the total internal resistance of the three cells, i.e., at the current $I = \dfrac{E_{total}}{2r_{total}}$, corresponding to the point on the graph where $V = \dfrac{E_{total}}{2}$.

questions.question: A cylindrical metallic wire is stretched to increase its length by 5%.Calculate the percentage change in its resistance.
questions.answer:
Percentage change in resistance is $10.25\%$ (increase).
Since volume $V = AL$ is constant when a wire is stretched, $R = \rho L^2/V$, so $R \propto L^2$.
With $L' = 1.05L$, $\dfrac{R'}{R} = (1.05)^2 = 1.1025$.
So the percentage increase in resistance $= (1.1025-1)\times 100\% = 10.25\%$.

questions.question: Two cells $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ in the given circuit diagram have an emf of $5 V$ and $9 V$ and internal resistance of $0.3 \Omega$ and $1.2 \Omega$ respectively. Calculate the value of current flowing through the resistance of $3 \Omega$.
questions.answer:
For two cells in parallel feeding an external resistance $R = 3\,\Omega$, the equivalent emf and internal resistance are $E_{eq} = \dfrac{E_1/r_1 + E_2/r_2}{1/r_1 + 1/r_2}$ and $r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1 r_2}{r_1+r_2}$.
Substituting, $E_{eq} = \dfrac{5/0.3 + 9/1.2}{1/0.3+1/1.2} = 5.8$ V and $r_{eq} = \dfrac{0.3\times1.2}{1.5} = 0.24\,\Omega$.
Current through $3\,\Omega$: $I = \dfrac{E_{eq}}{r_{eq}+R} = \dfrac{5.8}{3.24} \approx 1.79$ A.

questions.question: Write the mathematical relation between mobility and drift velocity of charge carriers in a conductor. Name the mobile charge carriers responsible for conduction of electric current in (i) an electrolyte (ii) an ionised gas.
questions.answer:
Mobility is defined as drift velocity per unit electric field: $\mu = \dfrac{v_d}{E}$.
(i) In an electrolyte, the mobile charge carriers are positive and negative ions.
(ii) In an ionised gas, the mobile charge carriers are electrons and positive ions (and sometimes negative ions).

questions.question: Draw $V$ - $I$ graph for ohmic and non-ohmic materials. Give one example for each.
questions.answer:
For an ohmic material, the $V$-$I$ graph is a straight line passing through the origin, showing $V \propto I$ (constant resistance); example: a nichrome wire/metallic resistor.
For a non-ohmic material, the $V$-$I$ graph is a curve (non-linear, and may not pass through the origin), showing that resistance changes with current/voltage; example: a junction diode.

questions.question: In a copper voltameter, a varying electric current, as shown in graph, is passed. The mass of copper deposited at the end of 30 seconds is $m$ grams. Using the graph, find the value of e.c.e. (electrochemical equivalent) of copper in g/C.
questions.answer:
The electrochemical equivalent is $Z = \dfrac{m}{q}$, where $q$ is the total charge passed, found as the area under the $I$-$t$ graph over the $30$ s interval.
For a graph rising linearly from $0$ to a peak current $I_0$ over $30$ s, $q = \dfrac{1}{2} \times I_0 \times 30 = 15 I_0$ C.
So $Z = \dfrac{m}{15 I_0}$ g/C, using the value of $I_0$ read from the given graph.

questions.question: (a) Explain the statement: "Current is a scalar although we represent current with an arrow". (b) Use Kirchhoff’s rules to find the current through $3 \Omega$ resistor in the circuit shown in the figure:
questions.answer:
(a) Current does not obey the law of vector addition (parallelogram/triangle law); at a junction, currents add or subtract algebraically as scalars, not according to their directions in space. The arrow on a current only indicates the sense of flow of positive charge along a specified conductor, not a direction associated with vector transformation properties, so current is treated as a scalar quantity with sign convention, not a vector.
(b) Apply Kirchhoff's junction rule (algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero) to assign currents to each branch, then apply the loop rule (algebraic sum of $IR$ drops and emfs is zero) to each independent closed loop of the circuit.
Solving the resulting simultaneous equations for the loop currents and substituting back gives the current through the $3\,\Omega$ resistor, taking care of the sign of each emf and $IR$ term according to the assumed current directions.

questions.question: (a) Establish the relation between drift velocity of electrons $(v_{d})$ and electric current $(I)$ in a conductor. (b) How is $v_{d}$ affected when the length of the conductor is doubled, keeping the voltage applied across the conductor constant?
questions.answer:
(a) Consider a conductor of length $l$, area of cross-section $A$, having $n$ free electrons per unit volume, each of charge $e$.
In time $dt$ each electron drifts a distance $v_d dt$, so all electrons in a volume $Av_d dt$ cross any cross-section.
Charge crossing in time $dt$: $dq = neAv_d dt$, so current $I = dq/dt = neAv_d$, i.e. $v_d = I/(neA)$.
(b) Since $v_d = eE\tau/m = eV\tau/(ml)$, we have $v_d \propto 1/l$ (V constant); when $l$ is doubled, $v_d$ becomes half its original value.

questions.question: State Kirchhoff’s rules. Using these rules, find the current flowing through branch FC in the given circuit.
questions.answer:
Kirchhoff's junction rule: the algebraic sum of currents meeting at a junction is zero, $\Sigma I = 0$, based on conservation of charge.
Kirchhoff's loop rule: the algebraic sum of emfs and $IR$ drops around any closed loop is zero, $\Sigma E = \Sigma IR$, based on conservation of energy.
To find the current in branch FC, assign an unknown current to it, apply the junction rule at F and C, and apply the loop rule to loops containing FC and the other branches/emfs.
Solving the resulting simultaneous equations gives the value of the current in FC; if the solved value is negative, the actual current flows opposite to the assumed direction.

questions.question: (a) The two Kirchhoff’s rules are based on law of conservation of two physical quantities. Name the quantities. (b) Find magnitude and direction of current in 1 $\Omega$ resistor in the given circuit.
questions.answer:
(a) Kirchhoff's junction rule is based on conservation of electric charge; Kirchhoff's loop rule is based on conservation of energy.
(b) Assign an unknown current $I$ to the $1\,\Omega$ resistor and unknown currents to the other branches.
Apply the junction rule at each node ($\Sigma I_{in} = \Sigma I_{out}$) and the loop rule ($\Sigma E = \Sigma IR$) to each independent closed loop containing the $1\,\Omega$ resistor.
Solving these simultaneous equations gives the magnitude of $I$; the sign obtained fixes its direction — positive means current flows as assumed, negative means it flows opposite to the assumed direction.

questions.question: (a) ’Current is a scalar quantity, although we represent current with an arrow.’ Explain. (b) Derive the balance condition of a Wheatstone Bridge.
questions.answer:
(a) Current is defined as $I = dq/dt$, the rate of flow of charge, and currents at a junction combine by simple algebraic addition ($\Sigma I = 0$), not by the vector (parallelogram) law.
Since it does not obey vector addition, current is a scalar; the arrow merely shows the sense of flow of positive charge, not a direction in the vector sense.
(b) In a Wheatstone bridge, resistances $P, Q, R, S$ form the four arms, a battery is across A and C, and a galvanometer is between B and D.
At balance, no current flows through the galvanometer, so the same currents $I_1$ (through P, Q) and $I_2$ (through R, S) flow in each pair, and $B$, $D$ are at the same potential.
Then $I_1 P = I_2 R$ and $I_1 Q = I_2 S$; dividing gives the balance condition $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$.

questions.question: (a) Two batteries of emfs $3$ V & $6$ V and internal resistances $0.2 \Omega$& $0.4 \Omega$ are connected in parallel. This combination is connected to a $4 \Omega$ resistor. Find: (i) the equivalent emf of the combination (ii) the equivalent internal resistance of the combination (iii) the current drawn from the combination OR (b) (i) A conductor of length $l$ is connected across an ideal cell of emf $E$. Keeping the cell connected, the length of the conductor is increased to $2l$ by gradually stretching it. If $R$ and $R^{'}$ are initial and final values of resistance and $v_{d}$ and $v^{'}$ are initial $d$ and final values of drift velocity, find the relation between (i) $R^{'}$ and $R$ and (ii) $v_{d}{}^{'}$ and $v_{d}$. (ii) When electrons drift in a conductor from lower to higher potential, does it mean that all the ’free electrons’ of the conductor are moving in the same direction?
questions.answer:
(a) For batteries in parallel: $E_{eq} = \dfrac{E_1/r_1 + E_2/r_2}{1/r_1 + 1/r_2}$ and $\dfrac{1}{r_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2}$.
(i) $E_{eq} = \dfrac{3/0.2 + 6/0.4}{1/0.2 + 1/0.4} = \dfrac{15+15}{5+2.5} = 4$ V.
(ii) $r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1 r_2}{r_1+r_2} = \dfrac{0.2 \times 0.4}{0.6} = \dfrac{2}{15}\,\Omega \approx 0.13\,\Omega$.
(iii) $I = \dfrac{E_{eq}}{R+r_{eq}} = \dfrac{4}{4+2/15} = \dfrac{30}{31} \approx 0.97$ A.
OR
(b) (i) On stretching to length $2l$ at constant volume, area becomes $A' = A/2$, so $R' = \rho(2l)/(A/2) = 4\rho l/A$, giving $R' = 4R$.
Since $E$ is constant, new current $I' = E/R' = I/4$; as $v_d = I/(neA)$, $v_d' = I'/(neA') = (I/4)/(ne \cdot A/2) = v_d/2$.
(ii) No. Free electrons also possess large random thermal velocities in all directions; only a small net drift velocity is superimposed on this random motion, giving an overall average flow opposite to the field, not identical individual motions.

questions.question: (a) A cell of e.m.f. E and internal resistance r is connected with a variable external resistance R and a voltmeter showing potential drop V across R. Obtain the relationship between V, E, R and r. (b) Draw the shape of the graph showing the variation of terminal voltage V of the cell as a function of current I drawn from it. How one can determine the e.m.f. of the cell and its internal resistance from this graph?
questions.answer:
(a) The terminal voltage equals emf minus the drop across internal resistance: $E = V + Ir$, where $I = V/R$ is the current drawn.
Substituting, $E = V + \dfrac{V}{R}r$, so $V = \dfrac{ER}{R+r}$, or equivalently $I = \dfrac{E-V}{r}$.
(b) The graph of $V$ versus $I$ is a straight line with negative slope, since $V = E - Ir$.
The intercept of this line on the $V$-axis (at $I = 0$) gives the emf $E$ of the cell.
The magnitude of the slope of the line gives the internal resistance $r$.

questions.question: (a) Define resistivity of a conductor. Discuss its dependence on temperature of the conductor and draw a plot of resistivity of copper as a function of temperature. (b) (i) "A low voltage battery from which high current is required must have low internal resistance." Justify. (ii) "A high voltage battery must have a large internal resistance." Justify.
questions.answer:
(a) Resistivity is defined as $\rho = \dfrac{RA}{l}$, the resistance offered by a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area; its SI unit is ohm-metre.
For metals, resistivity increases with temperature, $\rho_T = \rho_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]$, since increased thermal vibrations of ions reduce the relaxation time $\tau$ of electrons.
For copper, the plot of $\rho$ versus $T$ is an almost straight line rising with temperature, becoming slightly non-linear only at very low $T$.
(b)(i) Since $I = \dfrac{E}{R+r}$, a low emf $E$ can still supply a large current only if $r$ is small; a large $r$ would cause most of $E$ to drop across it as $Ir$, limiting $I$.
(ii) In a high voltage battery, a large $r$ keeps the current $I=E/r$ within a safe limit even if the terminals are accidentally short-circuited, protecting the circuit and user.

questions.question: (a) Define Electrical conductivity. Obtain the expression of electrical conductivity of a conductor in terms of number density and relaxation time of free electrons. (b) Explain qualitative change in resistivity of a conductor with temperature using expression obtained in (a).
questions.answer:
Electrical conductivity $\sigma$ is defined as the reciprocal of resistivity, $\sigma = 1/\rho = J/E$, where $J$ is current density and $E$ the applied field.
For a conductor with $n$ free electrons per unit volume, drift velocity $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$, where $\tau$ is relaxation time.
Current density $J = nev_d = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}E$, so comparing with $J=\sigma E$ gives $\sigma = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}$.
(b) As temperature rises, $n$ stays essentially constant but increased ionic vibrations reduce $\tau$, so $\sigma$ decreases and resistivity $\rho = m/(ne^2\tau)$ increases with temperature.

questions.question: (a) (i) Derive an expression for the resistivity of a conductor in terms of number density of free electrons and relaxation time. (ii) The figure shows the plot of current through a cross-section of wire over two different time intervals. Compare the charges ($Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$) that pass through the cross-section during these time intervals. OR (b) (i) A battery of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ is connected to a variable external resistance $R$. (I) Obtain the expression for current $I$ in the circuit and the value of maximum current the battery can supply. (II) Obtain the terminal voltage $V$ across the battery and its maximum possible value. (ii) The above battery sends a current $I_{1}$ when $R = R_{1}$ and a current $I_{2}$ when $R = R_{2}$. Obtain the internal resistance of the battery in terms of $I_{1}$, $I_{2}$, $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Under field $E$, drift velocity is $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$.
Current $I = neAv_d = \dfrac{ne^2A\tau}{m}E$; using $E=V/l$ and $I=V/R$ gives $R=\dfrac{ml}{ne^2\tau A}$.
Since $R=\rho l/A$, this gives $\rho = \dfrac{m}{ne^2\tau}$.
(ii) Charge equals the area under the current-time graph, $Q=\int I\,dt$. So $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are found as the areas under the curve over their respective intervals; the interval with the larger area (higher current sustained for longer time) carries the greater charge.
OR
(b)(i)(I) $I = \dfrac{E}{R+r}$; current is maximum when $R=0$, giving $I_{max} = \dfrac{E}{r}$.
(II) Terminal voltage $V = E-Ir = \dfrac{ER}{R+r}$; it is maximum when $R\to\infty$ (open circuit, $I\to0$), so $V_{max}=E$.
(ii) $I_1=\dfrac{E}{R_1+r}$ and $I_2=\dfrac{E}{R_2+r}$; solving these gives $r=\dfrac{I_1R_1-I_2R_2}{I_2-I_1}$.

questions.question: What is the difference between ’emf’ and ’terminal voltage’ of a cell? Two cells of emfs $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ and internal resistances $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ are connected in parallel. Derive an expression for the emf and internal resistance of the equivalent cell.
questions.answer:
EMF is the work done per unit charge by the cell in driving charge round the complete circuit, equal to the terminal voltage only when no current is drawn (open circuit).
Terminal voltage is the potential difference between the cell's terminals when current flows; it is less than emf due to the drop $Ir$ across internal resistance.
For two cells $E_1,r_1$ and $E_2,r_2$ in parallel, using $I_1=(E_1-V)/r_1$, $I_2=(E_2-V)/r_2$ and $I=I_1+I_2$, the combination behaves as a single cell with
$\dfrac{1}{r_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{r_1}+\dfrac{1}{r_2}$ and $E_{eq} = \dfrac{E_1r_2+E_2r_1}{r_1+r_2}$

questions.question: (a) Define the term ’drift velocity’ of conduction electrons in a conductor. (b) A conductor of length $l$ and area of cross-section $A$ is connected across an ideal battery of emf $V$. Derive the formula for the current density in terms of relaxation time $\tau$.
questions.answer:
(a) Drift velocity is the average velocity acquired by free electrons in a conductor under an applied electric field, superimposed on their random thermal motion.
(b) Field inside the conductor is $E=V/l$, so drift velocity $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m} = \dfrac{eV\tau}{ml}$.
Current $I = neAv_d$, so current density $J=\dfrac{I}{A} = nev_d = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}E = \dfrac{ne^2\tau V}{ml}$

questions.question: State Kirchhoff’s laws. Apply these laws to find the values of current flowing in the three branches of the given circuit.
questions.answer:
Kirchhoff's current law (junction rule): at any junction, the algebraic sum of currents is zero, i.e. total current entering equals total current leaving, from conservation of charge.
Kirchhoff's voltage law (loop rule): the algebraic sum of potential differences (including emfs) around any closed loop is zero, from conservation of energy.
To find the three branch currents, label them $I_1$, $I_2$, $I_3$ with assumed directions, apply the junction rule at the common node to get one equation relating them, then apply the loop rule to two independent closed loops of the circuit to get two more equations in terms of the given emfs and resistances.
Solving these three simultaneous equations gives the values of $I_1$, $I_2$ and $I_3$; a negative value for any current indicates its actual direction is opposite to the one assumed.

questions.question: Three cells $A$, $B$ and $C$ of emfs $2$ V, $3$ V and $5$ V respectively are connected in parallel to each other. Their internal resistances are $5 \Omega$, $5 \Omega$ and $1 \Omega$ respectively. Calculate the currents flowing through the cells $A$, $B$ and $C$.
questions.answer:
Using Millman's theorem, the common terminal voltage $V = \dfrac{\frac{E_A}{r_A}+\frac{E_B}{r_B}+\frac{E_C}{r_C}}{\frac{1}{r_A}+\frac{1}{r_B}+\frac{1}{r_C}}$
$V = \dfrac{\frac{2}{5}+\frac{3}{5}+\frac{5}{1}}{\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{5}+1} = \dfrac{6.0}{1.4} = 4.29$ V
Current through each cell, $I = \dfrac{E-V}{r}$:
$I_A = \dfrac{2-4.29}{5} = -0.46$ A (flows into $A$, charging it)
$I_B = \dfrac{3-4.29}{5} = -0.26$ A (flows into $B$, charging it)
$I_C = \dfrac{5-4.29}{1} = 0.71$ A (flows out of $C$, discharging it)

questions.question: Define ’current density’. Is it a scalar or a vector? An electric field $\vec{E}$ is maintained in a metallic conductor. If $n$ be the number of electrons (mass $m$, charge $-e$) per unit volume in the conductor and $_{2} \tau$ its relaxation time, show that the current density $\vec{j} = \sigma\vec{E}$, where $\sigma = \frac{ne\tau}{m}$.
questions.answer:
Current density $\vec{j}$ is the current flowing per unit cross-sectional area held normal to the direction of flow, $j = I/A$.
It is a vector quantity, directed along the flow of positive (conventional) current.
On applying $\vec{E}$, each electron feels force $-e\vec{E}$, giving acceleration $\vec{a} = -\dfrac{e\vec{E}}{m}$.
Average drift velocity $\vec{v}_d = \vec{a}\tau = -\dfrac{e\tau}{m}\vec{E}$
Current $I = neAv_d$, so $j = \dfrac{I}{A} = nev_d = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}E$
Thus $\vec{j} = \sigma\vec{E}$, with $\sigma = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}$, directed along $\vec{E}$.

questions.question: What is a Wheatstone bridge? Obtain the necessary conditions under which the Wheatstone bridge is balanced.
questions.answer:
A Wheatstone bridge is a network of four resistors $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ arranged in a closed loop, with a cell connected across one pair of opposite junctions and a galvanometer across the other pair, used to measure an unknown resistance.
At balance, no current flows through the galvanometer ($I_g = 0$).
Applying Kirchhoff's loop rule to the two loops: $I_1 P = I_2 R$ and $I_1 Q = I_2 S$
Dividing these gives the balance condition $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$

questions.question: The figure shows a circuit with three ideal batteries. Find the magnitude and direction of currents in the branches AG, BF and CD.
questions.answer:
Applying Kirchhoff's rules: assign unknown currents $I_1$, $I_2$, $I_3$ to branches $AG$, $BF$ and $CD$, with directions assumed at each junction.
Apply Kirchhoff's junction rule ($\Sigma I = 0$) at the common nodes to relate the three currents.
Apply Kirchhoff's voltage rule ($\Sigma \varepsilon = \Sigma IR$) around each independent closed loop containing the given emfs and resistances.
Solving the resulting simultaneous equations gives the magnitude of $I_1$, $I_2$, $I_3$; a positive value confirms the assumed direction, while a negative value means the actual current flows opposite to the assumed direction in that branch.

questions.question: Determine the current in branches $AB$, $AC$ and $BC$ of the network shown in figure.
questions.answer:
The network has three branches $AB$, $AC$, $BC$ meeting at common nodes, so Kirchhoff's rules are applied.
Assign unknown currents $I_1$ (in $AB$), $I_2$ (in $AC$), $I_3$ (in $BC$), with directions chosen at the junctions.
Junction rule: current entering a junction equals current leaving it, giving one equation relating $I_1$, $I_2$, $I_3$.
Loop rule: for each closed loop, $\Sigma \varepsilon = \Sigma IR$, using the emfs and resistances of that loop.
Solving these equations simultaneously gives the current in each branch; a negative result means the current actually flows opposite to the direction assumed.

questions.question: A battery of unknown emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ is connected in a circuit as shown in the figure. When the key (K) is open, the voltmeter reads $10.0$ V and ammeter reads $0$ A. In the closed circuit, the voltmeter reads $6.0$ V and ammeter reads $2.0$ A. Calculate: (a) emf of the battery, (b) internal resistance of the battery ($r$), and (c) external resistance ($R$).
questions.answer:
(a) With key open, no current flows, so the voltmeter reads the emf directly: $E = 10.0$ V
(b) With key closed, $E = V + Ir$, so $r = \dfrac{E-V}{I} = \dfrac{10.0-6.0}{2.0} = 2.0\ \Omega$
(c) External resistance $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{6.0}{2.0} = 3.0\ \Omega$

questions.question: A current of $1.6$ A flows through a wire when a potential difference of $1.0$ V is applied across it. The length and cross-sectional area of the wire are $1.0$ m and $1.0 \times 10^{-7}$ m $2$ respectively. Calculate: (a) Electric field across the wire (b) Current density (c) Average relaxation time ($\tau$) (Number density of free electrons in the wire is $9.0 \times 10^{28}$ m $-3$)
questions.answer:
(a) Electric field: $E = V/l = 1.0/1.0 = 1.0$ V/m
(b) Current density: $J = I/A = 1.6/(1.0 \times 10^{-7}) = 1.6 \times 10^{7}$ A/m$^2$
(c) Drift speed from $J = nev_d$: $v_d = J/(ne) = (1.6\times10^{7})/(9.0\times10^{28}\times1.6\times10^{-19}) = 1.11\times10^{-3}$ m/s
Relaxation time from $v_d = eE\tau/m$: $\tau = mv_d/(eE) = (9.1\times10^{-31}\times1.11\times10^{-3})/(1.6\times10^{-19}\times1.0) = 6.3\times10^{-15}$ s

questions.question: Find the current in branch $BM$ in the network shown:
questions.answer:
Assign an unknown current to every branch, including $BM$, using Kirchhoff's junction rule ($\sum I_{in} = \sum I_{out}$) at each node.
Apply Kirchhoff's loop rule, $\sum \varepsilon = \sum IR$, around each independent loop of the network that contains the branch $BM$, taking care of the sign convention for emfs and $IR$ drops.
Solve the resulting simultaneous equations for $I_{BM}$; if the network forms a balanced Wheatstone bridge with $M$ as the junction, the products of resistances of opposite arms are equal and $I_{BM} = 0$.

questions.question: Find the currents flowing through the branches $AB$ and $BC$ in the network shown.
questions.answer:
Label the unknown currents in branches $AB$, $BC$ and the other arms of the network, and apply Kirchhoff's junction rule at $B$ (and other nodes) so that the current entering equals the current leaving.
Apply Kirchhoff's loop rule, $\sum \varepsilon = \sum IR$, to each independent closed loop containing $AB$ and $BC$, using Ohm's law $V = IR$ for each resistor.
Solving the simultaneous linear equations obtained gives the numerical values of the currents through $AB$ and $BC$; equal currents result if the two branches are symmetric arms of a balanced network.

questions.question: In the given network, calculate: (i) effective resistance between points $A$ and $M$, and (ii) power supplied by the battery.
questions.answer:
(i) Combine resistors step by step using the series rule $R = R_1+R_2+\dots$ and the parallel rule $\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R_1}+\dfrac{1}{R_2}+\dots$, reducing the network progressively until a single equivalent resistance $R_{AM}$ between $A$ and $M$ is obtained; if the network cannot be reduced this way, Kirchhoff's laws are applied instead.
(ii) With the battery of emf $\varepsilon$ and internal resistance $r$ connected across $A$ and $M$, the current drawn is $I = \varepsilon/(R_{AM}+r)$, and the power supplied by the battery is $P = \varepsilon I$.

questions.question: (i) Define ’temperature coefficient of resistance’ of a metal. (ii) Show the variation of resistivity of copper with rise in temperature. (iii) The resistance of a wire is $10 \Omega$ at $27^{^{\circ}}$ C. Find its resistance at $-73^{^{\circ}}$ C. The temperature coefficient of resistance of the material of the wire is $1.70 \times 10^{-4 ^{\circ}}$ C $-1$.
questions.answer:
(i) Temperature coefficient of resistance is the fractional change in resistance per unit rise in temperature: $\alpha = \dfrac{R_T - R_0}{R_0\,\Delta T}$, its SI unit is $^{\circ}$C$^{-1}$ or K$^{-1}$.
(ii) For copper (a metal), resistivity increases almost linearly with temperature over ordinary ranges, $\rho_T = \rho_0(1+\alpha\Delta T)$, giving a straight line of positive slope that flattens and approaches a small residual resistivity as $T \to 0$ K.
(iii) $R_1 = 10\,\Omega$ at $T_1 = 27^{\circ}$C, $T_2 = -73^{\circ}$C, so $\Delta T = -100^{\circ}$C.
$R_2 = R_1(1+\alpha\Delta T) = 10[1+(1.70\times10^{-4})(-100)] = 10(0.983) = 9.83\ \Omega$

questions.question: A potential difference of $1.0$ V is applied across a conductor of length $5.0$ m and area of cross-section $1.0$ mm $2$. When current of $4.25$ A is passed through the conductor, calculate (i) the drift speed and (ii) relaxation time, of electrons. (Given number density of electrons in the conductor, $n = 8.5 \times 10^{28}$ m $-3$).
questions.answer:
Electric field: $E = V/l = 1.0/5.0 = 0.2$ V/m
(i) Drift speed from $I = nAev_d$: $v_d = I/(nAe) = 4.25/(8.5\times10^{28}\times1.0\times10^{-6}\times1.6\times10^{-19}) = 3.125\times10^{-4}$ m/s
(ii) Relaxation time from $v_d = eE\tau/m$: $\tau = mv_d/(eE) = (9.1\times10^{-31}\times3.125\times10^{-4})/(1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.2) = 8.9\times10^{-15}$ s

questions.question: Define current density and relaxation time. Derive an expression for resistivity of a conductor in terms of number density of charge carriers in the conductor and relaxation time.
questions.answer:
Current density $j$ is the current flowing per unit area of cross-section held normal to the direction of flow of charge; $j = I/A$, a vector quantity with SI unit $A/m^2$.
Relaxation time $\tau$ is the average time between two successive collisions of a free electron with the ions/atoms of the conductor.
On applying field $E$, drift velocity $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$.
Current $I = neAv_d$, so $j = \dfrac{I}{A} = nev_d = \dfrac{ne^2E\tau}{m}$.
Since $j = \sigma E$, conductivity $\sigma = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}$.
Resistivity $\rho = \dfrac{1}{\sigma} = \dfrac{m}{ne^2\tau}$.

questions.question: Two cells of emf $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ and internal resistances $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ are connected in parallel, with their terminals of the same polarity connected together. Obtain an expression for the equivalent emf of the combination.
questions.answer:
Let the common terminal voltage between the parallel combination be $V$.
Current delivered by each cell: $I_1 = \dfrac{E_1-V}{r_1}$, $I_2 = \dfrac{E_2-V}{r_2}$.
Total current $I = I_1+I_2 = \left(\dfrac{E_1}{r_1}+\dfrac{E_2}{r_2}\right) - V\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1}+\dfrac{1}{r_2}\right)$.
If the combination is replaced by a single cell of emf $E_{eq}$ and internal resistance $r_{eq}$, $I = \dfrac{E_{eq}-V}{r_{eq}}$.
Comparing: $\dfrac{1}{r_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{r_1}+\dfrac{1}{r_2}$ and $\dfrac{E_{eq}}{r_{eq}} = \dfrac{E_1}{r_1}+\dfrac{E_2}{r_2}$.
So $E_{eq} = \dfrac{E_1r_2+E_2r_1}{r_1+r_2}$.

questions.question: A potential difference $V$ is applied across a conductor of length $l$ and cross-sectional area $A$. Briefly explain how the current density $j$ in the conductor will be affected if (a) the potential difference $V$ is doubled, (b) the conductor were gradually stretched to reduce its cross-sectional area to $\frac{A}{4}$ and then the same potential difference $V$ is applied across it.
questions.answer:
Current density $j = \sigma E = \dfrac{\sigma V}{l}$, where $\sigma$ is the conductivity (a material property, unchanged).
(a) If $V$ is doubled, keeping $l$ and $A$ fixed, $j = \sigma V/l$ simply doubles.
(b) Stretching keeps the volume constant, so if $A$ becomes $A/4$, the new length becomes $l' = 4l$.
New density $j' = \dfrac{\sigma V}{l'} = \dfrac{\sigma V}{4l} = \dfrac{j}{4}$; the current density falls to one-fourth of its original value.

questions.question: A potential difference $V$ is applied across a conductor of length $l$ and uniform cross-section area $A$. How will the (i) electric field $E$, (ii) drift velocity $v_{d}$, and (iii) current density $j$ be affected when (a) $V$ is doubled and (b) $l$ is halved (keeping other factors constant)?
questions.answer:
$E = V/l$, $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$, $j = nev_d = \sigma E$.
(a) $V$ doubled, $l$ constant: $E$ doubles, so $v_d$ doubles and $j$ doubles.
(b) $l$ halved, $V$ constant: $E = V/l$ doubles, so $v_d$ doubles and $j$ doubles.
Thus in both cases $E$, $v_d$ and $j$ all become twice their original values.
