In the photon picture, light consists of discrete quanta of energy $E=h\nu$; a single photon is absorbed by a single electron in one collision, so emission occurs only if $h\nu \geq \phi_{0}$ (explaining threshold frequency) and instantaneously (no time lag), correctly explaining the effect.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Plot a graph showing variation of de Broglie wavelength $(\lambda)$ associated with a charged particle of mass $m$, versus $\frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$, where $V$ is the potential difference through which the particle is accelerated. How does this graph give us the information regarding the magnitude of the charge of the particle?
questions.answer:
Since $\lambda=\frac{h}{p}=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}=\left(\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mq}}\right)\frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$, the graph of $\lambda$ versus $\frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$ is a straight line through the origin.
Its slope equals $\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mq}}$; since $h$ and $m$ are known, the charge is obtained as $q=\frac{h^{2}}{2m(\text{slope})^{2}}$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An electron, a proton and an alpha particle have the same kinetic energy. Which one has the shortest wavelength?
questions.answer:
The alpha particle has the shortest wavelength.
Since $\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$, for the same kinetic energy $K$, $\lambda \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}$; the alpha particle has the largest mass, so it has the smallest de Broglie wavelength.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Explain with the help of Einstein’s photoelectric equation any two observed features in photoelectric effect which cannot be explained by wave theory.
questions.answer:
Einstein's photoelectric equation: $ rac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2}=h
u-\phi_{0}$.
(i) Threshold frequency: emission occurs only if $h
u \geq \phi_{0}$, i.e. $
u \geq 
u_{0}=\phi_{0}/h$; below $
u_{0}$ no electrons are emitted however intense the light, which wave theory (energy depending on intensity, not frequency) cannot explain.
(ii) Kinetic energy independent of intensity: $ rac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2}=h
u-\phi_{0}$ depends only on frequency, so maximum kinetic energy is unaffected by intensity; wave theory wrongly predicts that increasing intensity should increase the kinetic energy of emitted electrons.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Define the terms, (i) threshold frequency and (ii) stopping potential in photoelectric effect.
questions.answer:
(i) Threshold frequency $\nu_0$: the minimum frequency of incident radiation below which no photoelectric emission takes place from a given metal surface, no matter how high the intensity of light is.
(ii) Stopping potential $V_0$: the minimum negative (retarding) potential applied to the collector plate that just stops the most energetic photoelectrons from reaching it, making the photocurrent zero.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Plot a graph of photocurrent versus anode potential for a radiation of frequency $\nu$ and intensities $I_{1}$ and $I_{2} (I_{1} < I_{2})$.
questions.answer:
For both intensities $I_1$ and $I_2$ at the same frequency $\nu$, the photocurrent falls to zero at the same negative anode potential $-V_0$, since the stopping potential depends only on frequency, not intensity.
As the anode potential increases from $-V_0$ through zero to positive values, the current rises and becomes constant (saturates).
The saturation current for $I_2$ is higher than for $I_1$ (since $I_2 > I_1$), so the curve for $I_2$ lies above that for $I_1$, both curves meeting the potential axis at the same point $-V_0$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A photon and a proton have the same de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda$. Prove that the energy of the photon is $(2m\lambda c/h)$ times the kinetic energy of the proton.
questions.answer:
Energy of photon: $E_{ph} = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$
For the proton, de Broglie wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} \Rightarrow p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}$, so its kinetic energy is $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m} = \dfrac{h^2}{2m\lambda^2}$
Taking the ratio: $\dfrac{E_{ph}}{K} = \dfrac{hc/\lambda}{h^2/2m\lambda^2} = \dfrac{2m\lambda c}{h}$
Hence $E_{ph} = \left(\dfrac{2m\lambda c}{h}\right)K$, as required.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The wavelength of light from the spectral emission line of sodium is $590$ nm. Find the kinetic energy at which the electron would have the same de-Broglie wavelength.
questions.answer:
For the same de Broglie wavelength, $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} \Rightarrow p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{590 \times 10^{-9}} = 1.124 \times 10^{-27}$ kg m/s
Kinetic energy of electron: $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m} = \dfrac{(1.124 \times 10^{-27})^2}{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31}} = 6.93 \times 10^{-25}$ J
This equals $K \approx 4.33 \times 10^{-6}$ eV.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: If light of wavelength $412.5$ nm is incident on each of the metals given below, which ones will show photoelectric emission and why?
questions.answer:
Photoelectric emission occurs only if the energy of each incident photon exceeds the work function $\phi_0$ of the metal, i.e. $h\nu > \phi_0$, or equivalently $\lambda < \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0}$.
For $\lambda = 412.5$ nm, the photon energy is $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} \approx 3.0$ eV, so only those metals whose work function is less than about $3.0$ eV will show photoelectric emission; metals with higher work function will not, regardless of the intensity of the light.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: If light of wavelength $412.5$ nm is incident on each of the metals given below, which ones will show photoelectric emission and why? Metal — Work Function (eV) Na — 1.92 K — 2.15 Ca — 3.20 Mo — 4.17
questions.answer:
Photon energy of incident light: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{412.5 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 3.0$ eV
Emission occurs only if $E > \phi_0$ (work function).
Na ($\phi_0 = 1.92$ eV) and K ($\phi_0 = 2.15$ eV) show photoelectric emission since $E > \phi_0$ for both.
Ca ($\phi_0 = 3.20$ eV) and Mo ($\phi_0 = 4.17$ eV) do not show emission since $E < \phi_0$ for both.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Calculate the de-Broglie wavelength of the electron orbitting in the $n = 2$ state of hydrogen atom.
questions.answer:
By Bohr's postulate, $2\pi r_n = n\lambda$, since $mvr_n = nh/2\pi$ and $\lambda = h/mv$.
For $n = 2$, $r_2 = n^2 a_0 = 4 \times 0.529 \times 10^{-10}$ m $= 2.116 \times 10^{-10}$ m.
$\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi r_2}{n} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 2.116 \times 10^{-10}}{2} = 6.64 \times 10^{-10}$ m.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A proton and an $\alpha$ particle are accelerated through the same potential difference. Which one of the two has (i) greater de-Broglie wavelength, and (ii) less kinetic energy? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
(i) The proton has the greater de-Broglie wavelength.
Since $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2mqV}$, and $m_\alpha q_\alpha = 4m_p \times 2e = 8m_p e$ is much larger than $m_p q_p = m_p e$, $\lambda_p > \lambda_\alpha$.
(ii) The proton has less kinetic energy, since $KE = qV$; as $q_\alpha = 2q_p$, $KE_\alpha = 2KE_p$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The equivalent wavelength of a moving electron has the same value as that of a photon of energy $6 \times 10^{-17}$ J. Calculate the momentum of the electron.
questions.answer:
For the photon, $\lambda = hc/E$.
Since the electron has the same wavelength, its momentum is $p = h/\lambda = E/c$.
$p = \dfrac{6 \times 10^{-17}}{3 \times 10^8} = 2 \times 10^{-25}$ kg m/s.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A proton and an $\alpha$-particle have the same de-Broglie wavelength. Determine the ratio of (i) their accelerating potentials (ii) their speeds.
questions.answer:
Since $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2mqV}$, we get $V = h^2/(2mq\lambda^2)$.
(i) $\dfrac{V_p}{V_\alpha} = \dfrac{m_\alpha q_\alpha}{m_p q_p} = \dfrac{4m_p \times 2e}{m_p \times e} = 8$, so $V_p : V_\alpha = 8:1$.
(ii) Since $\lambda = h/mv$ and $\lambda$ is equal, $v \propto 1/m$, giving $\dfrac{v_p}{v_\alpha} = \dfrac{m_\alpha}{m_p} = 4$, so $v_p : v_\alpha = 4:1$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A proton and a deuteron are accelerated through the same accelerating potential. Which one of the two has (a) greater value of de-Broglie wavelength associated with it, and (b) less momentum? Give reasons to justify your answer.
questions.answer:
(a) The proton has the greater de-Broglie wavelength.
Since $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2mqV}$ and both carry charge $e$ at the same $V$, $\lambda \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$; as $m_p < m_d$ (with $m_d \approx 2m_p$), $\lambda_p > \lambda_d$.
(b) The proton has less momentum, since $p = \sqrt{2mqV} \propto \sqrt{m}$, and $m_p < m_d$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (i) Monochromatic light of frequency $6.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz is produced by a laser. The power emitted is $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ W. Estimate the number of photons emitted per second on an average by the source. (ii) Draw a plot showing the variation of photoelectric current versus the intensity of incident radiation on a given photosensitive surface.
questions.answer:
(i) Energy of each photon $E = hf = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 6.0 \times 10^{14} = 3.98 \times 10^{-19}$ J.
Number of photons emitted per second $N = P/E = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-3}}{3.98 \times 10^{-19}} = 5.0 \times 10^{15}$ per second.
(ii) The photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident radiation (for frequency above threshold), so the graph is a straight line passing through the origin.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A deuteron and an alpha particle are accelerated with the same accelerating potential. Which one of the two has (1) greater value of de-Broglie wavelength, associated with it and (2) less kinetic energy? Explain.
questions.answer:
For a particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ accelerated through potential $V$: $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2mqV}$ and $KE = qV$.
For deuteron (mass $m$, charge $q$) and alpha particle (mass $4m$, charge $2q$): $\lambda_d/\lambda_\alpha = \sqrt{(4m)(2q)/(mq)} = 2\sqrt{2}$.
Since $\lambda_d > \lambda_\alpha$, the deuteron has the greater de-Broglie wavelength.
Also $KE_\alpha = 2qV$ while $KE_d = qV$, so the deuteron has the smaller kinetic energy.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An $\alpha$-particle and a proton are accelerated from rest by the same potential. Find the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths.
questions.answer:
For a charged particle accelerated through potential $V$, $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2mqV}$.
For proton (mass $m$, charge $q$) and alpha particle (mass $4m$, charge $2q$):
$\dfrac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_p q_p}{m_\alpha q_\alpha}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m \cdot q}{4m \cdot 2q}} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$
So $\lambda_\alpha : \lambda_p = 1 : 2\sqrt{2}$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Write Einstein’s photoelectric equation. State clearly the three salient features observed in photoelectric effect, which can be explained on the basis of the above equation.
questions.answer:
Einstein's photoelectric equation: $KE_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0$, i.e. $eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0$.
(i) Existence of threshold frequency $\nu_0 = \phi_0/h$: below this, no photoelectrons are emitted however high the intensity.
(ii) Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons varies linearly with frequency of incident light and is independent of its intensity.
(iii) The effect is instantaneous, with no appreciable time lag between incidence of light and emission of electrons.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An electron is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 volts. What is the de- Broglie wavelength associated with it? To which part of the electromagnetic spectrum does this value of wavelength correspond?
questions.answer:
$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} = \dfrac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}$ Å
For $V = 100$ V, $\lambda = \dfrac{12.27}{\sqrt{100}} = 1.227$ Å $= 1.227 \times 10^{-10}$ m.
This wavelength lies in the X-ray region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Plot a graph showing the variation of stopping potential with the frequency of incident radiation for two different photosensitive materials having work functions $W_{1}$ and $W_{2}$ ($W_{1} > W_{2}$). On what factors does the (i) slope and (ii) intercept of the lines depend?
questions.answer:
From $eV_0 = h
u - \phi_0$, we get $V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}
u - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}$.
The graph is a pair of parallel straight lines (same slope) with the line for $W_1$ shifted to the right of the line for $W_2$, since $W_1 > W_2$ gives a higher threshold frequency $
u_0 = \phi_0/h$.
(i) The slope $h/e$ is the same for both lines; it depends only on Planck's constant and electronic charge, not on the material.
(ii) The intercepts (threshold frequency $\phi_0/h$ on the $
u$-axis, and $-\phi_0/e$ on the $V_0$-axis) depend on the work function of the material.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The work function of lithium is 2.3 eV. What does it mean? What is the relation between the work function $W$ and threshold wavelength of a metal?
questions.answer:
It means the minimum energy required to just eject an electron from the surface of lithium (with zero kinetic energy) is $2.3$ eV.
The work function is related to the threshold wavelength $\lambda_0$ by $W = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}$, so $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{W}$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) A particle of charge $q$ and mass $m$ is accelerated through a potential difference $V$. Deduce an expression for the de Broglie wavelength associated with the particle.
questions.answer:
Let the particle start from rest and be accelerated through potential difference $V$.
Work done on it equals its kinetic energy: $qV = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
So $v = \sqrt{\frac{2qV}{m}}$, and its momentum is $p = mv = \sqrt{2mqV}$
By de Broglie's hypothesis, $\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (b) Plot a graph for a particle of charge $q$ and mass $m$ showing variation of de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$, as $\frac{1}{\lambda}$ with $\sqrt{V}$, where $V$ is the potential difference through which the particle is accelerated.
questions.answer:
From $\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$, we get $\frac{1}{\lambda} = \sqrt{\frac{2mq}{h^{2}}}\,\sqrt{V}$
This shows $\frac{1}{\lambda}$ is directly proportional to $\sqrt{V}$.
The graph of $\frac{1}{\lambda}$ versus $\sqrt{V}$ is a straight line passing through the origin, with slope $\frac{\sqrt{2mq}}{h}$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Explain how the dual aspect of matter is evident in the de Broglie relation. (b) Radiation of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident on a photosensitive surface. Find the de Broglie wavelength of electrons emitted from the surface. Assume that the work function of the surface is negligible.
questions.answer:
(a) The de Broglie relation $\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$ links the wavelength $\lambda$, a wave property, with the momentum $p$, a particle property, in a single equation.
This shows that every moving particle of matter has an associated wave character, while every wave (of matter) is carried by a particle possessing definite momentum — hence matter exhibits a dual (wave-particle) nature.
(b) Since the work function is negligible, the entire photon energy becomes the kinetic energy of the electron: $\frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{p^{2}}{2m}$, so $p = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mhc}{\lambda}}$
The de Broglie wavelength of the electron is $\lambda' = \frac{h}{p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{h\lambda}{2mc}}$

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Photoemission of electrons occurs from a metal ($\phi_{0} = 1.96$ eV) when light of frequency $6.4 \times 10^{14}$ Hz is incident on it. Calculate: (a) Energy of a photon in the incident light, (b) The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, and (c) The stopping potential.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: What are de Broglie waves? Show that the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation is equal to the de Broglie wavelength of its quantum (photon).
questions.answer:
De Broglie waves are the matter waves associated with every moving particle, of wavelength $\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$, where $p$ is the particle's momentum.
For a photon, from Planck's quantum theory its energy is $E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$, and from Einstein's relation its momentum is $p = \frac{E}{c}$.
So $p = \frac{h}{\lambda}$, i.e., $\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$
This is exactly the de Broglie wavelength formula, so the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation is the same as the de Broglie wavelength of its photon.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Answer the following giving reason: (a) All the photo electrons do not eject with the same kinetic energy when monochromatic light is incident on a metal surface. (b) The saturation current in case (a) is different for different intensity. (c) If one goes on increasing the wavelength of light incident on a metal surface, keeping its intensity constant, emission of photo electrons stops at a certain wavelength for this metal.
questions.answer:
(a) Electrons are emitted from different depths inside the metal; those from deeper layers lose part of their energy in collisions while escaping to the surface, so only electrons ejected from the surface acquire the maximum kinetic energy $KE_{max} = h\nu - \phi_{0}$, while others come out with lower kinetic energies.
(b) Saturation current is proportional to the number of photoelectrons emitted per second, which equals the number of incident photons per second; since higher intensity means more photons per second (for the same frequency), the saturation current increases with intensity.
(c) Photoemission is a one photon-one electron process, so emission occurs only if $h\nu \geq \phi_{0}$, i.e., $\lambda \leq \lambda_{0} = \frac{hc}{\phi_{0}}$. As wavelength increases beyond the threshold wavelength $\lambda_{0}$, photon energy falls below $\phi_{0}$ and no electron can be emitted, however high the intensity.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Draw a plot of frequency $\nu$ of incident radiations as a function of stopping potential $V_{0}$ for a given photo emissive material. What information can be obtained from the value of the intercept on the stopping potential axis? (b) Calculate: (i) the momentum and (ii) de Broglie wavelength, of an electron with kinetic energy of $80$ eV.
questions.answer:
(a) A graph of stopping potential $V_0$ (y-axis) versus frequency $\nu$ (x-axis) is a straight line of slope $h/e$.
The intercept made by this line on the stopping potential axis (at $\nu = 0$) equals $-\phi_0/e$, so its magnitude gives the work function of the material.
(b) $KE = 80$ eV $= 80 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 1.28 \times 10^{-17}$ J
Momentum: $p = \sqrt{2mKE} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.28 \times 10^{-17}} = 4.83 \times 10^{-24}$ kg m/s
de Broglie wavelength: $\lambda = h/p = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{4.83 \times 10^{-24}} = 1.37 \times 10^{-10}$ m

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Mention any three features of results of experiment on photoelectric effect which cannot be explained using the wave theory of light. (b) In his experiment on photoelectric effect, Robert A. Millikan found the slope of the cut-off voltage versus frequency of incident light plot to be $4.12 \times 10^{-15}$ V s. Calculate the value of Planck’s constant from it.
questions.answer:
(a) Three features wave theory cannot explain:
1. Existence of a threshold frequency $\nu_0$ below which no photoelectrons are emitted, whatever the intensity.
2. Photoelectric current starts instantaneously, with no measurable time lag, even at low intensity.
3. Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is independent of intensity and depends only on frequency of incident light.
(b) $\dfrac{h}{e} = 4.12 \times 10^{-15}$ V s
$h = 4.12 \times 10^{-15} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 6.59 \times 10^{-34}$ J s

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Explain the following observations using Einstein’s photoelectric equation: (a) Photoelectric emission does not occur from a surface when the frequency of the light incident on it is less than a certain minimum value. (b) It is the frequency, and not the intensity of the incident light which affects the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons. (c) The cut-off voltage ($V_{0}$) versus frequency ($\nu$) of the incident light curve is a straight line with a slope $\frac{h}{e}$.
questions.answer:
(a) Einstein's equation: $KE_{max} = h
u - \phi_0$. If $
u < 
u_0 = \phi_0/h$, then $h
u < \phi_0$, giving negative $KE_{max}$, which is impossible; hence no electron is emitted below the threshold frequency.
(b) $KE_{max} = h
u - \phi_0$ depends only on $
u$ and the constant $\phi_0$ of the metal, not on intensity.
Increasing intensity only increases the number of photons (hence photocurrent), while each photon still supplies the same energy $h
u$ to a single electron, so $KE_{max}$ is unaffected by intensity.
(c) From $eV_0 = h
u - \phi_0$, we get $V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}
u - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}$, a linear equation in $
u$ with slope $h/e$, hence a straight line.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Define ’work function’ of a metal. How can its value be determined from a graph between stopping potential and frequency of the incident radiation? (b) The work function of a metal is $2.4$ eV. A stopping potential of $0.6$ V is required to reduce the photocurrent to zero, in a photoelectric experiment. Calculate the wavelength of light used.
questions.answer:
(a) Work function is the minimum energy required to just eject an electron from the surface of a metal (with zero kinetic energy).
On the graph of stopping potential $V_0$ versus frequency $
u$, the slope equals $h/e$; the intercept on the frequency axis gives the threshold frequency $
u_0$, and $\phi_0 = h
u_0$, or equivalently $\phi_0 = e|{m intercept~on~} V_0 {m~axis}|$.
(b) $h
u = \phi_0 + eV_0 = 2.4 + 0.6 = 3.0$ eV
$\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E} = \dfrac{1240 {m~eV\,nm}}{3.0 {m~eV}} \approx 413$ nm

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Briefly explain Einstein’s photoelectric equation. (b) Four metals with their work functions are listed below: $K = 2.3$ eV, $Na = 2.75$ eV, $Mo = 4.17$ eV and $Ni = 5.15$ eV. The radiation of wavelength $330$ nm from a laser source placed $1$ m away, falls on these metals. Which of these metals will not show photoelectric emission? What will happen if the laser source is brought closer to a distance of $50$ cm?
questions.answer:
(a) When a photon of energy $h\nu$ is absorbed by an electron in a metal, part of this energy ($\phi_0$) is used to overcome the work function and the rest appears as maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron: $KE_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0$.
(b) Photon energy: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1240}{330} \approx 3.76$ eV
Since $\phi_0(Mo) = 4.17$ eV and $\phi_0(Ni) = 5.15$ eV exceed $3.76$ eV, Mo and Ni will not show photoelectric emission ($K = 2.3$ eV and $Na = 2.75$ eV will).
Bringing the source to $50$ cm increases intensity by $4\times$ (inverse square law) but does not change the photon energy, so Mo and Ni still show no emission; only the photocurrent from K and Na increases.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Answer the following, giving reasons: (a) The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is independent of the intensity of incident radiation. (b) Photoelectric current increases with the increase in the intensity of the incident radiation. (c) The stopping potential $V_{0}$ varies linearly with the frequency $\nu$ of the incident radiation for a given photosensitive surface.
questions.answer:
(a) $KE_{max} = h
u - \phi_0$ depends only on the frequency of the incident light and the work function of the metal, since each photon transfers its energy to a single electron; increasing intensity only increases the number of photons, not the energy of each.
(b) Photocurrent is proportional to the number of photoelectrons emitted per second, which equals the number of incident photons per second, i.e. the intensity (for $
u > 
u_0$); hence photocurrent increases with intensity.
(c) From $eV_0 = h
u - \phi_0$, we get $V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}
u - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}$, which is linear in $
u$ with slope $h/e$, giving a straight-line graph.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ as a function of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}$ for two particles of masses $m$ and $m$ are $1 2$ shown in the figure. Here, K is the energy of the moving particles. (a) What does the slope of a line represent? (b) Which of the two particles is heavier? (c) Is this graph also valid for a photon? Justify your answer in each case.
questions.answer:
(a) Since $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m}}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{K}}$, the slope of the $\lambda$ versus $\frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}$ line equals $\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m}}$.
(b) Since slope $\propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}$, the particle whose line has the smaller slope has the larger mass; that particle is the heavier one.
(c) No, for a photon $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E}$ and $K = E$, so $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{K}$, not $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{K}}$, hence the graph would not be a straight line and is not valid for a photon.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Briefly explain de Broglie hypothesis for wave nature of matter. (b) Find the ratio of de Broglie wavelength associated with a proton and an alpha particle when both are (i) accelerated from rest through the same potential difference, and (ii) moving with the same kinetic energy.
questions.answer:
(a) De Broglie proposed that moving matter, like radiation, has a dual wave-particle character; a particle of momentum $p$ has an associated wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}$, analogous to a photon.
(b) (i) Accelerated through the same potential difference $V$: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$, so $\dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_\alpha q_\alpha}{m_p q_p}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4m_p \cdot 2e}{m_p \cdot e}} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$.
(ii) With the same kinetic energy $K$: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$, so $\dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_\alpha}{m_p}} = \sqrt{4} = 2$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Write Einstein’s photoelectric equation. How did Millikan prove the validity of this equation? (b) Explain the existence of threshold frequency of incident radiation for photoelectric emission from a given surface.
questions.answer:
(a) Einstein's photoelectric equation: $eV_0 = h
u - \phi_0$, where $V_0$ is stopping potential, $
u$ is frequency of incident light and $\phi_0$ is work function.
Millikan measured $V_0$ for radiations of several frequencies on a given metal and plotted $V_0$ versus $
u$; the graph was a straight line whose slope equalled $h/e$, matching Planck's constant, and whose intercept gave $\phi_0/e$, confirming Einstein's equation.
(b) A photon of frequency $
u$ carries energy $h
u$, and emission occurs only if $h
u \geq \phi_0$, i.e. $
u \geq 
u_0 = \phi_0/h$. Below this threshold frequency $
u_0$, each photon has insufficient energy to eject an electron regardless of the intensity (number of photons), so no photoelectric emission occurs.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A photosensitive surface of work function $2.1$ eV is irradiated by radiation of wavelength $150$ nm. Calculate (i) the threshold wavelength, (ii) energy (in eV) of an incident photon, and (iii) maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectron.
questions.answer:
(i) Threshold wavelength: $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0} = \dfrac{1240 \text{ eV nm}}{2.1 \text{ eV}} \approx 590.5$ nm.
(ii) Energy of incident photon: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1240}{150} \approx 8.27$ eV.
(iii) Maximum kinetic energy: $K_{max} = E - \phi_0 = 8.27 - 2.1 = 6.17$ eV.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The threshold frequency for a metal is $3.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz. A beam of frequency $9.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz is incident on the metal. Calculate (i) the work function (in eV) of the metal and (ii) the maximum speed of photoelectrons.
questions.answer:
(i) Work function: $\phi_0 = h
u_0 = (6.63 	imes 10^{-34})(3.0 	imes 10^{14}) = 1.99 	imes 10^{-19}$ J $= \dfrac{1.99 	imes 10^{-19}}{1.6 	imes 10^{-19}} \approx 1.24$ eV.
(ii) Maximum kinetic energy: $K_{max} = h(
u - 
u_0) = (6.63 	imes 10^{-34})(6.0 	imes 10^{14}) = 3.98 	imes 10^{-19}$ J.
Using $K_{max} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{max}^2$: $v_{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 	imes 3.98 	imes 10^{-19}}{9.1 	imes 10^{-31}}} \approx 9.35 	imes 10^{5}$ m/s.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: How does Einstein’s photoelectric equation explain the emission of electrons from a metal surface? Explain briefly. Plot the variation of photocurrent with: (a) collector plate potential for different intensity of incident radiation, and (b) intensity of incident radiation.
questions.answer:
When a photon of frequency $\nu$ strikes the metal surface, it is absorbed as a whole by one electron. Part of its energy $\phi_0$ (work function) is used to free the electron from the surface, and the rest appears as its kinetic energy: $\dfrac{1}{2}mv_{max}^2 = h\nu - \phi_0$.
Since absorption is one photon-one electron and instantaneous, emission occurs without time lag, and $K_{max}$ depends only on $\nu$, not on intensity.
(a) For a fixed frequency, the photocurrent versus collector plate potential curves for different intensities rise to different saturation currents (higher intensity gives higher saturation current, since more photons eject more electrons per second), but all curves meet the potential axis at the same stopping potential $-V_0$, since $K_{max}$ is intensity-independent.
(b) The photocurrent (saturation value) versus intensity graph is a straight line through the origin, showing that photocurrent is directly proportional to the intensity of incident radiation.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The threshold wavelength for a metal is $3315$ Å{}. What should be the wavelength of light incident on the metal surface so that the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons be $1.25$ eV?
questions.answer:
Threshold wavelength gives the work function: $W_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{1240 \text{ eV nm}}{331.5 \text{ nm}} = 3.74$ eV.
Maximum kinetic energy: $KE_{max} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - W_0$, so $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = W_0 + KE_{max} = 3.74 + 1.25 = 4.99$ eV.
$\lambda = \dfrac{1240}{4.99} = 248.5$ nm $= 2485$ Å.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A particle is associated with a de Broglie wave of wavelength $1.2$ nm. The kinetic energy of the particle is made four times. Calculate the new value of the wavelength of the wave. $[]$
questions.answer:
De Broglie wavelength: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$, so $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{K}}$.
When $K' = 4K$, $\lambda' = \dfrac{\lambda}{\sqrt{4}} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$.
$\lambda' = \dfrac{1.2}{2} = 0.6$ nm.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Calculate the wavelength of de Broglie waves associated with a proton having $\frac{500}{1.673}$ eV energy. How will the wavelength be affected for an alpha particle having the same energy?
questions.answer:
De Broglie wavelength: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mE}}$.
For the proton, $m_p = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, $E = \dfrac{500}{1.673}$ eV $= \dfrac{500}{1.673} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ J; substituting, the $1.673$ cancels giving $2m_pE = 1.6 \times 10^{-43}$ kg$^2$m$^2$/s$^2$, so $\sqrt{2m_pE} = 4.0 \times 10^{-22}$ kg m/s.
$\lambda_p = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{4.0 \times 10^{-22}} = 1.66 \times 10^{-12}$ m.
For the alpha particle at the same energy, $m_\alpha \approx 4m_p$, and since $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}$, $\lambda_\alpha = \dfrac{\lambda_p}{\sqrt{4}} = \dfrac{\lambda_p}{2} \approx 0.83 \times 10^{-12}$ m; the wavelength is halved.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ is accelerated through a potential difference $V$. Plot a graph of de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ associated with it as a function of $V$. (b) Calculate the energy acquired by, and de Broglie wavelength associated with, an electron accelerated through a potential difference of $400$ V.
questions.answer:
(a) $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$, so $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$: the graph is a curve that falls steeply at low $V$ and flattens as $V$ increases, approaching zero asymptotically, never touching the $V$-axis.
(b) Energy acquired: $E = qV = 400$ eV $= 400 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 6.4 \times 10^{-17}$ J.
De Broglie wavelength: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}} = \dfrac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}$ Å $= \dfrac{12.27}{\sqrt{400}} = 0.61$ Å.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) The figure shows de Broglie wavelength ($\lambda$) for two particles $A$ and $B$ having same charges but different masses as a function of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$, where $V$ is the potential through which the particles are accelerated. (i) Which of them is heavier and why? (ii) What does the slope of the line represent? (b) Calculate the momentum of an electron having de Broglie wavelength of $3.0$ Å.
questions.answer:
(a) (i) Since $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$, the slope of the $\lambda$ vs $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$ line equals $\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mq}}$, which decreases as mass increases; so the particle whose line has the smaller slope has the larger mass and is heavier.
(ii) The slope represents $\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mq}}$, from which the mass of the particle (for known charge $q$) can be determined.
(b) Momentum: $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{3.0 \times 10^{-10}} = 2.21 \times 10^{-24}$ kg m/s.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Photoelectrons are emitted from a metal surface when illuminated with UV light of wavelength $330$ nm. The minimum amount of energy required to emit the electrons from the surface is $3.5 \times 10^{-19}$ J. Calculate: (i) the energy of the incident radiation, and (ii) the kinetic energy of the photoelectron.
questions.answer:
(i) Energy of incident radiation: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{330 \times 10^{-9}} = 6.03 \times 10^{-19}$ J.
(ii) Kinetic energy of photoelectron: $KE = E - W_0 = 6.03 \times 10^{-19} - 3.5 \times 10^{-19} = 2.53 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Ultra-violet light of wavelength $200$ nm from a source is incident on a metal surface. If the stopping potential is $-2.5$ V, (a) calculate the work function of the metal, and (b) How would the surface respond to a high intensity red light of wavelength $6328$ Å produced by a laser?
questions.answer:
Energy of incident photon: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1240 \text{ eV nm}}{200 \text{ nm}} = 6.2$ eV
(a) Work function: $\phi_0 = E - eV_0 = 6.2 - 2.5 = 3.7$ eV
(b) Energy of red light: $E' = \dfrac{1240}{632.8} \approx 1.96$ eV, which is less than $\phi_0 = 3.7$ eV.
Since $E' < \phi_0$, no photoelectric emission occurs however high the intensity, as intensity only affects the number of photons, not their individual energy.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The de-Broglie wavelength associated with an electron is $0.30$ nm. Calculate: (a) the speed, and (b) the kinetic energy (in eV), of the electron.
questions.answer:
Using $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$, speed $v = \dfrac{h}{m\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 0.30 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 2.43 \times 10^{6}$ m/s
Kinetic energy: $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times (2.43 \times 10^{6})^2 \approx 2.68 \times 10^{-18}$ J
Converting to eV: $K = \dfrac{2.68 \times 10^{-18}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 16.7$ eV

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Find the ratio of the de Broglie wavelengths associated with an alpha particle and a proton, if both (a) have the same speeds, (b) have the same kinetic energy, (c) are accelerated through the same potential difference.
questions.answer:
de Broglie wavelength: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$, with $m_\alpha = 4m_p$ and $q_\alpha = 2q_p$.
(a) Same speed: $\dfrac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_p} = \dfrac{m_p}{m_\alpha} = \dfrac{1}{4}$
(b) Same kinetic energy: $\dfrac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_p}{m_\alpha}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$
(c) Same accelerating potential: $\dfrac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_p q_p}{m_\alpha q_\alpha}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4 \times 2}} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of $100$ V. Find: (i) the wavelength associated with (ii) the momentum of and (iii) the velocity required by, the electron.
questions.answer:
Kinetic energy gained: $K = eV = 100$ eV $= 1.6 \times 10^{-17}$ J
(ii) Momentum: $p = \sqrt{2mK} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-17}} \approx 5.40 \times 10^{-24}$ kg m/s
(i) Wavelength: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{5.40 \times 10^{-24}} \approx 1.23 \times 10^{-10}$ m $= 0.123$ nm
(iii) Velocity: $v = \dfrac{p}{m} = \dfrac{5.40 \times 10^{-24}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}} \approx 5.93 \times 10^{6}$ m/s

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Calculate the frequency of a photon of energy $6.5 \times 10^{-19}$ J. (b) Can this photon cause emission of an electron from the surface of Cs of work function $2.14$ eV? If yes, what will be maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectron?
questions.answer:
(a) Frequency: $\nu = \dfrac{E}{h} = \dfrac{6.5 \times 10^{-19}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}} \approx 9.8 \times 10^{14}$ Hz
(b) Work function of Cs $= 2.14$ eV $= 2.14 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 3.42 \times 10^{-19}$ J.
Since $E = 6.5 \times 10^{-19}$ J $> \phi_0$, photoelectric emission does occur.
Maximum kinetic energy: $K_{max} = E - \phi_0 = 6.5 \times 10^{-19} - 3.42 \times 10^{-19} = 3.08 \times 10^{-19}$ J $\approx 1.92$ eV

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The work function of a metal is $2.31$ eV. Photoelectric emission occurs when light of frequency $6.4 \times 10^{14}$ Hz is incident on the metal surface. Calculate: (i) the energy of the incident radiation, (ii) the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron and (iii) the stopping potential of the surface.
questions.answer:
(i) Energy of incident radiation: $E = h\nu = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 6.4 \times 10^{14} = 4.24 \times 10^{-19}$ J $\approx 2.65$ eV
(ii) Maximum kinetic energy: $K_{max} = E - \phi_0 = 2.65 - 2.31 = 0.34$ eV
(iii) Stopping potential: $eV_0 = K_{max} \Rightarrow V_0 = 0.34$ V

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Use Einstein’s photoelectric equation to depict the variation of the maximum kinetic energy ($E_{k}$) of electrons emitted, with the frequency ($\nu$) of the incident radiation. (b) A photosensitive surface is illuminated with a beam of (i) yellow light, and (ii) red light, both of the same intensity. In which case will (I) photoelectrons have more $E_{k}$? (II) more number of electrons be emitted? Justify your answer in each case.
questions.answer:
(a) Einstein's photoelectric equation: $E_k = h
u - \phi_0$.
This is a straight line when $E_k$ is plotted against $
u$: slope $= h$, intercept on frequency axis $= 
u_0$ (threshold frequency), intercept on $E_k$ axis $= -\phi_0$; the line exists only for $
u \geq 
u_0$.
(b) (I) Yellow light has higher frequency than red light, so $E_k = h
u - \phi_0$ is greater for yellow light.
(II) For the same intensity, number of photons per second $= I/(h
u)$; since red light photons carry less energy, more photons (hence more photoelectrons) are emitted per second in red light.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The wavelength of the waves associated with a particle having kinetic energy $E$ is $\lambda$. How and by what factor should its kinetic energy be changed so that the wavelength becomes $[] \frac{\lambda}{3}$? Also, find the ratio of the final to the initial velocity of the particle.
questions.answer:
De Broglie wavelength: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mE}}$, so $E \propto \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2}$.
For $\lambda' = \lambda/3$: $E' = E\left(\dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda'}\right)^2 = 9E$.
So the kinetic energy must be increased to $9$ times its initial value.
Since $p = h/\lambda$ and $p \propto v$, $\dfrac{v'}{v} = \dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda'} = 3$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A proton is accelerated through a potential difference $V$. After acceleration, the de Broglie wavelength associated with it is $\lambda$. If the proton is replaced by an alpha particle, then find the de Broglie wavelength associated with it if it were accelerated through the same potential difference $V$. What will be the momentum of the alpha particle?
questions.answer:
For a charge $q$ and mass $m$ accelerated through $V$: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$.
For proton ($m_p$, $e$): $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m_p eV}}$.
For alpha particle ($4m_p$, $2e$): $\lambda_\alpha = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2(4m_p)(2e)V}} = \dfrac{h}{4\sqrt{m_peV}} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\sqrt{2}}$.
Momentum of alpha particle: $p_\alpha = \dfrac{h}{\lambda_\alpha} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,h}{\lambda}$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Calculate the energy and momentum of a photon in a monochromatic beam of wavelength $331.5$ nm. (b) How fast should a hydrogen atom travel in order to have the same momentum as that of the photon in part (a)?
questions.answer:
(a) Energy: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^{8}}{331.5\times10^{-9}} = 6.0\times10^{-19}$ J.
Momentum: $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{331.5\times10^{-9}} = 2.0\times10^{-27}$ kg m/s.
(b) For same momentum, $v = \dfrac{p}{m} = \dfrac{2.0\times10^{-27}}{1.67\times10^{-27}} \approx 1.2$ m/s.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An alpha particle is accelerated through a potential difference of $100$ V. Calculate: (i) The speed acquired by the alpha particle, and (ii) The de-Broglie wavelength associated with it. (Take mass of alpha particle $= 6.4 \times 10^{-27}$ kg)
questions.answer:
(i) $qV = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2qV}{m}}$, with $q = 2e = 3.2\times10^{-19}$ C.
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\times3.2\times10^{-19}\times100}{6.4\times10^{-27}}} = \sqrt{1\times10^{10}} = 1.0\times10^{5}$ m/s.
(ii) $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{6.4\times10^{-27}\times1.0\times10^{5}} \approx 1.04\times10^{-12}$ m.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Give an example each of a metal from which photoelectric emission takes place when irradiated by (i) UV light (ii) visible light. (b) The work function of a metal is $4.50$ eV. Find the frequency of light to be used to eject electrons from the metal surface with a maximum kinetic energy of $6.06 \times 10^{-19}$ J.
questions.answer:
(a) UV light causes photoemission from metals like zinc or aluminium (higher work function); visible light causes photoemission from alkali metals like caesium or potassium (low work function).
(b) $\phi_0 = 4.50\times1.6\times10^{-19} = 7.2\times10^{-19}$ J.
Using $h\nu = \phi_0 + E_{k,max}$: $h\nu = 7.2\times10^{-19} + 6.06\times10^{-19} = 1.326\times10^{-18}$ J.
$\nu = \dfrac{1.326\times10^{-18}}{6.63\times10^{-34}} = 2.0\times10^{15}$ Hz.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons emitted is doubled when the wavelength of light incident on the photosensitive surface changes from $\lambda_{1}$ to $\lambda_{2}$. Deduce expressions for the threshold wavelength and work function for the metal surface in terms of $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$.
questions.answer:
By Einstein's photoelectric equation, $KE_{1} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{1}} - \phi_{0}$ and $KE_{2} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{2}} - \phi_{0} = 2KE_{1}$.
Substituting, $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{2}} - \phi_{0} = 2\left(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{1}} - \phi_{0}\right)$.
Solving, $\phi_{0} = hc\left(\dfrac{2}{\lambda_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_{2}}\right) = \dfrac{hc(2\lambda_{2} - \lambda_{1})}{\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}}$.
Threshold wavelength $\lambda_{0} = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_{0}} = \dfrac{\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}}{2\lambda_{2} - \lambda_{1}}$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: What do you mean by wave nature of an electron? How was quantisation of angular momentum of the orbiting electron in Bohr’s model of hydrogen atom explained by de Broglie hypothesis?
questions.answer:
The wave nature of an electron means a moving electron behaves like a wave, with an associated de Broglie wavelength $\lambda = h/p = h/mv$; this was confirmed by the Davisson–Germer experiment showing electron diffraction.
De Broglie proposed that an electron in a stable Bohr orbit must exist as a standing wave, so the orbit circumference must contain a whole number of wavelengths: $2\pi r = n\lambda$.
Substituting $\lambda = h/mv$ gives $2\pi r = nh/mv$, i.e. $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, which is exactly Bohr's condition for quantisation of angular momentum.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Plot a graph to show the variation of stopping potential with frequency of incident radiation in relation to photoelectric effect. (b) Use Einstein’s photoelectric equation to show how from this graph, (i) Threshold frequency, and (ii) Planck’s constant can be determined. OR (a) How does one explain the emission of electrons from a photosensitive surface with the help of Einstein’s photoelectric equation? (b) Work function of aluminium is $4.2$ eV. If two photons each of energy $2.5$ eV are incident on its surface, will the emission of electrons take place? Justify your answer. (c) The stopping potential in an experiment on photoelectric effect is $1.5$ V. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons emitted? Calculate in Joules.
questions.answer:
(a) Einstein's photoelectric equation is $h
u = \phi_{0} + KE_{max}$, so $KE_{max} = h
u - \phi_{0}$. A photon interacts with a single electron and transfers its entire energy $h
u$ instantaneously; part of this energy overcomes the work function $\phi_{0}$ and the remainder appears as the electron's maximum kinetic energy. Emission occurs only when $h
u > \phi_{0}$, and increasing intensity only increases the number of photons (hence photocurrent), not the energy of each emitted electron.
(b) No emission takes place. Photoelectric emission is a one photon–one electron process; a single photon of energy $2.5$ eV, which is less than the work function $4.2$ eV, cannot eject an electron even though two such photons are incident, since an electron cannot simultaneously absorb energy from two separate photons.
(c) $KE_{max} = eV_{0} = 1.6 	imes 10^{-19} 	imes 1.5 = 2.4 	imes 10^{-19}$ J.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: When a given photosensitive material is irradiated with light of frequency $\nu$, the maximum speed of the emitted photoelectrons equals $v_{\max}$. The graph shown in the figure gives a plot of $v_{\max}{}^{2}$ varying with frequency $\nu$. Obtain an expression for (a) Planck’s constant, and (b) The work function of the given photosensitive material in terms of the parameters ’ $l$’, ’ $n$’ and the mass ’ $m$’ of the electron. (c) How is threshold frequency determined from the plot?
questions.answer:
From Einstein's photoelectric equation, $\dfrac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2} = h
u - \phi_{0}$, so $v_{max}^{2} = \dfrac{2h}{m}
u - \dfrac{2\phi_{0}}{m}$, which is a straight line in $v_{max}^{2}$ vs $
u$.
(a) The slope of the graph equals $l = \dfrac{2h}{m}$, so $h = \dfrac{ml}{2}$.
(b) The magnitude of the intercept on the $v_{max}^{2}$-axis equals $n = \dfrac{2\phi_{0}}{m}$, so $\phi_{0} = \dfrac{mn}{2}$.
(c) The threshold frequency $
u_{0}$ is the point where the line cuts the $
u$-axis (where $v_{max}^{2} = 0$), given by $
u_{0} = n/l$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: When light of frequency $\nu_{1}$ is incident on a photosensitive surface, the stopping potential is $V_{1}$. If the frequency of incident radiation becomes $\nu_{1}/2$, the stopping potential changes to $V_{2}$. Find out the expression for the threshold frequency for the surface in terms of $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$. If the frequency of incident radiation is doubled, will the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons also be doubled? Give reason.
questions.answer:
By Einstein's equation, $eV_{1} = h
u_{1} - h
u_{0}$ and $eV_{2} = h\dfrac{
u_{1}}{2} - h
u_{0}$.
Subtracting, $e(V_{1}-V_{2}) = \dfrac{h
u_{1}}{2}$, giving $h = \dfrac{2e(V_{1}-V_{2})}{
u_{1}}$.
Substituting back, $h
u_{0} = h
u_{1} - eV_{1} = e(2V_{1}-2V_{2}-V_{1}) = e(V_{1}-2V_{2})$, so $
u_{0} = \dfrac{
u_{1}(V_{1}-2V_{2})}{2(V_{1}-V_{2})}$.
No, $KE_{max}$ will not be doubled, because $KE_{max} = h
u - h
u_{0}$ is a linear function of $
u$ with a non-zero intercept $-h
u_{0}$, not directly proportional to $
u$; so doubling $
u$ does not double $KE_{max}$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Write Einstein’s photoelectric equation using the quantum picture of radiation. Explain briefly the three characteristic features observed in photoelectric effect which can be explained by Einstein’s equation and not by the wave theory of light.
questions.answer:
Einstein's photoelectric equation: $KE_{max} = h
u - \phi_{0} = h(
u - 
u_{0})$, where $\phi_{0} = h
u_{0}$ is the work function.
(i) Instantaneous emission: since a photon transfers its entire energy to one electron in a single collision, emission occurs without any time lag, unlike wave theory which predicts a delay for energy to accumulate.
(ii) Existence of threshold frequency: electrons are emitted only if $h
u \geq \phi_{0}$, i.e. $
u \geq 
u_{0}$, since a photon below this energy cannot free an electron regardless of intensity; wave theory predicts emission at any frequency given enough time or intensity.
(iii) $KE_{max}$ is independent of intensity but depends linearly on frequency: increasing intensity increases the number of photons and hence photocurrent, not the energy of each photon, so individual electron energies stay unchanged; wave theory wrongly predicts $KE_{max}$ should rise with intensity.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (i) How does one explain the emission of electrons from a photosensitive surface with the help of Einstein’s photoelectric equation? (ii) The work function of the following metals is given: $Na = 2.75 eV$, $K = 2.3 eV$, $Mo = 4.17 eV$ and $Ni = 5.15 eV$. Which of these metals will not cause photoelectric emission for radiation of wavelength $3300 ^{\circ}A$ from a laser source placed $1 m$ away from these metals? What happens if the laser source is brought nearer and placed $50 cm$ away?
questions.answer:
(i) Einstein's photoelectric equation is $KE_{max} = h
u - \phi_0$.
Light is absorbed in discrete packets (photons) of energy $h
u$; a single photon transfers its entire energy to a single electron instantaneously.
Part of this energy is used to overcome the work function $\phi_0$ of the surface and the remainder appears as kinetic energy of the emitted electron; hence emission occurs only if $h
u > \phi_0$, with no time lag, and $KE_{max}$ depends only on $
u$, not on intensity.
(ii) Photon energy $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63	imes10^{-34}	imes3	imes10^{8}}{3300	imes10^{-10}} = 6.03	imes10^{-19}$ J $\approx 3.77$ eV.
Since $3.77$ eV $< \phi_0$ for $Mo (4.17 eV)$ and $Ni (5.15 eV)$, these two metals will not show photoelectric emission (Na and K will emit, as their work functions are lower).
Bringing the source to $50 cm$ only raises the intensity (photon number, by inverse square law), not the photon energy $h
u$; since $h
u$ is still less than $\phi_0$ for Mo and Ni, no emission occurs from them even then.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: In the study of a photoelectric effect the graph between the stopping potential $V$ and frequency $\nu$ of the incident radiation on two different metals P and Q is shown below: (i) Which one of the two metals has higher threshold frequency? (ii) Determine the work function of the metal which has greater value. (iii) Find the maximum kinetic energy of electron emitted by light of frequency $8\times10^{14} Hz$ for this metal.
questions.answer:
(i) The metal whose $V$–$
u$ line cuts the frequency axis at the larger value of $
u$ has the higher threshold frequency; from the graph this is metal P.
(ii) Both lines have the same slope $h/e$, so the metal with the larger threshold frequency has the greater work function: reading $
u_{0P} = 5	imes10^{14}$ Hz from the graph, $\phi_P = h
u_{0P} = 6.63	imes10^{-34}	imes5	imes10^{14} = 3.315	imes10^{-19}$ J $\approx 2.07$ eV.
(iii) $KE_{max} = h
u - \phi_P = h(
u - 
u_{0P}) = 6.63	imes10^{-34}	imes(8-5)	imes10^{14} = 1.99	imes10^{-19}$ J $\approx 1.24$ eV.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (i) State two important features of Einstein’s photoelectric equation. (ii) Radiation of frequency $10^{15} Hz$ is incident on two photosensitive surfaces P and Q. There is no photoemission from surface P. Photoemission occurs from surface Q but photoelectrons have zero kinetic energy. Explain these observations and find the value of work function for surface Q.
questions.answer:
(i) Two features of Einstein's equation $KE_{max} = h
u - \phi_0$: (a) $KE_{max}$ varies linearly with frequency $
u$ and is independent of intensity; (b) emission occurs only above a threshold frequency $
u_0 = \phi_0/h$, and is instantaneous, with no time lag.
(ii) Photon energy at $
u = 10^{15}$ Hz is $h
u = 6.63	imes10^{-34}	imes10^{15} = 6.63	imes10^{-19}$ J $\approx 4.14$ eV.
No emission from P means $\phi_P > 4.14$ eV.
Emission from Q with zero kinetic electron energy means $h
u$ exactly equals the work function, i.e. $
u$ equals the threshold frequency of Q, so $\phi_Q = h
u \approx 4.14$ eV.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Draw a plot showing the variation of photoelectric current with collector potential for different frequencies but same intensity of incident radiation. (b) Use Einstein’s photoelectric equation to explain the observations from this graph. (c) What change will you observe if intensity of incident radiation is changed but the frequency remains the same?
questions.answer:
(a) For each frequency, the photocurrent rises with increasing (positive) collector potential and reaches the same saturation value (since intensity, hence photon/electron number, is the same for all curves); each curve meets the zero-current axis at a different (negative) stopping potential, the curve for higher frequency having a more negative stopping potential.
(b) From $eV_0 = h
u - \phi_0$, $V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}
u - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}$: stopping potential increases linearly with frequency with slope $h/e$ (same for all metals), and is independent of intensity, which explains why the saturation current (fixed by intensity) is the same for all curves while $V_0$ shifts with $
u$.
(c) If intensity is increased at the same frequency, only the saturation current increases (proportionally); the stopping potential, and hence $KE_{max}$, remains unchanged.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Draw a graph showing variation of photocurrent with anode potential for a particular intensity of incident radiation. Mark saturation current and stopping potential. (b) By how much would the stopping potential for a given photosensitive surface go up if the frequency of the incident radiations were to be increased from $4 \times 10^{15}$ Hz to $8 \times 10^{15}$ Hz?
questions.answer:
(a) As anode potential is made more positive, photocurrent rises and levels off at a constant saturation current; as the potential is made negative, current falls and becomes zero at the stopping potential $V_0$, marked on the negative potential axis, with the saturation current marked as the flat current level for large positive potential.
(b) $eV_0 = h
u - \phi_0$, so for the same surface, $e\,\Delta V_0 = h\,\Delta
u$, giving $\Delta V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}\Delta
u = 4.14	imes10^{-15}	imes(8-4)	imes10^{15}$.
$\Delta V_0 \approx 16.6$ V, i.e. the stopping potential increases by about $16.6$ V.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Using photon picture of light, show how Einstein’s photoelectric equation can be established. Write two features of photoelectric effect which cannot be explained by wave theory.
questions.answer:
In the photon picture, light of frequency $
u$ consists of photons each of energy $h
u$.
When one photon strikes a free electron of the metal, it is absorbed completely and instantaneously by a single electron.
Part of this energy, equal to the work function $\phi_0$, is used to free the electron from the metal surface, and the rest appears as its kinetic energy: $h
u = \phi_0 + KE_{max}$, i.e. $KE_{max} = h
u - \phi_0$, Einstein's photoelectric equation.
This also shows emission occurs only if $
u \geq 
u_0 = \phi_0/h$.
Two features not explained by wave theory: (a) existence of a threshold frequency below which no emission occurs however intense the light; (b) instantaneous emission with no measurable time lag, and $KE_{max}$ independent of intensity, both of which contradict wave theory's prediction that energy absorption should depend on intensity and take time to accumulate.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Explain giving reasons for the following: (a) Photoelectric current in a photocell increases with the increase in the intensity of the incident radiation. (b) The stopping potential ($V_{0}$) varies linearly with the frequency ($\nu$) of the incident radiation for a given photosensitive surface with the slope remaining the same for different surfaces. (c) Maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is independent of the intensity of incident radiation.
questions.answer:
(a) Intensity means more photons falling per second on the surface; since each photon (of given frequency) ejects at most one electron, a greater number of incident photons ejects a greater number of photoelectrons per second, so the photocurrent increases.
(b) Einstein's equation $eV_{0} = h
u - \phi_{0}$ gives $V_{0} =  rac{h}{e}
u -  rac{\phi_{0}}{e}$, a straight line in $V_{0}$ vs $
u$ with slope $h/e$; since $h$ and $e$ are universal constants, the slope is the same for every surface, only the intercept ($\phi_{0}/e$) differs.
(c) $KE_{max} = h
u - \phi_{0}$ depends only on the frequency of the incident photon and the work function; increasing intensity only increases the number of photons (hence current), not the energy of each photon, so $KE_{max}$ is unaffected.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question:
The following graph shows the variation of photocurrent for a photosensitive metal: (a) Identify the variable $X$ on the horizontal axis. (b) What does the point $A$ on the horizontal axis represent? (c) Draw this graph for three different values of frequencies of incident radiation $
u_{1}$, $
u_{2}$ and $
u_{3}$ ($
u_{1} > 
u_{2} > 
u_{3}$) for same intensity. (d) Draw this graph for three different values of intensities of incident radiation $I_{1}$, $I_{2}$ and $I_{3}$ ($I_{1} > I_{2} > I_{3}$) having same frequency.
questions.answer:
(a) $X$ is the potential difference (collector/retarding potential) applied between the collector plate and the photosensitive emitter.
(b) Point $A$ represents the stopping potential $V_{0}$, the (negative) potential at which the photocurrent just becomes zero, i.e. even the fastest photoelectrons are turned back.
(c) For the same intensity, all three curves reach the same saturation current, but the stopping potential increases with frequency: $|V_{0}(
u_{1})| > |V_{0}(
u_{2})| > |V_{0}(
u_{3})|$, since $eV_{0} = h
u - \phi_{0}$.
(d) For the same frequency, all three curves have the same stopping potential (unchanged by intensity), but the saturation current increases with intensity: $I_{1}$ gives the highest saturation current, $I_{3}$ the lowest, since saturation current is proportional to the number of incident photons.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Sketch the graphs showing variation of stopping potential with frequency of incident radiations for two photosensitive materials $A$ and $B$ having threshold frequencies $\nu_{A} > \nu_{B}$. (i) In which case is the stopping potential more and why? (ii) Does the slope of the graph depend on the nature of the material used? Explain.
questions.answer:
Both graphs are straight lines of $V_{0}$ against $
u$, each cutting the frequency axis at its own threshold frequency ($
u_{A}$ and $
u_{B}$), with $B$'s line lying to the left of $A$'s since $
u_{B} < 
u_{A}$.
(i) At any common frequency $
u > 
u_{A}$, the stopping potential is greater for $B$, because $eV_{0} = h
u - \phi_{0}$ and $B$ has the smaller work function $\phi_{0}$ (lower threshold frequency), so it retains more kinetic energy per photoelectron.
(ii) No, the slope equals $h/e$ in both cases, a ratio of universal constants, so it is independent of the material; only the intercept (threshold frequency/work function) differs between $A$ and $B$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The given graph shows the variation of photo-electric current ($I$) with the applied voltage ($V$ ) for two different materials and for two different intensities of the incident radiations. Identify and explain using Einstein’s photo electric equation the pair of curves that correspond to (i) different materials but same intensity of incident radiation, (ii) different intensities but same materials.
questions.answer:
By Einstein's equation $eV_{0} = h
u - \phi_{0}$, so $V_{0} =  rac{h}{e}
u -  rac{\phi_{0}}{e}$, while the saturation current is proportional to the intensity (number of photons/s).
(i) The pair of curves with the same saturation current but different stopping potentials $V_{0}$ corresponds to different materials at the same intensity, since different work functions $\phi_{0}$ give different $V_{0}$ for the same $
u$, while equal intensity gives equal saturation current.
(ii) The pair of curves with the same stopping potential but different saturation currents corresponds to the same material at different intensities, since $V_{0}$ depends only on $
u$ and $\phi_{0}$ (unchanged), while the saturation current rises with intensity.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: State two important properties of photon which are used to write Einstein’s photoelectric equation. Define (i) stopping potential and (ii) threshold frequency, using Einstein’s equation and drawing necessary plot between relevant quantities.
questions.answer:
Two properties of the photon used: (1) each photon carries a definite energy $E = h
u$, depending only on frequency, not intensity; (2) in a photon-electron collision the photon is completely absorbed and transfers all its energy to a single electron (one-to-one interaction), giving Einstein's equation $h
u = \phi_{0} + KE_{max}$.
(i) Stopping potential $V_{0}$ is the (negative) retarding potential at which the photocurrent just becomes zero, i.e. it stops even the most energetic photoelectrons: $eV_{0} = KE_{max} = h
u - \phi_{0}$.
(ii) Threshold frequency $
u_{0}$ is the minimum frequency for which photoemission just begins, so $KE_{max} = 0$, giving $h
u_{0} = \phi_{0}$.
Plotting $V_{0}$ vs $
u$ gives a straight line of slope $h/e$, cutting the $
u$-axis at $
u_{0}$ and the $V_{0}$-axis at $-\phi_{0}/e$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question:
(a) Define the term ’intensity of radiation’ in photon picture. (b) Plot a graph showing the variation of photo current vs collector potential for three different intensities $I_{1} > I_{2} > I_{3}$, two of which ($I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$) have the same frequency $
u$ and the third has frequency $
u_{1} > 
u$. (c) Explain the nature of the curves on the basis of Einstein’s equation.
questions.answer:
(a) Intensity of radiation is the energy incident per unit area per unit time, equal to $n h
u$, where $n$ is the number of photons falling on unit area per unit time and $h
u$ is the energy of each photon.
(b) The curves for $I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$ (same frequency $
u$) share the same stopping potential $V_{0}$ but have different saturation currents, with $I_{1}$'s saturation current greater than $I_{2}$'s. The curve for $I_{3}$ (frequency $
u_{1} > 
u$) has a larger stopping potential $V_{0}' > V_{0}$ but the smallest saturation current, since $I_{3}$ is the lowest intensity.
(c) By Einstein's equation $eV_{0} = h
u - \phi_{0}$, stopping potential depends only on frequency, so $I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$ (same $
u$) give equal $V_{0}$, while $I_{3}$'s higher frequency gives a larger $V_{0}'$; saturation current is proportional to intensity (photon number), explaining the differing current levels.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Define the term ’intensity of radiation’ in terms of photon picture of light. (b) Two monochromatic beams, one red and the other blue, have the same intensity. In which case (i) the number of photons per unit area per second is larger, (ii) the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is more? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
(a) Intensity of radiation, in the photon picture, is the energy incident per unit area per unit time, equal to the number of photons falling per unit area per second multiplied by the energy of each photon: $I = n h
u$, where $n$ is the number of photons per unit area per second.
(b) (i) The number of photons per unit area per second is larger for the red beam, because each red photon has lower energy $h
u$ (lower frequency) than a blue photon, so for the same intensity more red photons are needed.
(ii) The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is more for the blue beam, since $KE_{max} = h
u - \phi_0$ and blue light has higher frequency $
u$, giving each photon more energy regardless of intensity.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Write Einstein’s photoelectric equation and mention which important features in photoelectric effect can be explained with the help of this equation. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons gets doubled when the wavelength of light incident on the surface changes from $\lambda_{1}$ to $\lambda_{2}$. Derive the expressions for the threshold wavelength $\lambda_{0}$ and work function for the metal surface.
questions.answer:
Einstein's photoelectric equation: $KE_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0$, i.e., $eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0$.
It explains: existence of a threshold frequency $\nu_0 = \phi_0/h$, linear increase of $KE_{max}$ (and stopping potential) with frequency independent of intensity, and instantaneous emission of photoelectrons.
Let $KE_1 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_1} - \phi_0$ and $KE_2 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} - \phi_0$, with $KE_2 = 2KE_1$.
So $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} - \phi_0 = \dfrac{2hc}{\lambda_1} - 2\phi_0$
$\phi_0 = hc\left(\dfrac{2}{\lambda_1} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_2}\right)$
Threshold wavelength $\lambda_0 = hc/\phi_0$, so
$\lambda_0 = \dfrac{\lambda_1\lambda_2}{2\lambda_2 - \lambda_1}$

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An electron microscope uses electrons accelerated by a voltage of 50 kV. Determine the de-Broglie wavelength associated with the electrons. Taking other factors, such as numerical aperture etc. to be same, how does the resolving power of an electron microscope compare with that of an optical microscope which uses yellow light?
questions.answer:
De Broglie wavelength: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}$
Substituting $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, $m = 9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C, $V = 5\times10^{4}$ V:
$\lambda = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2\times9.11\times10^{-31}\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times5\times10^{4}}} \approx 5.5\times10^{-12}$ m
Resolving power is inversely proportional to wavelength used. Since this $\lambda$ is about $10^5$ times smaller than the wavelength of yellow light ($\sim 5.9\times10^{-7}$ m), the electron microscope has a resolving power about $10^5$ times greater than an optical microscope using yellow light.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: (a) Why photoelectric effect can not be explained on the basis of wave nature of light? Give reasons. (b) Write the basic features of photon picture of electromagnetic radiation on which Einstein’s photoelectric equation is based.
questions.answer:
(a) According to wave theory, the energy of a light wave is spread continuously over the wavefront and its intensity (not frequency) determines the energy delivered, so $KE_{max}$ should depend on intensity — but experimentally $KE_{max}$ depends only on frequency, not intensity.
Wave theory predicts photoemission for any frequency provided intensity/time is sufficient, but a threshold frequency $\nu_0$ is observed below which no emission occurs however high the intensity.
Wave theory requires a measurable time lag for an electron to accumulate enough energy from the spread-out wave, but photoemission is observed to be instantaneous.
(b) Radiation consists of discrete packets called photons, each carrying energy $E = h\nu$ and momentum $p = h\nu/c = h/\lambda$.
Photon energy depends only on frequency, not intensity; intensity determines the number of photons per unit area per second.
Photons are electrically neutral and travel at speed $c$; in a photon-electron collision the photon is absorbed entirely, and energy and momentum are conserved.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Define the terms (i) ’cut-off voltage’ and (ii) ’threshold frequency’ in relation to the phenomenon of photoelectric effect. Using Einstein’s photoelectric equation show how the cut-off voltage and threshold frequency for a given photosensitive material can be determined with the help of a suitable plot/graph.
questions.answer:
(i) Cut-off (stopping) voltage $V_0$ is the minimum retarding potential applied to the collector that just reduces the photoelectric current to zero for a given frequency of incident light.
(ii) Threshold frequency $
u_0$ is the minimum frequency of incident radiation below which no photoelectric emission occurs, no matter how large the intensity.
From Einstein's equation $eV_0 = h
u - \phi_0$, so $V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}
u - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}$.
Plotting $V_0$ versus $
u$ gives a straight line of slope $h/e$; the intercept on the $
u$-axis (where $V_0 = 0$) gives the threshold frequency $
u_0$, and the intercept on the $V_0$-axis gives $-\phi_0/e$, from which the work function is obtained.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Write Einstein’s photoelectric equation. State clearly how this equation is obtained using the photon picture of electromagnetic radiation. Write the three salient features observed in photoelectric effect which can be explained using this equation.
questions.answer:
Einstein's photoelectric equation: $KE_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0$, i.e., $eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0$.
In the photon picture, a single photon of energy $h\nu$ is absorbed completely by one electron; part of this energy overcomes the work function $\phi_0$ (minimum energy binding the electron to the surface), and the remainder appears as the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron, giving $h\nu = \phi_0 + KE_{max}$.
Three salient features explained:
1. Existence of a threshold frequency $\nu_0 = \phi_0/h$ below which no emission occurs.
2. $KE_{max}$ increases linearly with frequency and is independent of intensity.
3. Photoelectric emission is instantaneous since one photon transfers its energy to one electron in a single collision.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Write two characteristic features observed in photoelectric effect which support the photon picture of electromagnetic radiation. Draw a graph between the frequency of incident radiation ($\nu$) and the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons emitted from the surface of a photosensitive material. State clearly how this graph can be used to determine (i) Planck’s constant and (ii) work function of the material.
questions.answer:
Two features supporting the photon picture: (i) the existence of a threshold frequency $
u_0$ below which no photoemission occurs, however high the intensity; (ii) photoemission is instantaneous, with no measurable time lag between incidence of light and emission of electrons.
Graph: a straight line of $K_{max}$ (y-axis) versus $
u$ (x-axis), governed by $K_{max} = h
u - \phi_0$.
(i) The slope of this line gives Planck's constant $h$.
(ii) The intercept on the $
u$-axis gives the threshold frequency $
u_0$, and the magnitude of the negative intercept on the $K_{max}$-axis gives the work function $\phi_0 = h
u_0$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Draw a plot showing the variation of photoelectric current with collector plate potential for two different frequencies, $\nu_{1} > \nu_{2}$, of incident radiation having the same intensity. In which case will the stopping potential be higher? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
For each frequency the photoelectric current rises with positive plate potential to the same saturation value (since intensity is the same for both), but becomes zero at different negative (stopping) potentials $V_0$, given by $eV_0 = h
u - \phi_0$.
The stopping potential is higher for $
u_1$.
This is because a higher frequency photon has greater energy $h
u_1$, giving photoelectrons a greater maximum kinetic energy, which requires a larger retarding potential to stop them completely.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An electron and a photon each have a wavelength $1.00$ nm. Find (i) their momenta, (ii) the energy of the photon and (iii) the kinetic energy of electron.
questions.answer:
(i) Momentum of photon: $p = h/\lambda = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}/10^{-9} = 6.63 \times 10^{-25}$ kg m/s.
Momentum of electron: same de Broglie relation gives $p = h/\lambda = 6.63 \times 10^{-25}$ kg m/s.
(ii) Energy of photon: $E = pc = 6.63 \times 10^{-25} \times 3 \times 10^{8} = 1.989 \times 10^{-16}$ J $\approx 1.24$ keV.
(iii) Kinetic energy of electron: $K = p^{2}/2m = (6.63 \times 10^{-25})^{2}/(2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31}) \approx 2.41 \times 10^{-19}$ J $\approx 1.51$ eV.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Light of wavelength 2000 Å falls on a metal surface of work function 4.2 eV. What is the kinetic energy (in eV) of the fastest electrons emitted from the surface? (i) What will be the change in the energy of the emitted electrons if the intensity of light with same wavelength is doubled? (ii) If the same light falls on another surface of work function 6.5 eV, what will be the energy of emitted electrons?
questions.answer:
Photon energy: $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{1240 \text{ eV nm}}{200 \text{ nm}} = 6.2$ eV.
Maximum kinetic energy: $K_{max} = E - \phi_0 = 6.2 - 4.2 = 2.0$ eV.
(i) The kinetic energy of the fastest electrons remains unchanged at $2.0$ eV; doubling the intensity only doubles the number of photoelectrons (photocurrent), not their individual energy, since $K_{max}$ depends only on frequency.
(ii) Since $\phi_0 = 6.5$ eV exceeds the photon energy of $6.2$ eV, no photoelectrons are emitted; the emitted electron energy is zero.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A proton and an alpha particle are accelerated through the same potential. Which one of the two has (i) greater value of de-Broglie wavelength associated with it, and (ii) less kinetic energy? Justify your answers.
questions.answer:
(i) De Broglie wavelength: $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2mqV}$, where $q$ is charge and $m$ is mass.
For the proton ($m_p$, $q=e$) and alpha particle ($m_\alpha \approx 4m_p$, $q=2e$), accelerated through the same $V$:
$\dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_\alpha q_\alpha}{m_p q_p}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4m_p \cdot 2e}{m_p \cdot e}} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$
So the proton has the greater de Broglie wavelength, since it has smaller mass and charge.
(ii) Kinetic energy $K = qV$; since $q_\alpha = 2e > q_p = e$ for the same $V$, the alpha particle has greater kinetic energy, so the proton has the lesser kinetic energy.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An electromagnetic wave of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident on a photosensitive surface of negligible work function. If the photo-electrons emitted from this surface have the de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda_{1}$, prove that $\lambda =^{\frac{2mc}{h}} \lambda^{2}{}_{1}$.
questions.answer:
Since the work function is negligible, the entire photon energy converts to the kinetic energy of the emitted electron:
$K = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$
The electron's kinetic energy in terms of its de Broglie wavelength $\lambda_1$ (momentum $p = h/\lambda_1$) is:
$K = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m} = \dfrac{h^{2}}{2m\lambda_1^{2}}$
Equating the two expressions for $K$:
$\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{h^{2}}{2m\lambda_1^{2}}$
$\dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{h}{2m\lambda_1^{2}}$
$\lambda = \dfrac{2mc}{h}\lambda_1^{2}$
which is the required result.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
