(b) A plane surface, in shape of a square of side $1$ cm is placed in an electric field $\vec{E} = (100$ N/C $)\hat{i}$ such that the unit vector normal to the surface is given by $\hat{n} = 0.8\hat{i} + 0.6\hat{k}$. Find the electric flux through the surface. $[]_{-9} 2$
questions.answer:
(a) Electric flux through a surface is the total number of electric field lines passing through it, $\phi_E=\int \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}$. Dimensions: $[\phi_E]=[E][A]=(MLT^{-3}A^{-1})(L^2)=ML^3T^{-3}A^{-1}$.
(b) Area $A=(1\text{ cm})^2=1\times10^{-4}$ m$^2$, $\vec{E}=100\hat{i}$ N/C, $\hat{n}=0.8\hat{i}+0.6\hat{k}$.
$\phi_E=\vec{E}\cdot(A\hat{n})=100\times1\times10^{-4}\times0.8=8\times10^{-3}$ Nm$^2$/C.

questions.question: (a) A uniformly charged large plane sheet has charge density $\sigma =\frac{1}{18\pi}\times 10$ C/m. Find the electric field at point A which is $50$ cm from the sheet. (b) Consider a straight line with three points P, Q and R, placed $50$ cm from the charged sheet on the right side as shown in the figure. At which of these points, does the magnitude of the electric field due to the sheet remain the same as that at point A and why?
questions.answer:
(a) For an infinite charged sheet, $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, which is independent of the distance from the sheet.
Using $\sigma=\dfrac{1}{18\pi}\times10^{-9}$ C/m$^2$ and $\varepsilon_0=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\times9\times10^9}$, $E_A=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}=1$ N/C, directed away from the sheet.
(b) Since the field of an infinite plane sheet does not depend on the distance from it, the magnitude of the field at P, Q and R (all on the same, right side of the sheet) is the same as at A, equal to $1$ N/C.

questions.question: Two small identical conducting spheres carrying charge $10 \mu$ C and $-20 \mu$ C when separated by a distance of $r$, experience a force $F$ each. If they are brought in contact and then separated to a distance of $\frac{r}{2}$, what is the new force between them in terms of $F$?
questions.answer:
Initial force: $F=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2}=\dfrac{k(10)(20)\times10^{-12}}{r^2}$ (attractive, unlike charges).
On contact, charge redistributes equally: $q'=\dfrac{10+(-20)}{2}=-5\,\mu$C on each sphere.
New force at separation $\dfrac{r}{2}$: $F'=\dfrac{k(5)(5)\times10^{-12}}{(r/2)^2}=\dfrac{k(100)\times10^{-12}}{r^2}$.
Taking the ratio, $\dfrac{F'}{F}=\dfrac{100}{200}=\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $F'=\dfrac{F}{2}$, and since both charges are now negative, the force is repulsive (unlike the original attractive force).

questions.question: Two small identical electric dipoles AB and CD, each of dipole moment $\vec{p}$ are kept at an angle of $120^{^{\circ}}$ to each other in an external electric field $\vec{E}$ pointing along the $x$-axis as shown in the figure. Find the (a) dipole moment of the arrangement, and (b) magnitude and direction of the net torque acting on it. OR In the figure given below, find the (a) equivalent capacitance of the network between points A and B. Given: $C_{1} = C_{5} = 8 \mu$ F, $C_{2} = C_{3} = C_{4} = 4 \mu$ F. (b) maximum charge supplied by the battery, and (c) total energy stored in the network.
questions.answer:
(a) Both dipoles have equal moment $p$, inclined at $120^\circ$ to each other, so by symmetry each makes $60^\circ$ with the $x$-axis (bisector).
Net dipole moment: $p_{net}=\sqrt{p^2+p^2+2p^2\cos120^\circ}=\sqrt{2p^2-p^2}=p$, directed along the $x$-axis, i.e. along $\vec{E}$.
(b) Net torque $\tau=p_{net}E\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{p}_{net}$ and $\vec{E}$.
Since $\vec{p}_{net}$ is parallel to $\vec{E}$ ($\theta=0^\circ$), the net torque $\tau=0$.

questions.question: (a) Two electric field lines cannot cross each other. Also, they cannot form closed loops. Give reasons. (b) A particle of charge $2 \mu$ C and mass $1.6$ g is moving with a velocity $4\hat{i}$ m s $-1$. At $t = 0$ the particle enters in a region having an electric field $\vec{E}$ (in NC $-1$) $= 80\hat{i} + 60\hat{j}$. Find the velocity of the particle at $t = 5$ s. OR In the figure given below, find the (a) equivalent capacitance of the network between points A and B. Given: $C_{1} = C_{5} = 4 \mu$ F, $C_{2} = C_{3} = C_{4} = 2 \mu$ F. (b) maximum charge supplied by the battery, and (c) total energy stored in the network.
questions.answer:
Electric field lines cannot cross because at the point of intersection the field would have two different directions, but the electric field at any point is unique, so two lines meeting there is impossible.
They cannot form closed loops because the electrostatic field is conservative, i.e. $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l} = 0$; a closed loop line would mean the field does net work on a charge taken around it, back to the same point, which is not allowed for a static field. Field lines therefore start on positive charges and end on negative charges (or at infinity).
Acceleration: $a_x = \dfrac{qE_x}{m} = \dfrac{2\times10^{-6}\times80}{1.6\times10^{-3}} = 0.1$ m s$^{-2}$, $a_y = \dfrac{qE_y}{m} = \dfrac{2\times10^{-6}\times60}{1.6\times10^{-3}} = 0.075$ m s$^{-2}$.
Using $\vec{v} = \vec{u} + \vec{a}t$: $v_x = 4 + 0.1\times5 = 4.5$ m s$^{-1}$, $v_y = 0 + 0.075\times5 = 0.375$ m s$^{-1}$.
So $\vec{v} = 4.5\hat{i} + 0.375\hat{j}$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: A hollow conducting sphere of inner radius $r_{1}$ and outer radius $r_{2}$ has a charge $Q$ on its surface. A point charge $-q$ is also placed at the centre of the sphere. (a) What is the surface charge density on the (i) inner and (ii) outer surface of the sphere? (b) Use Gauss’ law of electrostatics to obtain the expression for the electric field at a point lying outside the sphere. OR (a) An infinitely long thin straight wire has a uniform linear charge density $\lambda$. Obtain the expression for the electric field $E$ at a point lying at a distance $x$ from the wire, using Gauss’ law. (b) Show graphically the variation of this electric field $E$ as a function of distance $x$ from the wire.
questions.answer:
(a) Inside the conductor $\vec{E} = 0$, so any Gaussian surface drawn within the shell must enclose zero net charge. Since $-q$ sits at the centre, the inner surface must carry induced charge $+q$, giving $\sigma_{\text{inner}} = \dfrac{q}{4\pi r_1^2}$.
Since the shell carries total charge $Q$, the outer surface carries $Q - q$, giving $\sigma_{\text{outer}} = \dfrac{Q-q}{4\pi r_2^2}$.
(b) For a point outside at distance $r > r_2$, choose a spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r$; the enclosed charge is $-q + Q = (Q-q)$.
By Gauss' law, $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = E(4\pi r^2) = \dfrac{Q-q}{\epsilon_0}$, so $E = \dfrac{Q-q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}$, directed radially outward if $Q > q$.

questions.question: Derive an expression for the electric field due to a dipole of dipole moment $\vec{p}$ at a point on its perpendicular bisector. $2$
questions.answer:
Consider a dipole with charges $+q$ at A and $-q$ at B, separated by $2a$, dipole moment $\vec{p} = q(2a)$ directed from B to A. Let P be a point on the perpendicular bisector at distance $r$ from the centre O.
Distance of P from each charge: $AP = BP = \sqrt{r^2+a^2}$.
Field due to $+q$: $E_{+q} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2+a^2}$, along the line from A to P.
Field due to $-q$: $E_{-q}$, same magnitude, along the line from P to B.
Components perpendicular to the dipole axis cancel by symmetry; components along the axis (anti-parallel to $\vec{p}$) add, each equal to $E_{+q}\cos\theta$, where $\cos\theta = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{r^2+a^2}}$.
Total field: $E = 2\cdot\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2+a^2}\cdot\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{r^2+a^2}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}}$, directed opposite to $\vec{p}$.
For $r \gg a$: $E \approx \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^3}$.

questions.question: Two large charged plane sheets of charge densities $\sigma$ and $-2\sigma$ C/mare arranged vertically with a separation of $d$ between them. Deduce expressions for the electric field at points (i) to the left of the first sheet, (ii) to the right of the second sheet, and (iii) between the two sheets. OR A spherical conducting shell of inner radius $r_{1}$ and outer radius $r_{2}$ has a charge $Q$. (a) A charge $q$ is placed at the centre of the shell. Find out the surface charge density on the inner and outer surfaces of the shell. (b) Is the electric field inside a cavity (with no charge) zero; independent of the fact whether the shell is spherical or not? Explain.
questions.answer:
Field of an infinite sheet has magnitude $\dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$, directed away from a positive sheet and towards a negative sheet. Let sheet 1 ($\sigma$) be to the left of sheet 2 ($-2\sigma$), separated by $d$; take rightward as positive.
(i) Left of sheet 1: $E_1 = -\dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$ (away from sheet 1), $E_2 = +\dfrac{2\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$ (towards sheet 2). Net: $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$, directed towards the sheets.
(ii) Right of sheet 2: $E_1 = +\dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$, $E_2 = -\dfrac{2\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$. Net: $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$, directed towards the sheets.
(iii) Between the sheets: $E_1 = +\dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$, $E_2 = +\dfrac{2\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$. Net: $E = \dfrac{3\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$, directed from the positive sheet to the negative sheet.

questions.question: Four point charges $Q$, $q$, $Q$ and $q$ are placed at the corners of a square of side ’ $a$’ as shown in the figure. Find the (a) resultant electric force on a charge $Q$, and (b) potential energy of this system.
questions.answer:
(a) Let charges $Q, q, Q, q$ occupy corners A, B, C, D of the square in order, so Q at A has neighbours $q$ at B and D (distance $a$) and the other charge $Q$ at C (diagonal distance $a\sqrt2$).
Force from each neighbouring $q$: $F_1 = F_2 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{Qq}{a^2}$, mutually perpendicular; their resultant is $\sqrt2\,\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{Qq}{a^2}$, directed along the diagonal AC.
Force from the diagonal charge: $F_3 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{Q^2}{2a^2}$, also along AC.
Since both act along the same diagonal, total force on Q: $F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0 a^2}\left(\sqrt2\,Qq + \dfrac{Q^2}{2}\right)$, directed along the diagonal AC.
(b) Summing potential energy of all six pairs (four $Qq$ pairs at distance $a$, and $QQ$, $qq$ pairs at distance $a\sqrt2$):
$U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0 a}\left(4Qq + \dfrac{Q^2+q^2}{\sqrt2}\right)$.

questions.question: (a) Three point charges $q$, $-4q$ and $2q$ are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle $ABC$ of side ’ $l$’ as shown in the figure. Obtain the expression for the magnitude of the resultant electric force acting on the charge $q$. (b) Find out the amount of the work done to separate the charges at infinite distance.
questions.answer:
(a) Let $q$ be at A, $-4q$ at B, $2q$ at C of the equilateral triangle, side $l$.
Force on $q$ due to $-4q$: $F_1 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{4q^2}{l^2}$, attractive, directed along AB.
Force on $q$ due to $2q$: $F_2 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{2q^2}{l^2}$, repulsive, directed away from C, along CA extended.
The angle between $F_1$ and $F_2$ is $120^\circ$ (since $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$).
Resultant: $F = \sqrt{F_1^2+F_2^2+2F_1F_2\cos120^\circ} = \sqrt{F_1^2+F_2^2-F_1F_2}$, which gives $F = 2\sqrt3\,\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q^2}{l^2}$.
(b) Potential energy of the system: $U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0 l}\left[q(-4q) + (-4q)(2q) + (2q)(q)\right] = -\dfrac{10q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 l}$.
Work done to separate the charges to infinity equals $-U$ (since $U_\infty = 0$): $W = \dfrac{10q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 l}$.

questions.question: Four point charges Q, q, Q and q are placed at the corners of a square of side ’a’ as shown in the figure. Find the (a) resultant electric force on a charge Q, and (b) potential energy of this system. OR (a) Three point charges q, −4q and 2q are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle ABC of side ’ $l$’ as shown in the figure. Obtain the expression for the magnitude of the resultant electric force acting on the charge q. (b) Find out the amount of the work done to separate the charges at infinite distance.
questions.answer:
Let square $ABCD$ have $Q$ at $A$, $q$ at $B$, $Q$ at $C$ (diagonal to $A$), $q$ at $D$.
(a) Force on $Q$ at $A$ due to $q$ at $B$ and $q$ at $D$: each of magnitude $\frac{kQq}{a^2}$, mutually perpendicular, resultant $= \sqrt2\frac{kQq}{a^2}$ along diagonal $AC$.
Force due to $Q$ at $C$: $\frac{kQ^2}{2a^2}$, also along $AC$.
Total resultant force $= \sqrt2\dfrac{kQq}{a^2}+\dfrac{kQ^2}{2a^2}$, directed along the diagonal $AC$.
(b) $U=k\left[\dfrac{4Qq}{a}+\dfrac{Q^2+q^2}{\sqrt2\,a}\right]$, where $k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}$.

OR
Let $q$ be at $A$, $-4q$ at $B$, $2q$ at $C$ of equilateral triangle side $l$.
(a) Force on $q$ due to $-4q$: $F_1=\dfrac{4kq^2}{l^2}$ (attractive, along $AB$).
Force due to $2q$: $F_2=\dfrac{2kq^2}{l^2}$ (repulsive, along extension of $CA$), angle between them $120°$.
$F=\sqrt{F_1^2+F_2^2+2F_1F_2\cos120°}=\dfrac{2\sqrt3\,kq^2}{l^2}$
(b) $U=k\left[\dfrac{q(-4q)}{l}+\dfrac{(-4q)(2q)}{l}+\dfrac{(2q)(q)}{l}\right]=-\dfrac{10kq^2}{l}$
Work done to separate to infinity $=-U=\dfrac{10kq^2}{l}$

questions.question: (i) Derive the expression for electric field at a point on the equatorial line of an electric dipole. (ii) Depict the orientation of the dipole in (i) stable, (ii) unstable equilibrium in a uniform electric field.
questions.answer:
(i) Consider dipole $-q$ at $-a$ and $+q$ at $+a$; point $P$ on equatorial line at distance $r$ from centre.
Field due to each charge has magnitude $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2+a^2}$; axial components cancel, perpendicular (to axis) components add.
$E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{2qa}{(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}}$, directed opposite to $\vec p$.
For $r\gg a$: $E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^3}$
(ii) Stable equilibrium: $\vec p$ parallel to $\vec E$ ($\theta=0°$).
Unstable equilibrium: $\vec p$ antiparallel to $\vec E$ ($\theta=180°$).

questions.question: (i) Obtain the expression for the torque $\tau$ experienced by an electric dipole of dipole moment $\vec{p}$ in a uniform electric field, $\vec{E}$. (ii) What will happen if the field were not uniform?
questions.answer:
(i) Dipole of charges $+q,-q$ separated by $2a$, placed in field $\vec E$ making angle $\theta$ with $\vec p$.
Force on $+q$ = $qE$, on $-q$ = $qE$, equal and opposite, forming a couple.
Perpendicular distance between the two forces $=2a\sin\theta$.
Torque $=$ force $\times$ perpendicular distance $=qE(2a\sin\theta)=(q\cdot2a)E\sin\theta=pE\sin\theta$
In vector form, $\vec\tau=\vec p\times\vec E$.
(ii) If the field is non-uniform, the two equal and opposite forces $qE$ act at points of different field strength, so they no longer cancel; the dipole experiences a net force in addition to the torque, resulting in both translational and rotational motion.

questions.question: A long charged cylinder of linear charge density $+\lambda_{1}$ is surrounded by a hollow coaxial conducting cylinder of linear charge density $-\lambda_{2}$. Use Gauss’s law to obtain expressions for the electric field at a point (i) in the space between the cylinders, and (ii) outside the larger cylinder.
questions.answer:
Take a coaxial Gaussian cylinder of radius $r$ and length $l$.
(i) Between the cylinders ($a<r<b$): charge enclosed $=\lambda_1 l$.
By Gauss's law, $E(2\pi r l)=\dfrac{\lambda_1 l}{\epsilon_0}$
$E=\dfrac{\lambda_1}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$, directed radially outward.
(ii) Outside the larger cylinder ($r>b$): charge enclosed $=\lambda_1 l-\lambda_2 l$.
$E(2\pi r l)=\dfrac{(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)l}{\epsilon_0}$
$E=\dfrac{\lambda_1-\lambda_2}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$

questions.question: Define electric flux. Write its SI unit. Using Gauss’s law, deduce an expression for electric field intensity due to an infinitely long straight uniformly charged wire.
questions.answer:
Electric flux through a surface is the total number of electric field lines crossing it, $\phi=\vec E\cdot\vec A$ (or $\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A$ for a general surface). SI unit: $\text{N m}^2\text{C}^{-1}$.
For an infinite line charge of linear density $\lambda$, take a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $r$, length $l$.
By symmetry $\vec E$ is radial and constant in magnitude on the curved surface; flux through the flat ends is zero.
$\phi=E(2\pi r l)$, charge enclosed $=\lambda l$
$E(2\pi r l)=\dfrac{\lambda l}{\epsilon_0}$
$E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$, directed radially outward (for $\lambda>0$).

questions.question: Using Gauss’s law in electrostatics, deduce an expression for electric field intensity due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet. If another identical sheet is placed parallel to it, show that there is no electric field in the region between the two sheets.
questions.answer:
Consider an infinite plane sheet of surface charge density $\sigma$. Take a cylindrical (pillbox) Gaussian surface of cross-sectional area $A$, straddling the sheet symmetrically.
By symmetry, $\vec E$ is perpendicular to the sheet and equal in magnitude on both faces; flux through the curved surface is zero.
$\phi=EA+EA=2EA$, charge enclosed $=\sigma A$
$2EA=\dfrac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_0}\Rightarrow E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$, directed away from the sheet on each side.
If a second identical sheet (same $\sigma$) is placed parallel to the first, in the region between them the field of each sheet ($\sigma/2\epsilon_0$) points toward the other sheet, i.e., in opposite directions, so they cancel and the net field between the sheets is zero.

questions.question: A thin metallic spherical shell of radius $R$ carries a charge $Q$ on its surface. A point charge $Q/2$ is placed at the centre $C$ and another charge $+2Q$ is placed outside the shell at $A$ at a distance $x$ from the centre as shown in the figure. (i) Find the electric flux through the shell. (ii) State the law used. (iii) Find the force on the charges at the centre $C$ of the shell and at the point $A$.
questions.answer:
By Gauss's law, $\phi = \dfrac{q_{enc}}{\epsilon_0} = \dfrac{Q+Q/2}{\epsilon_0} = \dfrac{3Q}{2\epsilon_0}$; the charge $+2Q$ at $A$ lies outside the shell (Gaussian surface) and does not contribute.
Law used: Gauss's law, $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = q_{enc}/\epsilon_0$.
Force on charge at $C$: the shell's own charge produces zero field at any interior point (including the centre), so the net force on $Q/2$ at $C$ is zero.
Force on charge at $A$: for points outside, the shell (charge $Q$) and the central charge $Q/2$ together act like a point charge $3Q/2$ at the centre, so $F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{(3Q/2)(2Q)}{x^2} = \dfrac{3Q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 x^2}$, directed radially outward along $CA$ (repulsive).

questions.question: Find the electric field intensity due to a uniformly charged spherical shell at a point (i) outside the shell and (ii) inside the shell. Plot the graph of electric field with distance from the centre of the shell.
questions.answer:
(i) Outside ($r>R$): a Gaussian sphere of radius $r$ encloses the whole charge $Q$, so $E(4\pi r^2) = Q/\epsilon_0$, giving $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r^2}$, same as a point charge $Q$ at the centre.
(ii) Inside ($r<R$): the Gaussian sphere encloses no charge (all charge resides on the surface), so $E(4\pi r^2) = 0$, giving $E = 0$.
Graph: $E$ is zero for $0 \le r < R$, rises discontinuously to $E = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^2}$ at $r=R$, and then falls off as $1/r^2$ for $r>R$.

questions.question: Derive an expression for the electric field intensity at a point on the equatorial line of an electric dipole of dipole moment $\vec{P}$ and length $2a$. What is the direction of this field?
questions.answer:
Consider a dipole with $+q$ at $B$ and $-q$ at $A$, separated by $2a$, and a point $P$ on the equatorial line at distance $r$ from the centre $O$.
Distance of $P$ from each charge $= \sqrt{r^2+a^2}$, so each field has magnitude $E_+ = E_- = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2+a^2}$.
By symmetry the components of $E_+$ and $E_-$ perpendicular to the dipole axis cancel, while the components along the axis (antiparallel to $\vec{P}$) add.
Each axial component $= E_+ \cos\theta$, with $\cos\theta = a/\sqrt{r^2+a^2}$, so the resultant is $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{2qa}{(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{P}{(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}}$.
This field is directed opposite to $\vec{P}$ (antiparallel to the dipole moment).

questions.question: State Gauss’s law in electrostatics. A cube with each side ’ $a$’ is kept in an electric field given by $\vec{E} = Cx\hat{i}$, (as is shown in the figure) where $C$ is a positive dimensional constant. Find out (i) the electric flux through the cube, and (ii) the net charge inside the cube.
questions.answer:
Gauss's law: the total electric flux through any closed surface equals $1/\epsilon_0$ times the net charge enclosed, $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = q_{enc}/\epsilon_0$.
(i) For the cube, $\vec{E} = Cx\hat{i}$ has flux only through the two faces perpendicular to $x$: the face at $x=0$ has $E=0$, and the face at $x=a$ has $E = Ca$. Flux $= Ca\cdot a^2 - 0 = Ca^3$ (through other four faces $\vec{E}\perp d\vec{A}$, so flux $=0$).
(ii) By Gauss's law, $q_{enc} = \epsilon_0 \phi = \epsilon_0 C a^3$.

questions.question: Using Gauss’s law obtain the expression for the electric field due to a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius $R$ at a point outside the shell. Draw a graph showing the variation of electric field with $r$, for $r > R$ and $r < R$.
questions.answer:
Consider a spherical shell of radius $R$ with charge $Q$ uniformly distributed on its surface. To find $E$ at a point outside at distance $r>R$, take a concentric Gaussian sphere of radius $r$. By symmetry $\vec{E}$ is radial and constant in magnitude over this surface, so $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = E(4\pi r^2)$.
By Gauss's law this equals $Q/\epsilon_0$, giving $E(4\pi r^2) = Q/\epsilon_0$, so $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r^2}$, directed radially outward — same as a point charge $Q$ at the centre.
Graph: $E=0$ for $r<R$; at $r=R$, $E = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^2}$; for $r>R$, $E$ falls off as $1/r^2$.

questions.question: A thin conducting spherical shell of radius $R$ has charge $Q$ spread uniformly over its surface. Using Gauss’s law, derive an expression for an electric field at a point outside the shell. Draw a graph of electric field $E(r)$ with distance $r$ from the centre of the shell for $0 \leq r \leq\in fty$.
questions.answer:
Let the shell of radius $R$ carry charge $Q$ uniformly on its surface. For a point outside at distance $r>R$, choose a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r$. By symmetry $\vec{E}$ is radial and has the same magnitude everywhere on this surface, so $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = E(4\pi r^2) = q_{enc}/\epsilon_0 = Q/\epsilon_0$.
This gives $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r^2}$, directed radially outward, as though the entire charge were concentrated at the centre.
Graph of $E(r)$: zero for $0\le r<R$ (no enclosed charge), a sudden jump to $E = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^2}$ at $r=R$, then a smooth $1/r^2$ decrease as $r\to\infty$.

questions.question: State Gauss’s theorem in electrostatics. Apply this theorem to derive an expression for electric field intensity at a point near an infinitely long straight charged wire.
questions.answer:
Gauss's theorem: the total electric flux through any closed surface equals $1/\epsilon_0$ times the net charge enclosed, $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = q_{enc}/\epsilon_0$.
For an infinite line charge of linear density $\lambda$, choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ and length $l$, coaxial with the wire.
By symmetry $\vec{E}$ is radial and equal in magnitude at every point on the curved surface; flux through the flat ends is zero as $\vec{E}$ is parallel to them.
So $E(2\pi r l) = \lambda l/\epsilon_0$, giving $E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$, directed radially outward (for $\lambda>0$).

questions.question: What is electric flux? Write its S.I. units. Using Gauss’s theorem, deduce an expression for the electric field at a point due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet.
questions.answer:
Electric flux through a surface is the measure of the number of field lines crossing it, $\phi_E = \oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}$; its S.I. unit is $\text{N m}^2\text{C}^{-1}$ (or V m).
For an infinite plane sheet of surface charge density $\sigma$, take a cylindrical (pillbox) Gaussian surface with its flat faces of area $A$ parallel to the sheet, symmetric about it.
By symmetry $\vec{E}$ is perpendicular to the sheet on both faces, and flux through the curved surface is zero.
Total flux $= EA + EA = 2EA$, and $q_{enc} = \sigma A$, so $2EA = \sigma A/\epsilon_0$, giving $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$, directed away from the sheet on both sides.

questions.question: An electric dipole is held in a uniform electric field. (i) Using a suitable diagram, show that it does not undergo any translatory motion, and (ii) derive an expression for the torque acting on it and specify its direction.
questions.answer:
(i) In a uniform field $\vec{E}$, the force on $+q$ is $q\vec{E}$ along the field and on $-q$ is $q\vec{E}$ opposite to the field; these are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so the net force on the dipole is zero and it does not undergo translatory motion.
(ii) Since the two forces act at different points (separated by $2a\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{p}$ and $\vec{E}$), they form a couple.
Torque $= qE(2a\sin\theta) = (2qa)E\sin\theta = pE\sin\theta$, i.e. $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p}\times\vec{E}$.
Its direction is perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec{p}$ and $\vec{E}$, given by the right-hand rule, and it tends to align $\vec{p}$ along $\vec{E}$.

questions.question: State Gauss’ theorem in electrostatics. Using this theorem, derive the expression for the electric field intensity at any point outside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell.
questions.answer:
Gauss's theorem: the total electric flux through a closed surface equals $q_{enc}/\epsilon_0$, i.e. $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = q_{enc}/\epsilon_0$.
For a thin spherical shell of charge $q$ and radius $R$, consider a Gaussian sphere of radius $r > R$, concentric with the shell.
By symmetry $\vec{E}$ has the same magnitude at every point of this surface and is directed radially, so $E(4\pi r^2) = q/\epsilon_0$.
Hence $E = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2} = \dfrac{kq}{r^2}$, directed radially outward, showing the shell behaves as if the entire charge were concentrated at its centre.

questions.question: A beam of electrons moving horizontally with a velocity of $3 \times 10^{7}$ m/s enters a region between two plates as shown in the figure. A suitable potential difference is applied across the plates such that the electron beam just strikes the edge of the lower plate. Answer the following questions based on the above: (a) How long does an electron take to strike the edge? (b) What is the shape of the path followed by the electron and why? (c) Find the potential difference applied. OR (c) Find the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field which should be created in the space between the plates so that the electron beam goes straight undeviated.
questions.answer:
(i) Inside the plates the horizontal velocity $v = 3\times10^{7}$ m/s stays unchanged since no force acts along that direction, so if $l$ is the length of the plates, the time taken is $t = l/v$.
(ii) The electric field between the plates gives the electron a constant acceleration perpendicular to its initial velocity, exactly like a horizontally projected object under gravity; combining uniform horizontal motion with uniformly accelerated vertical motion produces a parabolic path.
(iii) If $d$ is the plate separation and the electron enters along the centre line, it must deflect $y = d/2$ to just graze the lower plate: $y = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ with $a = eV/(md)$ ($V$ = applied p.d., $m$ = electron mass), so $V = \dfrac{md^2}{e t^2}$.
OR (iii) For the beam to go straight, the magnetic force must balance the electric force: $evB = eE$, so $B = E/v = V/(vd)$, directed perpendicular to both $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{E}$ (into or out of the plane) such that $\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ opposes $\vec{E}$, as given by the right-hand rule.

questions.question: (a) An electric dipole consists of two point charges $q$ and $-q$ separated by a distance $2a$. Derive an expression for the electric field $\vec{E}$ due to this dipole at a point distant $r$ from the centre of the dipole on the equatorial plane. Write the expression for the electric field at a far off point, i.e. $r >> a$. (b) A dipole is placed in $x$- $y$ plane such that charges $q$ and $-q$ are located at $x = a$ and $x = b$ respectively. There exists an electric field $\vec{E} = 2x\hat{i}$ N/C in the region. Calculate the force $\vec{F}$ and torque $\tau$ experienced by the dipole. OR (a) Two cells of emf $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ with internal resistances $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ respectively, are connected in parallel by connecting their positive terminals together and negative terminals together. Deduce an expression for equivalent emf and equivalent internal resistance of the combination. (b) A parallel combination, as stated in (a) above, of two cells of emfs $E$ and $3E$ and internal resistances $R$ each is connected across a resistance $2R$. Find the current that flows through resistance $2R$.
questions.answer:
(a) Let $+q$ at A and $-q$ at B be separated by $2a$, and P lie on the equatorial line at distance $r$ from centre O.
Distance $AP = BP = \sqrt{r^2+a^2}$, so $E_A = E_B = \dfrac{kq}{r^2+a^2}$, directed along AP and PB respectively.
Components along the dipole axis cancel; components perpendicular to it add, giving $E = 2E_A\cos\theta$ with $\cos\theta = a/\sqrt{r^2+a^2}$.
So $E = \dfrac{2kqa}{(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{kp}{(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}}$, directed opposite to $\vec{p}$, where $p = 2qa$.
For $r >> a$: $E \approx \dfrac{p}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}$.
(b) Dipole moment $\vec{p} = q(a-b)\hat{i}$ (from $-q$ at $x=b$ to $+q$ at $x=a$).
Force: $\vec{F} = q\vec{E}(a) - q\vec{E}(b) = q(2a)\hat{i} - q(2b)\hat{i} = 2q(a-b)\hat{i}$ N, nonzero because the field is non-uniform.
Torque: $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p}\times\vec{E} = 0$, since $\vec{p}$ and $\vec{E}$ are both along $\hat{i}$ (parallel).

OR (a) With terminal p.d. $V$: $I_1 = (E_1-V)/r_1$, $I_2 = (E_2-V)/r_2$, total $I = I_1+I_2$.
Writing this as $I = (E_{eq}-V)/r_{eq}$ gives $E_{eq} = \dfrac{E_1 r_2 + E_2 r_1}{r_1+r_2}$ and $\dfrac{1}{r_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{r_1}+\dfrac{1}{r_2}$, i.e. $r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1 r_2}{r_1+r_2}$.
(b) Here $E_1=E$, $E_2=3E$, $r_1=r_2=R$: $E_{eq} = \dfrac{ER+3ER}{2R} = 2E$, and $r_{eq} = \dfrac{R^2}{2R} = R/2$.
With external resistance $2R$: $I = \dfrac{E_{eq}}{r_{eq}+2R} = \dfrac{2E}{R/2+2R} = \dfrac{4E}{5R}$.

questions.question: (i) Two infinitely long straight wires having linear charge densities $-\lambda$ and $3\lambda$ are held vertically parallel to each other, distance $r$ apart in free space. Find the nature and magnitude of the force/length exerted by one wire on the other.
questions.answer:
The field at distance $r$ from an infinite line charge of linear density $\lambda$ is $E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$, directed radially outward (or inward if $\lambda$ is negative).
Force per unit length on wire 2 (density $\lambda_2$) due to the field of wire 1 (density $\lambda_1$) at separation $r$ is $f = \lambda_2 E_1 = \frac{\lambda_1 \lambda_2}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$.
Here $\lambda_1 = -\lambda$, $\lambda_2 = 3\lambda$, so $f = \frac{-3\lambda^2}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$; magnitude $f = \frac{3\lambda^2}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$ per unit length.
Since the charge densities are of opposite sign, the force between the wires is attractive.

questions.question: (ii) A small hollow conducting sphere of radius $r_{1}$ is given a charge $Q$. It is surrounded by a concentric conducting spherical shell of inner radius $r_{2}$ and outer radius $r_{3}$, having charge $-3Q$. If a point charge $2q$ were kept at the centre, find: (I) the electric flux through a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius $x$ for (1) $x < r_{1}$, and (2) $r_{1} < x < r_{2}$. (II) electric field at a point distant $x$ from the centre for (1) $x > r_{3}$, and (2) $r_{1} < x < r_{2}$. (III) surface charge density on the inner surface of (1) sphere, and (2) shell.
questions.answer:
(I)(1) For $x < r_1$, only the point charge $2q$ at the centre is enclosed: $\phi = \frac{2q}{\epsilon_0}$.
(2) For $r_1 < x < r_2$, enclosed charge is $2q + Q$: $\phi = \frac{2q+Q}{\epsilon_0}$.
(II)(1) For $x > r_3$, total enclosed charge is $2q + Q - 3Q = 2q - 2Q$, so $E = \frac{2q-2Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 x^2}$, directed radially.
(2) For $r_1 < x < r_2$, $E = \frac{2q+Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 x^2}$, directed radially outward.
(III)(1) The point charge $2q$ induces $-2q$ on the inner surface of the sphere (radius $r_1$), so $\sigma = \frac{-2q}{4\pi r_1^2}$.
(2) The charge enclosed within the shell's cavity is $2q+Q$, inducing $-(2q+Q)$ on its inner surface (radius $r_2$), so $\sigma = \frac{-(2q+Q)}{4\pi r_2^2}$.

questions.question: (i) What is difference between an open surface and a closed surface? Draw elementary surface vector $d\vec{S}$ for a spherical surface S. (ii) Define electric flux through a surface. Give the significance of a Gaussian surface. A charge outside a Gaussian surface does not contribute to total electric flux through the surface. Why? (iii) A small spherical shell $S_{1}$ has point charges $q_{1} = -3 \mu$ C, $q_{2} = -2 \mu$ C and $q_{3} = 9 \mu$ C inside it. This shell is enclosed by another big spherical shell $S_{2}$. A point charge Q is placed in between the two surfaces $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$. If the electric flux through the surface $S_{2}$ is four times the flux through surface $S_{1}$, find charge Q.
questions.answer:
(i) An open surface has a boundary edge and two distinguishable sides (e.g. a disc or hemispherical cap); a closed surface encloses a volume and has no boundary edge (e.g. a sphere). For a spherical surface $S$, the elemental vector $d\vec{S}$ at every point is directed radially outward along the outward normal, with magnitude equal to the elemental area.
(ii) Electric flux through a surface is $d\phi = \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S}$, integrated over the surface; it measures the number of field lines crossing it. A Gaussian surface is an imaginary closed surface chosen so that $\vec{E}$ is either constant and normal, zero, or perpendicular to $d\vec{S}$ over parts of it, making $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S}$ easy to evaluate and charge easy to determine. A charge outside contributes zero net flux because every field line from it that enters the surface also leaves it, so the entering and leaving contributions cancel.
(iii) Flux through $S_1$: $\phi_1 = \frac{q_1+q_2+q_3}{\epsilon_0} = \frac{4\,\mu C}{\epsilon_0}$.
Flux through $S_2$: $\phi_2 = \frac{q_1+q_2+q_3+Q}{\epsilon_0} = \frac{(4\,\mu C + Q)}{\epsilon_0}$.
Given $\phi_2 = 4\phi_1$: $4 + Q = 16$, so $Q = 12\,\mu C$.

questions.question: (a) (i) Two point charges $+q$ and $-q$ are held at $(a, 0)$ and $(-a, 0)$ in $x$- $y$ plane. Obtain an expression for the net electric field due to the charges at a point $(0, y)$. Hence, find electric field at a far off point $(y \gg a)$. (ii) Three point charges of $-2$ nC, $-1$ nC, and $+5$ nC are kept at the vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ of an equilateral triangle of side $0.2$ m. Find the total amount of work done in shifting the charges from $A$ to $A_{1}$, $B$ to $B_{1}$ and $C$ to $C_{1}$. Here $A_{1}$, $B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ are the midpoints of sides $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$, respectively. OR (b) (i) Show that Gauss’s theorem is consistent with Coulomb’s law. Using it, derive an expression for the electric field due to a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius $r$ at a point at a distance $y$ from the centre of the shell such that (I) $y > r$, and (II) $y < r$. (ii) A point charge of $+2$ nC is kept at the origin of a threedimensional coordinate system. Find the type and magnitude of the charge which should be kept at $(0, 0, -6$ m $)$ so that the potential due to the system becomes zero at $(0, 0, 2$ m $)$.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Distance of $(0,y)$ from each charge is $\sqrt{a^2+y^2}$, and each field has magnitude $\frac{kq}{a^2+y^2}$.
By symmetry the $y$-components cancel and the $x$-components add, both pointing along $-x$ (antiparallel to $\vec{p}$, which points from $-q$ to $+q$).
Net field: $E = \frac{2kqa}{(a^2+y^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{p}{4\pi\epsilon_0 (a^2+y^2)^{3/2}}$, where $p = 2qa$, directed along $-x$.
For $y \gg a$: $E \approx \frac{p}{4\pi\epsilon_0 y^3}$, directed opposite to $\vec{p}$.
(ii) Initial side $r = 0.2$ m, final side (joining midpoints) $r' = 0.1$ m.
Sum of pairwise products: $q_Aq_B+q_Bq_C+q_Cq_A = (-2)(-1)+(-1)(5)+(5)(-2) = -13\ (\text{nC})^2$.
$W = U_f - U_i = k(-13\times10^{-18})\left(\frac{1}{0.1}-\frac{1}{0.2}\right) = 9\times10^9 \times(-13\times10^{-18})\times5$
$W = -5.85 \times 10^{-7}$ J.

questions.question: (a) (i) Obtain an expression for the electric potential due to a small dipole of dipole moment $\vec{p}$, at a point $\vec{r}$ from its centre, for much larger distances compared to the size of the dipole. (ii) Three point charges q, 2q and nq are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. If the potential energy of the system is zero, find the value of n. OR (b) (i) State Gauss’s Law in electrostatics. Apply this to obtain the electric field $\vec{E}$ at a point near a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet. (ii) Two long straight wires 1 and 2 are kept as shown in the figure. The linear charge density of the two wires are $\lambda_{1} = 10 \mu C/m$ and $\lambda_{2} = -20 \mu C/m$. Find the net force $\vec{F}$ experienced by an electron held at point P.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) For a dipole of charges $+q$ at distance $\frac{a}{r_1}$-type separations from a far point $P$ (position vector $\vec{r}$, $r \gg a$), the potentials add as $V = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{r_1}-\frac{1}{r_2}\right)$.
Using $r_1 \approx r - a\cos\theta$, $r_2 \approx r + a\cos\theta$ and binomial approximation:
$V = \frac{p\cos\theta}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{r}$ and dipole moment $\vec{p} = q(2a)$.
(ii) For charges $q$, $2q$, $nq$ at vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $d$:
$U = \frac{k}{d}\left[q(2q) + (2q)(nq) + (nq)(q)\right] = \frac{kq^2}{d}(2+3n)$.
Setting $U = 0$: $2 + 3n = 0 \Rightarrow n = -\frac{2}{3}$.

questions.question: (i) A charge $+Q$ is placed on a thin conducting spherical shell of radius $R$. Use Gauss’s theorem to derive an expression for the electric field at a point lying (i) inside and (ii) outside the shell. (ii) Show that the electric field for same charge density ($\sigma$) is twice in case of a conducting plate or surface than in a nonconducting sheet.
questions.answer:
(i) Choose a spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ concentric with the shell.
Inside ($r < R$): the Gaussian surface encloses no charge, so by $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} = \frac{q_{enc}}{\epsilon_0}$, $E = 0$.
Outside ($r > R$): enclosed charge is $Q$, and by symmetry $E$ is radial and uniform over the surface, so $E(4\pi r^2) = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0}$, giving $E = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}$, directed radially outward, same as that of a point charge $Q$ at the centre.
(ii) For a non-conducting sheet of surface charge density $\sigma$, charge exists on a single (geometric) surface with field lines emerging symmetrically on both sides; applying Gauss's law to a pillbox gives $2E\cdot A = \frac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_0}$, so $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$.
For a charged conductor, all charge resides on the outer surface and the field inside the conductor is zero; a pillbox straddling the surface then gives flux only through the outer face: $E\cdot A = \frac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_0}$, so $E = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}$.
Thus for the same $\sigma$, the field just outside a conductor is twice that of a non-conducting sheet.

questions.question: (i) Using Gauss’s law, show that the electric field $\vec{E}$ at a point due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet is given by $\vec{E} = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_{0}}\hat{n}$ where symbols have their usual meanings. (ii) Electric field $\vec{E}$ in a region is given by $\vec{E} = (5x^{2} + 2)\hat{i}$, where $E$ is in N/C and $x$ is in meters. A cube of side $10$ cm is placed in the region as shown in figure. Calculate (1) the electric flux through the cube, and (2) the net charge enclosed by the cube.
questions.answer:
(i) Choose a cylindrical (pill-box) Gaussian surface with flat circular faces of area $A$, one on each side of the sheet, axis perpendicular to it.
By symmetry $\vec{E}$ is perpendicular to the sheet with equal magnitude on both faces, so flux through the curved surface is zero and total flux $=EA+EA=2EA$.
Enclosed charge $=\sigma A$, so by Gauss's law $2EA=\sigma A/\varepsilon_0$, giving $E=\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$, directed away from the sheet along $\hat n$.
(ii) $\vec E$ has only an $x$-component, so flux is only through the two faces perpendicular to $x$-axis (side $L=0.1$ m), taken at $x=0$ and $x=0.1$ m.
At $x=0$: $E=2$ N/C, inward normal, $\Phi_1=-2\times(0.1)^2=-0.02$ N m$^2$/C
At $x=0.1$: $E=5(0.1)^2+2=2.05$ N/C, outward normal, $\Phi_2=2.05\times(0.1)^2=0.0205$ N m$^2$/C
Net flux $\Phi=5\times10^{-4}$ N m$^2$/C
$q=\varepsilon_0\Phi=8.85\times10^{-12}\times5\times10^{-4}=4.43\times10^{-15}$ C

questions.question: (i) A thin spherical shell of radius $R$ has a uniform surface charge density $\sigma$. Using Gauss’ law, deduce an expression for electric field (i) outside and (ii) inside the shell. (ii) Two long straight thin wires AB and CD have linear charge densities $10 \mu$ C/m and $-20 \mu$ C/m, respectively. They are kept parallel to each other at a distance $1$ m. Find magnitude and direction of the net electric field at a point midway between them.
questions.answer:
(i) Take a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r$.
Outside ($r>R$): enclosed charge $q=\sigma\times4\pi R^2$; by symmetry $\vec E$ is radial and uniform, so $E\times4\pi r^2=q/\varepsilon_0$, giving $E=\dfrac{\sigma R^2}{\varepsilon_0 r^2}$, directed radially outward.
Inside ($r<R$): $q_{enc}=0$, so $E=0$.
(ii) $E_1$ (due to AB, $+10\,\mu$C/m) at $r=0.5$ m: $E_1=\dfrac{2\times9\times10^9\times10\times10^{-6}}{0.5}=3.6\times10^5$ N/C, directed from AB towards CD.
$E_2$ (due to CD, $-20\,\mu$C/m) at $r=0.5$ m: $E_2=\dfrac{2\times9\times10^9\times20\times10^{-6}}{0.5}=7.2\times10^5$ N/C, also directed towards CD.
Both fields act in the same direction, so $E_{net}=E_1+E_2=1.08\times10^6$ N/C, directed from AB towards CD.

questions.question: (i) State Coulomb’s law in electrostatics and write it in vector form, for two charges. (ii) ’Gauss’s law is based on the inverse-square dependence on distance contained in the Coulomb’s law.’ Explain. (iii) Two charges $A$ (charge $q$) and $B$ (charge $2q$) are located at points $(0, 0)$ and $(a, a)$ respectively. Let $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ be the unit vectors along $x$-axis and $y$-axis respectively. Find the force exerted by $A$ on $B$, in terms of $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$.
questions.answer:
(i) Coulomb's law: the force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, acting along the line joining them.
Vector form: $\vec F_{12}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}\hat r_{21}$
(ii) By Gauss's law, $\Phi=\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=q/\varepsilon_0$. For a point charge $E\propto 1/r^2$, while the area of a spherical Gaussian surface $\propto r^2$, so $E\times A$ is independent of $r$; flux depends only on enclosed charge. This cancellation works only because Coulomb's law is inverse-square — for any other power of $r$, flux would depend on $r$ and Gauss's law would not hold.
(iii) $\vec r_{AB}=a\hat i+a\hat j$, $|\vec r_{AB}|=a\sqrt2$, $\hat r=\dfrac{\hat i+\hat j}{\sqrt2}$
$F=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q(2q)}{2a^2}=\dfrac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a^2}$
$\vec F=\dfrac{q^2}{4\sqrt2\,\pi\varepsilon_0 a^2}(\hat i+\hat j)$, directed from A to B.

questions.question: (i) Derive an expression for the electric field at a point on the equatorial plane of an electric dipole consisting of charges $q$ and $-q$ separated by a distance $2a$. (ii) The distance of a far off point on the equatorial plane of an electric dipole is halved. How will the electric field be affected for the dipole? (iii) Two identical electric dipoles are placed along the diagonals of a square $ABCD$ of side $\sqrt{2}$ m as shown in the figure. Obtain the magnitude and direction of the net electric field at the centre $(O)$ of the square.
questions.answer:
(i) Consider $+q$ at distance $a$ and $-q$ at $-a$ from centre O along the dipole axis; P is on the equatorial line at distance $r$ from O.
Distance of P from each charge $=\sqrt{r^2+a^2}$; field magnitude from each charge $=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2+a^2}$.
Components along the axis add, perpendicular components cancel by symmetry:
$E=2\times\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2+a^2}\times\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{r^2+a^2}}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}}$, directed opposite to $\vec p$; for $r\gg a$, $E\approx\dfrac{p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3}$.
(ii) Since $E\propto 1/r^3$, halving $r$ makes $E$ eight times its original value.
(iii) Diagonal $=2$ m, so each dipole's half-separation $a=1$ m and O is the dipole's own centre.
Exact field at a dipole's centre: $E=\dfrac{2kq}{a^2}=\dfrac{kp}{a^3}=kp$, directed opposite to that dipole's moment.
As the diagonals are perpendicular, $E_1=E_2=kp$ are perpendicular; $E_{net}=\sqrt{E_1^2+E_2^2}=\sqrt2\,kp=\sqrt2\times9\times10^9\,p$ N/C, directed parallel to a side of the square.

questions.question: (i) Use Gauss’ law to obtain an expression for the electric field due to an infinitely long thin straight wire with uniform linear charge density $\lambda$. (ii) An infinitely long positively charged straight wire has a linear charge density $\lambda$. An electron is revolving in a circle with a constant speed $v$ such that the wire passes through the centre, and is perpendicular to the plane, of the circle. Find the kinetic energy of the electron in terms of magnitudes of its charge and linear charge density $\lambda$ on the wire. (iii) Draw a graph of kinetic energy as a function of linear charge density $\lambda$.
questions.answer:
(i) Take a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $r$, length $l$, around the wire.
By symmetry $\vec E$ is radial and uniform on the curved surface; flux through the flat ends is zero.
$E\times2\pi rl=\lambda l/\varepsilon_0$, so $E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$, directed radially outward.
(ii) The Coulomb force provides the centripetal force: $eE=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$
$\dfrac{e\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\Rightarrow mv^2=\dfrac{e\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}$
$KE=\dfrac12 mv^2=\dfrac{e\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$, independent of the radius $r$.
(iii) Since $KE=\dfrac{e}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\lambda$, the graph of $KE$ versus $\lambda$ is a straight line through the origin with slope $\dfrac{e}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$.

questions.question: (a) (i) Define electric flux and write its SI unit. (ii) Use Gauss’ law to obtain the expression for the electric field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet. (iii) A cube of side $L$ is kept in space, as shown in the figure. An electric field $\vec{E} = (Ax + B)\hat{i}$ exists in the region. Find the net charge enclosed by the cube. OR (b) (i) Define electric potential at a point and write its SI unit. (ii) Two capacitors are connected in series. Derive an expression of the equivalent capacitance of the combination. (iii) Two point charges $+q$ and $-q$ are located at points $(3a, 0)$ and $(0, 4a)$ respectively in $x$- $y$ plane. A third charge $Q$ is kept at the origin. Find the value of $Q$, in terms of $q$ and $a$, so that the electrostatic potential energy of the system is zero.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Electric flux through a surface is the total number of electric field lines passing through it, $\Phi=\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A$. SI unit: N m$^2$/C.
(a)(ii) Using a pill-box Gaussian surface straddling the sheet, symmetry gives equal field $E$ on both flat faces (area $A$) with zero flux through the curved part: $2EA=\sigma A/\varepsilon_0$, so $E=\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$, directed away from the sheet.
(a)(iii) With one corner of the cube at the origin, faces perpendicular to $x$ at $x=0$ and $x=L$:
$\Phi_1$ (at $x=0$, inward) $=-BL^2$; $\Phi_2$ (at $x=L$, outward) $=(AL+B)L^2$
Net flux $\Phi=AL^3$ (other four faces contribute zero, as $\vec E\parallel\hat i$)
$q_{enc}=\varepsilon_0\Phi=\varepsilon_0AL^3$

OR

(b)(i) Electric potential at a point is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point without acceleration. SI unit: volt (V).
(b)(ii) For capacitors $C_1,C_2$ in series, the same charge $Q$ appears on each: $V_1=Q/C_1$, $V_2=Q/C_2$
Total potential difference $V=V_1+V_2=Q\left(\dfrac{1}{C_1}+\dfrac{1}{C_2}\right)$
Since $V=Q/C_{eq}$, $\dfrac{1}{C_{eq}}=\dfrac{1}{C_1}+\dfrac{1}{C_2}$
(b)(iii) $r_{+q,-q}=\sqrt{(3a)^2+(4a)^2}=5a$; distance of $+q$ from O $=3a$, of $-q$ from O $=4a$
Total P.E. $=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{Qq}{3a}-\dfrac{Qq}{4a}-\dfrac{q^2}{5a}\right]=0$
$Qq\left(\dfrac13-\dfrac14\right)=\dfrac{q^2}{5}\Rightarrow\dfrac{Qq}{12}=\dfrac{q^2}{5}$
$Q=\dfrac{12q}{5}=2.4q$

questions.question: Using Gauss law, derive expression for electric field due to a spherical shell of uniform charge distribution $\sigma$ and radius $R$ at a point lying at a distance $x$ from the centre of shell, such that (i) $0 < x < R$, and (ii) $x > R$.
questions.answer:
By Gauss's law, $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = q_{enc}/\epsilon_0$.
Consider a spherical shell of radius $R$ carrying uniform surface charge density $\sigma$, so total charge $q = \sigma \times 4\pi R^2$.
(i) For $0 < x < R$: draw a Gaussian sphere of radius $x$ inside the shell. Since no charge lies within this sphere, $q_{enc} = 0$, so $E \times 4\pi x^2 = 0$, giving $E = 0$.
(ii) For $x > R$: draw a Gaussian sphere of radius $x$ enclosing the whole shell, so $q_{enc} = \sigma \times 4\pi R^2$.
By symmetry $\vec{E}$ is radial and constant in magnitude over this sphere, so $E \times 4\pi x^2 = \dfrac{\sigma \times 4\pi R^2}{\epsilon_0}$.
Thus $E = \dfrac{\sigma R^2}{\epsilon_0 x^2}$, directed radially outward, same as that of a point charge $q$ placed at the centre.

questions.question: An electric field is uniform and acts along $+x$ direction in the region of positive $x$. It is also uniform with the same magnitude but acts in $-x$ direction in the region of negative $x$. The value of the field is $E = 200$ N/C for $x > 0$ and $E = -200$ N/C for $x < 0$. A right circular cylinder of length $20$ cm and radius $5$ cm has its centre at the origin and its axis along the $x$-axis so that one flat face is at $x = +10$ cm and the other is at $x = -10$ cm. Find: (i) The net outward flux through the cylinder. (ii) The net charge present inside the cylinder.
questions.answer:
The cylinder's two flat (circular) faces are perpendicular to the x-axis; the curved surface has its normal perpendicular to $E$ (which is purely along x), so flux through the curved surface is zero.
At the right face ($x=+10$ cm), $\vec{E}=200\hat{i}$ N/C and outward normal is $+\hat{i}$, so flux $=E\times A$.
At the left face ($x=-10$ cm), $\vec{E}=-200\hat{i}$ N/C and outward normal is $-\hat{i}$, so flux $=(-200)(-1)A=200\times A$, again positive.
Area $A=\pi r^2=\pi(0.05)^2=7.854\times10^{-3}$ m$^2$.
(i) Net outward flux $=2EA=2\times200\times7.854\times10^{-3}\approx3.14$ N m$^2$/C.
(ii) By Gauss's law, $q_{enc}=\epsilon_0\phi=8.854\times10^{-12}\times3.14\approx2.78\times10^{-11}$ C.

questions.question: (a) Use Gauss’s law to show that due to a uniformly charged spherical shell of radius $R$, the electric field at any point situated outside the shell at a distance $r$ from its centre is equal to the electric field at the same point, when the entire charge on the shell were concentrated at its centre. Also plot the graph showing the variation of electric field with $r$, for $r < R$ and $r \geq R$. (b) Two point charges of $+1 \mu$ C and $+4 \mu$ C are kept $30$ cm apart. How far from the $+1 \mu$ C charge on the line joining the two charges, will the net electric field be zero? OR (a) Two point charges $q_{1}$ and $q_{2}$ are kept $r$ distance apart in a uniform external electric field $\vec{E}$. Find the amount of work done in assembling this system of charges. (b) A cube of side $20$ cm is kept in a region as shown in the figure. An electric field $\vec{E}$ exists in the region such that the potential at a point is given by $V = 10x + 5$, where $V$ is in volt and $x$ is in m. Find the (i) electric field $\vec{E}$, and (ii) total electric flux through the cube.
questions.answer:
(a) For a uniformly charged shell of radius $R$ and total charge $q$, consider a Gaussian sphere of radius $r>R$ concentric with the shell.
By symmetry $\vec{E}$ is radial and uniform over this sphere, so Gauss's law gives $E\times4\pi r^2=q/\epsilon_0$, i.e. $E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2}$.
This is exactly the field of a point charge $q$ placed at the centre, since the enclosed charge and the geometry are the same as for a point charge.
Graph: $E=0$ for $r<R$; at $r=R$, $E$ jumps to $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{R^2}$; for $r>R$, $E$ falls off as $1/r^2$.
(b) Let the null point be at distance $d$ from $+1\mu$C charge (between the charges, since both are positive).
$\dfrac{1}{d^2}=\dfrac{4}{(30-d)^2}\Rightarrow 30-d=2d\Rightarrow d=10$ cm.
OR
(a) Work done $W=q_1V(\vec{r_1})+q_2V(\vec{r_2})+\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r}$, the first two terms being work against the external field and the last being mutual interaction energy.
(b) $V=10x+5\Rightarrow E_x=-\dfrac{dV}{dx}=-10$ V/m, so $\vec{E}=-10\hat{i}$ N/C (uniform, independent of $x$).
(ii) Since $\vec{E}$ is uniform, flux entering one face equals flux leaving the opposite face; net flux through the closed cube $=0$ (no charge enclosed).

questions.question: (a) An electric dipole of dipole moment $\vec{P}$ is placed in a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$ at an angle $\theta$ with it. Derive the expression for torque $(\tau)$ acting on it. Find the orientation of the dipole relative to the electric field for which torque on it is (i) maximum, and (ii) half of maximum. (b) Two point charges $q_{1} = +1 \mu$ C and $q_{2} = +4 \mu$ C are placed $2$ m apart in air. At what distance from $q_{1}$ along the line joining the two charges, will the net electric field be zero? OR (a) Derive an expression for the energy stored in a parallel plate capacitor of capacitance $C$ when charged up to voltage $V$. How is this energy stored in the capacitor? (b) A capacitor of capacitance $1 \mu$ F is charged by connecting a battery of negligible internal resistance and emf $10$ V across it. Calculate the amount of charge supplied by the battery in charging the capacitor fully.
questions.answer:
(a) A dipole of moment $\vec{P}=q(2a)\hat{n}$ in field $\vec{E}$ experiences equal and opposite forces $qE$ on its charges, separated by $2a\sin\theta$.
Torque $=$ force $\times$ perpendicular distance $=qE(2a\sin\theta)=(q\cdot2a)E\sin\theta=PE\sin\theta$, i.e. $\vec{\tau}=\vec{P}\times\vec{E}$.
(i) $\tau$ is maximum when $\sin\theta=1$, i.e. $\theta=90^\circ$, giving $\tau_{max}=PE$.
(ii) $\tau=\tau_{max}/2\Rightarrow\sin\theta=1/2\Rightarrow\theta=30^\circ$ (or $150^\circ$).
(b) Let null point be at distance $d$ from $q_1=1\mu$C (between the charges).
$\dfrac{1}{d^2}=\dfrac{4}{(2-d)^2}\Rightarrow2-d=2d\Rightarrow d=\dfrac{2}{3}$ m $\approx0.67$ m from $q_1$.
OR
(a) Work done in charging $=\int_0^Q \dfrac{q}{C}dq=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}=\dfrac{1}{2}CV^2$, stored as electrostatic energy in the field between the plates, with energy density $u=\dfrac{1}{2}\epsilon_0E^2$.
(b) $Q=CV=1\mu F\times10\text{ V}=10\mu$C.

questions.question: (a) Write two important characteristics of equipotential surfaces. (b) A thin circular ring of radius $r$ is charged uniformly so that its linear charge density becomes $\lambda$. Derive an expression for the electric field at a point $P$ at a distance $x$ from it along the axis of the ring. Hence, prove that at large distances ($x \gg r$), the ring behaves as a point charge. OR (a) State Gauss’s law on electrostatics and derive an expression for the electric field due to a long straight thin uniformly charged wire (linear charge density $\lambda$) at a point lying at a distance $r$ from the wire. (b) The magnitude of electric field (in NC $-1$) in a region varies with the distance $r$ (in m) as $E = 10r + 5$ By how much does the electric potential increase in moving from point at $r = 1$ m to a point at $r = 10$ m.
questions.answer:
(a) (i) No work is done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface, since potential is the same everywhere on it.
(ii) The electric field is always perpendicular to an equipotential surface at every point.
(b) Consider an element $dl$ of the ring at distance $\sqrt{x^2+r^2}$ from $P$; its field $dE=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{\lambda\,dl}{x^2+r^2}$, with components along and perpendicular to the axis.
By symmetry, perpendicular components cancel; axial components add: $E=\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{\lambda\,dl}{(x^2+r^2)}\cdot\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+r^2}}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{qx}{(x^2+r^2)^{3/2}}$, where $q=\lambda(2\pi r)$.
For $x\gg r$: $E\approx\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{x^2}$, same as a point charge $q$ at the centre.
OR
(a) Gauss's law: $\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}=q_{enc}/\epsilon_0$.
For an infinite line charge $\lambda$, take a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $r$, length $l$; flux is only through the curved surface, so $E(2\pi rl)=\lambda l/\epsilon_0\Rightarrow E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$.
(b) $V(10)-V(1)=-\displaystyle\int_1^{10}(10r+5)\,dr=-[5r^2+5r]_1^{10}=-(550-10)=-540$ V.
So the potential decreases by $540$ V (the "increase" is $-540$ V) on moving from $r=1$ m to $r=10$ m.

questions.question: Derive an expression for the electric field at any point on the equatorial line of an electric dipole.
questions.answer:
Consider a dipole of charges $-q$ at $A$ and $+q$ at $B$, separation $2a$, with point $P$ on the equatorial line at distance $x$ from the centre $O$.
Distance of $P$ from each charge is $\sqrt{x^2+a^2}$, so each charge produces field of magnitude $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{x^2+a^2}$ at $P$.
The components of these two fields perpendicular to the dipole axis cancel by symmetry, while components anti-parallel to $\vec{P}$ add up.
Each field makes angle $\theta$ with the axis where $\cos\theta=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}$, so resultant $E=2\times\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{x^2+a^2}\times\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q(2a)}{(x^2+a^2)^{3/2}}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{P}{(x^2+a^2)^{3/2}}$.
The direction of $\vec{E}$ is antiparallel to $\vec{P}$ (the dipole moment).
For $x\gg a$, $E\approx\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{P}{x^3}$.

questions.question: Two identical point charges, $q$ each, are kept $2$ m apart in air. A third point charge $Q$ of unknown magnitude and sign is placed on the line joining the charges such that the system remains in equilibrium. Find the position and nature of $Q$.
questions.answer:
Let charges $q$ be placed at points $A$ and $B$, $2$ m apart, and let $Q$ be placed at point $C$ on the line $AB$.
For $Q$ itself to be in equilibrium under forces from two equal charges $q$, by symmetry $C$ must be the midpoint of $AB$, i.e. $1$ m from each charge.
For the whole system to be in equilibrium, the charge at $A$ must also experience zero net force.
Force on $A$ due to $B$: $F_{AB} = \dfrac{kq^2}{(2)^2} = \dfrac{kq^2}{4}$, repulsive (directed away from $B$).
Force on $A$ due to $Q$: $F_{AQ} = \dfrac{kqQ}{(1)^2}$.
For this to cancel $F_{AB}$, it must be attractive, so $Q$ must be of opposite sign to $q$, i.e. negative.
Equating magnitudes: $\dfrac{kq^2}{4} = kq|Q| \Rightarrow |Q| = \dfrac{q}{4}$
Hence $Q = -\dfrac{q}{4}$, located at the midpoint of the line joining the two charges.

questions.question: (a) Define electric flux. Is it a scalar or a vector quantity? A point charge $q$ is at a distance of $d/2$ directly above the centre of a square of side $d$, as shown in the figure. Use Gauss’ law to obtain the expression for the electric flux through the square. (b) If the point charge is now moved to a distance ’ $d$’ from the centre of the square and the side of the square is doubled, explain how the electric flux will be affected.
questions.answer:
(a) Electric flux through a surface is the total number of electric field lines crossing it, $\phi = \oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}$; it is a scalar quantity.
Imagine a cube of side $d$ with the given square as one face and the charge $q$ placed at the centre of the cube (since $q$ is at height $d/2$ above the centre of the square).
By Gauss' law, total flux through the closed cube is $\phi_{cube} = \dfrac{q}{\epsilon_0}$.
By symmetry this is shared equally among the 6 faces, so flux through the square is $\phi = \dfrac{q}{6\epsilon_0}$.
(b) Now imagine a cube of side $2d$ (equal to the new side of the square) with the charge at its centre, since the charge is at distance $d$, which is half of $2d$, directly above the centre. The square of side $2d$ is again exactly one face of this larger cube, so the flux through it is still $\phi = \dfrac{q}{6\epsilon_0}$. Thus the flux through the square remains unchanged.

questions.question: (a) Use Gauss’ law to derive the expression for the electric field $(\vec{E})$ due to a straight uniformly charged infinite line of charge density $\lambda$ C/m. (b) Draw a graph to show the variation of $E$ with perpendicular distance $r$ from the line of charge. (c) Find the work done in bringing a charge $q$ from perpendicular distance $r_{1}$ to $r_{2} (r_{2} > r_{1})$.
questions.answer:
(a) Consider an infinite line of charge with linear density $\lambda$. By symmetry, $\vec{E}$ is radial, perpendicular to the line, with equal magnitude at all points equidistant from it. Choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ and length $l$, coaxial with the line.
Flux through the curved surface: $\phi = E(2\pi r l)$; flux through the flat ends is zero since $\vec{E}$ is parallel to them.
Charge enclosed: $q = \lambda l$.
By Gauss' law: $E(2\pi r l) = \dfrac{\lambda l}{\epsilon_0} \Rightarrow E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$, directed radially outward for $\lambda > 0$.
(b) $E$ decreases with $r$ as a hyperbola, $E \propto 1/r$, falling steeply near the line and approaching zero for large $r$.
(c) $W = q\displaystyle\int_{r_1}^{r_2} E\,dr = \dfrac{q\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0}\ln\left(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}\right)$, positive for $r_2 > r_1$ and like charges, since work is done against the repulsive field.

questions.question: (a) Derive an expression for the electric field $\vec{E}$ due to a dipole of length $^{'}2a^{'}$ at a point distant $r$ from the centre of the dipole on the axial line. (b) Draw a graph of $E$ versus $r$ for $r >> a$. (c) If this dipole were kept in a uniform external electric field $\vec{E}_{0}$, diagrammatically represent the position of the dipole in stable and unstable equilibrium and write the expressions for the torque acting on the dipole in both the cases.
questions.answer:
(a) Let a dipole have charge $-q$ at $A$ and $+q$ at $B$, separated by $2a$, with dipole moment $p = q(2a)$. For a point $P$ on the axial line at distance $r$ from the centre $O$:
Field due to $+q$ (distance $r-a$): $E_{+q} = \dfrac{kq}{(r-a)^2}$, away from $B$.
Field due to $-q$ (distance $r+a$): $E_{-q} = \dfrac{kq}{(r+a)^2}$, toward $A$.
Both act along the same direction (from $-q$ to $+q$), so net field is
$E = kq\left(\dfrac{1}{(r-a)^2}-\dfrac{1}{(r+a)^2}\right) = \dfrac{4kqar}{(r^2-a^2)^2} = \dfrac{2kpr}{(r^2-a^2)^2}$
For $r>>a$: $E \approx \dfrac{2kp}{r^3} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{2p}{r^3}$, along the direction of $\vec{p}$.
(b) For $r>>a$, $E$ falls steeply with $r$ as $E\propto 1/r^3$, decreasing faster than for a single point charge.
(c) In stable equilibrium, $\vec{p}$ is parallel to $\vec{E}_0$ ($\theta = 0°$); torque $\tau = pE_0\sin\theta = 0$, and any small angular displacement is restored.
In unstable equilibrium, $\vec{p}$ is antiparallel to $\vec{E}_0$ ($\theta = 180°$); torque $\tau = pE_0\sin180° = 0$, but a small displacement causes it to move further away, not return.

questions.question: (a) Use Gauss’s theorem to find the electric field due to a uniformly charged infinitely large plane thin sheet with surface charge density $\sigma$. (b) An infinitely large thin plane sheet has a uniform surface charge density $+\sigma$. Obtain the expression for the amount of work done in bringing a point charge $q$ from infinity to a point, distant $r$, in front of the charged plane sheet.
questions.answer:
(a) Consider an infinite plane sheet with uniform surface charge density $\sigma$. By symmetry, $\vec{E}$ is perpendicular to the sheet and has equal magnitude at equal distances on either side. Take a cylindrical (pillbox) Gaussian surface of cross-sectional area $A$, symmetric about the sheet, with its flat faces parallel to the sheet.
Flux through the two flat faces: $\phi = EA + EA = 2EA$ (no flux through the curved surface).
Charge enclosed: $q = \sigma A$.
By Gauss' law: $2EA = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_0} \Rightarrow E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$, directed away from the sheet on both sides (for $\sigma > 0$).
(b) Since $E = \sigma/2\epsilon_0$ is uniform and independent of distance from the sheet, the work done in bringing a charge $q$ from infinity to a point at distance $r$ in front of the sheet is
$W = qEr = \dfrac{q\sigma r}{2\epsilon_0}$

questions.question: (i) Use Gauss’s law to find the electric field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet. What is the direction of field for positive and negative charge densities? (ii) Find the ratio of the potential differences that must be applied across the parallel and series combination of two capacitors $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ with their capacitances in the ratio $1: 2$ so that the energy stored in the two cases becomes the same. OR (i) If two similar large plates, each of area $A$ having surface charge densities $+\sigma$ and $-\sigma$ are separated by a distance $d$ in air, find the expressions for (a) field at points between the two plates and on outer side of the plates. Specify the direction of the field in each case. (b) the potential difference between the plates. (c) the capacitance of the capacitor so formed. (ii) Two metallic spheres of radii $R$ and $2R$ are charged so that both of these have same surface charge density $\sigma$. If they are connected to each other with a conducting wire, in which direction will the charge flow and why?
questions.answer:
(i) Using a pillbox Gaussian surface across an infinite charged sheet of density $\sigma$, Gauss' law gives $2EA = \sigma A/\epsilon_0$, so $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$. For positive $\sigma$, $\vec{E}$ points away from the sheet on both sides; for negative $\sigma$, $\vec{E}$ points toward the sheet on both sides.
(ii) Let $C_1 = C$, $C_2 = 2C$. In parallel: $C_p = 3C$; in series: $C_s = \dfrac{2C}{3}$.
Energy stored: $\tfrac12 C_p V_p^2 = \tfrac12 C_s V_s^2 \Rightarrow 3C V_p^2 = \dfrac{2C}{3}V_s^2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{V_p^2}{V_s^2} = \dfrac{2}{9}$
So $V_p : V_s = \sqrt{2} : 3$

OR

(i)(a) Between the plates: $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}$, directed from the $+\sigma$ plate to the $-\sigma$ plate.
Outside the plates (on the outer sides): $E = 0$, as the fields due to the two sheets cancel.
(b) Potential difference: $V = Ed = \dfrac{\sigma d}{\epsilon_0}$
(c) Capacitance: $C = \dfrac{Q}{V} = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\sigma d/\epsilon_0} = \dfrac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}$
(ii) Potential of a charged sphere of radius $r$ with surface density $\sigma$: $V = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} = \dfrac{\sigma r}{\epsilon_0}$, so $V \propto r$. The sphere of radius $2R$ is at higher potential than the sphere of radius $R$. When connected by a wire, charge flows from the sphere of radius $2R$ to the sphere of radius $R$ (higher to lower potential) until their potentials become equal.

questions.question: (a) "The outward electric flux due to charge $+Q$ is independent of the shape and size of the surface which encloses it." Give two reasons to justify this statement. (b) Two identical circular loops ’1’ and ’2’ of radius R each have linear charge densities $-\lambda$ and $+\lambda$ C/m respectively. The loops are placed coaxially with their centres $R\sqrt{3}$ distance apart. Find the magnitude and direction of the net electric field at the centre of loop ’1’.
questions.answer:
(a) Reason 1: Total flux depends only on the charge enclosed (a consequence of Coulomb's law and the $1/r^2$ nature of $\vec E$), so it cannot depend on the surface's shape or size.
Reason 2: A closed surface subtends a solid angle of exactly $4\pi$ steradians at an internal point charge irrespective of its shape/size, and since $\Phi=Q/\varepsilon_0$ follows from this solid angle, it stays the same for every enclosing surface.
(b) Field at the centre of loop 1 due to its own charge is zero, since a uniformly charged ring produces zero field at its own centre by symmetry.
Field due to loop 2 (axial field of a ring, $Q=2\pi R\lambda$, at $x=R\sqrt3$): $E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Qx}{(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}}$
Here $x^2+R^2=4R^2$, so $(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}=8R^3$, giving $E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(2\pi R\lambda)(R\sqrt3)}{8R^3}=\dfrac{\sqrt3\lambda}{16\varepsilon_0R}$
Since loop 2 carries $+\lambda$, this is the net field at the centre of loop 1, of magnitude $\dfrac{\sqrt3\lambda}{16\varepsilon_0R}$, directed along the axis away from loop 2 (from loop 2 towards loop 1).

questions.question: (a) An electric dipole of dipole moment $\vec{p}$ consists of point charges $+q$ and $-q$ separated by a distance $2a$ apart. Deduce the expression for the electric field $\vec{E}$ due to the dipole at a distance $x$ from the centre of the dipole on its axial line in terms of the dipole moment $\vec{p}$. Hence show that in the limit $x \gg a$, $\vec{E} \rightarrow2\vec{p}/(4\pi\varepsilon_{0}x^{3})$. (b) Given the electric field in the region $\vec{E} = 2x\hat{i}$, find the net electric flux through the cube and the charge enclosed by it.
questions.answer:
(a) Let P lie on the axial line at distance $x$ from the centre $O$ of the dipole ($x>a$). Distance of P from $+q$ is $(x-a)$ and from $-q$ is $(x+a)$.
$E_{+q}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{(x-a)^2}$, directed away from $+q$; $E_{-q}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{(x+a)^2}$, directed towards $-q$.
Both point in the same direction (along $\vec p$), so $E=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{1}{(x-a)^2}-\dfrac{1}{(x+a)^2}\right]=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{4ax}{(x^2-a^2)^2}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2px}{(x^2-a^2)^2}$, where $p=q(2a)$.
For $x\gg a$, $(x^2-a^2)^2\approx x^4$, so $\vec E\to\dfrac{2\vec p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0x^3}$, along the direction of $\vec p$.
(b) Take a cube of side $a$ with edges parallel to the axes, one face at $x$ and the opposite face at $x+a$. Since $\vec E=2x\hat i$ is along x, only these two faces contribute.
Flux $\Phi=E(x+a)a^2-E(x)a^2=2(x+a)a^2-2xa^2=2a^3$
Charge enclosed $q=\varepsilon_0\Phi=2\varepsilon_0a^3$

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram of Van de Graaff generator. State its working principle to show how by introducing a small charged sphere into a larger sphere, a large amount of charge can be transferred to the outer sphere. State the use of this machine and also point out its limitations. OR (a) Deduce the expression for the torque acting on a dipole of dipole moment $\vec{p}$ in the presence of a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$. (b) Consider two hollow concentric spheres, $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$, enclosing charges $2Q$ and $4Q$ respectively as shown in the figure. (i) Find out the ratio of the electric flux through them. (ii) How will the electric flux through the sphere $S_{1}$ change if a medium of dielectric constant ’ $\varepsilon_{r}$’ is introduced in the space inside $S_{1}$ in place of air? Deduce the necessary expression.
questions.answer:
Principle: Van de Graaff generator works on two facts — (i) electric discharge from sharp points (corona/spray discharge) sprays charge easily onto a moving belt, and (ii) charge given to a hollow conductor always moves to its outer surface, however much charge is already there, because the field inside a charged conductor is zero.
Diagram description: a large hollow metal sphere S mounted on an insulating column stands over two pulleys carrying an insulating belt; a spray comb near the lower pulley is connected to a high-voltage source (a few tens of kV) and sprays positive charge onto the belt by corona discharge; a collecting comb inside the sphere, connected to its inner surface, removes this charge from the belt.
Working: the belt, driven by a motor, carries the sprayed charge up into the sphere; the collecting comb removes it completely (field inside the hollow sphere is zero, so charge cannot stay on the belt) and it appears on the outer surface. Since new charge keeps being deposited on an already-charged outer surface, the potential of the sphere rises continuously, till limited by leakage.
Use: to accelerate charged particles (protons, ions) to energies of a few MeV for nuclear physics research.
Limitation: yes, there is an upper limit — the field around the sphere cannot exceed the dielectric strength of air ($\approx3\times10^6\text{ V/m}$), beyond which air ionises and charge leaks away by sparking; this is reduced by enclosing the machine in high-pressure gas (e.g. $SF_6$).

questions.question: Explain the principle of a device that can build up high voltages of the order of a few million volts. Draw a schematic diagram and explain the working of this device. Is there any restriction on the upper limit of the high voltages set up in this machine? Explain. OR (a) Define electric flux. Write its S.I. units. (b) Using Gauss’s law, prove that the electric field at a point due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet is independent of the distance from it. (c) How is the field directed if (i) the sheet is positively charged, (ii) negatively charged?
questions.answer:
(a) Electric flux through a surface is the total number of electric field lines crossing it, $\Phi=\displaystyle\int\vec E\cdot d\vec A$. Its SI unit is $N\,m^2\,C^{-1}$ (equivalently, $V\,m$).
(b) Consider an infinite plane sheet with uniform surface charge density $\sigma$. By symmetry, $\vec E$ is perpendicular to the sheet and has the same magnitude at all points equidistant from it, pointing away on both sides (for $\sigma>0$).
Choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface of cross-sectional area $A$, with the sheet passing through its middle so that the two flat faces are equidistant from the sheet. Flux through the curved surface is zero (E parallel to it); flux through each flat face is $EA$.
Total flux $=2EA$. Charge enclosed $=\sigma A$.
By Gauss's law, $2EA=\dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}$, so $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, which does not contain $r$ — hence independent of distance from the sheet.
(c) (i) Positively charged sheet: $\vec E$ points away from the sheet on both sides.
(ii) Negatively charged sheet: $\vec E$ points towards the sheet on both sides.

questions.question: State Gauss’ theorem in electrostatics. Apply it to find the electric field strength at a point near a long straight conductor carrying electric charge.
questions.answer:
Gauss's theorem: the total electric flux through any closed surface equals $1/\varepsilon_0$ times the total charge enclosed by it, $\displaystyle\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$.
For a long straight conductor with uniform linear charge density $\lambda$, by symmetry $\vec E$ is radial and has the same magnitude at every point at a given perpendicular distance $r$ from the wire.
Choose a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ and length $l$. Flux through the two flat end faces is zero (E is parallel to them); flux through the curved surface is $E(2\pi rl)$.
Charge enclosed $=\lambda l$.
By Gauss's theorem: $E(2\pi rl)=\dfrac{\lambda l}{\varepsilon_0}$
$E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$, directed radially outward (for $\lambda>0$), perpendicular to the wire.

questions.question: What is the magnitude of a point electric charge chosen so that the electric field due to it at a point 50 cm away has magnitude $2.0 N C^{-1}$?
questions.answer:
$E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r^2}$, so $Q=4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2E=\dfrac{r^2E}{k}$
Substituting $r=0.5$ m, $E=2.0\ N C^{-1}$, $k=9\times10^9\ N m^2C^{-2}$:
$Q=\dfrac{(0.5)^2\times2.0}{9\times10^9}=\dfrac{0.5}{9\times10^9}\approx5.6\times10^{-11}$ C

questions.question: (a) Using Gauss’ law, derive an expression for the electric field intensity at any point outside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius $R$ and charge density $\sigma C/m^{2}$. Draw the field lines when the charge density of the sphere is (i) positive, (ii) negative. (b) A uniformly charged conducting sphere of $2.5 m$ in diameter has a surface charge density of $100 \mu C/m^{2}$. Calculate the (i) Charge on the sphere (ii) Total electric flux passing through the sphere
questions.answer:
(a) Consider a thin spherical shell of radius $R$ carrying uniform surface charge density $\sigma$.
To find $\vec{E}$ at a point outside at distance $r$ ($r > R$), choose a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r$.
By symmetry, $\vec{E}$ is radial and of the same magnitude at every point on this surface.
Applying Gauss's law: $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = q_{enc}/\epsilon_0$, so $E(4\pi r^2) = \sigma(4\pi R^2)/\epsilon_0$.
Thus $E = \dfrac{\sigma R^2}{\epsilon_0 r^2} = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}$, directed radially outward, where $q = \sigma \cdot 4\pi R^2$ — the shell behaves as if all charge were concentrated at its centre.
Field lines: (i) for positive $\sigma$, lines point radially outward from the shell; (ii) for negative $\sigma$, lines point radially inward toward the shell.
(b) $R = 1.25$ m, $\sigma = 100 \times 10^{-6}$ $C/m^2$.
(i) $q = \sigma \times 4\pi R^2 = 100 \times 10^{-6} \times 4\pi \times (1.25)^2 \approx 1.96 \times 10^{-3}$ C.
(ii) $\phi = q/\epsilon_0 = \dfrac{1.96 \times 10^{-3}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 2.22 \times 10^{8}$ $Nm^2/C$.

questions.question: (a) Derive an expression for the torque experienced by an electric dipole kept in a uniform electric field. (b) Calculate the work done to dissociate the system of three charges placed on the vertices of a triangle as shown.
questions.answer:
(a) Consider a dipole of charges $+q$ and $-q$ separated by distance $2a$, placed in a uniform field $\vec{E}$ making angle $\theta$ with the dipole moment $\vec{p}$.
Force on $+q$ is $qE$ along $\vec{E}$; force on $-q$ is $qE$ opposite to $\vec{E}$.
The net force is zero, but the two equal, opposite, parallel forces form a couple.
Torque = magnitude of one force $\times$ perpendicular distance between the forces $= qE(2a\sin\theta) = pE\sin\theta$, since $p = q(2a)$.
