Since $r \ll R$, this field may be taken as uniform over the smaller loop, so flux linked with it is $\phi_r = B\pi r^2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I \pi r^2}{2R}$.
Mutual inductance $M = \dfrac{\phi_r}{I} = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi r^2}{2R}$.

questions.question: A rectangular conductor MNPQ with a movable arm MN (resistance $r$) is kept in a uniform magnetic field as shown in the figure. Resistance of arms MQ, QP and PN are negligible. Obtain the expression for the: (a) current induced in the loop specifying its direction, and (b) power required to move the arm.
questions.answer:
(a) As MN moves with velocity $v$ in field $B$, motional emf $\varepsilon = Blv$, so induced current $I = \dfrac{Blv}{r}$.
By Lenz's law (Fleming's right-hand rule), the induced current opposes the change in flux; its direction in the arm is from $N$ to $M$ if the flux is increasing into the page as the loop area grows.
(b) The magnetic force opposing motion is $F = BIl = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{r}$, so the power required to move the arm at constant velocity is $P = Fv = \dfrac{B^2l^2v^2}{r}$, equal to the power dissipated $I^2r$.

questions.question: State the basic principle behind the working of an ac generator. Briefly describe its working and obtain the expression for the instantaneous value of emf induced.
questions.answer:
The ac generator works on the principle of electromagnetic induction: when a coil is rotated in a uniform magnetic field, the magnetic flux linked with it changes continuously, inducing an emf in the coil.
Working: a rectangular coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ is rotated with angular velocity $\omega$ about an axis perpendicular to a uniform field $B$, using slip rings and brushes to connect it to the external circuit.
If the coil is in the plane of $B$ at $t=0$, flux at time $t$ is $\phi = NBA\cos\omega t$.
Induced emf $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = \varepsilon_0\sin\omega t$, where $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$.

questions.question: Two concentric circular coils X and Y of radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2} (r_{1} > r_{2})$ having $N_{1}$ and $N_{2}$ turns respectively are placed coaxially with centres coinciding. Obtain an expression for (i) the mutual inductance for the arrangement, and (ii) the magnetic flux linked with coil Y when current $I$ flows through coil X.
questions.answer:
(i) Let current $I$ flow through coil X (radius $r_1$, turns $N_1$). Field at the common centre is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N_1 I}{2r_1}$.
Since $r_2 < r_1$, this field is nearly uniform over coil Y, so flux linked with one turn of Y is $B\pi r_2^2$, and with $N_2$ turns: $\phi_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 \pi r_2^2 I}{2r_1}$.
Mutual inductance $M = \dfrac{\phi_2}{I} = \dfrac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 \pi r_2^2}{2r_1}$.
(ii) Flux linked with Y is $\phi_2 = MI = \dfrac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 \pi r_2^2 I}{2r_1}$.

questions.question: What are eddy currents? Why does the pendulum plate with holes or slots reduce electromagnetic damping? How are the eddy currents minimised in the core of a transformer? Why is the electromagnetic braking effect smooth in a train?
questions.answer:
Eddy currents are induced circulating currents set up in the bulk of a conductor when the magnetic flux linked with it changes.
A pendulum plate with holes or slots reduces the area available for eddy current loops, increasing their resistance and reducing their magnitude, so electromagnetic damping decreases and the pendulum keeps oscillating.
In a transformer core, eddy currents are minimised by using a laminated core (thin sheets insulated from each other), which breaks the conducting paths and increases resistance to eddy current flow, reducing energy loss as heat.
In train braking, strong eddy currents induced in the wheels (or rotating drums) by an applied field oppose the motion smoothly without mechanical contact, giving a jerk-free, gradual braking effect.

questions.question: (a) Differentiate between self inductance and mutual inductance. (b) The mutual inductance of two coaxial coils is $2$ H. The current in one coil is changed uniformly from zero to $0.5$ A in $100$ ms. Find the: (i) change in magnetic flux through the other coil. (ii) emf induced in the other coil during the change.
questions.answer:
(a) Self inductance is the property of a single coil by which a changing current in it induces an emf in itself, given by $\varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$.
Mutual inductance is the property of two coils by which a changing current in one coil induces an emf in the neighbouring coil, given by $\varepsilon_2 = -M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}$.
(b) (i) $\Delta\phi = M\Delta I = 2 \times 0.5 = 1$ Wb
(ii) $\varepsilon = M\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.5}{0.1} = 10$ V

questions.question: Draw the labelled diagram of an AC generator. Briefly explain its working and obtain the expression for the emf produced in the coil.
questions.answer:
Diagram: a rectangular coil ABCD of $N$ turns mounted on an axle between the poles of a strong magnet, its ends connected to slip rings that touch fixed carbon brushes joined to the external circuit.
Working: as the axle is rotated by an external agent with angular velocity $\omega$, the flux linked with the coil changes, inducing an alternating emf that drives current through the external circuit via the brushes.
Taking the coil in the plane of $B$ at $t=0$, flux $\phi = NBA\cos\omega t$.
Induced emf $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = \varepsilon_0\sin\omega t$, an alternating emf of amplitude $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$.

questions.question: When a conducting loop of resistance $10 \Omega$ and area $10$ cm $2$ is removed from an external magnetic field acting normally, the variation of induced current in the loop with time is shown in the figure. Find the (i) total charge passed through the loop. (ii) change in magnetic flux through the loop. (iii) magnitude of the magnetic field applied.
questions.answer:
(i) Total charge $q$ equals the area under the current-time graph, $q = \int I\,dt$; reading the graph (a triangular/rectangular $i$–$t$ variation) gives this area directly in coulombs.
(ii) Since $q = \dfrac{\Delta\phi}{R}$, the change in flux is $\Delta\phi = qR$, obtained by multiplying the charge found above by $R = 10\ \Omega$.
(iii) As the loop is withdrawn completely, $\Delta\phi = BA$ (final flux zero), so the field is $B = \dfrac{\Delta\phi}{A}$, with $A = 10\ \text{cm}^2 = 10\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$.

questions.question: Define mutual inductance and write its S.I. unit.
questions.answer:
Mutual inductance of a pair of coils is the property by virtue of which a change of current in one coil induces an emf in the neighbouring coil.
If $I_1$ is the current in coil 1, the flux linked with coil 2 is $N_2\Phi_2 = MI_1$, so $M = \dfrac{N_2\Phi_2}{I_1}$
The induced emf is $\varepsilon_2 = -M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}$
S.I. unit of mutual inductance is henry (H), where $1\text{ H} = 1\text{ Wb/A} = 1\text{ V s/A}$.

questions.question: (a) How are eddy currents generated in a conductor which is subjected to a magnetic field? (b) Write two examples of their useful applications. (c) How can the disadvantages of eddy currents be minimized?
questions.answer:
(a) When a bulk conductor moves in, or is placed in, a changing magnetic field, the magnetic flux through it changes. By Faraday's law this induces circulating currents (eddy currents) within the body of the conductor itself, flowing in closed loops perpendicular to the field.
(b) Uses: (i) electromagnetic braking in trains, (ii) induction furnaces for melting metals; also used in speedometers and energy meters.
(c) Eddy current losses (heating) are minimised by using laminated cores (thin, insulated sheets) instead of solid metal blocks, which increases resistance to the eddy current paths and reduces their magnitude.

questions.question: The figure shows a rectangular conducting frame MNOP of resistance $R$ placed partly in a perpendicular magnetic field $\vec{B}$ and moved with velocity $\vec{v}$ as shown in the figure. Obtain the expressions for the (a) force acting on the arm ’ON’ and its direction, and (b) power required to move the frame to get a steady emf induced between the arms MN and PO.
questions.answer:
Let arm ON (length $l$) lie inside the field $B$ while the frame moves with velocity $v$.
(a) Motional emf: $\varepsilon = Bvl$, induced current $I = \dfrac{Bvl}{R}$
Force on ON: $F = BIl = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}$, directed opposite to $\vec{v}$ (by Lenz's law, opposing the motion).
(b) To keep $v$ constant this force must be balanced by an equal external force, so power required is
$P = Fv = \dfrac{B^2l^2v^2}{R}$, which equals the rate of heat dissipation in $R$.

questions.question: Define mutual inductance between a pair of coils. Derive an expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids of same length wound one over the other.
questions.answer:
Mutual inductance of a pair of coils is the flux linked with one coil per unit current in the other: $M = \dfrac{N_2\Phi_2}{I_1}$
Consider two coaxial solenoids of length $l$ and cross-sectional area $A$, with $N_1, N_2$ turns (turns per length $n_1=N_1/l$, $n_2=N_2/l$), one wound over the other.
Current $I_1$ in solenoid 1 produces field $B_1 = \mu_0 n_1 I_1$ inside it.
This field also passes through each turn of solenoid 2, so flux linkage $N_2\Phi_2 = n_2 l \cdot \mu_0 n_1 I_1 \cdot A$
Hence $M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l = \dfrac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 A}{l}$

questions.question: Define self-inductance of a coil. Obtain the expression for the energy stored in an inductor $L$ connected across a source of emf.
questions.answer:
Self-inductance of a coil is the property by which it opposes any change of current through itself; the induced emf is $\varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$
When current $I$ grows from $0$ to $I$ against this back emf, work done in time $dt$ is $dW = |\varepsilon| I\, dt = LI\, dI$
Total work done (stored as magnetic energy) is
$W = \int_0^I LI\, dI = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^2$
Thus the energy stored in the inductor is $U = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^2$.

questions.question: Define mutual inductance between a pair of coils. Derive an expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids of same length wound one over the other. OR Define self-inductance of a coil. Obtain the expression for the energy stored in an inductor $L$ connected across a source of emf.
questions.answer:
Mutual inductance of a pair of coils is the flux linked with one coil per unit current in the other: $M = \dfrac{N_2\Phi_2}{I_1}$
Consider two coaxial solenoids of length $l$ and cross-sectional area $A$, with $N_1, N_2$ turns (turns per length $n_1=N_1/l$, $n_2=N_2/l$), one wound over the other.
Current $I_1$ in solenoid 1 produces field $B_1 = \mu_0 n_1 I_1$ inside it.
This field also passes through each turn of solenoid 2, so flux linkage $N_2\Phi_2 = n_2 l \cdot \mu_0 n_1 I_1 \cdot A$
Hence $M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l = \dfrac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 A}{l}$

questions.question: State Lenz’s law. Illustrate, by giving an example, how this law helps in predicting the direction of the current in a loop in the presence of a changing magnetic flux. In a given coil of self-inductance of 5 mH, current changes from 4 A to 1 A in 30 ms. Calculate the emf induced in the coil.
questions.answer:
Lenz's law: the direction of an induced emf (or current) is such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it, consistent with conservation of energy.
Example: when the N-pole of a bar magnet is moved towards a coil, the induced current flows so as to make the near face of the coil a N-pole, repelling the magnet and opposing its approach.
Given $L = 5$ mH, $dI = 1-4 = -3$ A, $dt = 30$ ms $=0.03$ s
$\varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt} = -5\times10^{-3}\times\dfrac{-3}{0.03} = 0.5$ V

questions.question: (a) A rod of length $l$ is moved horizontally with a uniform velocity ’v’ in a direction perpendicular to its length through a region in which a uniform magnetic field is acting vertically downward. Derive the expression for the emf induced across the ends of the rod. (b) How does one understand this motional emf by invoking the Lorentz force acting on the free charge carriers of the conductor? Explain.
questions.answer:
(a) In time $dt$ the rod of length $l$ sweeps area $dA = lv\, dt$, so flux change $d\Phi = B\, l v\, dt$
Induced emf: $\varepsilon = \dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = Bvl$
(b) Free charges in the rod move with velocity $v$ along with it and experience a Lorentz force $\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$, which pushes positive charges to one end and negative charges to the other.
This charge separation creates an electric field $E$ inside the rod; equilibrium is reached when $qE = qvB$, i.e. $E = vB$.
The potential difference across the rod is then $V = El = Bvl$, which is the motional emf.

questions.question: A metallic rod of length ’ $l$’ is rotated with a frequency $\nu$ with one end hinged at the centre and the other end at the circumference of a circular metallic ring of radius $r$, about an axis passing through the centre and perpendicular to the plane of the ring. A constant uniform magnetic field $B$ parallel to the axis is present every where. Using Lorentz force, explain how emf is induced between the centre and the metallic ring and hence obtain the expression for it.
questions.answer:
Consider an element of the rod at distance $x$ from the centre, of length $dx$, rotating with angular speed $\omega = 2\pi\nu$.
Its linear velocity is $v = \omega x$, so free charges in it experience a Lorentz force per unit charge (effective field) $E = vB = B\omega x$, directed along the rod.
This drives charge along the rod, giving an elemental emf $d\varepsilon = B\omega x\, dx$
Integrating from the centre ($x=0$) to the rim ($x=l$):
$\varepsilon = \int_0^l B\omega x\, dx = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^2 = \pi B \nu l^2$
The rod thus acts as a source of emf $\varepsilon = \pi\nu Bl^2$ between the centre and the ring.

questions.question: (a) Define self inductance. Write its S.I. units. (b) Derive an expression for self inductance of a long solenoid of length $l$, cross-sectional area $A$ having $N$ number of turns.
questions.answer:
(a) Self-inductance of a coil is numerically equal to the emf induced in it when the rate of change of current through it is unity, $L = -\varepsilon/(dI/dt)$; also $L = N\Phi/I$.
S.I. unit: henry (H).
(b) For a long solenoid, turns per unit length $n = N/l$, and current $I$ produces field $B = \mu_0 n I = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{l}$ inside.
Flux linked with all turns: $N\Phi = N\cdot B\cdot A = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A I}{l}$
Since $N\Phi = LI$, $L = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l}$

questions.question: (i) State Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction. (ii) A jet plane is travelling towards west at a speed of $1800 km/h$. What is the voltage difference developed between the ends of the wing having a span of $25 m$, if the Earth’s magnetic field at the location has a magnitude of $5 \times 10^{-4} T$ and the dip angle is $30^{^{\circ}}$?
questions.answer:
(i) Faraday's law states that the induced e.m.f. in a circuit is equal to the negative rate of change of magnetic flux linked with it: $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}$.
(ii) Speed $v = 1800 \text{ km/h} = 500 \text{ m/s}$
Vertical component of Earth's field, $B_v = B\sin\delta = 5\times 10^{-4}\times\sin30^{\circ} = 2.5\times 10^{-4}$ T
Voltage developed: $\varepsilon = B_v l v = 2.5\times 10^{-4}\times 25\times 500 = 3.125$ V

questions.question: A metallic rod of length $l$ is rotated at a constant angular speed $\omega$, normal to a uniform magnetic field $B$. Derive an expression for the current induced in the rod, if the resistance of the rod is $R$.
questions.answer:
Consider a rod of length $l$ rotating with angular speed $\omega$ about one end, normal to field $B$.
An element $dr$ at distance $r$ from the axis has speed $v = r\omega$, giving elemental e.m.f. $d\varepsilon = Bv\,dr = B\omega r\,dr$.
Total e.m.f.: $\varepsilon = \int_0^l B\omega r\,dr = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$
Induced current: $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R} = \dfrac{B\omega l^2}{2R}$

questions.question: Explain with the help of a labelled diagram the underlying principle and working of a step-up transformer. Why cannot such a device be used to step up d.c. voltage?
questions.answer:
Principle: A step-up transformer works on the principle of mutual induction — a changing current in the primary coil produces a changing flux which induces an e.m.f. in the secondary coil wound on the same soft-iron core.
Diagram: primary coil ($N_p$ turns) and secondary coil ($N_s$ turns, with $N_s > N_p$) wound on a laminated soft-iron core, primary connected to a.c. source, secondary to load.
Working: A.c. voltage $V_p$ applied to primary sets up alternating flux in the core, which links the secondary and induces $V_s$, with $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} > 1$.
It cannot step up d.c. voltage because d.c. produces a constant, unchanging flux, so $\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = 0$ and no e.m.f. is induced in the secondary.

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram of an a.c. generator. Explain briefly its principle and working.
questions.answer:
Diagram: A rectangular coil (armature) of $N$ turns rotates about an axis, in a uniform magnetic field $B$ between the pole pieces of a magnet, with its ends connected to slip rings that touch fixed carbon brushes connected to the external circuit.
Principle: It works on the principle of electromagnetic induction — when a coil rotates in a magnetic field, the magnetic flux linked with it changes continuously, inducing an alternating e.m.f. in the coil.
Working: As the coil is rotated (by mechanical means, e.g. steam/water turbine) with angular speed $\omega$, the flux $\phi = BA\cos\omega t$ changes, inducing e.m.f. $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$, which drives an alternating current through the external circuit via the slip rings and brushes.

questions.question: How is the mutual inductance of a pair of coils affected when: (i) separation between the coils is increased? (ii) the number of turns of each coil is increased? (iii) a thin iron sheet is placed between the two coils, other factors remaining the same? Explain your answer in each case.
questions.answer:
(i) When separation between coils increases, mutual inductance decreases, since less flux from one coil links the other, and $M \propto \dfrac{1}{d}$ (approximately).
(ii) When the number of turns of each coil increases, mutual inductance increases, since $M \propto N_1 N_2$, as flux linkage with each turn adds up.
(iii) When a thin iron sheet (ferromagnetic core) is placed between the coils, mutual inductance increases greatly, because the iron sheet has high permeability $\mu_r$, which increases the flux linkage between the coils, and $M \propto \mu_r$.

questions.question: Explain, with the help of a diagram, the principle and working of an a.c. generator. Write the expression for the e.m.f. generated in the coil in terms of its speed of rotation.
questions.answer:
Diagram: A rectangular armature coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ rotates about an axis perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B$, with its ends joined to slip rings that make contact with stationary brushes connected to the external circuit.
Principle: The generator works on the principle of electromagnetic induction; rotating the coil in the magnetic field changes the flux linked with it, inducing an alternating e.m.f.
Working: If the coil rotates with angular speed $\omega$ starting from the plane of the coil along $B$, the flux at time $t$ is $\phi = BA\cos\omega t$, so by Faraday's law the induced e.m.f. is
$\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = \varepsilon_0\sin\omega t$, where $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$ is the peak e.m.f.

questions.question: A circular coil of N turns and radius R, is kept normal to a magnetic field, given by $B = B_{0} \cos \omega t$. Deduce an expression for e.m.f. induced in this coil. State the rule which helps to detect the direction of induced current.
questions.answer:
Flux linked with the coil: $\phi = NB\pi R^2 = N\pi R^2 B_0\cos\omega t$
Induced e.m.f. by Faraday's law: $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = N\pi R^2 B_0\omega\sin\omega t$
Thus the e.m.f. is alternating with peak value $\varepsilon_0 = N\pi R^2 B_0\omega$.
The direction of the induced current is given by Lenz's law, which states that the induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it (consistent with conservation of energy).

questions.question: Read the following paragraph and answer the questions. Consider the experimental set up shown in the figure. This jumping ring experiment is an outstanding demonstration of some simple laws of Physics. A conducting non-magnetic ring is placed over the vertical core of a solenoid. When current is passed through the solenoid, the ring is thrown off. Answer the following questions: (i) Explain the reason of jumping of the ring when the switch is closed in the circuit. (ii) What will happen if the terminals of the battery are reversed and the switch is closed? Explain. (iii) Explain the two laws that help us understand this phenomenon.
questions.answer:
(i) When the switch is closed, the increasing current in the solenoid produces a rapidly increasing magnetic flux through the ring. By Lenz's law, an induced current flows in the ring in a direction that opposes this increase, making the ring behave like a magnet with its top face having the same polarity as the top of the solenoid; the resulting repulsive force pushes the ring up, and it jumps off.
(ii) If the battery terminals are reversed, the ring still jumps off in the same way (upward), because the induced current in the ring always opposes the change in flux regardless of the direction of the current in the solenoid, so the repulsion effect is unchanged.
(iii) The phenomenon is explained by Faraday's law (a changing flux induces an e.m.f., and hence an eddy current, in the ring) and Lenz's law (the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the increasing flux, producing a repulsive force that throws the ring off).

questions.question: Ram is a student of class $X$ in a village school. His uncle gifted him a bicycle with a dynamo fitted in it. He was very excited to get it. While cycling during night, he could light the bulb and see the objects on the road. He, however, did not know how this device works. He asked this question to his teacher. The teacher considered it an opportunity to explain the working to the whole class. Answer the following questions: (a) State the principle and working of a dynamo. (b) Write two values each displayed by Ram and his school teacher.
questions.answer:
(a) A dynamo works on the principle of electromagnetic induction: when a coil rotates in a magnetic field (or a magnet rotates near a coil), the flux linked with the coil changes continuously, inducing an e.m.f. Mechanical energy of the rotating bicycle wheel turns a small magnet/coil inside the dynamo, generating an alternating e.m.f. $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\sin\omega t$, which drives current through the bulb, lighting it.
(b) Values displayed by Ram: curiosity, eagerness to learn, respect for elders.
Values displayed by the teacher: attentiveness to students' questions, dedication to teaching, willingness to use practical examples to explain science.

questions.question: A group of students while coming from the school noticed a box marked "Danger H.T. 2200 V" at a substation in the main street. They did not understand the utility of such a high voltage, while they argued, the supply was only 220 V. They asked their teacher this question the next day. The teacher thought it to be an important question and therefore explained to the whole class. Answer the following questions: (i) What device is used to bring the high voltage down to low voltage of a.c. current and what is the principle of its working? (ii) Is it possible to use this device for bringing down the high dc voltage to the low voltage? Explain. (iii) Write the values displayed by the students and the teacher.
questions.answer:
(i) A transformer is used to step down (or step up) a.c. voltage. It works on the principle of mutual induction: an alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing flux in the laminated iron core, which induces an e.m.f. in the secondary coil, with $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$.
(ii) It cannot be used for d.c. voltage, because d.c. produces a steady, unchanging flux in the core, so $\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = 0$ and no e.m.f. is induced in the secondary coil.
(iii) Values displayed by the students: curiosity, scientific temperament, willingness to question and understand.
Values displayed by the teacher: patience, dedication, encouraging student inquiry through explanation.

questions.question: (a) State Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction. (b) Derive an expression for the self-inductance of an air-filled long solenoid of length $l$ and cross-sectional area $A$ having $N$ turns. (c) A conducting rod of length 50 cm, with one end pivoted, is rotated with angular speed of 60 rpm in a uniform magnetic field of 4.0 mT directed perpendicular to the plane of rotation of rod. Find the emf induced in the rod. OR (a) Draw a labelled diagram of a step-up transformer. State the principle on which it works and obtain the ratio of secondary voltage to primary voltage in terms of number of turns and currents in the two coils. (b) The ratio of the number of turns in the primary to the secondary of an ideal transformer is $1: 5$. If 5 kW power at 200 V is supplied to the primary, find (i) current in the primary, and (ii) output voltage.
questions.answer:
(a) Faraday's law: whenever the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an emf is induced in it, given by $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}$.

(b) For a solenoid of length $l$, area $A$, $N$ turns carrying current $I$: field inside $B = \mu_0\dfrac{N}{l}I$.
Flux per turn $\phi = BA = \mu_0\dfrac{N}{l}IA$.
Flux linkage $N\phi = \mu_0\dfrac{N^2A}{l}I = LI$.
So $L = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l}$.

(c) $l = 0.5$ m, $\omega = 60$ rpm $= 2\pi$ rad/s, $B = 4.0\times10^{-3}$ T.
$\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\times4.0\times10^{-3}\times2\pi\times(0.5)^2$
$\varepsilon = 3.14\times10^{-3}$ V $= 3.14$ mV.

questions.question: (a) (i) With the help of a labelled diagram, explain the principle, construction and working of an a.c. generator. (ii) Deduce an expression for the induced emf in the coil of the generator.
questions.answer:
Principle: electromagnetic induction — an emf is induced in a coil when the magnetic flux linked with it changes, which is achieved by rotating a coil in a uniform magnetic field.

Construction: it consists of an armature (a rectangular coil of $N$ turns wound on a soft-iron core), strong field magnets producing a uniform field $B$, two slip rings attached to the coil ends that rotate with the coil, and carbon brushes pressed against the slip rings connecting the coil to the external circuit.

Working: the coil is rotated with angular speed $\omega$ about an axis perpendicular to $B$ by an external mechanical source (e.g. turbine); the flux linked with it changes continuously, inducing an alternating emf that reverses every half rotation, delivered to the external circuit through the brushes.

Derivation: if the coil's normal makes angle $\theta = \omega t$ with $B$, flux $\phi = NBA\cos\omega t$.
Induced emf $e = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$, where $e_0 = NBA\omega$.

questions.question: (b) If $T$ is the time period of the rotation of the coil, at what values of $T$ in a cycle, the emf generated is maximum?
questions.answer:
The induced emf is maximum when the rate of change of flux is maximum, i.e. when the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field (coil normal perpendicular to $B$).
For $e = e_0\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{T}\right)$, this occurs at $t = \dfrac{T}{4}, \dfrac{3T}{4}, \dfrac{5T}{4}, ...$
That is, at odd multiples of $T/4$ within each cycle.

questions.question: (i) State Lenz’s law and explain that it follows the law of conservation of energy.
questions.answer:
Lenz's law: the direction of an induced emf (or current) is always such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it.
This follows conservation of energy because work must be done against the opposing induced effect to change the flux, and this work done is what appears as the electrical energy of the induced current.
If the induced current instead aided the change in flux, the flux would increase further, driving still more current without any external work being done, creating energy from nothing.
Since this is impossible, the induced current must oppose the change, consistent with energy conservation.

questions.question: (ii) Write the dimensional formula for self-inductance. The current in a coil changes from $8$· $0$ A to $2$· $0$ A in $0$· $6$ s. If an average emf induced in the coil is $50$ V, calculate the self-inductance of the coil.
questions.answer:
Dimensional formula of self-inductance: $[L] = [M^1 L^2 T^{-2} A^{-2}]$ (from $\varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$).

Given: $dI = 8.0 - 2.0 = 6.0$ A, $dt = 0.6$ s, $\varepsilon = 50$ V.
$L = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{dI/dt} = \dfrac{50}{6.0/0.6} = \dfrac{50}{10}$
$L = 5$ H.

questions.question: (a) (i) State Lenz’s law and explain how this law is a consequence of conservation of energy principle. (ii) A square shaped loop of side $\ell$ is initially lying outside a region of uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ as shown in the figure. The loop is moved towards right with a constant velocity $v$ till it goes out of the region of magnetic field. (I) What will be the directions of induced current when the loop enters the field and when it leaves the field? (II) Draw the plots showing the variation of magnetic flux $\phi$ linked with the loop with time $t$ and variation of induced emf $E$ with time $t$. Mark the relevant values of $E$, $\phi$ and $t$ on the graphs. OR (b) (i) Differentiate between peak and rms values of alternating current. How are they related? (ii) A current element $X$ is connected across an ac source of emf $V = V_{0} \sin 2\pi\nu t$. It is found that the voltage leads the current in phase by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ radian. If element $X$ was replaced by element $Y$, the voltage lags behind the current in phase by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ radian. (I) Identify elements $X$ and $Y$ by drawing phasor diagrams. (II) Obtain the condition of resonance when both elements $X$ and $Y$ are connected in series to the source and obtain expression for resonant frequency. What is the impedance value in this case?
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Lenz's law: the direction of induced current is always such as to oppose the change in magnetic flux that produces it.
It follows conservation of energy because work has to be done against the induced opposing effect to change the flux, and this work done gets converted into the electrical energy of the induced current.
If the induced current aided the change instead, flux would keep increasing and drive more current with no external work, creating energy from nothing, which is impossible.

(a)(ii)(I) As the loop enters the field, flux increases, so by Lenz's law the induced current flows in a sense that opposes this increase (say anticlockwise).
As the loop leaves the field, flux decreases, so the induced current flows in the opposite sense (clockwise), opposing the decrease.

(a)(ii)(II) $\phi$-$t$ graph: $\phi = 0$ till the loop reaches the field; rises linearly to a maximum value $B\ell^2$ while entering (over time $t = \ell/v$); stays constant at $B\ell^2$ while fully inside; falls linearly to zero while leaving.
$E$-$t$ graph: $E = 0$ before entering and while fully inside; $E = -B\ell v$ (constant) while entering; $E = +B\ell v$ (constant, opposite sign) while leaving; $E = 0$ after leaving.

questions.question: (a) (i) Define self-inductance of a coil. Derive the expression for the energy required to build up a current $I$ in a coil of self-inductance $L$. (ii) The currents passing through two inductors of self-inductances $10$ mH and $20$ mH increase with time at the same rate. Draw graphs showing the variation of: (I) the magnitude of emf induced with the rate of change of current in each inductor. (II) the energy stored in each inductor with the current flowing through it. OR (b) (i) Define the term mutual inductance. Deduce the expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids of the same length having different radii and different number of turns. (ii) The current through an inductor is uniformly increased from zero to $2$ A in $40$ s. An emf of $5$ mV is induced during this period. Find the flux linked with the inductor at $t = 10$ s.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Self-inductance is the property of a coil by which it opposes any change in the current flowing through it, defined by $\phi = LI$, so $\varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$.
Derivation of energy: work done against the back emf in time $dt$ is $dW = \varepsilon I\,dt = L\dfrac{dI}{dt}I\,dt = LI\,dI$.
Total work to build current from $0$ to $I$: $W = \int_0^I LI\,dI = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^2$.
This work is stored as magnetic energy in the inductor.

(a)(ii)(I) Since $\varepsilon = L\left(\dfrac{dI}{dt}\right)$, the $\varepsilon$ vs $dI/dt$ graph is a straight line through the origin; the slope for $L = 20$ mH is twice as steep as that for $L = 10$ mH.

(a)(ii)(II) Since $W = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^2$, the $W$ vs $I$ graph is a parabola through the origin for each coil; for the same current, the $20$ mH curve lies above (rises faster than) the $10$ mH curve.

questions.question: (i) A rectangular coil of $N$ turns and area of cross-section $A$ is rotated at a steady angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform magnetic field. Obtain an expression for the emf induced in the coil at any instant of time. (ii) Two coplanar and concentric circular loops $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are placed coaxially with their centres coinciding. The radii of $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are $1$ cm and $100$ cm respectively. Calculate the mutual inductance of the loops. (Take $\pi^{2} = 10$)
questions.answer:
(i) Let the coil's normal make angle $\theta = \omega t$ with $B$ at time $t$.
Flux linked: $\phi = NBA\cos\omega t$.
Induced emf: $e = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$, where $e_0 = NBA\omega$.

(ii) For two coplanar, concentric loops with $r_1 \ll r_2$, treating the field of the larger loop as uniform over the smaller one:
$M = \dfrac{\mu_0\pi r_1^2}{2r_2}$
$M = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times\pi\times(0.01)^2}{2\times1} = 2\pi^2\times10^{-11}$ H
Using $\pi^2 = 10$: $M = 2\times10^{-10}$ H.

questions.question: (i) With the help of a diagram, briefly explain the construction and working of ac generator. (ii) An electron is revolving around a proton in an orbit of radius $r$ with a speed $v$. Obtain expression for magnetic moment associated with the electron.
questions.answer:
(i) Principle: electromagnetic induction — a coil rotated in a uniform magnetic field has changing flux, inducing an alternating emf.
Construction: armature coil ($N$ turns) on a soft-iron core, field magnets producing uniform $B$, slip rings fixed to the coil rotating with it, and carbon brushes touching the slip rings to connect to the external circuit.
Working: as the coil rotates with angular speed $\omega$, the flux linked changes continuously, inducing emf $e = e_0\sin\omega t$ (with $e_0 = NBA\omega$) which reverses direction every half cycle and is delivered via the brushes.

(ii) An electron revolving in a circle of radius $r$ with speed $v$ constitutes a current $I = \dfrac{e}{T} = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}$.
Magnetic moment $\mu = I\times A = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}\times\pi r^2$
$\mu = \dfrac{evr}{2}$.

questions.question: (i) Define coefficient of self-induction. Obtain an expression for self-inductance of a long solenoid of length $l$, area of cross-section $A$ having $N$ turns. (ii) Calculate the self-inductance of a coil using the following data obtained when an AC $[]$ source of frequency $\frac{200}{\pi}$ Hz and a DC source is applied across the coil. AC Source: $V$ (V), $I$ (A) = (3.0, 0.5), (6.0, 1.0), (9.0, 1.5). DC Source: $V$ (V), $I$ (A) = (4.0, 1.0), (6.0, 1.5), (8.0, 2.0).
questions.answer:
(i) Coefficient of self-induction ($L$) is the flux linkage per unit current in a coil: $\phi = LI$, or equivalently $\varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$.
For a solenoid of length $l$, area $A$, $N$ turns: $B = \mu_0\dfrac{N}{l}I$, flux linkage $N\phi = \mu_0\dfrac{N^2A}{l}I = LI$.
So $L = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l}$.

(ii) From AC data, $V/I = 6.0$ Ω throughout, so impedance $Z = 6$ Ω.
From DC data, $V/I = 4.0$ Ω throughout, so resistance $R = 4$ Ω (inductor offers no reactance to DC).
$Z^2 = R^2 + (\omega L)^2 \Rightarrow 36 = 16 + (\omega L)^2 \Rightarrow \omega L = \sqrt{20}$ Ω
$\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi\times\dfrac{200}{\pi} = 400$ rad/s
$L = \dfrac{\sqrt{20}}{400} \approx 11.2\times10^{-3}$ H $= 11.2$ mH.

questions.question: (i) With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the principle and working of an ac generator.Hence, obtain an expression for the instantaneous value of the emf generated. (ii) The coil of an ac generator consists of $100$ turns of wire, each of area $0.5$ m $2$. The resistance of the wire is $100 \Omega$. The coil is rotating in a magnetic field of $0.8$ T perpendicular to its axis of rotation, at a constant angular speed of $60$ radian per second. Calculate the maximum emf generated and power dissipated in the coil.
questions.answer:
(i) Principle: When a coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field, the magnetic flux linked with it changes continuously, inducing an emf (electromagnetic induction).
Construction: A rectangular armature coil $ABCD$ of $N$ turns rotates about an axis perpendicular to a uniform field $\vec{B}$ between the pole pieces of a magnet. The coil ends are joined to two slip rings, against which carbon brushes press to connect the coil to the external circuit.
If the normal to the coil makes angle $\omega t$ with $\vec{B}$ at time $t$, flux $\phi = NBA\cos\omega t$.
Induced emf $e = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$, where $e_0 = NBA\omega$ is the peak emf.
(ii) $e_0 = NBA\omega = 100 \times 0.8 \times 0.5 \times 60 = 2400$ V.
Power dissipated $P = \dfrac{e_0^2}{2R} = \dfrac{(2400)^2}{2 \times 100} = 28800$ W.

questions.question: A conducting rod $PQ$ of length $20$ cm and resistance $0$· $1 \Omega$ rests on two smooth parallel rails of negligible resistance $AA^{'}$ and $CC^{'}$. It can slide on the rails and the arrangement is positioned between the poles of a permanent magnet producing uniform magnetic field $B = 0$· $4$ T. The rails, the rod and the magnetic field are in three mutually perpendicular directions as shown in the figure. If the ends $A$ and $C$ of the rails are short circuited, find the (i) external force required to move the rod with uniform velocity $v = 10$ cm/s, and (ii) power required to do so.
questions.answer:
Motional emf: $e = Blv = 0.4 \times 0.2 \times 0.1 = 8 \times 10^{-3}$ V.
Induced current: $I = e/R = 8\times10^{-3}/0.1 = 0.08$ A.
(i) For uniform velocity, the applied force balances the magnetic force on the current-carrying rod: $F = BIl = 0.4 \times 0.08 \times 0.2 = 6.4 \times 10^{-3}$ N.
(ii) Power required $P = Fv = 6.4\times10^{-3} \times 0.1 = 6.4 \times 10^{-4}$ W (equal to $I^2R$, the rate of heat dissipation).

questions.question: (a) Derive an expression for the induced emf developed when a coil of $N$ turns, and area of cross-section $A$, is rotated at a constant angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform magnetic field $B$. (b) A wheel with $100$ metallic spokes each $0.5$ m long is rotated with a speed of $120$ rev/min in a plane normal to the horizontal component of the Earth’s magnetic field. If the resultant magnetic field at that place is $4 \times 10^{-4}$ T and the angle of dip at the place is $30^{^{\circ}}$, find the emf induced between the axle and the rim of the wheel. OR (a) Derive the expression for the magnetic energy stored in an inductor when a current $I$ develops in it. Hence, obtain the expression for the magnetic energy density. (b) A square loop of sides $5$ cm carrying a current of $0.2$ A in the clockwise direction is placed at a distance of $10$ cm from an infinitely long wire carrying a current of $1$ A as shown. Calculate (i) the resultant magnetic force, and (ii) the torque, if any, acting on the loop.
questions.answer:
(a) When a coil of $N$ turns, area $A$, rotates with angular speed $\omega$ in field $B$, the flux at time $t$ is $\phi = NBA\cos\omega t$.
Induced emf $e = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$, with peak value $e_0 = NBA\omega$.
(b) $\omega = 2\pi\nu = 2\pi \times \dfrac{120}{60} = 4\pi$ rad/s.
Horizontal component $B_H = B\cos\delta = 4\times10^{-4}\cos30^\circ = 3.46\times10^{-4}$ T.
Each spoke acts as a rotating rod; emf between axle and rim: $e = \dfrac{1}{2}B_H\omega l^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 3.46\times10^{-4}\times4\pi\times(0.5)^2 \approx 5.4\times10^{-4}$ V (same for all spokes, in parallel, so net emf is this value).

questions.question: (a) A metallic rod of length ’ $l$’ and resistance ’ $R$’ is rotated with a frequency ’ $\nu$’ with one end hinged at the centre and the other end at the circumference of a circular metallic ring of radius ’ $l$’, about an axis passing through the centre and perpendicular to the plane of the ring. A constant and uniform magnetic field ’ $B$’ parallel to the axis is present everywhere. (i) Derive the expression for the induced emf and the current in the rod. (ii) Due to the presence of current in the rod and of the magnetic field, find the expression for the magnitude and direction of the force acting on this rod. (iii) Hence, obtain an expression for the power required to rotate the rod. (b) A copper coil is taken out of a magnetic field with a fixed velocity. Will it be easy to remove it from the same field if its ohmic resistance is increased? OR (a) A rectangular coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field. Obtain an expression for induced emf and current at any instant. Also find their peak values. Show the variation of induced emf versus angle of rotation $(\omega t)$ on a graph. (b) An iron bar falling through the hollow region of a thick cylindrical shell made of copper experiences a retarding force. What can you conclude about the nature of the iron bar? Explain.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) An element $dr$ at radius $r$ moving with speed $v = \omega r$ has emf $de = B(\omega r)dr$.
Total emf $e = \int_0^l B\omega r\,dr = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$, where $\omega = 2\pi\nu$.
Current $I = \dfrac{e}{R} = \dfrac{B\omega l^2}{2R}$.
(ii) Force on current-carrying rod in field $B$: $F = BIl = \dfrac{B^2\omega l^3}{2R}$, directed tangentially, opposing the rotation of the rod (Lenz's law).
(iii) Power required $P = eI = \dfrac{B^2\omega^2 l^4}{4R}$ (equal to the ohmic power dissipated).
(b) Yes, it becomes easier. Increasing the resistance reduces the induced current $I = e/R$, so the retarding (opposing) force $F = BIl$ decreases, so less external force is needed to remove the coil.

questions.question: (a) State the principle of an ac generator and explain its working with the help of a labelled diagram. Obtain the expression for the emf induced in a coil having $N$ turns each of cross-sectional area $A$, rotating with a constant angular speed ’ $\omega$’ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$, directed perpendicular to the axis of rotation. (b) An aeroplane is flying horizontally from west to east with a velocity of $900$ km/hour. Calculate the potential difference developed between the ends of its wings having a span of $20$ m. The horizontal component of the Earth’s magnetic field is $5 \times 10^{-4}$ T and the angle of dip is $30^{^{\circ}}$.
questions.answer:
(a) Principle: A coil rotating in a magnetic field experiences a change in flux linkage, which induces an alternating emf (electromagnetic induction).
The armature coil, mounted between magnetic poles, is connected through slip rings and brushes to the external circuit.
Flux at time $t$: $\phi = NBA\cos\omega t$; induced emf $e = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$.
(b) $v = 900$ km/h $= 250$ m/s, $l = 20$ m.
Vertical component $B_V = B_H\tan\delta = 5\times10^{-4}\times\tan30^\circ = 2.89\times10^{-4}$ T.
Only $B_V$ contributes to emf across the horizontal wings: $e = B_V l v = 2.89\times10^{-4}\times20\times250 \approx 1.44$ V.

questions.question: (a) Draw a labelled diagram of AC generator. Derive the expression for the instantaneous value of the emf induced in the coil. (b) A circular coil of cross-sectional area $200 cm^{2}$ and 20 turns is rotated about the vertical diameter with angular speed of $50 rad s^{-1}$ in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $3.0 \times 10^{-2} T$. Calculate the maximum value of the current in the coil. OR (a) Draw a labelled diagram of a step-up transformer. Obtain the ratio of secondary to primary voltage in terms of number of turns and currents in the two coils. (b) A power transmission line feeds input power at $2200 V$ to a step-down transformer with its primary windings having 3000 turns. Find the number of turns in the secondary to get the power output at $220 V$.
questions.answer:
(a) In an ac generator, a coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ rotates with angular speed $\omega$ between magnet poles, connected to the external circuit via slip rings and brushes.
Flux $\phi = NBA\cos\omega t$; induced emf $e = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$, with $e_0 = NBA\omega$.
(b) $e_0 = NBA\omega = 20 \times 3\times10^{-2} \times 0.02 \times 50 = 0.6$ V.
Maximum current $i_0 = \dfrac{e_0}{R}$, where $R$ is the resistance of the coil circuit.

questions.question: (a) State Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction. (b) The magnetic field through a circular loop of wire $12$ cm in radius and $8$· $5 \Omega$ resistance, changes with time as shown in the figure. The magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the loop. Calculate the induced current in the loop and plot it as a function of time. (c) Show that Lenz’s law is a consequence of conservation of energy. OR (a) Describe, with the help of a suitable diagram, the working principle of a step-up transformer. Obtain the relation between input and output voltages in terms of the number of turns of primary and secondary windings and the currents in the input and output circuits. (b) Given the input current $15$ A and the input voltage of $100$ V for a step-up transformer having $90\%$ efficiency, find the output power and the voltage in the secondary if the output current is $3$ A.
questions.answer:
(a) Faraday's law: The magnitude of the emf induced in a circuit is equal to the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with it: $e = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}$.
(b) Induced current $I = \dfrac{e}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R}\left|\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}\right| = \dfrac{A}{R}\left|\dfrac{dB}{dt}\right|$, where $A = \pi r^2 = \pi(0.12)^2 = 0.0452$ m$^2$.
For each interval of the given $B$-$t$ graph, $I$ is constant and equal to $\dfrac{A}{R}\times(\text{slope of that segment})$, with sign given by Lenz's law; $I = 0$ wherever $B$ is constant. The current-time plot is thus a step (rectangular) graph mirroring the slopes of the $B$-$t$ graph.
(c) By Lenz's law, the induced emf opposes the change producing it, so work must be done against this opposition to change the flux; this work appears as electrical energy which is dissipated as heat. If the induced effects aided the change instead, energy would be created from nothing, violating conservation of energy. Hence Lenz's law is consistent with energy conservation.

questions.question: (a) Draw a labelled diagram of an ac generator. Obtain the expression for the emf induced in the rotating coil of $N$ turns each of cross-sectional area $A$, in the presence of a magnetic field $\vec{B}$. (b) A horizontal conducting rod $10$ m long extending from east to west is falling with a speed $5.0$ m s $-1$ at right angles to the horizontal component of the Earth’s magnetic field, $0.3 \times 10^{-4}$ Wb m $-2$. Find the instantaneous value of the emf induced in the rod.
questions.answer:
(a) In an ac generator, a coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ rotates with angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform field $\vec{B}$, connected to the external circuit through slip rings and brushes.
Flux $\phi = NBA\cos\omega t$; induced emf $e = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$, $e_0 = NBA\omega$.
(b) $e = B_Hlv = 0.3\times10^{-4} \times 10 \times 5.0 = 1.5\times10^{-3}$ V.

questions.question: (a) When a bar magnet is pushed towards (or away) from the coil connected to a galvanometer, the pointer in the galvanometer deflects. Identify the phenomenon causing this deflection and write the factors on which the amount and direction of the deflection depends. State the laws describing this phenomenon. (b) Sketch the change in flux, emf and force when a conducting rod $PQ$ of resistance $R$ and length $l$ moves freely to and fro between $A$ and $C$ with speed $v$ on a rectangular conductor placed in uniform magnetic field as shown in the figure.
questions.answer:
(a) Phenomenon: electromagnetic induction.
The deflection (magnitude of induced emf) depends on: (1) the rate of relative motion between magnet and coil (or speed of the magnet), (2) the strength of the magnet, and (3) the number of turns and area of the coil; the direction of deflection depends on the direction of relative motion of the magnet.
Laws: Faraday's first law states an emf is induced whenever flux linked with a circuit changes; his second law states $e = -N\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}$. Lenz's law gives the direction: the induced emf/current opposes the change in flux that produces it.
(b) As the rod moves from $A$ to $C$, flux $\phi = Blx$ increases linearly with position, so the $\phi$-$t$ graph rises linearly; on the return stroke it falls linearly, giving a triangular wave.
Emf $e = -Blv$ has constant magnitude $Blv$ during each stroke but reverses sign when the rod reverses direction, giving a square wave.
Force $F = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}$ always opposes the rod's velocity (Lenz's law), so it also has constant magnitude and reverses sign in phase with the emf.

questions.question: Draw a necessary arrangement for winding of primary and secondary coils in a step-up transformer. State its underlying principle and derive the relation between the primary and secondary voltages in terms of number of primary and secondary turns. Mention the two basic assumptions used in obtaining the above relation. State any two causes of energy loss in actual transformers.
questions.answer:
Principle: A step-up transformer works on mutual induction — a changing current in the primary coil produces a changing flux that induces an emf in the secondary coil.
Construction: Primary (fewer turns, $N_p$) and secondary (more turns, $N_s$) coils are wound on the same laminated soft-iron core so that nearly all flux is linked with both.
Since the same flux $\phi$ links each turn of both coils, emf per turn is equal: $\dfrac{e_p}{N_p} = \dfrac{e_s}{N_s}$, so $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$.
For an ideal transformer (no power loss), $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$, giving $\dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = \dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{I_p}{I_s}$.
Assumptions: (1) There is no flux leakage — the same flux links both windings at every instant. (2) The resistance of the windings is negligible, so there is no $I^2R$ loss.
Two causes of energy loss: (1) Copper loss — $I^2R$ heating in the winding resistances. (2) Core loss — due to hysteresis and eddy currents in the iron core.

questions.question: (a) Define mutual inductance and write its S.I. units. (b) Derive an expression for the mutual inductance of two long co-axial solenoids of same length wound one over the other. (c) In an experiment, two coils $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ are placed close to each other. Find out the expression for the emf induced in the coil $c_{1}$ due to a change in the current through the coil $c_{2}$.
questions.answer:
(a) Mutual inductance of a pair of coils is the property by virtue of which an emf is induced in one coil due to a change of current in the neighbouring coil: $\Phi_1 = M_{12} I_2$. SI unit: henry ($\mathrm{H}$), where $1\ \mathrm{H} = 1\ \mathrm{Wb/A}$.

(b) Consider two long coaxial solenoids of length $l$, wound one over the other, with $n_1$, $n_2$ turns per unit length and inner radius $r_1$ (area $A_1 = \pi r_1^2$). Current $I_1$ in solenoid 1 produces field $B_1 = \mu_0 n_1 I_1$ inside it.
Flux linked with solenoid 2 (which surrounds solenoid 1): $\Phi_2 = n_2 l \times B_1 A_1 = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A_1 l\, I_1$.
So $M_{21} = \Phi_2/I_1 = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A_1 l$. By reciprocity, $M_{12} = M_{21} = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A_1 l$.

(c) By Faraday's law, the emf induced in $c_1$ due to a changing current $I_2$ in $c_2$ is $e_1 = -M\dfrac{dI_2}{dt}$, the negative sign showing that the induced emf opposes the change producing it (Lenz's law).

questions.question: (a) Describe a simple experiment (or activity) to show that the polarity of emf induced in a coil is always such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change of magnetic flux that produces it. (b) The current flowing through an inductor of self inductance L is continuously increasing. Plot a graph showing the variation of (i) Magnetic flux versus the current (ii) Induced emf versus $dI/dt$ (iii) Magnetic potential energy stored versus the current. OR (a) Draw a schematic sketch of an ac generator describing its basic elements. State briefly its working principle. Show a plot of variation of (i) Magnetic flux and (ii) Alternating emf versus time generated by a loop of wire rotating in a magnetic field. (b) Why is choke coil needed in the use of fluorescent tubes with ac mains?
questions.answer:
(a) Connect a coil to a sensitive galvanometer and push the north pole of a bar magnet towards the coil: the galvanometer deflects, showing an induced current whose direction (by the right-hand rule) makes the coil face behave like a north pole, repelling the approaching magnet, i.e. opposing the increasing flux. When the magnet is withdrawn, the deflection reverses; the induced current now attracts the magnet, opposing the decreasing flux. In both cases the induced current opposes the change of flux causing it, confirming Lenz's law.

(b) (i) $\Phi$ versus $I$: a straight line through the origin, since $\Phi = LI$, slope $= L$.
(ii) $e$ versus $dI/dt$: a straight line through the origin, since $e = L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$, slope $= L$.
(iii) $U$ versus $I$: an upward-opening parabola, since $U = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^2$, energy increasing as the square of current.

questions.question: State Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction. Figure shows a rectangular conductor PQRS in which the conductor PQ is free to move in a uniform magnetic field $B$ perpendicular to the plane of the paper. The field extends from $x = 0$ to $x = b$ and is zero for $x > b$. Assume that only the arm PQ possesses resistance $r$. When the arm PQ is pulled outward from $x = 0$ to $x = 2b$ and is then moved backward to $x = 0$ with constant speed $v$, obtain the expressions for the flux and the induced emf. Sketch the variations of these quantities with distance $0 \leq x \leq2b$. OR Draw a schematic diagram of a step-up transformer. Explain its working principle. Deduce the expression for the secondary to primary voltage in terms of the number of turns in the two coils. In an ideal transformer, how is this ratio related to the currents in the two coils? How is the transformer used in large scale transmission and distribution of electrical energy over long distances?
questions.answer:
Faraday's law: whenever the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an emf is induced in it, equal to the negative rate of change of flux linkage: $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$.
Let $PQ$ have length $l$, moving with speed $v = dx/dt$.
Outward, $0\le x\le b$: $\Phi = Blx$, so $\varepsilon = -Blv$ (constant magnitude $Blv$).
Outward, $b\le x\le 2b$: field is zero, $\Phi = Bbl$ (constant), so $\varepsilon = 0$.
Return, $2b\to b$: still $\varepsilon = 0$, since the field is zero there.
Return, $b\to 0$: $\Phi = Blx$ decreases, so $\varepsilon = +Blv$, opposite in sign to the outward journey (Lenz's law).
Sketch: $\Phi$-$x$ rises linearly from $0$ to $Bbl$ for $0\le x\le b$, stays constant at $Bbl$ over $b\le x\le 2b$, then falls linearly back to $0$ as $x$ returns from $b$ to $0$.
$\varepsilon$-$x$ is a step pulse: $+Blv$ for $0<x<b$ (outward), $0$ for $b<x<2b$, and $-Blv$ for $b>x>0$ (return).

questions.question: (a) State the principle on which AC generator works. Draw a labelled diagram and explain its working. (b) A conducting rod held horizontally along East-West direction is dropped from rest from a certain height near the Earth’s surface. Why should there be an induced emf across the ends of the rod? Draw a plot showing the instantaneous variation of emf as a function of time from the instant it begins to fall. OR (a) State the principle of a step-up transformer. Explain, with the help of a labelled diagram, its working. (b) Describe briefly any two energy losses, giving the reasons for their occurrence in actual transformers.
questions.answer:
(a) Principle: electromagnetic induction — a coil rotated with constant angular velocity $\omega$ in a uniform magnetic field $B$ has a changing flux linkage, so an emf is induced. Elements: a field magnet, an armature coil (of $N$ turns, area $A$) rotated by mechanical energy, two slip rings fixed to the coil's ends, and brushes pressing on the rings to connect the coil to an external circuit. With $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$, the induced emf is $e = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$.

(b) As the horizontal E–W rod falls, it moves with increasing speed through the vertical component $B_v$ of the Earth's magnetic field, and the free charges experience a force $qv B_v$ along the rod, producing a motional emf $e = B_v l v$. Since $v = gt$, $e = B_v l g t$ increases linearly with time; the $e$–$t$ graph is a straight line through the origin with slope $B_v l g$.

questions.question: State the working of a.c. generator with the help of a labelled diagram. The coil of an a.c. generator having $N$ turns, each of area $A$, is rotated with a constant angular velocity $\omega$. Deduce the expression for the alternating e.m.f. generated in the coil. What is the source of energy generation in this device?
questions.answer:
Working: an a.c. generator works on the principle of electromagnetic induction — an armature coil ($N$ turns, area $A$) is rotated with constant angular velocity $\omega$ in a uniform field $B$ between the poles of a field magnet; the ends of the coil are connected via slip rings and brushes to the external circuit. As the coil rotates, the flux linked with it changes, inducing an emf; a mechanical source (turbine, engine) supplies the energy to rotate the coil.

Derivation: let the plane of the coil make angle $\theta = \omega t$ with the field direction at time $t$ (coil starting in the plane of $B$). Flux linked: $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$.
By Faraday's law, $e = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$, where $e_0 = NBA\omega$ is the peak emf.

Source of energy: the mechanical energy used to rotate the coil against the opposing (Lenz's law) torque is converted into electrical energy.

questions.question: (a) Derive the expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids of same length $l$ having radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ ($r_{2} > r_{1}$ and $l \gg r_{2}$). (b) Show that mutual inductance of solenoid 1 due to solenoid 2, $M_{12}$, is the same as that of 2 due to 1 i.e. $M_{21}$. (c) A power transmission line feeds power at 2200 V with a current of 5 A to a step down transformer with its primary winding having 4000 turns. Calculate the number of turns and the current in the secondary in order to get output power at 220 V.
questions.answer:
(a) For two coaxial solenoids of length $l$ wound one over the other, with $n_1$, $n_2$ turns per unit length and radii $r_1 < r_2$ ($l \gg r_2$): current $I_1$ in solenoid 1 gives $B_1 = \mu_0 n_1 I_1$ inside it (area $A_1 = \pi r_1^2$). Flux linked with solenoid 2: $\Phi_2 = n_2 l B_1 A_1 = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A_1 l I_1$, so $M_{21} = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A_1 l$.

(b) By symmetry of the derivation (interchanging 1 and 2, and noting the flux common region is still $A_1$, the smaller area), $M_{12} = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A_1 l = M_{21}$, i.e., $M_{12} = M_{21} = M$.

(c) Since $\dfrac{N_2}{N_1} = \dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$: $N_2 = 4000 \times \dfrac{220}{2200} = 400$ turns.
For an ideal transformer, $V_1 I_1 = V_2 I_2$: $I_2 = \dfrac{2200 \times 5}{220} = 50\ \mathrm{A}$.

questions.question: Describe briefly, with the help of a labelled diagram, the basic elements of an A.C. generator. State its underlying principle. Show diagrammatically how an alternating emf is generated by a loop of wire rotating in a magnetic field. Write the expression for the instantaneous value of the emf induced in the rotating loop.
questions.answer:
An a.c. generator has: (i) a field magnet producing a uniform magnetic field $B$, (ii) an armature coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ wound on a soft-iron core mounted on a rotating axle, (iii) two slip rings attached to the coil's ends, and (iv) carbon brushes pressing against the slip rings, connecting the coil to the external circuit.
Principle: electromagnetic induction — rotating the coil in the field changes the flux linked with it, inducing an emf.
As the coil (starting in the plane of $B$) rotates with angular velocity $\omega$, the flux is $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$, a cosine curve versus time; the induced emf $e = -d\Phi/dt = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$, a sine curve, $90^\circ$ out of phase with $\Phi$.
Instantaneous emf: $e = e_0\sin\omega t$, where $e_0 = NBA\omega$.

questions.question: (a) What are eddy currents? Write their two applications. (b) Figure shows a rectangular conducting loop $PQSR$ in which arm $RS$ of length $l$ is movable. The loop is kept in a uniform magnetic field $B$ directed downward perpendicular to the plane of the loop. The arm $RS$ is moved with a uniform speed $v$. Deduce an expression for (i) the emf induced across the arm $RS$, (ii) the external force required to move the arm, and (iii) the power dissipated as heat.
questions.answer:
(a) Eddy currents are induced currents that circulate in loops within the body of a bulk conductor when the magnetic flux linked with it changes. Applications: (1) electromagnetic braking in trains, (2) induction furnaces for melting metals.

(b) (i) As $RS$ moves with speed $v$, the motional emf induced is $\varepsilon = Bvl$.
(ii) Induced current $I = \varepsilon/R = Bvl/R$ ($R$ = resistance of the circuit) experiences a retarding force by Lenz's law; to keep $RS$ moving at constant speed, the external force must equal this: $F = BIl = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}$.
(iii) Power dissipated as heat: $P = I^2R = \dfrac{B^2l^2v^2}{R}$, which equals the power delivered by the external force, $Fv$.

questions.question: (a) State Lenz’s law.Give one example to illustrate this law."The Lenz’s law is a consequence of the principle of conservation of energy." Justify this statement. (b) Deduce an expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids but having different radii and different number of turns.
questions.answer:
(a) Lenz's law: the direction of an induced emf (or current) is always such as to oppose the change in magnetic flux that produces it. Example: when a bar magnet's north pole is pushed towards a coil, the induced current flows so as to make the near face of the coil a north pole, repelling the magnet and opposing its approach.
This is a consequence of energy conservation: work must be done against the opposing induced force to change the flux, and this mechanical work is converted into electrical energy. If the induced current instead aided the change, flux would increase further with no external work, creating energy from nothing, violating conservation of energy.

(b) For two coaxial solenoids of length $l$, turns per unit length $n_1, n_2$ and radii $r_1 < r_2$: field of solenoid 1, $B_1 = \mu_0 n_1 I_1$, links solenoid 2 only over area $A_1 = \pi r_1^2$, giving $\Phi_2 = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A_1 l\, I_1$, so $M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A_1 l$.

questions.question: An electromagnetic wave passes from vacuum into a dielectric medium with relative electrical permittivity $(3/2)$ and relative magnetic permeability $(8/3)$. Then, its: (A) wavelength is doubled and frequency remains unchanged. (B) wavelength is doubled and frequency is halved. (C) wavelength is halved and frequency remains unchanged. (D) wavelength and frequency both will remain unchanged.
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Refractive index $n = \sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}\times\frac{8}{3}} = 2$, so speed $v = c/n = c/2$ while frequency stays fixed by the source, hence wavelength $\lambda = v/f$ is halved.

questions.question: Electromagnetic waves used in a diagnostic tool in medicine have a wavelength range: (A) 1 nm to $10^{-3}$ nm (B) 400 nm to 1 nm (C) 1 mm to 700 nm (D) 0.1 m to 1 mm
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Diagnostic imaging (X-rays) uses electromagnetic waves of wavelength range $1$ nm to $10^{-3}$ nm.

questions.question: Electromagnetic waves used for purification of water are: (A) X-rays (B) Ultraviolet rays (C) Infrared rays (D) Ultrasonic rays
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Ultraviolet rays kill bacteria and germs, and hence are used for purifying water.

questions.question: Welders wear special glass goggles or face masks with glass windows to protect their eyes from: (A) Infrared rays (B) Ultraviolet rays (C) X-rays (D) Microwaves
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Welding arcs emit intense ultraviolet rays which can damage the eyes, so goggles with UV-absorbing glass are used.

questions.question: An electromagnetic wave is propagating along $x$-axis. At any instant, the phase difference (in radian) between the electric field $(\vec{E})$ and the magnetic field $(\vec{B})$ associated with the wave is: (A) zero (B) $\frac{\pi}{4}$ (C) $\frac{\pi}{2}$ (D) $\pi$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
In an electromagnetic wave, $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ oscillate in phase, so their phase difference is zero.

questions.question: The expressions of magnetic fields associated with four electromagnetic waves are given below: I. $B= (4\times10^{-7}$ T $) \sin[0$· $7\times10^{3}x+1$· $4\times10^{11}t]$ II. $B= (2\times10^{-7}$ T $) \sin[0$· $6\times10^{3}x+ ^{1}{}^{2} 1$· $5\times10^{11}t]$ III. $B= (3\times10^{-6}$ T $) \sin[0$· $5\times10^{3}x+1$· $5\times10^{11}t]$ IV. $B= (5\times10^{-7}$ T $) \sin[0$· $2\times ^{3}{}^{4} 10^{4}x + 4$· $8 \times 10^{11}t]$ Which wave is travelling in free space? (A) I (B) II (C) III (D) IV
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
For free space, $v = \omega/k = c = 3\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$, and only wave III gives $\dfrac{1.5\times10^{11}}{0.5\times10^{3}} = 3\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: The electric field and the magnetic field components of an electromagnetic wave travelling in vacuum are represented as $E = m \sin(\alpha z -\beta t)$ and $B = n \sin(\alpha z -\beta t)$, where $m$, $n$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants characterising the wave. Then: (A) $\frac{m}{n}= \frac{\alpha}{\beta}$ (B) $\frac{m}{n}= \frac{\beta}{\alpha}$ (C) $\frac{n}{m}= \frac{\beta}{\alpha}$ (D) $\frac{n}{m}= \alpha\beta$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
For a wave of form $\sin(\alpha z-\beta t)$, the wave speed $c = \beta/\alpha = E_0/B_0$, so $\dfrac{m}{n} = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}$.

questions.question: A plane electromagnetic wave travels through a medium and the magnetic field associated with it is given by $B = 5 \times 10^{-8} \sin(3 \times 10^{10} t -150 x)$ T, where $x$ is in metres and $t$ is in seconds. The velocity of the wave is: (A) $2$· $0 \times 10^{8}$ m s $-1$ (B) $4$· $5 \times 10^{7}$ m s $-1$ (C) $3$· $5 \times 10^{7}$ m s $-1$ (D) $2$· $5 \times 10^{8}$ m s $-1$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
$v = \dfrac{\omega}{k} = \dfrac{3\times10^{10}}{150} = 2.0\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: The ratio of amplitude of electric field to the amplitude of the magnetic field associated with an electromagnetic wave propagating in glass $(n = 1$ · $5)$ is: (A) $3 \times 10^{8}$ m s $-1$ (B) $2 \times 10^{8}$ m s $-1$ (C) $3$ · $3 \times 10^{-9}$ m s $-1$ (D) $5 \times 10^{-9}$ m s $-1$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
$\dfrac{E_0}{B_0} = v = \dfrac{c}{n} = \dfrac{3\times10^{8}}{1.5} = 2\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: The magnetic field in a plane electromagnetic wave travelling in glass $(n = 1.5)$ is given by $B= (2 \times 10^{-7}$ T $) \sin(\alpha x + 1.5 \times 10^{11} t)$ where $x$ is in metres and $t$ is in seconds. The $^{y}$ value of $\alpha$ is: (A) $0.5 \times 10^{3}$ m $-1$ (B) $6.0 \times 10^{2}$ m $-1$ (C) $7.5 \times 10^{2}$ m $-1$ (D) $1.5 \times 10^{3}$ m $-1$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
$v = c/n = 2\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$, so $\alpha = \dfrac{\omega}{v} = \dfrac{1.5\times10^{11}}{2\times10^{8}} = 7.5\times10^{2}$ m$^{-1}$.

questions.question: The given diagram exhibits the relationship between the wavelength of the electromagnetic waves and the energy of photon associated with them. The three points $P$, $Q$ and $R$ marked on the diagram may correspond respectively to: (A) X-rays, microwaves, UV radiation (B) X-rays, UV radiation, microwaves (C) UV radiation, microwaves, X-rays (D) Microwaves, UV radiation, X-rays
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
Since photon energy $E = hc/\lambda$ increases as wavelength decreases, the points of increasing energy (decreasing $\lambda$) correspond to microwaves, UV radiation and X-rays respectively.

questions.question: Which one of the following correctly represents the change in wave characteristics (all in vacuum) from microwaves to X-rays in electromagnetic spectrum? (A) Speed: Remains same; Wavelength: Decreases; Frequency: Remains same (B) Speed: Remains same; Wavelength: Decreases; Frequency: Increases (C) Speed: Increases; Wavelength: Increases; Frequency: Decreases (D) Speed: Remains same; Wavelength: Increases; Frequency: Remains same
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
In vacuum all electromagnetic waves travel with the same speed $c$; since $c = \nu\lambda$, going from microwaves to X-rays the wavelength decreases and frequency increases while speed remains unchanged.

questions.question: X-rays are more harmful to human beings than ultraviolet radiations because X-rays: (A) have frequency lower than that of ultraviolet radiations. (B) have wavelength smaller than that of ultraviolet radiations. (C) move faster than ultraviolet radiations in air. (D) are mechanical waves but ultraviolet radiations are electromagnetic waves.
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
X-rays have a smaller wavelength than UV radiation, hence higher frequency and greater photon energy $E = h\nu$, making them more penetrating and harmful.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Out of Infrared and radio waves, the radio waves show more diffraction effect. Reason (R): Radio waves have greater frequency than infrared waves. (A) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A). (B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A). (C) Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false. (D) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Radio waves, having a longer wavelength than infrared waves, diffract more (Assertion is true), but this is because radio waves have lower, not greater, frequency than infrared waves, so the Reason is false.

questions.question: The amplitude of electric field in an electromagnetic wave in free space is $1000$ V m $-1$. The amplitude of the magnetic field in this electromagnetic wave is: (A) $3.0 \times 10^{-6}$ T (B) $3.33 \times 10^{-6}$ T (C) $3.0 \times 10^{-11}$ T (D) $3.33 \times 10^{-11}$ T
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
$B_0 = E_0/c = 1000/(3 \times 10^{8}) = 3.33 \times 10^{-6}$ T.

questions.question: The electric field in space between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor (each of area $2.5 \times 10^{-3}$ m $2$) is changing at the rate of $4 \times 10^{6}$ V m $-1$ s $-1$. The displacement current between the plates of the capacitor is: (A) $1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ A (B) $3.47 \times 10^{-8}$ A (C) $8.85 \times 10^{-8}$ A (D) $6.32 \times 10^{-4}$ A
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
$I_d = \varepsilon_0 A \dfrac{dE}{dt} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 4 \times 10^{6} = 8.85 \times 10^{-8}$ A.

questions.question: In an electromagnetic wave travelling in free space, the amplitude of magnetic field is $6.0 \times 10^{-4}$ T. The amplitude of its electric field is: (A) $2 \times 10^{-4}$ V m $-1$ (B) $1.5 \times 10^{12}$ V m $-1$ (C) $1.8 \times 10^{5}$ V m $-1$ (D) $0.3 \times 10^{4}$ V m $-1$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
$E_0 = cB_0 = 3 \times 10^{8} \times 6.0 \times 10^{-4} = 1.8 \times 10^{5}$ V m$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Which of the following rays coming from the Sun plays an important role in maintaining the Earth’s warmth? (A) Infrared rays (B) $\gamma$ rays (C) UV rays (D) Visible light rays
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Infrared rays from the Sun are absorbed by the Earth's surface and greenhouse gases, keeping the Earth warm.

questions.question: The dimensions of $(\mu\varepsilon)$, where $\varepsilon$ is permittivity and $\mu$ is permeability of a medium, are: (A) $[M^{0}L^{-1}T]$ (B) $[M^{0}L^{-2}T^{2}]$ (C) $[M^{-1}L^{-2}T^{-1}]$ (D) $[M^{1}L^{1}T^{-1}]$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Since $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}$, $\mu\varepsilon = 1/c^{2}$, which has dimensions $[M^{0}L^{-2}T^{2}]$.

questions.question: Assertion (A): EM waves do not require a medium for their propagation. Reason (R): EM waves are transverse waves. Select the correct answer: (A) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A). (B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A). (C) Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false. (D) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Both statements are true, but EM waves need no medium because they consist of mutually sustaining oscillating electric and magnetic fields, not because of their transverse character, so R does not explain A.

questions.question: In the four regions, I, II, III and IV, the electric fields are described as: Region I: $E_{y} = E_{0} \sin(kz -\omega t)$ Region II: $E_{y} = E_{0}$ Region III: $E_{y} = E_{0} \sin kz$ Region IV: $E_{y} = E_{0} \cos kz$ The displacement current will exist in the region: (A) I (B) IV (C) II (D) III
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Displacement current $I_d = \varepsilon_0 \dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$ requires a time-varying electric field; only in Region I does $E_y = E_0\sin(kz-\omega t)$ depend on time, while in the other regions the field is static (independent of $t$), so displacement current exists only in Region I.

questions.question: The electric and magnetic fields of electromagnetic waves are: (A) In the same phase and perpendicular to each other. (B) In the same phase and not perpendicular to each other. (C) Not in the same phase but are perpendicular to each other. (D) Neither in the same phase nor perpendicular to each other.
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
In an electromagnetic wave, $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ oscillate in the same phase and are mutually perpendicular, both being perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.

questions.question: The first scientist who produced and observed electromagnetic waves of wavelengths in the range $25$ mm $-5$ mm was: (A) J.C. Maxwell (B) H.R. Hertz (C) J.C. Bose (D) G. Marconi
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
J.C. Bose was the first to produce and study electromagnetic waves of millimetre wavelength range ($25$ mm to $5$ mm).

questions.question: Electromagnetic waves with wavelength 10 nm are called: (A) Infrared waves (B) Ultraviolet rays (C) Gamma rays (D) X-rays
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Electromagnetic waves of wavelength $10$ nm lie in the ultraviolet range ($400$ nm to about $1$ nm).

questions.question: Welders wear special glass goggles or face masks with glass windows to protect their eyes from radiations produced by welding arcs. These radiations are: (A) X-rays (B) Ultraviolet rays (C) Infrared waves (D) Gamma rays
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Welding arcs produce ultraviolet rays, which can damage the eyes, so protective goggles with UV-absorbing glass are used.

questions.question: In four regions I, II, III and IV, the magnetic field is given by: I. $B_{y} = B_{0} \sin kz$ II. $B_{y} = B_{0} \cos kz$ III. $B_{y} = B_{0} \sin(kz-\omega t)$ IV. $B_{y} = B_{0} \sin kz+B_{0} \cos kz$ The electromagnetic wave will exist in the region: (A) IV (B) I (C) III (D) II
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Only $B_{y} = B_{0} \sin(kz-\omega t)$ has the form of a travelling wave $f(kz-\omega t)$, satisfying the wave equation, while the others are either time-independent or not valid wave solutions.

questions.question: Which one of the following has the highest frequency? (A) Infrared rays (B) Gamma rays (C) Radio waves (D) Microwaves
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength among the given options and hence, by $\nu = c/\lambda$, the highest frequency.

questions.question: Electromagnetic waves with frequency $1.0 \times 10^{18}$ Hz are known as: (A) Infrared rays (B) Ultraviolet rays (C) X-rays (D) Gamma rays
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
A frequency of $1.0 \times 10^{18}$ Hz corresponds to a wavelength of about $3 \times 10^{-10}$ m, which lies in the X-ray region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

questions.question: A plane electromagnetic wave is travelling in air in $+x$ direction. At a particular moment, its electric field $\vec{E}$ is along $+y$ direction. At that moment, the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is along: (A) $+z$ direction and in phase with $\vec{E}$ (B) $-z$ direction and in phase with $\vec{E}$ (C) $+z$ direction and out of phase with $\vec{E}$ (D) $-z$ direction and out of phase with $\vec{E}$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Since $\vec{E} \times \vec{B}$ must point along the direction of propagation $+\hat{x}$, with $\vec{E}$ along $+\hat{y}$, $\vec{B}$ must be along $+\hat{z}$, and in an electromagnetic wave $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ oscillate in phase.

questions.question: The phase difference between electric field $\vec{E}$ and magnetic field $\vec{B}$ in an electromagnetic wave propagating along $z$-axis is (A) zero (B) $\pi$ (C) $\frac{\pi}{2}$ (D) $\frac{\pi}{4}$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
The electric and magnetic field vectors of an electromagnetic wave oscillate in the same phase, so the phase difference between them is zero.

questions.question: The electromagnetic waves used to purify water are: (A) Infrared rays (B) Ultraviolet rays (C) X-rays (D) Gamma rays
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Ultraviolet rays have germicidal action and are used to disinfect and purify water by killing bacteria and other microorganisms.
