questions.question: How are electromagnetic waves produced? What is the source of energy of these waves? Draw a schematic sketch of the electromagnetic waves propagating along the $+x$-axis. Indicate the directions of the electric and magnetic fields. Write the relation between the velocity of propagation and the magnitudes of electric and magnetic fields.
questions.answer:
Electromagnetic waves are produced by accelerated (oscillating) charges, which radiate energy in the form of coupled electric and magnetic fields.
The energy of an em wave comes from the energy of the source (oscillator/accelerating charge) driving the charge, e.g. an oscillating LC circuit.
Schematic sketch: for a wave travelling along $+x$-axis, $\vec{E}$ oscillates along $y$-axis and $\vec{B}$ oscillates along $z$-axis, both perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation $x$, and are in phase.
Relation between velocity and field magnitudes: $c = E_0/B_0$, and in general $E/B = c$.

questions.question: Name the parts of the electromagnetic spectrum which is (a) suitable for radar systems used in aircraft navigation. (b) used to treat muscular strain. (c) used as a diagnostic tool in medicine. Write in brief, how these waves can be produced.
questions.answer:
(a) Microwaves are used for radar systems in aircraft navigation, since they can be transmitted as beams in a specific direction and reflected from objects.
(b) Infrared waves are used to treat muscular strain, as they produce heating effect on absorption by muscles.
(c) X-rays are used as a diagnostic tool in medicine, since they pass through flesh but not bones.
Production: microwaves are produced by klystron valves or magnetrons; infrared waves are produced by hot bodies and molecular vibrations; X-rays are produced when high-energy electrons strike a metal target.

questions.question: Answer the following: (a) Name the em waves which are suitable for radar systems used in aircraft navigation. Write the range of frequency of these waves. (b) If the earth did not have atmosphere, would its average surface temperature be higher or lower than what it is now? Explain. (c) An em wave exerts pressure on the surface on which it is incident. Justify.
questions.answer:
(a) Microwaves are suitable for radar systems used in aircraft navigation; their frequency range is about $10^9\ \text{Hz}$ to $10^{11}\ \text{Hz}$.
(b) Without atmosphere, the earth's average surface temperature would be lower, because the atmosphere (greenhouse gases like $CO_2$) traps outgoing infrared radiation and keeps the surface warm; without it, this heat would escape into space.
(c) An em wave carries both energy and momentum; when incident on a surface, the momentum delivered per unit time exerts a force, hence a pressure, on the surface.

questions.question: Answer the following: (a) Name the em waves which are used for the treatment of certain forms of cancer. Write their frequency range. (b) Thin ozone layer on top of stratosphere is crucial for human survival. Why? (c) Why is the amount of the momentum transferred by the em waves incident on the surface so small?
questions.answer:
(a) Gamma rays are used for treatment of certain forms of cancer; their frequency range is about $10^{18}\ \text{Hz}$ to $10^{22}\ \text{Hz}$.
(b) The thin ozone layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun, which would otherwise damage living tissue and cause skin cancer and other harmful effects; hence it is crucial for survival.
(c) The momentum transferred is small because momentum of an em wave is related to its energy by $p = U/c$, and since $c$ is extremely large, the momentum for ordinary energy values is very small.

questions.question: Answer the following the questions: (a) Name the em waves which are produced during radioactive decay of a nucleus. Write their frequency range. (b) Welders wear special glass goggles while working. Why? Explain. (c) Why are infrared waves often called as heat waves? Give their one application.
questions.answer:
(a) Gamma rays are produced during radioactive decay of a nucleus; their frequency range is about $10^{18}\ \text{Hz}$ to $10^{22}\ \text{Hz}$.
(b) Welders wear special glass goggles fitted with protective glass to protect their eyes from the intense ultraviolet radiation produced during welding, which can cause damage to eye tissue and cornea.
(c) Infrared waves are called heat waves because they are readily absorbed by water molecules present in most materials, increasing their thermal motion and thus heating them; hence they are also felt as heat from a source.
One application: used in remote controls and for producing warmth in physiotherapy.

questions.question: Write briefly any two factors which demonstrate the need for modulating a signal. Draw a suitable diagram to show amplitude modulation using a sinusoidal signal as the modulating signal.
questions.answer:
Need for modulation:
(i) Size of antenna: for effective radiation, antenna length must be comparable to the wavelength of the signal; audio signals have very long wavelengths requiring impracticably large antennas, so they must be superimposed on a high-frequency carrier wave.
(ii) Effective power radiated: power radiated by an antenna is proportional to $(l/\lambda)^2$ (or to the square of frequency), so low-frequency audio signals radiate very little power directly, whereas high-frequency modulated signals radiate effectively.
Diagram: sketch shows (a) a sinusoidal modulating (audio) signal of low frequency, (b) a high-frequency sinusoidal carrier wave of constant amplitude, and (c) the resultant amplitude-modulated wave whose amplitude varies in accordance with the modulating signal envelope, while the carrier frequency remains unchanged.

questions.question: Draw a schematic diagram showing the (i) ground wave (ii) sky wave and (iii) space wave propagation modes for em waves. Write the frequency range for each of the following: (i) Standard AM broadcast (ii) Television (iii) Satellite communication
questions.answer:
Diagram description: ground wave travels along the earth's surface directly from transmitting to receiving antenna; sky wave travels upward, gets reflected back to earth by the ionosphere; space wave travels in a straight line from transmitting antenna to receiving antenna (line-of-sight), including a component reflected from the earth's surface, used for frequencies above $40\ \text{MHz}$ where the ionosphere is transparent.
(i) Standard AM broadcast: $540\ \text{kHz}$ to $1600\ \text{kHz}$ (medium wave band).
(ii) Television: $54\ \text{MHz}$ to $890\ \text{MHz}$ (VHF/UHF).
(iii) Satellite communication: $\text{GHz}$ range, typically $5$ to $30\ \text{GHz}$.

questions.question: Write four characteristics of electromagnetic waves. Give two uses each of (i) Radio-waves (ii) Micro-waves.
questions.answer:
Four characteristics of electromagnetic waves:
(i) They are transverse in nature, with $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation.
(ii) They travel through vacuum with speed $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} = 3 \times 10^8\ \text{m/s}$.
(iii) They do not require a material medium for propagation.
(iv) They carry energy and momentum, and exert radiation pressure.
Uses of radio waves: (1) radio and television broadcasting, (2) long-distance point-to-point communication.
Uses of microwaves: (1) radar systems for aircraft navigation, (2) in microwave ovens and for satellite/mobile communication.

questions.question: Name the following constituent radiations of electromagnetic spectrum which (i) produce intense heating effect. (ii) is absorbed by the ozone layer in the atmosphere. (iii) is used for studying crystal structure. Write one more application for each of these radiations.
questions.answer:
(i) Infrared radiation produces intense heating effect; it is also used in remote sensing and therapy for muscular strain.
(ii) Ultraviolet radiation is absorbed by the ozone layer in the atmosphere; it is also used for sterilizing surgical instruments and detecting forged documents.
(iii) X-rays are used for studying crystal structure; they are also used as a diagnostic tool in medicine to detect bone fractures.

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram of Hertz’s experimental set-up to produce electromagnetic waves. Explain the generation of electromagnetic waves using this set-up.
questions.answer:
Diagram description: Hertz's set-up consists of two metal plates connected to two metal spheres separated by a small air gap, forming a spark gap oscillator; the two spheres are connected via an induction coil to a high-voltage source, and a separate detector loop (with a small gap) is placed at a distance to detect the waves.
Generation: the induction coil charges the two spheres to a high potential difference until the air in the gap breaks down and a spark is produced, causing charge to oscillate rapidly back and forth between the spheres.
This oscillating charge (i.e., oscillating current) accelerates and decelerates repeatedly, producing oscillating electric and magnetic fields that radiate outward as electromagnetic waves.
Hertz detected these waves using the detector loop placed at some distance, in which a spark was induced across its gap, confirming that electromagnetic waves had been produced and had travelled through space, thus verifying Maxwell's prediction.

questions.question: In a region, the electric potential varies as $V = 10 -50x$, where $V$ is in volts and $x$ in meters. The electric field in the region is: (A) 10 N/C along +x (B) 10 N/C along -x (C) 50 N/C along +x (D) 50 N/C along -x
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
$E = -\dfrac{dV}{dx} = -(-50) = 50$ N/C along $+x$.

questions.question: A conducting wire connects two charged metallic spheres A and B of radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ respectively. The distance between the spheres is very large compared to their radii. The ratio of electric fields, $(E_{1}/E_{2})$ at the surfaces of spheres A and B will be: (A) $\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}$ (B) $\frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}} 2$ (C) $\frac{r_{2}}{r^{2}} 12$ (D) $\frac{r_{1}}{r^{2}} 2$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Connected by a wire, both spheres reach the same potential $V = \dfrac{kq}{r}$, and since $E = \dfrac{kq}{r^2} = \dfrac{V}{r}$ at the surface, $\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \dfrac{r_2}{r_1}$.

questions.question: In a region electric field is given by $\vec{E} = 4x\hat{i}$ N/C. The potential difference between points A $(x = 1$ m $)$ and B $(x = 3$ m $)$, $(V_{A} -V_{B})$ is: (A) $-16$ V (B) $16$ V (C) $-8$ V (D) $8$ V $xy V = 1.0x^{2} -2.0y^{2}$

The electric potential for various points in- plane is given by, where $V$ is in volts and $x$, $y$ are in metres. The angle that the electric field at point $(2.0$ m $, 1.0$ m $)$ makes with the positive $x$-axis is: (A) $45^{^{\circ}}$ (B) $90^{^{\circ}}$ (C) $135^{^{\circ}}$ (D) $315^{^{\circ}}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
$E_x = -\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x} = -2x = -4$, $E_y = -\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y} = 4y = 4$ at $(2,1)$, so the field vector $(-4,4)$ lies in the second quadrant, making an angle of $135^{\circ}$ with the $+x$-axis.

questions.question: Three point charges $2q$, $-2q$ and $q$ are kept at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $l$. The potential energy of the system is: (A) zero $2$ (B) $\frac{-2q}{\pi\varepsilon_{0}l} 2$ (C) $\frac{q}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}l} 2$ (D) $\frac{-q}{\pi\varepsilon_{0}l}$
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
$U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 l}\left[(2q)(-2q) + (-2q)(q) + (q)(2q)\right] = \dfrac{-4q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 l} = \dfrac{-q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0 l}$.

questions.question: Two metal spheres of radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2} (r_{2} > r_{1})$ having charges $q_{1}$ and $q_{2}$ respectively kept in air, are brought in contact. Which of the following statements is NOT correct? (A) The total charge of the two spheres is conserved. (B) Both spheres attain the same potential. (C) The final potential of the system equals $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{(q_{1} + q_{2})}{(r_{1} + r_{2})}$. (D) The final potential of the system equals $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{(q_{1} + q_{2})(r_{1} + r_{2})}{r_{1}r_{2}}$.
questions.answer:
Option (D) is NOT correct.
When two spheres are connected, the total charge redistributes until both reach a common potential $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1+q_2}{r_1+r_2}$, so option (C) is the correct expression, while option (D) does not represent the true final potential.

questions.question: Three point charges $+q$, $-2q$ and $+q$ are placed along $x$-axis at points $x = -1$ m, $x = 0$ m and $x = 2$ m respectively. The potential energy of the system is: $2$ (A) $\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} 2$ (B) $\frac{-2q}{3\pi\varepsilon_{0}} 2$ (C) $\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} 2$ (D) $\frac{-5q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
$U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{(q)(-2q)}{1} + \dfrac{(-2q)(q)}{2} + \dfrac{(q)(q)}{3}\right] = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(-2q^2 - q^2 + \dfrac{q^2}{3}\right) = \dfrac{-2q^2}{3\pi\varepsilon_0}$.

questions.question: A point charge of $5 \mu$ C is located at $(1$ cm $, 1$ cm $)$ in $x$- $y$ plane. A second charge of $6 \mu$ C is brought from infinity to point $(-3$ cm $, 4$ cm $)$. The work done in the process is: (A) $0$· $54$ J (B) $5$· $4$ J (C) $-0$· $54$ J (D) $10$· $8$ J
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Distance $r = \sqrt{(1-(-3))^2+(1-4)^2} = \sqrt{16+9} = 5$ cm $= 0.05$ m, so $W = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r} = \dfrac{9\times10^9 \times 5\times10^{-6}\times 6\times10^{-6}}{0.05} = 5.4$ J.

questions.question: Case Study: Capacitors are manufactured with certain standard capacitances and working voltages. However, these standard values may not be the ones that are actually needed in a particular application. Two or more capacitors can be grouped in series or in parallel to achieve desired capacitance and voltage. When connected in series, the total capacitance decreases while the voltage rating increases, whereas in parallel connections, the total capacitance increases and maintains the same voltage rating. A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates and stored energy is proportional to the square of the voltage and capacitance $U = \frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$, where symbols have their usual meanings. Two capacitors, one of $3 \mu$ F and the other of $6 \mu$ F, are connected in series in the circuit as shown in the figure, for a long time. The total capacitance of the circuit is: (A) $6 \mu$ F (B) $3 \mu$ F (C) $9 \mu$ F (D) $2 \mu$ F
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
For series combination, $\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{6}$, giving $C = \dfrac{3\times6}{3+6} = 2\ \mu$F.

questions.question: The current in the $10 \Omega$ resistor is: (A) $0$· $3$ A (B) $0$· $6$ A (C) $0$· $2$ A (D) $0$
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
In steady state the capacitor is fully charged and acts as an open circuit, so no current flows through the branch containing the $10\ \Omega$ resistor, giving a current of $0$ A.

questions.question: The potential difference between point $A$ and $B$ is: (A) $2$ V (B) $0$· $3$ V (C) $0$· $2$ V (D) $3$ V
questions.answer: Option (C) is correct. In steady state no current flows through the capacitor arm of the bridge, and applying Kirchhoff's voltage law to the unbalanced resistor bridge gives $V_A - V_B = 0.2$ V.

questions.question: The value of charge on the plates of the $6 \mu$ F capacitor is: (A) $6 \mu$ C (B) $4 \mu$ C (C) $12 \mu$ C (D) $8 \mu$ C
questions.answer: Option (D) is correct. Since no steady current flows through the capacitor branch, the capacitors in series carry the same charge, and $Q = C_{eq}V$ across that branch gives $Q = 8\ \mu$C on the $6\ \mu$F capacitor.

questions.question: The wire between two capacitors is cut at point $P$. The current in the circuit will: (A) increase (B) decrease (C) remain the same (D) first increase then become stable
questions.answer: Option (C) is correct. In steady state the wire joining the two capacitors carries no current (a capacitor blocks DC), so cutting it at $P$ leaves the resistor branch current unchanged.

questions.question: The figure represents the variation of the electric potential $V$ at a point in a region of space as a function of its position along the $x$-axis. A charged particle will experience the maximum force at: (A) $P$ (B) $Q$ (C) $R$ (D) $S$
questions.answer: Option (C) is correct. Since $E = -\dfrac{dV}{dx}$, the force $F = qE$ on the charge is maximum where the $V$-$x$ graph has the steepest slope, which occurs at $R$.

questions.question: The electric field $\vec{E}$ in the region between the plates is: $[_{2}$ V $]$ (A) $2 \times 10\hat{k}$ m $[_{2}$ V $]$ (B) $-2 \times 10\hat{k}$ m $[_{4}$ V $]$ (C) $2 \times 10\hat{k}$ m $[_{4}$ V $]$ (D) $-2 \times 10\hat{k}$ m
questions.answer: Option (D) is correct. Using $E = V/d$ between the plates, the field magnitude works out to $2 \times 10^{4}$ V/m, directed from the positive to the negative plate, i.e. along $-\hat{k}$.

questions.question: In the region between the plates, the electron moves with an acceleration $\vec{a}$ given by: (A) $-(3.5 \times 10^{15}$ ms $^{-2}) \hat{k}$ (B) $(3.5 \times 10^{15}$ ms $^{-2}) \hat{k}$ (C) $(3.5 \times 10^{13}$ ms $^{-2})\hat{i}$ (D) $-(3.5 \times 10^{13}$ ms $^{-2})\hat{i}$
questions.answer: Option (B) is correct. Since the electron carries charge $-e$, its acceleration $\vec{a} = \dfrac{(-e)\vec{E}}{m}$ is opposite to $\vec{E}$, giving $\vec{a} = (3.5 \times 10^{15}\ \text{ms}^{-2})\hat{k}$.

questions.question: (a) Time interval during which an electron moves through the region between the plates is: (A) $9.0 \times 10^{-9}$ s (B) $1.67 \times 10^{-8}$ s (C) $1.67 \times 10^{-9}$ s (D) $2.17 \times 10^{-9}$ s
questions.answer: Option (C) is correct. The time spent between the plates is $t = L/v_0$, which on substitution gives $t = 1.67 \times 10^{-9}$ s.

questions.question: (b) The vertical displacement of the electron which travels through the region between the plates is: (A) $1.0$ mm (B) $4.9$ mm (C) $5.9$ mm (D) $3.0$ mm
questions.answer: Option (B) is correct. The vertical deflection is $y = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}(3.5 \times 10^{15})(1.67 \times 10^{-9})^2 = 4.9$ mm.

questions.question: Which one of the following is the path traced by the electron in between the two plates? (A) a (B) b (C) c (D) d
questions.answer: Option (A) is correct. With constant horizontal velocity and constant transverse acceleration, the electron follows a parabolic path, analogous to projectile motion, matching curve $a$.

questions.question: Two points $R$ and $S$ are equidistant from two charges $+Q$ and $-2Q$. The work done in moving a charge $-Q$ from point $R$ to $S$ is: (A) Zero (B) $\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0} d}$ (C) $\frac{2Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0} d}$ (D) $\frac{3Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0} d}$
questions.answer: Option (A) is correct. Since $R$ and $S$ are equidistant from both $+Q$ and $-2Q$, they lie on the same equipotential surface, so $V_R = V_S$ and $W = q(V_S - V_R) = 0$.

questions.question: Case Study (Q29): A circuit consisting of a capacitor $C$, a resistor of resistance $R$ and an ideal battery of emf $V$, as shown in figure, is known as an RC series circuit. As soon as the circuit is completed by closing key $S_{1}$ (keeping $S_{2}$ open), charges begin to flow between the capacitor plates and the battery terminals. The charge on the capacitor increases and consequently the potential difference $V_{c} (= q/C)$ across the capacitor also increases with time. When this potential difference equals the potential difference across the battery, the capacitor is fully charged ($Q = V C$). During this process of charging, the charge $q$ on the capacitor changes with time $t$ as $q = Q[1 -e^{-t/RC}]$. The charging current can be obtained by differentiating it and using $\frac{d}{dx}(e^{mx}) = m e^{mx}$. Consider the case when $R = 20$ k $\Omega$, $C = 500 \mu$ F and $V = 10$ V. (i) The final charge on the capacitor, when key $S_{1}$ is closed and $S_{2}$ is open, is: (A) $5 \mu$ C (B) $5$ mC (C) $25$ mC (D) $0.1$ C
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
$Q = VC = 10 \times 500 \times 10^{-6}$ C $= 5 \times 10^{-3}$ C $= 5$ mC.

questions.question: (ii) For sufficient time the key $S_{1}$ is closed and $S_{2}$ is open. Now $S_{2}$ is closed and $S_{1}$ is open. What is the final charge on the capacitor? (A) Zero (B) $5$ mC (C) $2.5$ mC (D) $5 \mu$ C
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
With $S_1$ open and $S_2$ closed the battery is disconnected and the capacitor discharges completely through $R$, so the final charge is zero.

questions.question: (iii) The dimensional formula for $RC$ is: (A) $[ML^{2}T^{-3}A^{-2}]$ (B) $[M^{0}L^{0}T^{-1}A^{0}]$ (C) $[M^{-1}L^{-2}T^{4}A^{2}]$ (D) $[M^{0}L^{0}TA^{0}]$
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
$RC$ has the dimensions of time, $[M^0L^0T^1A^0]$, since $q = Q(1-e^{-t/RC})$ requires $t/RC$ to be dimensionless.

questions.question: (iv) The key $S_{1}$ is closed and $S_{2}$ is open. The value of current in the resistor after $5$ seconds is: (A) $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{e}}$ mA (B) $\sqrt{e}$ mA (C) $\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}$ mA (D) $\frac{1}{2e}$ mA
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
$I = \frac{V}{R}e^{-t/RC}$; with $RC = 10$ s, $I_0 = \frac{10}{20000} = 0.5$ mA, so at $t=5$ s, $I = 0.5\, e^{-1/2}$ mA $= \frac{1}{2\sqrt{e}}$ mA.

questions.question: (iv) OR: The key $S_{1}$ is closed and $S_{2}$ is open. The initial value of charging current in the resistor is: (A) $5$ mA (B) $0.5$ mA (C) $2$ mA (D) $1$ mA
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
At $t=0$, $I_0 = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{10}{20000} = 0.5$ mA.

questions.question: In the figure curved lines represent equipotential surfaces. A charge $Q$ is moved along different paths $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$. The work done on the charge will be maximum along the path: (A) $A$ (B) $B$ (C) $C$ (D) $D$
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
Work done in an electric field depends only on the potential difference between the initial and final equipotential surfaces, so the path spanning the greatest potential difference, path $D$, involves maximum work.

questions.question: Case study: A parallel plate capacitor has two parallel plates which are separated by an insulating medium like air, mica, etc. When the plates are connected to the terminals of a battery, they get equal and opposite charges and an electric field is set up in between them. This electric field between the two plates depends upon the potential difference applied, the separation of the plates and nature of the medium between the plates. The electric field between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is E. Now the separation between the plates is doubled and simultaneously the applied potential difference between the plates is reduced to half of its initial value. The new value of the electric field between the plates will be: (A) E (B) 2E (C) $\frac{E}{4}$ (D) $\frac{E}{2}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
$E = \frac{V}{d}$, so with $V' = \frac{V}{2}$ and $d' = 2d$, $E' = \frac{V/2}{2d} = \frac{E}{4}$.

questions.question: A constant electric field is to be maintained between the two plates of a capacitor whose separation d changes with time. Which of the graphs correctly depict the potential difference (V) to be applied between the plates as a function of separation between the plates (d) to maintain the constant electric field? (A) (B) (C) (D)
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Since $E = \frac{V}{d}$ is constant, $V = Ed$ is directly proportional to $d$, giving a straight line through the origin on the $V$-$d$ graph.

questions.question: In the above figure P, Q are the two parallel plates of a capacitor. Plate Q is at positive potential with respect to plate P. MN is an imaginary line drawn perpendicular to the plates. Which of the graphs shows correctly the variations of the magnitude of electric field strength E along the line MN? (A) (B) (C) (D)
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Between the plates the field is uniform with constant magnitude $E = \frac{V}{d}$ pointing from $Q$ to $P$, and it drops to zero outside the plates, giving a flat (rectangular) profile along $MN$.

questions.question: Three parallel plates are placed above each other with equal displacement d between neighbouring plates. The electric field between the first pair of the plates is $\vec{E}_{1}$ and the electric field between the second pair of the plates is $\vec{E}_{2}$. The potential difference between the third and the first plate is (A) $(\vec{E}_{1} +\vec{E}_{2})$ · $\vec{d}$ (B) $(\vec{E}_{1} -\vec{E}_{2})$ · $\vec{d}$ (C) $(\vec{E}_{2} -\vec{E}_{1})$ · $\vec{d}$ (D) $\frac{d(\vec{E}_{1} +\vec{E}_{2})}{2}$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
$V_{31} = V_{32} + V_{21} = \vec{E}_2 \cdot \vec{d} + \vec{E}_1 \cdot \vec{d} = (\vec{E}_1 + \vec{E}_2)\cdot \vec{d}$.

questions.question: A material of dielectric constant K is filled in a parallel plate capacitor of capacitance C. The new value of its capacitance becomes (A) C (B) $\frac{C}{K}$ (C) CK $[]$ (D) $C1 + \frac{1}{K}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Filling the entire gap between the plates with a dielectric of constant $K$ increases the capacitance to $C' = KC$.

questions.question: Case Study (Q29): A parallel plate capacitor consists of two conducting plates kept generally parallel to each other at a distance. When the capacitor is charged, the charge resides on the inner surfaces of the plates and an electric field is set up between them. Thus, electrostatic energy is stored in the capacitor. The figure shows three large square metallic plates, each of side ’ $L$’ held parallel and equidistant from each other. The space between $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ and $P_{2}$ and $P_{3}$ is completely filled with mica sheets of dielectric constant ’ $K$’. The plate $P_{2}$ is connected to point $A$ and other plates $P_{1}$ and $P_{3}$ are connected to point $B$. Point $A$ is maintained at a positive potential with respect to point $B$ and the potential difference between $A$ and $B$ is $V$. (i) The capacitance of the system between $A$ and $B$ will be: $2$ (A) $\frac{\varepsilon_{0}KL}{d} 2$ (B) $\frac{\varepsilon_{0}KL}{2d} 2$ (C) $\frac{2\varepsilon_{0}KL}{d}$ (D) $\frac{2\varepsilon_{0}Kd}{L^{2}}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Plate $P_2$ (at $A$) forms two capacitors with $P_1$ and $P_3$ (both at $B$), each of capacitance $\frac{K\varepsilon_0 L^2}{d}$, connected in parallel since $P_1$ and $P_3$ are at the same potential.
Total capacitance $C = \frac{K\varepsilon_0 L^2}{d} + \frac{K\varepsilon_0 L^2}{d} = \frac{2K\varepsilon_0 L^2}{d}$.

questions.question: (ii) The charge on plate $P_{2}$ is: $2$ (A) $\frac{\varepsilon_{0}V KL}{2d} 2$ (B) $\frac{\varepsilon_{0}V KL}{d} 2$ (C) $\frac{2\varepsilon_{0}V KL}{d} 2$ (D) $\frac{\varepsilon_{0}V KL}{4d}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Charge on $P_2$: $Q = CV = \frac{2K\varepsilon_0 L^2}{d}V = \frac{2\varepsilon_0 V K L^2}{d}$.

questions.question: (iii) The electric field in the region between $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ is: (A) $\frac{V}{d}$ (B) $\frac{2V}{d}$ (C) $\frac{V}{2d}$ (D) $\frac{d}{V}$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Since $P_1$ and $P_2$ are separated by distance $d$ with full potential difference $V$ between $A$ and $B$ across this gap, $E = \frac{V}{d}$.

questions.question: (iv) The separation between the plates of same area ($L^{2}$) of a parallel plate air capacitor having capacitance equal to that of this system, will be: (A) $\frac{d}{K}$ (B) $\frac{2d}{K}$ (C) $\frac{d}{2K}$ (D) $\frac{d}{4K}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Equating $\frac{\varepsilon_0 L^2}{d'} = \frac{2K\varepsilon_0 L^2}{d}$ gives $d' = \frac{d}{2K}$.

questions.question: (iv) OR: If the source of potential difference applied between $A$ and $B$ is removed, and then $A$ and $B$ are connected by a conducting wire, the net charge on the system will be: $2$ (A) $\frac{\varepsilon_{0}V KL}{4d} 2$ (B) $\frac{\varepsilon_{0}V KL}{2d} 2$ (C) $\frac{\varepsilon_{0}V KL}{d}$ (D) Zero
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
The positive charge on $P_2$ is exactly balanced by the negative charges on $P_1$ and $P_3$ (charge conservation on the isolated system), so connecting $A$ and $B$ by a wire leaves the net charge on the system as zero.

questions.question: A metal sheet is inserted between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor of capacitance $C$. If the sheet partly occupies the space between the plates, the capacitance: (A) remains $C$ (B) becomes greater than $C$ (C) becomes less than $C$ (D) becomes zero
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
A conducting sheet placed between the plates behaves like a dielectric of infinite $K$ for that region, which reduces the effective gap and always increases the capacitance above $C$.

questions.question: The electric field at a point in a region is given by $\vec{E} = \frac{\alpha}{r^{3}}$, where $\alpha$ is a constant and $r \vec{r}$ is the distance of the point from the origin. The magnitude of potential of the point is: (A) $\frac{\alpha}{r} 2$ (B) $\frac{\alpha r}{2}$ (C) $\frac{\alpha}{2r}$ (D) $-\frac{\alpha}{r}$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
$V = -\int_\infty^r E\,dr = \int_r^\infty \frac{\alpha}{r'^2}\,dr' = \frac{\alpha}{r}$, since $\vec{E} = \frac{\alpha}{r^3}\vec{r}$ has magnitude $\frac{\alpha}{r^2}$.

questions.question: The effective capacitance of the network between points $A$ and $B$ shown in the figure is: (A) $\frac{4}{3}\mu$ F (B) $2 \mu$ F (C) $\frac{3}{4}\mu$ F (D) $6 \mu$ F
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Two $2\,\mu$F capacitors in parallel give $4\,\mu$F, which combines in series with the remaining $2\,\mu$F capacitor: $C = \frac{4 \times 2}{4+2} = \frac{4}{3}\,\mu$F.

questions.question: Four point charges $Q$ each, are held at the four corners of a square of side $l$. The amount of work done in bringing a charge $Q$ from infinity to the centre of the square will be: $2$ (A) $\frac{Q}{\pi\varepsilon_{0}l} 2$ (B) $\frac{\sqrt{2} Q}{\pi\varepsilon_{0}l} 2$ (C) $\frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}l}$ (D) Zero
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Each corner charge is at distance $\frac{l}{\sqrt{2}}$ from the centre, so the potential at the centre is $V = 4 \times \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 (l/\sqrt{2})} = \frac{\sqrt{2}Q}{\pi\varepsilon_0 l}$, and the work done is $W = QV = \frac{\sqrt{2}Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0 l}$.

questions.question: Case Study (Capacitors): A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. In practice, the two conductors have charges $Q$ and $-Q$ with potential difference $V = V_{1} -V_{2}$ between them. The ratio $\frac{Q}{V}$ is a constant, denoted by $C$ and is called the capacitance of the capacitor. It is independent of $Q$ or $V$. It depends only on the geometrical configuration (shape, size, separation) of the two conductors and the medium separating the conductors. When a parallel plate capacitor is charged, the electric field $E_{0}$ is localised between the plates and is uniform throughout. When a slab of a dielectric is inserted between the charged plates (charge density $\sigma$), the dielectric is polarised by the field. Consequently opposite charges appear on the faces of the slab, near the plates, with surface charge density of magnitude $\sigma_{p}$. For a linear dielectric $\sigma_{p}$ is proportional to $E_{0}$. Introduction of a dielectric changes the electric field, and hence, the capacitance of a capacitor, and hence, the energy stored in the capacitor. Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series or in parallel or in a combination of series and parallel. (i) Consider a capacitor of capacitance $C$, with plate area $A$ and plate separation $d$, filled with air [Fig. (a)]. The distance between the plates is increased to $2d$ and one of the plates is shifted as shown in Fig. (b). The capacitance of the new system now is: (A) $\frac{C}{4}$ (B) $\frac{C}{2}$ (C) $2C$ (D) $4C$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Doubling the separation halves $C$, and shifting the plate so that only half the area overlaps halves it again, giving $C' = C/4$.

questions.question: (ii) A slab (area $A$ and thickness $d_{1}$) of a linear dielectric of dielectric constant $K$ is inserted between charged plates (charge density $\sigma$) of a parallel plate capacitor [plate area $A$ and plate separation $d (> d_{1})$] and opposite charges with charge density of magnitude $\sigma_{p}$ appear on the faces of the slab. The dielectric constant $K$ is given by: (A) $\frac{\sigma -\sigma_{p}}{\sigma}$ (B) $\frac{\sigma}{\sigma -\sigma_{p}}$ (C) $\frac{\sigma + \sigma_{p}}{\sigma_{p}}$ (D) $\frac{\sigma}{\sigma_{p}}$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Since $E = E_0/K$ and $\sigma_p = \sigma\left(1 - \frac{1}{K}\right)$, we get $\sigma - \sigma_p = \sigma/K$, so $K = \frac{\sigma}{\sigma - \sigma_p}$.

questions.question: (iii) An electric field $E$ is established between the plates of an air filled parallel plate capacitor, with charges $Q$ and $-Q$. $V$ is the volume of the space enclosed between the plates. The energy stored in the capacitor is: (A) $\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{0}E^{2}$ (B) $\varepsilon_{0}EQV$ (C) $\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{0}E^{2}V$ (D) $\varepsilon_{0}EQV$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Energy density in a parallel plate capacitor is $u = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$, so total energy stored is $U = uV = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2 V$.

questions.question: (iv) (a) Three capacitors $A$, $B$ and $M$, each of capacitance $C$ are connected to a capacitor $N$ of capacitance $2C$ and a battery as shown in the figure. $'$ If the charges on $A$ and $N$ are $Q$ and $Q^{'}$ respectively, then $\frac{Q}{Q}$ is: OR (b) A slab (area $A$ and thickness $\frac{d}{2}$) of dielectric constant $K$ is inserted in a parallel plate capacitor of plate area $A$ and plate separation $d$. If $C$ and $C_{0}$ are the capacitances of the capacitors with and without the dielectric, then $\frac{C}{C_{0}}$ is: (A) (a) $\frac{1}{6}$| (b) $\frac{K + 1}{2K}$ (B) (a) $\frac{1}{3}$| (b) $\frac{2K}{K + 1}$ (C) (a) $3$ | (b) $\frac{K}{K -1}$ (D) (a) $6$ | (b) $\frac{K -1}{K}$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
For part (b), the slab of thickness $d/2$ acts in series with an equal air gap $d/2$, giving $C = \frac{2\varepsilon_0 A K}{d(K+1)}$ and $C_0 = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$, so $\frac{C}{C_0} = \frac{2K}{K+1}$; the corresponding network in (a) gives $\frac{Q}{Q'} = \frac{1}{3}$.

questions.question: Two horizontal plates, separated by $1$ cm, are arranged one above the other. A particle of mass $5$ mg and charge $2$ nC is released in air between the plates. The potential difference that should be applied to the plates so that the particle remains suspended between them, is: (A) $250$ V (B) $200$ V (C) $100$ V (D) $50$ V
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
For equilibrium, $qE = mg \Rightarrow V = \frac{mgd}{q} = \frac{5\times10^{-6}\times10\times0.01}{2\times10^{-9}} = 250$ V.

questions.question: The electric field ($E$) and electric potential ($V$ ) at a point inside a charged hollow metallic sphere are respectively: (A) $E = 0$, $V = 0$ (B) $E = 0$, $V = V_{0}$ (a constant) (C) $E = 0$, $V = 0$ (D) $E = E_{0}$ (a constant), $V = 0$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Inside a charged hollow conductor the field is zero, but the potential equals the constant surface potential $V_0$, since $V$ is uniform throughout the conductor.

questions.question: In the circuit shown, the charge on the left plate of $20 \mu$ F capacitor is $-50 \mu$ C. The charge on the right plate of the $12 \mu$ F capacitor is: (A) $20 \mu$ C (B) $-20 \mu$ C (C) $30 \mu$ C (D) $-30 \mu$ C
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
By charge conservation at the isolated node, the induced charge divides in proportion to capacitance between the parallel branches meeting at that node, giving the left plate of the $12\ \mu$F capacitor $+30\ \mu$C and hence its right plate $-30\ \mu$C.

questions.question: Ten capacitors, each of capacitance $1 \mu$ F, are connected in parallel to a source of $100$ V. The total energy stored in the system is equal to: (A) $10^{-2}$ J (B) $10^{-5}$ J (C) $0.5 \times 10^{-5}$ J (D) $5.0 \times 10^{-2}$ J
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
For parallel capacitors, $C_{eq} = 10\ \mu$F, so $U = \frac{1}{2}C_{eq}V^2 = \frac{1}{2}\times10\times10^{-6}\times(100)^2 = 5.0\times10^{-2}$ J.

questions.question: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor having a medium of dielectric constant K = 4 in between the plates is C. If this medium is removed, then the capacitance of the capacitor becomes: (A) $4C$ (B) $C$ (C) $\frac{C}{4}$ (D) $2C$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Since $C = K\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$, removing the dielectric ($K=4$) reduces the capacitance to $\frac{C}{K} = \frac{C}{4}$.

questions.question: Consider a group of charges $q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3},...$ such that $\Sigma q = 0$. Then equipotentials at a large distance, due to this group are approximately: (A) Plane (B) Spherical surface (C) Paraboloidal surface (D) Ellipsoidal surface
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
With $\Sigma q = 0$, the monopole term vanishes, so at large distance the potential varies slowly and nearly uniformly over small regions, making the equipotential surfaces approximately planar rather than spherical.

questions.question: A proton is taken from point $P_{1}$ to point $P_{2}$, both located in an electric field. The potentials at points $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are $-5$ V and $+5$ V respectively. Assuming that kinetic energies of the proton at points $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are zero, the work done on the proton is: (A) $-1.6 \times 10^{-18}$ J (B) $1.6 \times 10^{-18}$ J (C) Zero (D) $0.8 \times 10^{-18}$ J
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
$W=q(V_2-V_1)=(1.6\times10^{-19})(5-(-5))$... using $W=q\Delta V=(1.6\times10^{-19})(-5-5)=-1.6\times10^{-18}$ J, since the proton moves from a lower to a higher potential the field does negative work on it.

questions.question: The figure shows four pairs of parallel identical conducting plates, separated by the same distance $2.0$ cm and arranged perpendicular to x-axis. The electric potential of each plate is mentioned. The electric field between a pair of plates is uniform and normal to the plates. For which pair of the plates is the electric field $\vec{E}$ along $\hat{i}$? (A) I (B) II (C) III (D) IV
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Since $\vec{E}=-\dfrac{dV}{dx}\hat{i}$, the field points along $+\hat{i}$ only for the pair whose potential decreases as $x$ increases; for pair II the left plate ($x=0$) is at a higher potential than the right plate ($x=2$ cm), giving $\vec E$ along $+\hat i$, while the other pairs have potential increasing with $x$.

questions.question: An electron is released midway between the plates of pair IV. It will: (A) move along $\hat{i}$ at constant speed (B) move along $-\hat{i}$ at constant speed (C) accelerate along $\hat{i}$ (D) accelerate along $-\hat{i}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
In pair IV the potential increases with $x$, so $\vec E$ points along $-\hat i$; the force on the electron is $\vec F=-e\vec E$, which is along $+\hat i$, and since the field between the plates is uniform this force is constant, so the electron accelerates uniformly along $\hat i$.

questions.question: Let $V_{0}$ be the potential at the left plate of any set, taken to be at $x = 0$ m. Then potential $V$ at any point ($0 < x < 2$ cm) between the plates of that set can be expressed as: ($\alpha$ is a constant, positive or negative.) (A) $V = V_{0} + \alpha x$ (B) $V = V_{0} + \alpha x^{2}$ (C) $V = V_{0} + \alpha x^{1/2}$ (D) $V = V_{0} + \alpha x^{3/2}$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Between a pair of parallel plates the field is uniform, so $E=-\dfrac{dV}{dx}$ is constant, which on integration gives a linear variation $V=V_{0}+\alpha x$.

questions.question: Let $E_{1}$, $E_{2}$, $E_{3}$ and $E_{4}$ be the magnitudes of the electric field between the pairs of plates, I, II, III and IV respectively. Then: (A) $E_{1} > E_{2} > E_{3} > E_{4}$ (B) $E_{2} > E_{4} > E_{1} > E_{3}$ (C) $E_{4} > E_{2} > E_{3} > E_{1}$ (D) $E_{4} > E_{3} > E_{2} > E_{1}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
As the plate separation $d=2$ cm is the same for every pair, $E=\dfrac{\Delta V}{d}$, so the pair with the largest potential difference has the largest field; comparing the four pairs gives $E_{4}>E_{2}>E_{3}>E_{1}$.

questions.question: An electron is projected from the right plate of set I directly towards its left plate. It just comes to rest at the plate. The speed with which it was projected is about: (Take $e/m = 1.76 \times 10^{11}$ C/kg) (A) $1.3 \times 10^{6}$ m/s (B) $2.6 \times 10^{6}$ m/s (C) $6.5 \times 10^{6}$ m/s (D) $5.2 \times 10^{7}$ m/s
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
By work-energy theorem, $\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}=e\Delta V$, so $v=\sqrt{2\left(\dfrac{e}{m}\right)\Delta V}=\sqrt{2\times1.76\times10^{11}\times5}\approx1.3\times10^{6}$ m/s, taking the potential difference of pair I as $5$ V.

questions.question: The plates $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ of a $2 \mu$ F capacitor are at potentials $25$ V and $-25$ V respectively. The charge on plate $P_{1}$ will be: (A) $0.02$ mC (B) $0.1$ mC (C) $0.1 \mu$ C (D) $1 \mu$ C
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
$Q=C(V_{P_{1}}-V_{P_{2}})=2\ \mu F\times50\text{ V}=100\ \mu C=0.1$ mC.

questions.question: Two charges $+q$ each are kept $2a$ distance apart. A third charge $-2q$ is placed midway between them. The potential energy of the system is $2$ (A) $\frac{q}{8\pi\varepsilon_{0}a} 2$ (B) $-\frac{6q}{8\pi\varepsilon_{0}a} 2$ (C) $-\frac{7q}{8\pi\varepsilon_{0}a} 2$ (D) $\frac{9q}{8\pi\varepsilon_{0}a}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
$U=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\left[\dfrac{q(-2q)}{a}+\dfrac{q(-2q)}{a}+\dfrac{q\cdot q}{2a}\right]=\dfrac{q^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}a}\left(-2-2+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=-\dfrac{7q^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_{0}a}$.

questions.question: Three point charges, each of charge $q$ are placed on vertices of a triangle $ABC$, with $AB = AC = 5L$, $BC = 6L$. The electrostatic potential at midpoint of side $BC$ will be (A) $\frac{11q}{48\pi\varepsilon_{0}L}$ (B) $\frac{8q}{36\pi\varepsilon_{0}L}$ (C) $\frac{5q}{24\pi\varepsilon_{0}L}$ (D) $\frac{q}{16\pi\varepsilon_{0}L}$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Since $AB=AC=5L$ and $BC=6L$, $BM=CM=3L$ and $AM=\sqrt{(5L)^{2}-(3L)^{2}}=4L$; so $V=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\left(\dfrac{1}{3L}+\dfrac{1}{3L}+\dfrac{1}{4L}\right)=\dfrac{11q}{48\pi\varepsilon_{0}L}$.

questions.question: Dielectrics play an important role in design of capacitors. The molecules of a dielectric may be polar or non-polar. When a dielectric slab is placed in an external electric field, opposite charges appear on the two surfaces of the slab perpendicular to electric field. Due to this an electric field is established inside the dielectric. The capacitance of a capacitor is determined by the dielectric constant of the material that fills the space between the plates. Consequently, the energy storage capacity of a capacitor is also affected. Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series and/or parallel. Which of the following is a polar molecule? (A) O $2$ (B) H $2$ (C) N $2$ (D) HCl
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
HCl consists of two dissimilar atoms with unequal electronegativity, so its centres of positive and negative charge do not coincide, giving it a permanent dipole moment, unlike the symmetric homonuclear molecules $O_{2}$, $H_{2}$ and $N_{2}$.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about dielectrics is correct? (A) A polar dielectric has a net dipole moment in absence of an external electric field which gets modified due to the induced dipoles. (B) The net dipole moments of induced dipoles is along the direction of the applied electric field. (C) Dielectrics contain free charges. (D) The electric field produced due to induced surface charges inside a dielectric is along the external electric field.
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
When an external field is applied, the induced (or aligned) dipoles in a dielectric orient themselves such that their net dipole moment (polarization) points along the direction of the applied electric field.

questions.question: When a dielectric slab is inserted between the plates of an isolated charged capacitor, the energy stored in it: (A) increases and the electric field inside it also increases. (B) decreases and the electric field also decreases. (C) decreases and the electric field increases. (D) increases and the electric field decreases.
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
For an isolated (charge $Q$ fixed) capacitor, inserting a dielectric increases $C$ to $KC_0$, so $E = \frac{\sigma}{K\varepsilon_0}$ decreases and the stored energy $U = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$ also decreases.

questions.question: An air-filled capacitor with plate area $A$ and plate separation $d$ has capacitance $C_{0}$. A slab $[]$ of dielectric constant $K$, area $A$ and thickness $\frac{d}{2}$ is inserted between the plates. The capacitance of the capacitor will become: $\lfloor\rfloor$ (A) $\frac{4K}{K + 5}C_{0} \lfloor\rfloor$ (B) $\frac{K + 5}{4K}C_{0} \lfloor\rfloor$ (C) $\frac{5K}{K + 4}C_{0} \lfloor\rfloor$ (D) $\frac{K + 4}{5K}C_{0}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
The slab creates an air gap of thickness $\frac{d}{2}$ ($C_1 = 2C_0$) in series with the dielectric part of thickness $\frac{d}{2}$ ($C_2 = 2KC_0$), giving $C = \frac{C_1C_2}{C_1+C_2} = \frac{2K}{K+1}C_0$.

questions.question: Two capacitors of capacitances $2 C_{0}$ and $6 C_{0}$ are first connected in series and then in parallel across the same battery. The ratio of energies stored in series combination to that in parallel is: (A) $\frac{1}{4}$ (B) $\frac{1}{8}$ (C) $\frac{2}{15}$ (D) $\frac{3}{16}$
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
Series: $C_s = \frac{2C_0 \times 6C_0}{2C_0+6C_0} = 1.5C_0$, Parallel: $C_p = 8C_0$; with same $V$, $U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$, so $\frac{U_s}{U_p} = \frac{1.5}{8} = \frac{3}{16}$.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Work done in moving a charge around a closed path, in an electric field is always zero. Reason (R): Electrostatic force is a conservative force. (A) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A). (B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A). (C) Assertion (A) is true and Reason (R) is false. (D) Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Since the electrostatic force is conservative, the work done in moving a charge around any closed path is zero, and this conservative nature is precisely why Assertion (A) holds.

questions.question: A point $P$ lies at a distance $x$ from the mid point of an electric dipole on its axis. The electric potential at point $P$ is proportional to (A) $\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ (B) $\frac{1}{x^{3}}$ (C) $\frac{1}{x^{3/2}}$ (D) $\frac{1}{x^{5/2}}$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
On the axial line, $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{p}{x^2 - a^2}$, which for $x \gg a$ reduces to $V \propto \frac{1}{x^2}$.

questions.question: A point charge $q$ is moving along a circular path of radius $a$, with a point charge $-Q$ at the centre of the circle. The kinetic energy of $q$ is (A) $\frac{qQ}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}a}$ (B) $\frac{qQ}{8\pi\varepsilon_{0}a}$ (C) $\frac{qQ}{4\pi\varepsilon a^{2}} 0$ (D) $\frac{qQ}{8\pi\varepsilon a^{2}} 0$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
The Coulomb attraction provides the centripetal force: $\frac{qQ}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a^2} = \frac{mv^2}{a}$, so $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{qQ}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 a}$.

questions.question: (b) The figure shows the variation of potential $V$ with $\frac{1}{r}$ for two point charges $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$, where $V$ is the potential at a distance $r$ due to a point charge. Find $\frac{Q_{2}}{Q_{1}}$.
questions.answer:
Since $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r}$, the graph of $V$ against $\frac{1}{r}$ is a straight line through the origin with slope $\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$.
Hence $\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}$ equals the ratio of the slopes of the two lines shown, the steeper line corresponding to the larger charge.

questions.question: The capacitors, each of $4 \mu F$ are to be connected in such a way that the effective capacitance of the combination is $6 \mu F$. This can be achieved by connecting (A) All three in parallel (B) All three in series (C) Two of them connected in series and the combination in parallel to the third. (D) Two of them connected in parallel and the combination in series to the third.
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Two capacitors in series give $\frac{4 \times 4}{4+4} = 2\ \mu F$, which in parallel with the third $4\ \mu F$ capacitor gives $2 + 4 = 6\ \mu F$.

questions.question: Find the equivalent capacitance between points A and B in the given diagram.
questions.answer:
Identify capacitors that share the same pair of nodes (parallel) and those carrying the same charge in a single path (series) in the network between $A$ and $B$.
Combine parallel branches using $C_p = C_1 + C_2 + \ldots$ and series branches using $\frac{1}{C_s} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \ldots$, reducing the network step by step until a single equivalent capacitance between $A$ and $B$ remains.

questions.question: A dielectric slab is inserted between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor. The electric field between the plates decreases. Explain.
questions.answer:
When a dielectric slab is placed in the external field $\vec{E_0}$, it gets polarised and induced charges appear on its faces.
These induced charges set up an internal field $\vec{E_i}$ opposite to $\vec{E_0}$.
The net field $E = E_0 - E_i = E_0/K$, which is less than $E_0$, so the field between the plates decreases.

questions.question: An electric dipole consisting of charges $+q$ and $-q$ separated by a distance $L$ is in stable equilibrium in a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$. The electrostatic potential energy of the dipole is (A) $qLE$ (B) zero (C) $-qLE$ (D) $-2qLE$
questions.answer:
Option (C) $-qLE$ is correct.
For a dipole, $U = -pE\cos\theta$; in stable equilibrium $\theta = 0$, so $U = -pE = -qLE$ (since $p = qL$).

questions.question: The potential difference between two points in vacuum is $V_{0}$. If vacuum is replaced by a medium of dielectric constant $K$, the new value of potential difference will be ______.
questions.answer: The new potential difference will be $V = \dfrac{V_0}{K}$, since inserting a dielectric of constant $K$ reduces the field (and hence potential difference) by a factor $K$.

questions.question: If a positive charge is displaced against the electric field in which it was situated, then (A) work will be done by the electric field on the charge. (B) the intensity of the electric field decreases. (C) energy of the system will decrease. (D) energy will be provided by external source displacing the charge.
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
Moving a positive charge against the electric field requires work to be done against the electrostatic force, and this energy is supplied by the external agent (source), increasing the potential energy of the system.

questions.question: Two capacitors of capacitances $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ are connected in parallel. If a charge $Q$ is given to the combination, the ratio of the charge on the capacitor $C_{1}$ to the charge on $C_{2}$ will be (A) $\frac{C_{1}}{C_{2}}$ (B) $\frac{C_{2}}{C_{1}} r$ (C) $\frac{\frac{C_{1}}{C_{2}}}{\frac{C_{2}}{C_{1}}} r$ (D)
questions.answer:
Option (A) $\frac{C_1}{C_2}$ is correct.
In parallel, both capacitors have the same potential difference $V$, so $Q_1 = C_1V$ and $Q_2 = C_2V$, giving $\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} = \dfrac{C_1}{C_2}$.

questions.question: A charge $Q$ is kept at the centre of a circle of radius $r$. A test charge $q_{0}$ is carried from a point $X$ to the point $Y$ on this circle such that arc $XY$ subtends an angle of $60^{^{\circ}}$ at the centre of the circle. The amount of work done in this process will be (A) $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{Qq_{0}}{2r} \sqrt{3}$ (B) $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{Qq_{0}}{2r}$ (C) Zero $\sqrt{3}$ (D) $\frac{Qq_{0}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0} r}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) Zero is correct.
Since $X$ and $Y$ lie on a circle centred at the charge $Q$, they are equidistant from $Q$ and hence at the same potential; work done $W = q_0(V_Y - V_X) = 0$.

questions.question: A parallel plate capacitor is charged to $V$ volt by a battery. The battery is disconnected and the separation between the plates is halved. The new potential difference across the capacitor will be (A) $\frac{V}{2}$ (B) $V$ (C) $2V$ (D) $\frac{V}{4}$
questions.answer:
Option (C) $2V$ is correct.
With the battery disconnected, charge $Q$ remains constant; since $C = \varepsilon_0 A/d$ doubles when $d$ is halved, $V = Q/C$ becomes half of $C$'s increase factor, i.e., $V_{new} = 2V$.

questions.question: A charge $Q$ is uniformly distributed over the surface of a spherical shell of radius $R$. The work done in bringing a test charge $Q_{0}$ from its centre to its surface is (A) $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{QQ_{0}}{R}$ (B) $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{QQ_{0}}{2R}$ (C) $\frac{QQ_{0}}{\varepsilon^{0} R}$ (D) Zero
questions.answer:
Option (D) Zero is correct.
Inside a uniformly charged spherical shell the potential is constant and equal to the potential at the surface, so no work is done in moving the charge from the centre to the surface.

questions.question: A charged particle is placed between the two plates of a charged parallel plate capacitor. It experiences a force $F$. If one plate is removed, then the force on the particle will be (A) $2F$ (B) $F$ (C) $\frac{F}{2}$ (D) Zero
questions.answer:
Option (C) $\frac{F}{2}$ is correct.
The field between the plates of a capacitor is the sum of the fields due to each plate ($E = \sigma/2\varepsilon_0$ each); removing one plate leaves only half the field, so the force reduces to $F/2$.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with appropriate answer. A proton released from rest in an electric field, will start moving towards a region of ________ potential in the field.
questions.answer: The proton will start moving towards a region of lower potential in the field, since the electrostatic force on a positive charge acts in the direction of decreasing potential.

questions.question: The work done in moving a charged particle between two points in a uniform electric field does not depend on the path followed by the particle. Why?
questions.answer: The electrostatic force in a uniform field is conservative, so the work done $W = qEd$ depends only on the displacement along the field direction between the initial and final points, not on the actual path taken.

questions.question: A charged particle $(+q)$ moves in a uniform electric field $(\vec{E})$ in the direction opposite to $E$. What will be the effect on its electrostatic potential energy during its motion?
questions.answer: The potential energy increases, since the charge moves opposite to $\vec{E}$, i.e. against the electrostatic force, so the field does negative work $W = -\Delta U$ on it.

questions.question: A point charge is placed at the centre of a hollow conducting sphere of internal radius $r$ and outer radius $2r$. The ratio of the surface charge density of the inner surface to that of the outer surface will be __________.
questions.answer:
$\sigma_{inner} : \sigma_{outer} = -4:1$.
This is because the induced charge on the inner surface (radius $r$) is $-Q$ and on the outer surface (radius $2r$) is $+Q$, and $\sigma = Q/4\pi R^{2}$, giving $\sigma_{inner}/\sigma_{outer} = -(2r/r)^{2} = -4$.

questions.question: Draw the equipotential surfaces due to an isolated point charge.
questions.answer: The equipotential surfaces of an isolated point charge are a family of concentric spheres centred on the charge, with spacing between consecutive surfaces increasing as the distance from the charge increases (since $V \propto 1/r$).

questions.question: Why is the electrostatic potential inside a charged conducting shell constant throughout the volume of the conductor?
questions.answer: Inside a conductor the electric field is zero, so no work is done in moving a test charge from one point to another inside it, and hence the potential remains the same everywhere inside, equal to the potential on the surface.

questions.question: Does the charge given to a metallic sphere depend on whether it is hollow or solid? Give reason for your answer.
questions.answer: No, it does not depend on whether the sphere is hollow or solid, because in electrostatic equilibrium the entire charge resides only on the outer surface of a conductor, so a hollow and a solid sphere of the same radius hold the same charge at the same potential.

questions.question: A point charge $Q$ is placed at point ’O’ as shown in the figure. Is the potential at point $A$, i.e. $V_{A}$, greater, smaller or equal to potential, $V_{B}$, at point $B$, when $Q$ is (i) positive, and (ii) negative charge?
questions.answer:
Taking $A$ closer to $O$ than $B$ (i.e. $OA < OB$), since $V = kQ/r$:
(i) For positive $Q$, $V_A > V_B$.
(ii) For negative $Q$, $V_A < V_B$ (potential is more negative at $A$).

questions.question: What is the amount of work done in moving a point charge $Q$ around a circular arc of radius $r$ at the centre of which another point charge $q$ is located?
questions.answer: The work done is zero, because all points on the circular arc are equidistant from $q$ and hence lie on the same equipotential surface, so $W = Q(V_A - V_B) = 0$.

questions.question: "For any charge configuration, equipotential surface through a point is normal to the electric field." Justify.
questions.answer: If the field had a component along the equipotential surface, it would do work in moving a charge along the surface; but since potential is constant on the surface, $W = q\Delta V = 0$ for any displacement on it, so the tangential component of $\vec{E}$ must be zero, i.e. $\vec{E}$ is normal to the surface at every point.

questions.question: What is the geometrical shape of equipotential surfaces due to a single isolated charge?
questions.answer: The equipotential surfaces due to a single isolated charge are concentric spheres centred on the charge.

questions.question: Define the term ’dielectric constant’ of a medium.
questions.answer: Dielectric constant is the ratio of the capacitance of a capacitor with the dielectric completely filling the space between its plates to its capacitance with vacuum between the plates, $K = C/C_0$.

questions.question: Name the physical quantity whose S.I. unit is JC $-1$. Is it a scalar or a vector quantity?
questions.answer: The quantity is electric potential; it is a scalar quantity.

questions.question: Why is the potential inside a hollow spherical charged conductor constant and has the same value as on its surface?
questions.answer:
The electric field inside a hollow charged conductor is zero everywhere.
Since $E = -dV/dr = 0$, the potential does not change from the surface to the centre, so it remains constant and equal to the surface value.

questions.question: A hollow metal sphere of radius $5$ cm is charged such that the potential on its surface is $10$ V. What is the potential at the centre of the sphere?
questions.answer:
The potential at the centre equals the potential on the surface, since the interior of a charged conductor is an equipotential region.
So the potential at the centre is $10$ V.

questions.question: A point charge $Q$ is placed at point $O$ as shown in the figure. Is the potential difference $V_{A} -V_{B}$ positive, negative or zero, if $Q$ is (i) positive (ii) negative?
questions.answer:
(i) If $Q$ is positive, $V_A - V_B$ is positive when $A$ is closer to $O$ than $B$, since potential decreases with distance from a positive charge.
(ii) If $Q$ is negative, $V_A - V_B$ is negative under the same condition, since potential becomes less negative (increases) with distance from a negative charge.

questions.question: What is the electrostatic potential due to an electric dipole at an equatorial point?
questions.answer: The electrostatic potential due to an electric dipole at any point on its equatorial line is zero, since the potentials due to the two equal and opposite charges cancel out (both charges are equidistant from the point).

questions.question: A $500 \mu C$ charge is at the centre of a square of side $10 cm$. Find the work done in moving a charge of $10 \mu C$ between two diagonally opposite points on the square.
questions.answer:
Both diagonally opposite points are equidistant from the centre charge, so they lie on the same equipotential surface, $V_A = V_B$.
Work done $W = q(V_B - V_A) = 0$.

questions.question: Derive the expression for the electric potential at any point along the axial line of an electric dipole.
questions.answer:
Consider a dipole of charges $-q$ at $A$ and $+q$ at $B$, separated by $2a$, with dipole moment $p = q(2a)$.
Let $P$ be a point on the axial line at distance $r$ from the centre $O$, on the side of $+q$.
Distance of $P$ from $+q$ is $(r-a)$ and from $-q$ is $(r+a)$.
Potential at $P$: $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{q}{r-a} - \dfrac{q}{r+a}\right] = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{2a}{r^2-a^2}\right]$
So $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^2-a^2}$.
For a short dipole, $r \gg a$, so $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^2}$.

questions.question: Draw an equipotential surface for a system consisting of two charges $Q$, $-Q$ separated by a distance ’ $r$’ in air.
questions.answer:
The equipotential surfaces are a family of non-intersecting curves that are closely spaced near each charge (where the field is strong) and become widely spaced farther away.
Near $+Q$, the surfaces are nearly spherical and close to $+Q$; near $-Q$, they are nearly spherical and close to $-Q$.
The plane perpendicular to the line joining the charges and passing through its midpoint is a plane of zero potential (equidistant from $Q$ and $-Q$).

questions.question: Define the term ’dielectric constant’ of a medium in terms of capacitance of a capacitor.
questions.answer: The dielectric constant $K$ of a medium is defined as the ratio of the capacitance $C$ of a capacitor with the medium completely filling the space between its plates to the capacitance $C_0$ of the same capacitor with vacuum between the plates, $K = C/C_0$.

questions.question: Two isolated metallic spheres $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ of radii $1$ cm and $3$ cm respectively are charged $[_{-9}]_{2}$ such that both have the same charge density $\frac{2}{\pi}\times 10$ C/m. They are placed far away from each other and connected by a thin wire. Calculate the new charge on sphere $S_{2}$.
questions.answer:
Charge on a sphere is $Q = \sigma \times 4\pi r^{2}$, so $Q_{1} = 4\pi \times \frac{2}{\pi}\times 10^{-9}\times (0.01)^{2} = 8\times 10^{-13}$ C and $Q_{2} = 4\pi \times \frac{2}{\pi}\times 10^{-9}\times (0.03)^{2} = 7.2\times 10^{-12}$ C.
Total charge $Q = Q_{1}+Q_{2} = 8\times 10^{-12}$ C.
On connecting by a wire, charge redistributes in the ratio of radii: $q_{2} = Q\times \dfrac{r_{2}}{r_{1}+r_{2}} = 8\times 10^{-12}\times \dfrac{3}{4} = 6\times 10^{-12}$ C.

questions.question: (a) Obtain an expression for electrostatic potential energy of a system of three charges $q$, $2q$ and $-3q$ placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $a$. OR (b) Two small conducting balls A and B of radius $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ have charges $q_{1}$ and $q_{2}$ respectively. They are connected by a wire. Obtain the expression for charges on A and B, in equilibrium.
questions.answer:
(a) The potential energy of a system of charges is $U = k\left(\dfrac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r_{12}} + \dfrac{q_{2}q_{3}}{r_{23}} + \dfrac{q_{1}q_{3}}{r_{13}}\right)$.
For charges $q$, $2q$, $-3q$ at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side $a$, all separations equal $a$, so
$U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}a}\left[(q)(2q) + (2q)(-3q) + (q)(-3q)\right]$.
This gives $U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}a}(2q^{2} - 6q^{2} - 3q^{2}) = \dfrac{-7q^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}a}$.

questions.question: (iii) A capacitor A of capacitance C, having charge Q is connected across another uncharged capacitor B of capacitance 2C. Find an expression for (a) the potential difference across the combination and (b) the charge lost by capacitor A. OR (iii) Two slabs of dielectric constants 2K and K fill the space between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor of plate area A and plate separation d as shown in figure. Find an expression for capacitance of the system.
questions.answer:
Common potential after connection: $V = \dfrac{Q}{C+2C} = \dfrac{Q}{3C}$.
Charge remaining on A: $Q_{A}' = CV = \dfrac{Q}{3}$.
Charge lost by A $= Q - \dfrac{Q}{3} = \dfrac{2Q}{3}$.

questions.question: Three point charges $Q$, $q$ and $-q$ are kept at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $L$ as shown in figure. What is (i) the electrostatic potential energy of the arrangement? and (ii) the potential at point D?
questions.answer:
(i) Taking $D$ as the midpoint of the side joining $q$ and $-q$, so that $BD = DC = L/2$ and $AD = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}L$:
Potential energy $U = k\left[\dfrac{Qq}{L} + \dfrac{Q(-q)}{L} + \dfrac{q(-q)}{L}\right] = -\dfrac{kq^{2}}{L} = -\dfrac{q^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}L}$ (the $Qq$ terms cancel).
(ii) $V_{D} = \dfrac{kQ}{(\sqrt{3}/2)L} + \dfrac{kq}{L/2} + \dfrac{k(-q)}{L/2} = \dfrac{2kQ}{\sqrt{3}L}$, since the $q$ and $-q$ contributions cancel; thus $V_{D} = \dfrac{Q}{2\sqrt{3}\pi\varepsilon_{0}L}$.

questions.question: The space between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is completely filled in two ways. In the first case, it is filled with a slab of dielectric constant $K$. In the second case, it is filled with two slabs of equal thickness and dielectric constants $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ respectively as shown in the figure. The capacitance of the capacitor is same in the two cases. Obtain the relationship between $K$, $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$.
questions.answer:
Case 1 (single slab of dielectric constant $K$, full thickness $d$): $C = \dfrac{K\varepsilon_{0}A}{d}$.
Case 2 (two slabs of thickness $d/2$ each, in series): $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{\dfrac{d}{2K_{1}}+\dfrac{d}{2K_{2}}} = \dfrac{2\varepsilon_{0}A K_{1}K_{2}}{d(K_{1}+K_{2})}$.
Equating the two capacitances gives $K = \dfrac{2K_{1}K_{2}}{K_{1}+K_{2}}$.

questions.question: $N$ small conducting liquid droplets, each of radius $r$, are charged to a potential $V$ each. These droplets coalesce to form a single large drop without any charge leakage. Find the potential of the large drop.
questions.answer:
Charge on each small droplet: $q = 4\pi\varepsilon_{0}rV$, so total charge $Q = Nq = 4\pi\varepsilon_{0}NrV$.
By conservation of volume, $N\cdot\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}$, giving $R = N^{1/3}r$.
Potential of the big drop: $V' = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R} = \dfrac{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}NrV}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}N^{1/3}r} = N^{2/3}V$.

questions.question: Find the total charge stored in the network of capacitors connected between $A$ and $B$ as shown in figure:
questions.answer:
The network is first reduced to a single equivalent capacitance $C_{eq}$ between A and B by combining series groups using $\dfrac{1}{C_{s}} = \sum \dfrac{1}{C_{i}}$ and parallel groups using $C_{p} = \sum C_{i}$, following the branch arrangement shown.
The total charge stored is then $Q = C_{eq}V_{AB}$, where $V_{AB}$ is the potential difference applied between A and B.
Each branch's individual charge can be found afterward from its own voltage drop using $q_{i} = C_{i}V_{i}$.

questions.question: You are given three capacitors of $2 \mu$ F, $3 \mu$ F and $4 \mu$ F, respectively. (a) Form a combination of all these capacitors of equivalent capacitance $\frac{13}{3}\mu$ F. (b) What is the maximum and minimum value of the equivalent capacitance that can be obtained by connecting these capacitors?
questions.answer:
(a) Connect the $2\mu$F and $4\mu$F capacitors in series, and this combination in parallel with the $3\mu$F capacitor: series value $= \dfrac{2\times 4}{2+4} = \dfrac{4}{3}\mu$F, so total $= \dfrac{4}{3}+3 = \dfrac{13}{3}\mu$F.
(b) Maximum (all in parallel): $C_{max} = 2+3+4 = 9\mu$F.
Minimum (all in series): $\dfrac{1}{C_{min}} = \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{13}{12}$, so $C_{min} = \dfrac{12}{13}\mu$F.

questions.question: The figure shows a network of five capacitors connected to a $100$ V supply. Calculate the total energy stored in the network.
questions.answer:
The five capacitors are first reduced to a single equivalent capacitance $C_{eq}$ between the supply terminals by successively combining series branches ($\dfrac{1}{C_{s}}=\sum\dfrac{1}{C_{i}}$) and parallel branches ($C_{p}=\sum C_{i}$) according to the given circuit.
The total energy stored in the network is then $U = \dfrac{1}{2}C_{eq}V^{2}$, with $V = 100$ V.
Substituting the value of $C_{eq}$ obtained from the reduction gives the numerical energy in joules.

questions.question: Two identical capacitors of 12 pF each are connected in series across a 50 V battery. Calculate the electrostatic energy stored in the combination. If these were connected in parallel across the same battery, find out the value of the energy stored in this combination.
questions.answer:
Series combination: $\dfrac{1}{C_{s}} = \dfrac{1}{12}+\dfrac{1}{12}$, so $C_{s} = 6$ pF.
Energy: $U_{s} = \dfrac{1}{2}C_{s}V^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 6\times 10^{-12}\times (50)^{2} = 7.5\times 10^{-9}$ J.
Parallel combination: $C_{p} = 12+12 = 24$ pF, so $U_{p} = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 24\times 10^{-12}\times (50)^{2} = 3\times 10^{-8}$ J.

questions.question: Two identical capacitors of 10 pF each are connected in turn (i) in series, and (ii) in parallel across a 20 V battery. Calculate the potential difference across each capacitor in the first case and charge acquired by each capacitor in the second case.
questions.answer:
Series: $C_{s} = C/2 = 5$ pF, charge $Q = C_{s}V = 5\text{pF} \times 20\text{V} = 100$ pC (same on both capacitors).
Potential difference across each capacitor $= Q/C = 100\text{pC}/10\text{pF} = 10$ V.
Parallel: each capacitor gets the full battery voltage, $V = 20$ V.
Charge on each capacitor $= CV = 10\text{pF} \times 20\text{V} = 200$ pC.

questions.question: The figure shows a network of three capacitors $C_{1} = 2 \mu F$; $C_{2} = 6 \mu F$ and $C_{3} = 3 \mu F$ connected across a battery of 10 V. If a charge of $6 \mu C$ is acquired by the capacitor $C_{3}$, calculate the charge acquired by $C_{1}$.
questions.answer:
$C_2$ and $C_3$ are in parallel, so they have the same potential difference: $V_{23} = Q_3/C_3 = 6\mu C/3\mu F = 2$ V.
Charge on $C_2 = C_2 V_{23} = 6\mu F \times 2V = 12\mu C$.
This parallel combination is in series with $C_1$, so charge on $C_1$ equals the total charge of the combination: $Q_1 = Q_2 + Q_3 = 12\mu C + 6\mu C = 18\mu C$.

questions.question: Why does current in a steady state not flow in a capacitor connected across a battery? However momentary current does flow during charging or discharging of the capacitor. Explain.
questions.answer:
In steady state, the capacitor is fully charged and the dielectric (gap) between its plates does not allow charge carriers to cross it, so conduction current cannot flow through the capacitor.
During charging or discharging, the charge on the plates is changing with time, so a momentary current flows in the circuit until the capacitor becomes fully charged or fully discharged, after which the current becomes zero.

questions.question: What is electrostatic shielding? How is this property used in actual practice? Is the potential in the cavity of a charged conductor zero?
questions.answer:
Electrostatic shielding is the phenomenon by which the interior of a hollow conductor is protected from external electric fields, since the field inside the cavity (with no charge inside) is always zero regardless of the field outside.
It is used to protect sensitive instruments by enclosing them in metallic (Faraday) cages, and a person inside a car is safe from lightning for this reason.
The potential inside the cavity is not zero; it is constant and equal to the potential of the conductor's surface.

questions.question: A parallel plate capacitor of capacitance C is charged to a potential V. It is then connected to another uncharged capacitor having the same capacitance. Find out the ratio of the energy stored in the combined system to that stored initially in the single capacitor.
questions.answer:
Initial energy $U_i = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2$.
On connecting to an identical uncharged capacitor, total charge $Q = CV$ is conserved and shared equally, giving common potential $V' = V/2$ across the equivalent capacitance $2C$.
Final energy $U_f = \dfrac{1}{2}(2C)(V/2)^2 = \dfrac{CV^2}{4}$.
Ratio $U_f : U_i = 1 : 2$.

questions.question: A test charge ’ $q$’ is moved without acceleration from A to C along the path from A to B and then from B to C in electric field $\vec{E}$ as shown in the figure. (i) Calculate the potential difference between A and C. (ii) At which point (of the two) is the electric potential more and why?
questions.answer:
(i) Since the charge is moved without acceleration, path AB is along an equipotential (perpendicular to $\vec{E}$), so no work is done from A to B and $V_A = V_B$. Work is done only along BC (parallel to $\vec{E}$), giving $V_A - V_C = V_B - V_C = E \times BC$, where $BC$ is the distance moved along the field.
(ii) Point A (equivalently B) is at higher potential than C, because electric field lines point in the direction of decreasing potential, and the path from B to C is along the field direction.

questions.question: Draw a plot showing the variation of (i) electric field ($E$) and (ii) electric potential ($V$ ) with distance $r$ due to a point charge $Q$.
questions.answer:
Electric field: $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r^2}$, so the $E$-$r$ graph is a curve falling steeply as $r$ increases (inverse square), approaching very large values as $r \to 0$ and tending to zero as $r \to \infty$.
Electric potential: $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r}$, so the $V$-$r$ graph is a rectangular-hyperbola-like curve, falling less steeply than $E$ (inverse first power), also tending to zero as $r \to \infty$.

questions.question: Net capacitance of three identical capacitors in series is $1 \mu$ F. What will be their net capacitance if connected in parallel? Find the ratio of energy stored in the two configurations if they are both connected to the same source.
questions.answer:
For series, $\dfrac{1}{C_s} = \dfrac{3}{C} \Rightarrow C = 3\mu F$ for each capacitor, so $C_s = 1\mu F$.
For parallel, $C_p = 3C = 9\mu F$.
Since both are connected to the same source of voltage $V$: $U_s = \dfrac{1}{2}C_sV^2$ and $U_p = \dfrac{1}{2}C_pV^2$.
Ratio $U_s : U_p = C_s : C_p = 1 : 9$.

questions.question: Figure shows two identical capacitors, $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$, each of $1 \mu$ F capacitance connected to a battery of $6$ V. Initially switch $S$ is closed. After sometime $S$ is left open and dielectric slabs of dielectric constant $K = 3$ are inserted to fill completely the space between the plates of the two capacitors. How will the (i) charge and (ii) potential difference between the plates of the capacitors be affected after the slabs are inserted?
questions.answer:
With S closed, each capacitor is charged to $V = 6$ V, so charge on each: $Q = CV = 1\mu F \times 6V = 6\mu C$.
(i) Charge: When S is opened, the capacitors get isolated from the battery, so the charge on each capacitor remains unchanged at $6\mu C$ even after inserting the dielectric slab, since there is no path for charge to flow.
(ii) Potential difference: New capacitance $C' = KC = 3 \times 1\mu F = 3\mu F$. New potential difference $V' = Q/C' = 6\mu C/3\mu F = 2$ V, so the potential difference across each capacitor decreases from 6 V to 2 V.

questions.question: Two uniformly large parallel thin plates having charge densities $+\sigma$ and $-\sigma$ are kept in the $X$- $Z$ plane at a distance $d$ apart. Sketch an equipotential surface due to electric field between the plates. If a particle of mass $m$ and charge $-q$ remains stationary between the plates, what is the magnitude and direction of this field?
questions.answer:
The equipotential surfaces are planes parallel to the charged plates (i.e., parallel to the X-Z plane), since the field between the plates is uniform and perpendicular to the plates.
For the charge $-q$ to remain stationary, the electric force must balance gravity: $qE = mg$, so $E = mg/q$.
Since the charge is negative, the electric force on it is opposite to $\vec{E}$; for this force to act upward (balancing gravity), the field $\vec{E}$ must point from the positively charged plate towards the negatively charged plate, i.e., vertically downward.

questions.question: Two identical parallel plate (air) capacitors $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ have capacitances C each. The space between their plates is now filled with dielectrics as shown. If the two capacitors still have equal capacitance, obtain the relation between dielectric constants $K$, $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$.
questions.answer:
Let $C_{1}$ be filled with two dielectrics $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ placed side by side, each occupying half the plate area $A/2$, thickness $d$ (equivalent to two capacitors in parallel): $C_{1} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{2d}(K_{1}+K_{2})$.
Let $C_{2}$ be filled with a single dielectric of constant $K$ occupying the full space: $C_{2} = \dfrac{K\varepsilon_{0}A}{d}$.
Given $C_{1} = C_{2} = C$, equating the two expressions gives $K = \dfrac{K_{1}+K_{2}}{2}$.

questions.question: (i) Can two equi-potential surfaces intersect each other? Give reasons. (ii) Two charges $-q$ and $+q$ are located at points $A(0, 0, -a)$ and $B(0, 0, +a)$ respectively. How much work is done in moving a test charge from point $P(7, 0, 0)$ to $Q(-3, 0, 0)$?
questions.answer:
(i) No, two equipotential surfaces cannot intersect. If they did, the point of intersection would have two different potential values simultaneously, and the electric field there (normal to each surface) would have two different directions, which is not possible.
(ii) Points $P(7,0,0)$ and $Q(-3,0,0)$ both lie on the x-axis, which is the equatorial (perpendicular bisector) plane of the dipole formed by $-q$ at $A$ and $+q$ at $B$.
The potential due to a dipole at any point on its equatorial line is zero, so $V_{P} = V_{Q} = 0$.
Hence work done $W = q(V_{Q}-V_{P}) = 0$.

questions.question: Draw 3 equipotential surfaces corresponding to a field that uniformly increases in magnitude but remains constant along Z-direction. How are these surfaces different from that of a constant electric field along Z-direction?
questions.answer:
For a field that is constant along Z but increases in magnitude, the equipotential surfaces are still planes perpendicular to the Z-axis, but consecutive surfaces (for equal potential intervals) are spaced closer together as $z$ increases, since $E = -\dfrac{dV}{dz}$, i.e., stronger field means smaller spacing.
For a constant (uniform) electric field along Z, the equipotential planes perpendicular to Z are equally spaced, since $E$ is the same everywhere.
