If the field is directed perpendicular to the velocity of the particle, find the radius of the circular path described by the particle. Mention the condition under which the particle in this region (i) describes a helical path, and (ii) goes straight undeviated.
questions.answer:
Kinetic energy $= 8.0$ MeV $= 8.0 \times 1.6\times10^{-13}$ J $= 1.28\times10^{-12}$ J
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2KE}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\times1.28\times10^{-12}}{6.4\times10^{-27}}} = 2.0\times10^{7}$ m/s
$r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{6.4\times10^{-27}\times2.0\times10^{7}}{3.2\times10^{-19}\times0.5} = 0.8$ m
(i) The particle describes a helical path when its velocity makes an angle other than $0^{\circ}$, $90^{\circ}$, or $180^{\circ}$ with $\vec{B}$, i.e., it has both parallel and perpendicular components to $\vec{B}$.
(ii) The particle goes straight undeviated when its velocity is parallel or antiparallel to $\vec{B}$ (angle $0^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$).

questions.question: (a) The figure given below shows three straight long parallel conductors (1), (2) and (3) kept in x-y plane, carrying currents $2I$, $I$ and $3I$ respectively as shown in figure. Find the magnitude and direction of: (i) net magnetic field at a point on conductor (1) and (ii) net magnetic force acting on unit length of conductor (1), due to conductors (2) and (3). OR (b) A rectangular loop of sides $l$ and $b$ and resistance ’R’ is kept in a region in which the magnetic field varies as $B = B_{0} \sin \omega t$. (i) Derive expression for the emf induced in the loop. (ii) Find the effective value of current that flows in the loop.
questions.answer:
(b) Let the loop of area $A = lb$ lie with its plane perpendicular to $\vec{B}$.
Flux: $\Phi = B_0 A \sin\omega t = B_0 lb \sin\omega t$
Induced emf: $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = -B_0 lb\,\omega\cos\omega t$
Peak emf: $\varepsilon_0 = B_0 lb\,\omega$
Induced current: $I(t) = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R} = \dfrac{B_0 lb\,\omega}{R}\cos\omega t$, so peak current $I_0 = \dfrac{B_0 lb\,\omega}{R}$
Effective (rms) current: $I_{rms} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{B_0 lb\,\omega}{\sqrt{2}\,R}$

questions.question: Write the expression for the magnetic field due to a current element in vector form. Consider a $1$ cm segment of a wire, centered at the origin, carrying a current of $10$ A in positive $x$-direction. Calculate the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ at a point $(1$ m $, 1$ m $, 0)$.
questions.answer:
The magnetic field due to a current element is given by the Biot-Savart law:
$d\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,d\vec{l}\times\hat{r}}{r^2}$
Here $I\,d\vec{l} = 10 \times 0.01\,\hat{i} = 0.1\,\hat{i}$ A m, position vector to $(1,1,0)$ is $\vec{r} = \hat{i}+\hat{j}$, so $r = \sqrt{2}$ m and $\hat{r} = \dfrac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}}$.
$d\vec{l}\times\hat{r} = 0.01\hat{i}\times\dfrac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{0.01}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{k}$
$\vec{B} = \dfrac{10^{-7}\times10\times0.01}{\sqrt{2}\times2}\hat{k} \approx 3.54\times10^{-9}\ \hat{k}$ T

questions.question: Using Biot-Savart law, derive expression for the magnetic field ($\vec{B}$) due to a circular current carrying loop at a point on its axis and hence at its centre.
questions.answer:
Consider a circular loop of radius $r$ carrying current $I$, with point $P$ on its axis at distance $x$ from the centre.
By Biot-Savart law, a current element $Id\vec{l}$ produces $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl}{r^2+x^2}$, perpendicular to the line joining the element to $P$.
Resolving $dB$ into axial ($dB\sin\phi$) and radial ($dB\cos\phi$) components, where $\sin\phi = \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{r^2+x^2}}$: the radial components cancel in pairs by symmetry, and axial components add.
$B = \displaystyle\oint dB\sin\phi = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi(r^2+x^2)}\cdot\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{r^2+x^2}}\times 2\pi r = \dfrac{\mu_0 I r^2}{2(r^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$
At the centre, $x = 0$, so $B_{centre} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$

questions.question: (a) Define magnetic moment of a current-carrying coil. Write its SI unit. (b) A coil of $60$ turns and area $1.5 \times 10^{-3}$ m $2$ carrying $2$ A current lies in a vertical plane. It experiences a torque of $0.12$ Nm when placed in a uniform horizontal magnetic field. The torque acting on the coil changes to $0.05$ Nm after the coil is rotated about its diameter by $90^{^{\circ}}$, in the magnetic field. Find the magnitude of the magnetic field.
questions.answer:
(a) Magnetic moment of a current-carrying coil is the product of current and the area enclosed by the coil, $\vec{m} = NI\vec{A}$, directed along the normal to the coil (right-hand rule). Its SI unit is $\text{A m}^2$.
(b) $N=60$, $A=1.5\times10^{-3}$ m$^2$, $I=2$ A. Initially $\tau_1 = NIAB\sin\theta$; after rotating $90^{\circ}$, $\tau_2 = NIAB\sin(90^{\circ}-\theta) = NIAB\cos\theta$.
So $\tau_1^2+\tau_2^2 = (NIAB)^2$
$NIAB = \sqrt{0.12^2+0.05^2} = \sqrt{0.0169} = 0.13$
$NIA = 60\times2\times1.5\times10^{-3} = 0.18$
$B = \dfrac{0.13}{0.18} \approx 0.72$ T

questions.question: As shown in figure, a particle of charge $q$ is moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ at a distance ’ $d$’ from a long straight wire carrying a current ’ $I$’. At this instant, it is subjected to a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$ such that the particle keeps moving undeviated. In terms of unit vectors $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$, find: (a) the magnetic field $\vec{B}$, (b) the magnetic force $\vec{F}_{m}$, and (c) the electric field $\vec{E}$ acting on the charge.
questions.answer:
Take the wire along the $y$-axis carrying current $I$ in the $+\hat{j}$ direction, with the particle at perpendicular distance $d$ along the $x$-axis, moving with $\vec{v}=v\hat{j}$ (parallel to the wire, so $d$ stays constant).
(a) $\vec{B}=-\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}\hat{k}$
(b) $\vec{F}_m=q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}=-\dfrac{\mu_0 I q v}{2\pi d}\hat{i}$
(c) For undeviated motion $q\vec{E}+\vec{F}_m=0$, so $\vec{E}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I v}{2\pi d}\hat{i}$.

questions.question: In a region of a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$, a negatively charged particle is moving with a constant velocity $\vec{v} = -v\hat{j}$ near a long straight conductor coinciding with $XX^{'}$ axis $^{y}$ and carrying current I towards $-X$ axis. The particle remains at a distance d from the conductor. (i) Draw diagram showing direction of electric and magnetic fields. (ii) What are the various forces acting on the charged particle? (iii) Find the value of $v_{y}$ in terms of E, d and I.
questions.answer:
(i) Wire along the $x$-axis with current towards $-\hat{i}$; the particle is at distance $d$ along $+\hat{j}$ from it. The magnetic field at the particle's location is along $-\hat{k}$ (into the page); the required electric field is along $-\hat{i}$ so that its force balances the magnetic force.
(ii) Two forces act: the electric force $-q\vec{E}$ and the magnetic force $-q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ (gravity is neglected). Since the particle moves with constant velocity, these two forces must be equal and opposite.
(iii) $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$, and balance gives $qE=qvB$, so $v=\dfrac{E}{B}=\dfrac{2\pi d E}{\mu_0 I}$.

questions.question: Two infinitely long conductors kept along $XX^{'}$ and $Y Y^{'}$ axes are carrying current $I$ and $1 I_{2}$ along $-X$ axis and $-Y$ axis respectively. Find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field produced at point P(X, Y).
questions.answer:
Field of the wire along $XX'$ (current $I_1$ along $-\hat{i}$) at $P(x,y)$: $\vec{B}_1=-\dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi y}\hat{k}$
Field of the wire along $YY'$ (current $I_2$ along $-\hat{j}$) at $P(x,y)$: $\vec{B}_2=\dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi x}\hat{k}$
Both fields are along the $z$-axis (perpendicular to the plane), so they add algebraically:
$\vec{B}_{net}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\left(\dfrac{I_2}{x}-\dfrac{I_1}{y}\right)\hat{k}$
Magnitude $=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\left|\dfrac{I_2}{x}-\dfrac{I_1}{y}\right|$, directed out of the plane ($+\hat{k}$) if $\dfrac{I_2}{x}>\dfrac{I_1}{y}$, otherwise into the plane.

questions.question: (a) Write vector form of Biot-Savart law. (b) Two insulated long straight wires, each carrying $2.0$ A current are kept along $xx^{'}$ and $yy^{'}$ axis as shown in the figure. Find the magnitude and direction of resultant magnetic field at point $P(4$ m $, 5$ m $)$.
questions.answer:
(a) $d\vec{B}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,d\vec{l}\times\hat{r}}{r^2}$
(b) With current along $+\hat{i}$ on the $x$-axis and along $+\hat{j}$ on the $y$-axis, at $P(4,5)$:
$B_1=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(5)}=\dfrac{2\times10^{-7}\times2}{5}=8\times10^{-8}$ T, directed out of the page.
$B_2=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(4)}=\dfrac{2\times10^{-7}\times2}{4}=1\times10^{-7}$ T, directed into the page.
Since they are opposite, net field $B=B_2-B_1=2\times10^{-8}$ T, directed into the page.

questions.question: (a) A charged particle $q$ moving with a velocity $\vec{v}$ is subjected to a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ acting perpendicular to $\vec{v}$. If a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$ is also set up in the region along the direction of $\vec{B}$, describe the path followed by the particle and draw its shape. (b) How will the magnetic field inside a long solenoid be affected when: (i) the radius of the turns of the solenoid is increased, (ii) the length of solenoid as well as the total number of its turns are doubled?
questions.answer:
(a) Since $\vec{v}\perp\vec{B}$, the perpendicular velocity component causes uniform circular motion in the plane perpendicular to $\vec{B}$, while $\vec{E}\parallel\vec{B}$ continuously accelerates the particle along $\vec{B}$. The two combine to give a helical path whose pitch keeps increasing along the direction of $\vec{B}$ (an expanding helix, unlike the uniform-pitch helix formed with $E=0$).
(b) (i) $B=\mu_0 n I$ inside a solenoid is independent of the radius of turns, so it remains unchanged.
(ii) Doubling both length and number of turns keeps $n=N/L$ the same, so $B$ remains unchanged.

questions.question: (a) In which cases does a charged particle not experience a force in a magnetic field? (b) A square loop $MNPK$ of side ’ $l$’ carrying a current ’ $I_{2}$’ is kept close to a long straight wire in the same plane and the wire carries a steady current $I_{1}$, as shown in the figure. Obtain the magnitude of magnetic force exerted by the wire on the loop.
questions.answer:
(a) A charged particle experiences no magnetic force when it is at rest ($v=0$), when $\vec{v}$ is parallel or antiparallel to $\vec{B}$ (since $\vec{v}\times\vec{B}=0$), or when $\vec{B}=0$.
(b) Let the near side of the loop be at distance $x$ from the wire. The near and far sides (each of length $l$) experience unequal forces due to the non-uniform field of the wire, while the other two sides' forces cancel by symmetry. Net force:
$F=\dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 l}{2\pi}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}-\dfrac{1}{x+l}\right)$, directed toward the wire (if the near-side current is parallel to $I_1$).

questions.question: An electron of mass $m$ and charge $-e$ is revolving anticlockwise around the nucleus of an atom. (a) Obtain the expression for the magnetic dipole moment ($\mu$) of the atom. $(\frac{e}{2m})$ (b) If $\vec{L}$ is the angular momentum of electron, show that $\mu = -L$.
questions.answer:
(a) Current due to orbiting electron: $I=\dfrac{e}{T}=\dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}$
Magnetic moment: $\mu=IA=\dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}\times\pi r^2=\dfrac{evr}{2}$
Since $L=mvr$, this gives $\mu=\left(\dfrac{e}{2m}\right)L$.
(b) For anticlockwise motion of the electron, $\vec{L}$ points out of the orbital plane (right-hand rule). Since the electron's charge is negative, the conventional current is clockwise, so $\vec{\mu}$ points into the plane, i.e. opposite to $\vec{L}$. Hence, taking the vector nature into account, $\vec{\mu}=-\dfrac{e}{2m}\vec{L}$.

questions.question: (a) Use Ampere’s law to derive the expression for the magnetic field due to a long straight current carrying wire of infinite length. (b) Why is Ampere’s law used for the derivation in (a) above and not Biot-Savart’s law? Explain.
questions.answer:
(a) Consider a circular Amperian loop of radius $r$ centred on the wire, in a plane perpendicular to it. By symmetry, $\vec{B}$ has the same magnitude everywhere on the loop and is tangential to it. Applying Ampere's law:
$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l}=\mu_0 I_{enc}$
$B(2\pi r)=\mu_0 I$
$B=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$
(b) Ampere's law is used because the current distribution has high symmetry (cylindrical symmetry about the wire), which allows $B$ to be taken out of the integral and the field found algebraically. Using Biot-Savart's law would require integrating the contribution of every current element along the infinite wire, which is a much longer vector integration for the same result.

questions.question: A rectangular loop carries a current of $1$ A. A straight long wire carrying $2$ A current is kept near the loop in the same plane as shown in the figure. Find: (i) the torque acting on the loop, and (ii) the magnitude and direction of the net force on the loop.
questions.answer:
Since the rectangular loop lies in the same plane as the wire, the field due to the wire at every point of the loop is perpendicular to that plane, so the loop's magnetic moment $\vec{m}$ (also perpendicular to the plane) is parallel or antiparallel to $\vec{B}$.
(i) $\vec{\tau}=\vec{m}\times\vec{B}=0$, since the angle between $\vec{m}$ and $\vec{B}$ is $0°$ or $180°$.
(ii) The field is non-uniform (stronger nearer the wire), so the forces on the near and far sides (parallel to the wire) are unequal:
$F_{net}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 l}{2\pi}\left(\dfrac{1}{a}-\dfrac{1}{a+b}\right)$, directed toward the wire, where $a$ is the distance of the near side and $b$ the width of the loop.

questions.question: (a) (i) Write Biot-Savart’s law in vector form. (ii) Two identical circular coils $A$ and $B$, each of radius $R$, carrying currents $I$ and $\sqrt{3} I$ respectively, are placed concentrically in $XY$ and $Y Z$ planes respectively. Find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field at their common centre. OR (b) (i) A rectangular loop of sides $l$ and $b$ carries a current $I$ clockwise. Write the magnetic moment $\vec{m}$ of the loop and show its direction in a diagram. (ii) The loop is placed in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ and is free to rotate about an axis which is perpendicular to $\vec{B}$. Prove that the loop experiences no net force, but a torque $\tau =\vec{m} \times\vec{B}$.
questions.answer:
(a) (i) $d\vec{B}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,d\vec{l}\times\hat{r}}{r^2}$
(ii) Field of coil A (in the $XY$ plane) at the centre is along its axis, the $Z$-axis: $B_A=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$
Field of coil B (in the $YZ$ plane) at the centre is along its axis, the $X$-axis: $B_B=\dfrac{\mu_0 \sqrt3 I}{2R}$
Since $B_A$ and $B_B$ are mutually perpendicular:
$B_{net}=\sqrt{B_A^2+B_B^2}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\sqrt{1+3}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{R}$
Direction: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{B_B}{B_A}=\sqrt3 \Rightarrow \theta=60°$ from the $Z$-axis (towards the $X$-axis).

questions.question: A proton with kinetic energy $1.3384 \times 10^{-14}$ J moving horizontally from north to south, enters a uniform magnetic field $B$ of $2.0$ mT directed eastward. Calculate: (a) the speed of the proton (b) the magnitude of acceleration of the proton (c) the radius of the path traced by the proton [Take $(q/m)$ for proton $= 1.0 \times 10^{8}$ C/kg]
questions.answer:
(a) $KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, with $m = q/(q/m) = 1.6\times10^{-19}/1.0\times10^{8} = 1.6\times10^{-27}$ kg.
$v = \sqrt{2\,KE/m} = \sqrt{2\times1.3384\times10^{-14}/1.6\times10^{-27}} \approx 4.1\times10^{6}$ m/s.
(b) Force $F = qvB$, so $a = F/m = (q/m)vB = 1.0\times10^{8}\times4.1\times10^{6}\times2.0\times10^{-3} \approx 8.2\times10^{11}$ m/s$^2$.
(c) $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{v}{(q/m)B} = \dfrac{4.1\times10^{6}}{1.0\times10^{8}\times2.0\times10^{-3}} \approx 20.4$ m.
The force $q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ is vertically upward, so the proton curves upward in a vertical circle of this radius.

questions.question: A circular coil with cross-sectional area $0.2$ cm $2$ carries a current of $4$ A. It is kept in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $0.5$ T normal to the plane of the coil. Calculate: (a) the net force on the coil. (b) the torque on the coil. (c) the average force on each electron in the coil due to the magnetic field. The free electron density in the material of the coil is $10^{28}$ m $-3$.
questions.answer:
(a) For a current loop in a uniform field, the net force is always zero: $\vec{F}_{net} = 0$.
(b) Since $\vec{B}$ is normal to the plane of the coil, the magnetic moment $\vec{m}$ (also normal to the loop) is parallel to $\vec{B}$, so $\tau = mB\sin\theta = 0$.
(c) Drift velocity: $v_d = \dfrac{I}{neA} = \dfrac{4}{10^{28}\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.2\times10^{-4}} = 1.25\times10^{-4}$ m/s.
Force per electron $= ev_dB = 1.6\times10^{-19}\times1.25\times10^{-4}\times0.5 = 1.0\times10^{-23}$ N, directed toward the centre of the coil.

questions.question: (a) Two long, straight, parallel conductors carry steady currents in opposite directions. Explain the nature of the force of interaction between them. Obtain an expression for the magnitude of the force between the two conductors. Hence define one ampere. OR (b) Obtain an expression for the torque $\tau$ acting on a current carrying loop in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$. Draw the necessary diagram.
questions.answer:
(a) Each current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field that exerts a force on the other. For currents in opposite directions, the field of one wire at the other is such that the force is repulsive; for currents in the same direction it is attractive.
Field due to wire 1 at wire 2: $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}$.
Force on length $l$ of wire 2: $F = B_1 I_2 l = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 l}{2\pi d}$.
Force per unit length: $\dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$.
Definition of ampere: one ampere is that current which, when maintained in each of two infinitely long, straight, parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed $1$ m apart in vacuum, produces a force of $2\times10^{-7}$ N per metre of length between them.

questions.question: Two long straight parallel conductors carrying currents, exert a force on each other. Why? Derive an expression for the force per unit length between two long straight parallel conductors carrying currents in opposite directions. Explain the nature of the force between these conductors.
questions.answer:
Each current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field; the other current-carrying conductor placed in this field experiences a force $\vec{F} = I\vec{l}\times\vec{B}$, so the two conductors exert forces on each other.
Field due to wire 1 (current $I_1$) at wire 2, distance $d$ away: $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}$.
Force on length $l$ of wire 2 carrying current $I_2$: $F = B_1 I_2 l = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 l}{2\pi d}$, so force per unit length is $\dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$.
By Newton's third law, wire 1 experiences an equal and opposite force. For currents in opposite directions the force is repulsive; for currents in the same direction it is attractive.

questions.question: A rectangular loop of area $\vec{A}$, carrying current $I$, is placed in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$. With the help of a suitable diagram, derive an expression, in vector form, for the torque acting on the loop.
questions.answer:
Consider a rectangular loop of sides $a$ and $b$ (area $A = ab$), carrying current $I$, placed in a uniform field $\vec{B}$, with its normal $\hat{n}$ making angle $\theta$ with $\vec{B}$.
The two sides of length $a$ perpendicular to $B$'s component experience forces $F = IbB$ that form a couple, while the other two sides experience forces along the same line (no torque).
The perpendicular distance between the two forces is $a\sin\theta$, so torque $\tau = F\times a\sin\theta = IbB\times a\sin\theta = IAB\sin\theta$.
Since $\tau = IAB\sin\theta$ is the magnitude of $\vec{m}\times\vec{B}$ where $\vec{m} = I\vec{A}$ is the magnetic moment (direction given by the right-hand rule),
$$\vec{\tau} = \vec{m}\times\vec{B} = I\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$$

questions.question: An electron (charge $-e$, mass $m$) is revolving around a nucleus, in a hydrogen atom, in a circle of radius $r$. Derive an expression, in vector form, for the magnetic dipole moment, $\mu$, in terms of its orbital angular momentum $\vec{L}$. What is gyromagnetic ratio?
questions.answer:
The electron of charge $-e$ moving with speed $v$ in a circle of radius $r$ constitutes a current $I = \dfrac{e}{T} = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}$ (magnitude).
This is equivalent to a magnetic moment of magnitude $\mu = IA = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}\times\pi r^2 = \dfrac{evr}{2}$.
Orbital angular momentum: $L = mvr$, so $\mu = \dfrac{e}{2m}L$.
Since the electron's charge is negative, $\vec{\mu}$ is opposite to $\vec{L}$:
$$\vec{\mu} = -\dfrac{e}{2m}\vec{L}$$
The gyromagnetic ratio is $\mu/L = e/2m = 8.8\times10^{10}$ C/kg, a constant independent of $r$ or $v$.

questions.question: A circular loop of radius $10$ cm carrying current of $1.0$ A lies in $x$- $y$ plane. A long straight wire lies in the same plane parallel to $x$-axis at a distance of $20$ cm as shown in figure. Find the direction and value of current that has to be maintained in the wire so that the net magnetic field at $O$ is zero.
questions.answer:
Field at centre $O$ due to the loop: $B_{loop} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} = \dfrac{\mu_0(1.0)}{2(0.10)} = 5\mu_0$.
Field at $O$ due to the straight wire, distance $d = 0.20$ m: $B_{wire} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_w}{2\pi d}$.
For net field to be zero, $B_{wire} = B_{loop}$:
$\dfrac{\mu_0 I_w}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \Rightarrow I_w = \dfrac{\pi d I}{R} = \dfrac{\pi\times0.20\times1.0}{0.10} = 2\pi \approx 6.28$ A.
The current in the wire must flow in the direction that makes its field at $O$ (perpendicular to the plane, by the right-hand rule) point opposite to the field produced by the loop's current.

questions.question: Two long insulated straight wires carrying currents of $3$ A and $5$ A are arranged in $XY$ plane as shown in figure. Find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic fields at points $P_{1}(2$ m $, 2$ m $)$ and $P_{2}(-1$ m $, 1$ m $)$.
questions.answer:
Taking the wire along the $X$-axis to carry $3$ A (in the $+x$ direction) and the wire along the $Y$-axis to carry $5$ A (in the $+y$ direction), field magnitude from each is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$, with $\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi} = 2\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
At $P_1(2,2)$: $B_1$ (from $3$A wire, $r=2$) $= 3\times10^{-7}$ T along $+z$; $B_2$ (from $5$A wire, $r=2$) $= 5\times10^{-7}$ T along $-z$.
Net field at $P_1 = 2\times10^{-7}$ T, directed into the page ($-z$).
At $P_2(-1,1)$: $B_1$ (from $3$A wire, $r=1$) $= 6\times10^{-7}$ T along $+z$; $B_2$ (from $5$A wire, $r=1$) $= 1\times10^{-6}$ T along $+z$.
Net field at $P_2 = 1.6\times10^{-6}$ T, directed out of the page ($+z$).

questions.question: An infinite straight conductor is kept along $X^{'}X$ axis and carries a current $I$. A charge $q$ at point $P(0, r)$ starts moving with velocity $\vec{v} = v_{0}\hat{j}$ as shown in figure. Find the direction and magnitude of force initially experienced by the charge.
questions.answer:
Magnetic field at $P(0,r)$ due to the wire carrying current $I$ along $X'X$: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$, directed along $\hat{z}$ (out of the plane), by the right-hand rule.
Force on the charge: $\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B} = q(v_0\hat{j})\times(B\hat{k}) = qv_0B\,\hat{i}$.
So the initial force is directed along the $X$-axis (parallel to the current), with magnitude
$$F = \dfrac{\mu_0 I q v_0}{2\pi r}$$

questions.question: (i) State and explain Ampere’s circuital law. (ii) Two long straight parallel wires separated by $20$ cm, carry $5$ A and $10$ A current respectively, in the same direction. Find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field at a point midway between them.
questions.answer:
(i) Ampere's circuital law states that the line integral of the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ around any closed loop equals $\mu_0$ times the total current enclosed by the loop: $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{enc}$. It is used to find $\vec{B}$ for current distributions with symmetry, such as a long straight wire, solenoid, or toroid.
(ii) At the midpoint, distance from each wire $d = 0.10$ m.
$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0(5)}{2\pi(0.10)} = 1.0\times10^{-5}$ T; $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0(10)}{2\pi(0.10)} = 2.0\times10^{-5}$ T.
Since currents are in the same direction, the two fields at the midpoint are opposite in direction.
Net field $= B_2 - B_1 = 1.0\times10^{-5}$ T $= 10\ \mu$T, in the direction of the field due to the $10$ A wire.

questions.question: An electron moving with a velocity $\vec{v} = (1.0 \times 10^{7}$ m/s $)\hat{i} + (0.5 \times 10^{7}$ m/s $)\hat{j}$ enters a region of uniform magnetic field $\vec{B} = (0.5$ mT $)\hat{j}$. Find the radius of the circular path described by it. While rotating; does the electron trace a linear path too? If so, calculate the linear distance covered by it during the period of one revolution. $[^{8}]$
questions.answer:
Only the velocity component perpendicular to $\vec{B}$ produces circular motion; here $\vec{B}$ is along $\hat{j}$, so $v_\perp = v_x = 1.0\times10^{7}$ m/s and $v_\parallel = v_y = 0.5\times10^{7}$ m/s.
Radius: $r = \dfrac{mv_\perp}{eB} = \dfrac{9.1\times10^{-31}\times1.0\times10^{7}}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.5\times10^{-3}} \approx 0.114$ m.
Since there is a velocity component parallel to $\vec{B}$, the electron also moves along the field direction, so its path is helical, not purely circular.
Time period: $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{eB} \approx 7.15\times10^{-8}$ s, so linear distance (pitch) $= v_\parallel T \approx 0.5\times10^{7}\times7.15\times10^{-8} \approx 0.36$ m.

questions.question: An electron is moving with a velocity $\vec{v} =\frac{3 \times 10}{\pi}$ m/s $\hat{i}$. It enters a region of magnetic field $\vec{B} = (91$ mT $)\hat{k}$. (a) Calculate the magnetic force $\vec{F}$ acting on electron and the radius of its path. (b) Trace the path described by it.
questions.answer:
Here $\vec{v} = v\hat{i}$ with $v \approx 9.55\times10^{6}$ m/s and $\vec{B} = 91\times10^{-3}\hat{k}$ T, so $\vec{v} \perp \vec{B}$.
(a) Force: $\vec{F} = -e(\vec{v}\times\vec{B}) = evB\hat{j}$, magnitude $F = evB \approx 1.6\times10^{-19}\times9.55\times10^{6}\times0.091 \approx 1.39\times10^{-13}$ N.
Radius: $r = \dfrac{mv}{eB} = \dfrac{9.1\times10^{-31}\times9.55\times10^{6}}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.091} \approx 6.0\times10^{-4}$ m.
(b) Since $\vec{v}\perp\vec{B}$, the electron describes a circular path in the $xy$-plane, with the centre in the direction of the initial force (along $+\hat{j}$).

questions.question: Two circular loops A and B, each of radius 3 m, are placed coaxially at a distance of 4 m. They carry currents of 3 A and 2 A in opposite directions respectively. Find the net magnetic field at the centre of loop A.
questions.answer:
Field due to loop A at its own centre: $B_A = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_A}{2R} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times3}{2\times3} \approx 6.28\times10^{-7}$ T.
Field due to loop B (radius $R=3$ m, current 2 A) at A's centre, distance $x=4$ m on axis: $B_B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_B R^2}{2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2\times9}{2\times(25)^{3/2}} \approx 9.05\times10^{-8}$ T.
Since the currents are opposite, $B_A$ and $B_B$ oppose each other, so net field $B_{net} = B_A - B_B \approx 5.38\times10^{-7}$ T, directed along the axis in the sense of $B_A$.

questions.question: Two infinitely long parallel conductors A and B, separated by 2 cm, carry 6 A and 2 A currents in opposite directions respectively. Find: (a) the net magnetic field at a point midway between A and B. (b) the force acting per unit length on B.
questions.answer:
Distance of midpoint from each wire, $d = 1$ cm $= 0.01$ m.
$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times6}{2\pi\times0.01} = 1.2\times10^{-4}$ T, $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2}{2\pi\times0.01} = 4\times10^{-5}$ T.
(a) For opposite currents, the two fields at the midpoint act in the same direction, so $B_{net} = B_1+B_2 = 1.6\times10^{-4}$ T.
(b) $f = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times6\times2}{2\pi\times0.02} = 1.2\times10^{-4}$ N/m, repulsive since the currents are antiparallel.

questions.question: A current carrying circular loop and a straight wire bent partly in the form of a semicircle are placed as shown in the figure. Find the magnitude and direction of net magnetic field at point O.
questions.answer:
At the centre O, the straight parts of the wire that lie along a line passing through O contribute zero field, since $d\vec{l}\times\hat{r} = 0$ for them.
The circular loop of radius $R$ contributes $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$ at its centre, directed into or out of the page as given by the right-hand rule for the current direction shown.
The semicircular arc of radius $r$ contributes $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4r}$ at O, its direction found the same way.
The net field at O is the vector sum $B = B_1 \pm B_2$ (add if both are into/out of the page in the same sense, subtract if opposite), directed perpendicular to the plane of the figure.

questions.question: (a) Briefly describe how the current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer can be increased. (b) A galvanometer shows full scale deflection for current $I_{g}$. A resistance $R_{1}$ is required to convert it into a voltmeter of range $(0 -V )$ and a resistance $R_{2}$ to convert it into a voltmeter of range $(0 -2V )$. Find the resistance of the galvanometer.
questions.answer:
(a) Current sensitivity $I_s = \dfrac{NBA}{k}$ can be increased by increasing the number of turns $N$, using a stronger magnetic field $B$, increasing the coil area $A$, or using a suspension with smaller torsional constant $k$.
(b) For range $(0,V)$: $R_1 + G = \dfrac{V}{I_g}$; for range $(0,2V)$: $R_2 + G = \dfrac{2V}{I_g}$.
Subtracting: $R_2 - R_1 = \dfrac{V}{I_g}$.
Substituting back: $G = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - R_1 = (R_2-R_1) - R_1 = R_2 - 2R_1$.

questions.question: Write an expression of magnetic moment associated with a current $(I)$ carrying circular coil of radius $r$ having $N$ turns.
questions.answer:
Magnetic moment of the coil: $m = NIA = NI\pi r^{2}$.
It is directed along the axis of the coil, given by the right-hand thumb rule for the current direction.

questions.question: Define current sensitivity of a galvanometer. Write its expression.
questions.answer:
Current sensitivity of a galvanometer is the deflection produced per unit current flowing through it.
It is given by $I_s = \dfrac{\theta}{I} = \dfrac{NBA}{k}$, where $N$ is the number of turns, $B$ the magnetic field, $A$ the coil area, and $k$ the torsional constant of the suspension.

questions.question: Consider the above mentioned coil placed in $Y Z$ plane with its centre at the origin. Derive expression for the value of magnetic field due to it at point $(x, 0, 0)$.
questions.answer:
Consider a circular coil of $N$ turns, radius $r$, in the $YZ$-plane carrying current $I$, and point P at $(x,0,0)$ on its axis.
By Biot-Savart law, each current element $Id\vec{l}$ produces $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{Idl}{r^2+x^2}$, directed perpendicular to the line joining the element to P.
$dB$ can be resolved into a component along the axis ($dB\cos\phi$) and one perpendicular to it ($dB\sin\phi$), where $\cos\phi = \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{r^2+x^2}}$; the perpendicular components cancel by symmetry around the loop, while the axial components add up.
Net field: $B = \int dB\cos\phi = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi(r^2+x^2)} \times \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{r^2+x^2}} \times 2\pi r N$, giving $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I r^2}{2(r^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$, directed along the $x$-axis.

questions.question: A galvanometer has resistance $G$ and shows full scale deflection for current $I_{g}$. (i) How can it be converted into an ammeter to measure current up to $I_{0} (I_{0} > I_{g})$? (ii) What is the effective resistance of this ammeter?
questions.answer:
(i) A small resistance called a shunt, $S = \dfrac{I_g G}{I_0 - I_g}$, is connected in parallel with the galvanometer; this bypasses the excess current $(I_0-I_g)$, allowing the combination to read up to $I_0$.
(ii) Effective resistance: $R_A = \dfrac{GS}{G+S} = \dfrac{GI_g}{I_0}$, which is very small (less than $G$), as required for an ideal ammeter.

questions.question: A square loop of side ’ $a$’ carrying a current $I_{2}$ is kept at distance $x$ from an infinitely long straight wire carrying a current $I_{1}$ as shown in the figure. Obtain the expression for the resultant force acting on the loop.
questions.answer:
Force per unit length between two long parallel wires separated by distance $r$ is $f = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r}$.
The near side of the loop (distance $x$ from wire, current parallel to $I_1$) is attracted with force $F_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 a}{2\pi x}$.
The far side (distance $x+a$, current antiparallel) is repelled with force $F_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 a}{2\pi (x+a)}$.
Forces on the other two sides are equal, opposite and act along the same line, so they cancel.
Since $F_1 > F_2$, the net force on the loop is attractive, towards the wire:
$F = F_1 - F_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 a}{2\pi}\left(\dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{1}{x+a}\right)$

questions.question: Derive the expression for the torque acting on a current carrying loop placed in a magnetic field.
questions.answer:
Consider a rectangular loop of sides $a$ (along which current flows) and $b$, carrying current $I$, placed in a uniform field $\vec{B}$ with its normal making angle $\theta$ with $\vec{B}$.
The two sides of length $b$, being perpendicular to $B$, experience forces $F = BIb$ each, equal and opposite, forming a couple.
The perpendicular distance between these forces (moment arm) is $a\sin\theta$.
Torque, $\tau = F \times a\sin\theta = BIab\sin\theta = BIA\sin\theta$, where $A = ab$.
For a coil of $N$ turns, $\tau = NIAB\sin\theta = mB\sin\theta$, where $m = NIA$ is the magnetic moment.
In vector form, $\vec{\tau} = \vec{m} \times \vec{B}$.

questions.question: Explain the significance of a radial magnetic field when a current carrying coil is kept in it.
questions.answer:
In a radial magnetic field, the field lines are always directed along the radius of the circular coil, so $\vec{B}$ lies in the plane of the coil at every position of the coil.
This makes the angle between the normal to the coil and $\vec{B}$ always $90°$, so $\sin\theta = 1$ for all deflections.
Hence the deflecting torque $\tau = NIAB$ remains constant (independent of the angle of rotation) and is directly proportional to the current $I$.
This ensures a linear, uniform scale in the moving coil galvanometer.

questions.question: State the underlying principle of a moving coil galvanometer.
questions.answer:
A current-carrying coil placed in a uniform (radial) magnetic field experiences a torque $\tau = NIAB\sin\theta$, which tends to rotate it.
This deflecting torque is balanced by a restoring torque $k\phi$ due to a spring, where $k$ is the torsional constant and $\phi$ the deflection.
At equilibrium, $NIAB = k\phi$, giving $\phi = \dfrac{NAB}{k}I$, so the deflection is directly proportional to the current passed through the coil.

questions.question: Give two reasons to explain why a galvanometer cannot as such be used to measure the value of the current in a given circuit.
questions.answer:
(i) A galvanometer has a relatively high resistance; connecting it directly in a circuit changes the resistance of the circuit and alters the current to be measured.
(ii) A galvanometer is highly sensitive and gives full-scale deflection for a very small current (of the order of a few $\mu A$ or $mA$); it is not designed for or calibrated to read larger currents directly, and would be damaged if a large current were passed through it.

questions.question: Define the terms: (i) voltage sensitivity and (ii) current sensitivity of a galvanometer.
questions.answer:
(i) Voltage sensitivity is the deflection produced per unit voltage applied: $V_s = \dfrac{\phi}{V} = \dfrac{NAB}{kR}$, where $R$ is the coil resistance.
(ii) Current sensitivity is the deflection produced per unit current passed: $I_s = \dfrac{\phi}{I} = \dfrac{NAB}{k}$.
Here $N, A, B, k$ have their usual meanings (turns, area, field, torsional constant).

questions.question: Two infinitely long straight wires $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ carrying currents $I$ and $2I$ flowing in the same directions are kept ’ $d$’ distance apart. Where should a third straight wire $A_{3}$ carrying current $1.5 I$ be placed between $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ so that it experiences no net force due to $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$? Does the net force acting on $A_{3}$ depend on the current flowing through it?
questions.answer:
Let $A_3$ be placed at distance $x$ from $A_1$ (so at distance $d-x$ from $A_2$).
For zero net force, the forces per unit length due to $A_1$ and $A_2$ must be equal and opposite:
$\dfrac{\mu_0 I (1.5I)}{2\pi x} = \dfrac{\mu_0 (2I)(1.5I)}{2\pi (d-x)}$
This gives $d - x = 2x$, so $x = \dfrac{d}{3}$.
Thus $A_3$ should be placed at a distance $d/3$ from $A_1$ (and $2d/3$ from $A_2$).
Since the current $I_3$ (here $1.5I$) cancels out from both sides of the equation, the equilibrium position of $A_3$ does not depend on the current it carries.

questions.question: A proton, a deuteron and an alpha particle, are accelerated through the same potential difference and then subjected to a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$, perpendicular to the direction of their motions. Compare (i) their kinetic energies, and (ii) if the radius of the circular path described by proton is $5$ cm, determine the radii of the paths described by deuteron and alpha particle.
questions.answer:
Kinetic energy gained: $KE = qV$, so $KE_p : KE_d : KE_\alpha = q_p : q_d : q_\alpha = e : e : 2e = 1:1:2$.
Radius of circular path: $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$, and since $v = \sqrt{2qV/m}$, we get $r = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mV}}{B}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \propto \sqrt{m/q}$.
Using $m_p=1, q_p=1$; $m_d=2, q_d=1$; $m_\alpha=4, q_\alpha=2$ (in units of proton mass and charge):
$r_p : r_d : r_\alpha = 1 : \sqrt{2} : \sqrt{2}$
Given $r_p = 5$ cm, $r_d = r_\alpha = 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.07$ cm.

questions.question: (a) Briefly explain how a galvanometer is converted into an ammeter. (b) A galvanometer coil has a resistance of $15 \Omega$ and it shows full scale deflection for a current of $4$ mA. Convert it into an ammeter of range $0$ to $6$ A. OR (a) Briefly explain how a galvanometer is converted into a voltmeter. (b) A voltmeter of a certain range is constructed by connecting a resistance of $980 \Omega$ in series with a galvanometer. When the resistance of $470 \Omega$ is connected in series, the range gets halved. Find the resistance of the galvanometer.
questions.answer:
(a) A galvanometer is converted into an ammeter by connecting a small resistance called a shunt ($S$) in parallel with the galvanometer coil, so that most of the current bypasses the galvanometer and only a small fraction $I_g$ flows through it, protecting it and extending its range.
(b) $G = 15\,\Omega$, $I_g = 4\times10^{-3}$ A, $I = 6$ A.
Using $I_g G = (I - I_g)S$:
$S = \dfrac{I_g G}{I - I_g} = \dfrac{0.004 \times 15}{5.996} \approx 0.01\,\Omega$

questions.question: A particle of charge $q$ and mass $m$ is moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ in the positive x-direction. (a) It is subjected to a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ directed along negative z-direction. Explain briefly the trajectory it would describe. (b) When the particle is subjected simultaneously to both the magnetic and electric fields directed along the z-axis and y-axis respectively, obtain the condition when the particle will go undeflected.
questions.answer:
(a) The magnetic force $\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ acts perpendicular to $\vec{v}$ at every instant, so it changes only the direction of velocity, not its speed.
This constant-magnitude, always-perpendicular force provides centripetal force, so the particle moves in a circle of radius $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$ in the plane perpendicular to $\vec{B}$ (the x-y plane).
(b) With $\vec{E}$ along y and $\vec{B}$ along z, the electric force $qE$ and magnetic force $qvB$ act along the y-direction, in opposite senses.
The particle goes undeflected when these forces balance: $qE = qvB$, i.e., $v = \dfrac{E}{B}$.

questions.question: (a) Depict the magnetic field lines due to a circular current carrying loop showing the direction of field lines. (b) A current $I$ is flowing in a conductor placed along the x-axis as shown in the figure. Find the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field due to a small current element $d\vec{l}$ lying at the origin at points (i) $(0, d, 0)$ and (ii) $(0, 0, d)$.
questions.answer:
(a) The field lines of a circular current loop are concentric circles near the wire that become larger and straighten out near the centre, forming a pattern like that of a bar magnet, with direction given by the right-hand thumb rule (curl fingers along current, thumb gives field direction).
(b) By Biot-Savart law, $d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\, d\vec{l}\times \hat{r}}{r^2}$, with $d\vec{l} = dl\,\hat{x}$ at the origin.
(i) At $(0,d,0)$: $\hat{r}=\hat{y}$, so $d\vec{l}\times\hat{r} = dl\,\hat{z}$, giving $d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0 I\, dl}{4\pi d^2}$, directed along $+\hat{z}$.
(ii) At $(0,0,d)$: $\hat{r}=\hat{z}$, so $d\vec{l}\times\hat{r} = -dl\,\hat{y}$, giving $d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0 I\, dl}{4\pi d^2}$, directed along $-\hat{y}$.

questions.question: State the principle of a moving coil galvanometer. Explain its working and obtain the expression for the deflection produced due to the current passed through the coil. Define current sensitivity. OR Explain how a galvanometer can be converted into an ammeter of a given range. Derive an expression for shunt resistance and current for full scale deflection. Find the effective resistance of the ammeter.
questions.answer:
Principle: A current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a torque, $\tau = NIAB\sin\theta$, which tends to rotate it.
Working: The coil is suspended between concave pole pieces with a soft iron core producing a radial field, so $\theta = 90^\circ$ always and the deflecting torque is $\tau_d = NIAB$.
This is balanced by the restoring torque of the suspension, $\tau_r = k\theta$, where $k$ is the torsional constant.
At equilibrium, $NIAB = k\theta$, so $I = \left(\frac{k}{NAB}\right)\theta$, i.e., $\theta \propto I$.
Current sensitivity, $I_s = \frac{\theta}{I} = \frac{NAB}{k}$, is the deflection per unit current.

questions.question: Describe the working principle of a moving coil galvanometer. Why is it necessary to use (i) a radial magnetic field and (ii) a cylindrical soft iron core in a galvanometer? Write the expression for current sensitivity of the galvanometer. Can a galvanometer as such be used for measuring the current? Explain. OR (a) Define the term ’self-inductance’ and write its S.I. unit. (b) Obtain the expression for the mutual inductance of two long co-axial solenoids $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ wound one over the other, each of length $L$ and radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ and $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ number of turns per unit length, when a current $I$ is set up in the outer solenoid $S_{2}$.
questions.answer:
Principle: The galvanometer works on the fact that a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a deflecting torque, $\tau = NIAB$.
(i) A radial field is used so that the plane of the coil always remains parallel to $B$, making $\tau$ independent of $\theta$ and giving a linear scale.
(ii) The cylindrical soft iron core concentrates the field lines, increasing $B$ and hence sensitivity, and also helps make the field radial.
At equilibrium, $NIAB = k\theta$, so current sensitivity $I_s = \frac{\theta}{I} = \frac{NAB}{k}$.
A galvanometer cannot directly measure current as it is sensitive only to very small currents, is uncalibrated in amperes, and has resistance that would alter the circuit current; it must be converted into an ammeter using a shunt.

questions.question: An electron of mass $m_{e}$ revolves around a nucleus of charge $+Ze$. Show that it behaves like a tiny magnetic dipole. Hence prove that the magnetic moment associated with it is expressed as $\mu = -\frac{e}{2m_{e}}L$, where $\vec{L}$ is the orbital angular momentum of the electron. Give the significance of negative sign.
questions.answer:
An electron of charge $-e$ moving with speed $v$ in a circular orbit of radius $r$ is equivalent to a current loop with current $I = \frac{e}{T} = \frac{ev}{2\pi r}$ (magnitude), directed opposite to its velocity since its charge is negative.
This current loop has a magnetic moment $\mu = IA = \frac{ev}{2\pi r}\times \pi r^2 = \frac{evr}{2}$.
The orbital angular momentum is $L = m_e v r$, so $\mu = \frac{e}{2m_e}L$.
Since the conventional current is opposite to the electron's motion, $\vec{\mu}$ is antiparallel to $\vec{L}$: $\vec{\mu} = -\frac{e}{2m_e}\vec{L}$.
The negative sign shows that the magnetic moment and orbital angular momentum vectors point in opposite directions, a consequence of the electron's negative charge.

questions.question: (a) Write the expression for the force $\vec{F}$ acting on a particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$. Under what conditions will it move in (i) a circular path and (ii) a helical path? (b) Show that the kinetic energy of the particle moving in magnetic field remains constant.
questions.answer:
(a) The magnetic force is $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v}\times \vec{B})$.
(i) If $\vec{v}$ is entirely perpendicular to $\vec{B}$, the force is constant in magnitude and always perpendicular to $\vec{v}$, so the particle moves in a circular path.
(ii) If $\vec{v}$ has a component along $\vec{B}$ as well as perpendicular to it, the perpendicular component gives circular motion while the parallel component gives uniform motion along $\vec{B}$; the resultant path is a helix.
(b) Since $\vec{F}$ is always perpendicular to $\vec{v}$, the work done, $dW = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}\,dt = 0$. As no work is done, the speed and hence the kinetic energy of the particle remains unchanged.

questions.question: Using Biot-Savart law, deduce the expression for the magnetic field at a point $(x)$ on the axis of a circular current carrying loop of radius $R$. How is the direction of the magnetic field determined at this point? OR The figure shows three infinitely long straight parallel current carrying conductors. Find the (i) magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field at point $A$ lying on conductor 1, (ii) magnetic force on conductor 2.
questions.answer:
Consider a circular loop of radius $R$ carrying current $I$, and a point $P$ on its axis at distance $x$ from the centre. For a current element $Idl$, the distance to $P$ is $\sqrt{R^2+x^2}$, and by Biot-Savart law $dB = \frac{\mu_0 I\, dl}{4\pi (R^2+x^2)}$, directed perpendicular to the line joining the element to $P$.
Resolving $dB$ into components along and perpendicular to the axis, the perpendicular components cancel in pairs by symmetry, while the axial components add up:
$B = \int dB\sin\theta = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$, where $\sin\theta = R/\sqrt{R^2+x^2}$.
The direction of $\vec{B}$ is along the axis, given by the right-hand thumb rule (curling fingers along current direction, thumb points along field).

questions.question: (a) State the condition under which a charged particle moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ goes undeflected in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$. (b) An electron, after being accelerated through a potential difference of $10^{4}$ V, enters a uniform magnetic field of $0$ · $04$ T, perpendicular to its direction of motion. Calculate the radius of curvature of its trajectory.
questions.answer:
(a) The particle goes undeflected when its velocity $\vec{v}$ is parallel or antiparallel to $\vec{B}$, since then $\vec{v}\times\vec{B} = 0$ and the magnetic force is zero.
(b) Speed after acceleration: $eV = \frac{1}{2}m_ev^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\frac{2eV}{m_e}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times10^4}{9.1\times10^{-31}}} = 5.93\times10^7$ m/s.
Radius of curvature: $r = \frac{m_ev}{eB} = \frac{9.1\times10^{-31}\times5.93\times10^7}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.04}$
$r \approx 8.43\times10^{-3}$ m.

questions.question: A proton and an $\alpha$-particle move perpendicular to a magnetic field. Find the ratio of radii of the circular paths described by them when both (i) have equal momenta, and (ii) were accelerated through the same potential difference.
questions.answer:
Radius of circular path: $r = \frac{mv}{qB} = \frac{p}{qB}$.
(i) Equal momenta: $\frac{r_p}{r_\alpha} = \frac{q_\alpha}{q_p} = \frac{2e}{e} = 2$, so $r_p : r_\alpha = 2 : 1$.
(ii) Same accelerating potential $V$: $qV = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\frac{2qV}{m}}$, so $r = \frac{1}{B}\sqrt{\frac{2mV}{q}}$, i.e., $r \propto \sqrt{m/q}$.
$\frac{r_p}{r_\alpha} = \sqrt{\frac{m_p/e}{4m_p/2e}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}$, so $r_p : r_\alpha = 1 : \sqrt{2}$.

questions.question: (a) State Biot - Savart law and express this law in the vector form. (b) Two identical circular coils, $P$ and $Q$ each of radius $R$, carrying currents $1$ A and $\sqrt{3}$ A respectively, are placed concentrically and perpendicular to each other lying in the $XY$ and $Y Z$ planes. Find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field at the centre of the coils.
questions.answer:
(a) Biot-Savart law states that the magnetic field due to a current element $I\,d\vec{l}$ at a point is directly proportional to $I$, $dl$, $\sin\theta$ (angle between $d\vec{l}$ and $\hat{r}$), and inversely proportional to $r^2$: $d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\, d\vec{l}\times \hat{r}}{r^2}$.
(b) Field due to $P$ (in $XY$ plane) at centre: $B_P = \frac{\mu_0(1)}{2R}$, directed along $z$-axis.
Field due to $Q$ (in $YZ$ plane) at centre: $B_Q = \frac{\mu_0(\sqrt{3})}{2R}$, directed along $x$-axis.
Since $B_P \perp B_Q$: $B_{net} = \sqrt{B_P^2+B_Q^2} = \frac{\mu_0}{2R}\sqrt{1+3} = \frac{\mu_0}{R}$.
Direction: $\tan\theta = \frac{B_Q}{B_P} = \sqrt{3} \Rightarrow \theta = 60^\circ$ from the axis of coil $P$.

questions.question: Two identical loops $P$ and $Q$ each of radius $5$ cm are lying in perpendicular planes such that they have a common centre as shown in the figure. Find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field at the common centre of the two coils, if they carry currents equal to $3$ A and $4$ A respectively.
questions.answer:
Field at centre due to each loop (perpendicular to its own plane): $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.
For $P$ ($I_1=3$ A): $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0(3)}{2(0.05)} = 30\mu_0$, along its axis.
For $Q$ ($I_2=4$ A): $B_2 = \frac{\mu_0(4)}{2(0.05)} = 40\mu_0$, along its axis, perpendicular to $B_1$ since the loops are in perpendicular planes.
Net field: $B_{net} = \sqrt{B_1^2+B_2^2} = \mu_0\sqrt{30^2+40^2} = 50\mu_0 = 50\times4\pi\times10^{-7}$
$B_{net} \approx 6.28\times10^{-5}$ T.
Direction: $\tan\theta = \frac{B_2}{B_1} = \frac{4}{3} \Rightarrow \theta \approx 53^\circ$ from the axis of loop $P$.

questions.question: Use Biot-Savart law to derive the expression for the magnetic field on the axis of a current carrying circular loop of radius $R$. Draw the magnetic field lines due to a circular wire carrying current $I$.
questions.answer:
Consider a circular loop of radius $R$ carrying current $I$, centre $O$. Let $P$ be a point on the axis at distance $x$ from $O$. For a current element $Id\vec l$, distance to $P$ is $r=\sqrt{R^2+x^2}$, and $d\vec l \perp \vec r$, so by Biot-Savart law $dB=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,dl}{r^2}$.
Resolving $dB$ into axial and perpendicular components, the perpendicular components of diametrically opposite elements cancel; axial components ($dB\cos\theta$, $\cos\theta=R/r$) add up.
$B=\int dB\cos\theta=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2\pi R\cdot R}{(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}I=\frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$
At the centre ($x=0$), $B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.
Field lines: concentric circles close to the wire, becoming straight and parallel to the axis at the centre, resembling the pattern of a bar magnet.

questions.question: How is a galvanometer converted into a voltmeter and an ammeter? Draw the relevant diagrams and find the resistance of the arrangement in each case. Take resistance of galvanometer as $G$.
questions.answer:
Voltmeter: a high resistance $R$ is connected in series with the galvanometer so that it draws negligible current from the circuit, $R=\frac{V}{I_g}-G$. Combined resistance $=G+R=\frac{V}{I_g}$, which is large, and this combination is connected across the element whose voltage is to be measured.
Ammeter: a low resistance (shunt) $S$ is connected in parallel with the galvanometer, $S=\frac{I_gG}{I-I_g}$. Combined resistance $=\frac{GS}{G+S}$, which is very small, and this combination is inserted in series in the circuit.

questions.question: State Ampere’s circuital law. Use this law to find magnetic field due to straight infinite current carrying wire. How are the magnetic field lines different from the electrostatic field lines?
questions.answer:
Ampere's circuital law: the line integral of $\vec B$ around any closed path equals $\mu_0$ times the current enclosed: $\oint \vec B\cdot d\vec l=\mu_0 I_{enc}$.
For an infinite straight wire, choose a circular Amperian loop of radius $r$ around the wire; by symmetry $B$ is constant in magnitude and tangential everywhere: $B(2\pi r)=\mu_0 I\Rightarrow B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.
Difference: magnetic field lines always form closed loops (no beginning or end), whereas electrostatic field lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges (or infinity) and are never closed.

questions.question: State the principle of working of a galvanometer. A galvanometer of resistance G is converted into a voltmeter to measure upto V volts by connecting a resistance $R_{1}$ in series with the coil. If a resistance $R_{2}$ is connected in series with it, then it can measure upto V/2 volts. Find the resistance, in terms of $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$, required to be connected to convert it into a voltmeter that can read upto 2 V. Also find the resistance G of the galvanometer in terms of $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$.
questions.answer:
Principle: a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a torque $\tau=NIAB$, causing deflection proportional to current.
Given $V=I_g(G+R_1)$ and $\frac{V}{2}=I_g(G+R_2)$.
Dividing: $2=\frac{G+R_1}{G+R_2}\Rightarrow G=R_1-2R_2$
For $2V$: $2V=I_g(G+R)$; comparing with $V=I_g(G+R_1)$ gives $G+R=2(G+R_1)$, so
$R=G+2R_1=3R_1-2R_2$

questions.question: (a) State Ampere’s circuital law, expressing it in the integral form. (b) Two long coaxial insulated solenoids, $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ of equal lengths are wound one over the other as shown in the figure. A steady current "I" flow through the inner solenoid $S_{1}$ to the other end B, which is connected to the outer solenoid $S_{2}$ through which the same current "I" flows in the opposite direction so as to come out at end A. If $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ are the number of turns per unit length, find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field at a point (i) inside on the axis and (ii) outside the combined system.
questions.answer:
(a) Ampere's circuital law (integral form): $\oint \vec B\cdot d\vec l=\mu_0 I_{enc}$.
(b) Since the same current $I$ returns from $S_1$ through $S_2$ in the opposite sense, the two solenoids carry currents in opposite directions.
(i) Inside, on the axis (well within both solenoids): fields due to $S_1$ and $S_2$ oppose each other, so
$B=\mu_0(n_1-n_2)I$, directed along the axis in the sense of the solenoid with larger $n$.
(ii) Outside the combined system: field of a long solenoid outside itself is negligible, so $B=0$.

questions.question: A rectangular loop of wire of size $4$ cm $\times 10$ cm carries a steady current of $2$ A. A straight long wire carrying $5$ A current is kept near the loop as shown. If the loop and the wire are coplanar, find (i) the torque acting on the loop and (ii) the magnitude and direction of the force on the loop due to the current carrying wire.
questions.answer:
Torque $=0$: since the loop and wire are coplanar, the field $\vec B$ of the wire at every point of the loop is perpendicular to the plane of the loop, i.e. parallel to $\vec m$, so $\vec\tau=\vec m\times \vec B=0$.
Force: with the wire parallel to the 10 cm side, near side at $d_1=1$ cm and far side at $d_2=5$ cm,
$F_1=\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 l}{2\pi d_1}=2\times10^{-5}$ N (attractive), $F_2=\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 l}{2\pi d_2}=4\times10^{-6}$ N (repulsive)
Net force $=F_1-F_2=1.6\times10^{-5}$ N, directed towards the wire.

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram of a moving coil galvanometer and explain its working. What is the function of radial magnetic field inside the coil?
questions.answer:
Diagram: a rectangular coil of many turns wound on a light non-magnetic frame with a soft-iron cylindrical core, suspended by a phosphor-bronze strip between the concave pole pieces of a strong permanent magnet, giving a radial field; the strip also connects to a pointer/scale.
Working: when current $I$ flows through the coil in field $B$, it experiences a torque $\tau=NIAB$, causing rotation until balanced by the restoring torque $k\theta$ of the suspension: $NIAB=k\theta\Rightarrow \theta=\frac{NAB}{k}I$, so deflection is proportional to current.
Function of radial field: keeps the plane of the coil always parallel to $B$ at every deflection, making $\tau$ proportional to $I$ for all positions, giving a linear, uniformly-divided scale.

questions.question: Write the expression for the magnetic moment ($\vec{m}$) due to a planar square loop of side ’ $l$’ carrying a steady current I in a vector form. In the given figure this loop is placed in a horizontal plane near a long straight conductor carrying a steady current $I_{1}$ at a distance $l$ as shown. Give reasons to explain that the loop will experience a net force but no torque. Write the expression for this force acting on the loop.
questions.answer:
$\vec m=Il^2\hat n$, direction given by the right-hand rule, normal to the plane of the loop.
Since the loop is coplanar with the wire, the field $\vec B$ due to the wire at every point of the loop is perpendicular to the plane containing the wire and the loop, i.e. parallel to $\vec m$; hence $\vec\tau=\vec m\times \vec B=0$.
Net force arises because the two sides of the loop parallel to the wire lie at unequal distances $l$ and $2l$:
$F=\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I}{2\pi}\left(\frac{1}{l}-\frac{1}{2l}\right)=\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I}{4\pi}$, directed towards the wire.

questions.question: A long straight wire of a circular cross-section of radius ’ $a$’ carries a steady current ’ $I$’. The current is uniformly distributed across the cross-section. Apply Ampere’s circuital law to calculate the magnetic field at a point ’ $r$’ in the region for (i) $r < a$ and (ii) $r > a$.
questions.answer:
Ampere's law: $\oint \vec B\cdot d\vec l=\mu_0 I_{enc}$
(i) For $r<a$: current enclosed $I_{enc}=I\frac{\pi r^2}{\pi a^2}=\frac{Ir^2}{a^2}$
$B(2\pi r)=\mu_0\frac{Ir^2}{a^2}\Rightarrow B=\frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi a^2}$
(ii) For $r>a$: $I_{enc}=I$
$B(2\pi r)=\mu_0 I\Rightarrow B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$

questions.question: State the underlying principle of working of a moving coil galvanometer. Give two reasons why a galvanometer can not be used as such to measure current in a given circuit. Name any two factors on which the current sensitivity of a galvanometer depends.
questions.answer:
Principle: a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a torque $\tau=NIAB$, and its deflection is proportional to the current through it.
Reasons it cannot be used directly to measure current: (i) it is highly sensitive and gives full-scale deflection for very small currents (of the order of microamperes), so it cannot measure larger currents without damage; (ii) it has an appreciable resistance $G$, so inserting it directly in series would alter the current being measured.
Current sensitivity $I_s=\frac{NBA}{k}$ depends on the number of turns $N$ and the area $A$ of the coil.

questions.question: Derive the expression for force per unit length between two long straight parallel current carrying conductors. Hence define one ampere.
questions.answer:
Consider two long straight parallel conductors carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$, separated by distance $r$ in air.
The magnetic field due to conductor 1 at the location of conductor 2 is $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi r}$, directed perpendicular to conductor 2.
Force on a length $l$ of conductor 2 is $F = B_1 I_2 l = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 l}{2\pi r}$.
So force per unit length is $f = \frac{F}{l} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r}$; it is attractive if the currents are in the same direction and repulsive if opposite.
Definition of ampere: if $I_1 = I_2 = 1$ A and $r = 1$ m, then $f = 2 \times 10^{-7}$ N/m.
One ampere is the current which, when maintained in each of two infinitely long straight parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed $1$ m apart in vacuum, produces a force of $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N per metre of length on each conductor.

questions.question: If a particle of charge $q$ is moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ along the z-axis and the magnetic field $B$ is acting along the x-axis, use the expression $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times\vec{B})$ to find the direction of the force $\vec{F}$ acting on it. A beam of proton passes undeflected with a horizontal velocity $v$, through a region of electric and magnetic fields, mutually perpendicular to each other and normal to the direction of the beam. If the magnitudes of the electric and magnetic fields are $50 KV/m$ and $50 mT$ respectively, calculate (i) Velocity $v$ of the beam (ii) Force with which it strikes a target on a screen, if the proton beam current is equal to $0.80 mA$.
questions.answer:
With $\vec{v} = v\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = B\hat{i}$, $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B}) = qvB(\hat{k}\times\hat{i}) = qvB\hat{j}$.
So the force on the (positive) charge is along the $+y$-axis, perpendicular to both $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$.
Since the proton beam is undeflected, the electric and magnetic forces balance: $qE = qvB$, giving $v = \frac{E}{B} = \frac{50\times10^{3}}{50\times10^{-3}} = 1.0\times10^{6}$ m/s.
Number of protons striking the target per second, $n = \frac{I}{e} = \frac{0.80\times10^{-3}}{1.6\times10^{-19}} = 5\times10^{15}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.
Force with which the beam strikes the target $= n\times m_p v = 5\times10^{15}\times1.67\times10^{-27}\times10^{6} = 8.35\times10^{-6}$ N.

questions.question: A galvanometer with a coil of resistance $120 \Omega$ shows full scale deflection for a current of $2.5$ mA. How will you convert the galvanometer into an ammeter of range $0$ to $7.5$ A? Determine the net resistance of the ammeter. When an ammeter is put in a circuit, does it read slightly less or more than the actual current in the original circuit? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter, a small resistance (shunt) $S$ is connected in parallel with the galvanometer coil so that most of the current bypasses the coil.
Using $I_gG = (I-I_g)S$: $S = \frac{I_gG}{I-I_g} = \frac{2.5\times10^{-3}\times120}{7.5-2.5\times10^{-3}} \approx 0.04\ \Omega$.
Net resistance of the ammeter $= \frac{GS}{G+S} = \frac{120\times0.04}{120.04} \approx 0.04\ \Omega$.
An ammeter reads slightly less than the actual current, because an ideal ammeter should have zero resistance; the real ammeter has this small finite resistance which, when inserted in series, slightly increases the total circuit resistance and reduces the current below its original value.

questions.question: Two straight, parallel, current carrying conductors are kept at a distance $r$ from each other, in air. The direction of current in both the conductors is the same. Find the magnitude and direction of the force between them. Hence define one ampere.
questions.answer:
Let two parallel straight conductors carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ in the same direction be separated by distance $r$.
The field due to conductor 1 at conductor 2 is $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi r}$, so the force per unit length on conductor 2 is $f = B_1I_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r}$, directed towards conductor 1 (by Fleming's left-hand rule).
Since currents are in the same direction, the conductors attract each other with this force per unit length.
Definition of ampere: if $I_1 = I_2 = 1$ A and $r = 1$ m, $f = 2\times10^{-7}$ N/m; one ampere is the current in each of two infinitely long parallel conductors, $1$ m apart in vacuum, that produces a force of $2\times10^{-7}$ N per metre length between them.

questions.question: A galvanometer is used to detect or/and measure small currents in an electrical circuit. It essentially works on the fact that a current-carrying coil experiences a deflecting torque when placed in a magnetic field. This deflection in the coil can be measured and it is related to the current flowing in the coil, the number of turns in the coil, area of the coil and the magnetic field. A hair spring attached to the coil provides a counter torque and helps in measuring the deflection. A galvanometer can be converted to an ammeter or a voltmeter of desired range by using suitable resistances.
questions.answer:
(i) Working principle: the deflecting torque on the coil, $\tau_d = NIAB\sin\theta$, is balanced by the restoring torque of the spring, $\tau_r = k\theta$, giving $I = \frac{k}{NAB}\theta$, so deflection $\theta$ is directly proportional to current $I$.
(ii) Role of the hairspring: it provides a restoring torque proportional to the twist, produces a linear scale, and brings the coil/pointer back to zero when no current flows.
(iii) Conversion to ammeter: a small resistance (shunt) is connected in parallel with the galvanometer coil, so that most of the current bypasses the coil and only $I_g$ passes through it.
(iv) Conversion to voltmeter: a high resistance is connected in series with the galvanometer, so that only a small current $I_g$ flows for the full range of voltage to be measured.

questions.question: Briefly explain various ways to increase the strength of magnetic field produced by a given solenoid.
questions.answer:
For a solenoid, $B = \mu_0 n I$ (air core), where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length and $I$ is the current.
The field can be increased by increasing the current $I$ flowing through the solenoid.
It can also be increased by increasing the number of turns per unit length $n$, i.e. winding the turns more closely.
Inserting a soft iron (ferromagnetic) core inside the solenoid greatly increases the field, since $B = \mu I n$ and the permeability $\mu$ of soft iron is much greater than $\mu_0$.

questions.question: Seema’s uncle was advised by his doctor to have an MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) scan of his brain. Her uncle felt it to be expensive and wanted to postpone it. When Seema learnt about this, she took the help of her family and also approached the doctor, who also offered a substantial discount. She then convinced her uncle to undergo the test to enable the doctor to know the condition of his brain. The information thus obtained greatly helped the doctor to treat him properly. Based on the above paragraph, answer the following questions: (a) What according to you are the values displayed by Seema, her family and the doctor? (b) What could be the possible reason for MRI test to be so expensive? (c) Assuming that MRI test was performed using a magnetic field of $0.1$ T, find the minimum and maximum values of the force that the magnetic field could exert on a proton (charge $= 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C) moving with a speed of $10^{4}$ m/s.
questions.answer:
(a) Seema shows compassion, initiative and concern for family well-being; her family shows unity and support; the doctor shows empathy and social responsibility by offering a discount.
(b) MRI machines use powerful superconducting magnets that must be cooled with liquid helium, along with sophisticated electronics, software and highly trained personnel, making the installation and running costs very high.
(c) $F = qvB\sin\theta$; minimum force occurs when $\theta = 0^{\circ}$ (velocity parallel to field), giving $F_{min} = 0$; maximum force occurs when $\theta = 90^{\circ}$, giving $F_{max} = qvB = 1.6\times10^{-19}\times10^{4}\times0.1 = 1.6\times10^{-16}$ N.

questions.question: (a) (i) A rectangular loop of sides $a$ and $b$ carrying current $I$ is placed in a magnetic field $B$ such that its area vector $\vec{A}$ makes an angle $\theta$ with $\vec{B}$. With the help of a suitable diagram, show that the torque $\tau$ acting on the loop is given by $\tau =\vec{m} \times\vec{B}$, where $m(= I\vec{A})$ is the magnetic dipole moment of the loop. (ii) A circular coil of 100 $[]$ turns and radius $\frac{10}{\sqrt{\pi}}$ cm carrying current of $5.0$ A is suspended vertically in a uniform horizontal magnetic field of $2.0$ T. The field makes an angle $30^{^{\circ}}$ with the normal to the coil. Calculate: (I) the magnetic dipole moment of the coil, and (II) the magnitude of the counter torque that must be applied to prevent the coil from turning.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Consider a rectangular loop PQRS of sides $a$ (PQ, RS) and $b$ (QR, SP) carrying current $I$, placed in field $\vec{B}$ with area vector $\vec{A}$ making angle $\theta$ with $\vec{B}$.
The sides of length $b$ each experience a force of magnitude $F = BIb$, in opposite directions, forming a couple.
The perpendicular distance between these two forces is $a\sin\theta$.
So torque $\tau = F\times a\sin\theta = BIb\times a\sin\theta = BI(ab)\sin\theta = BIA\sin\theta$.
Since $m = IA$ is directed along the normal to the loop, this can be written vectorially as $\vec{\tau} = \vec{m}\times\vec{B}$.
(ii) Area $A = \pi r^2 = \pi\left(\frac{0.1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^2 = 0.01$ m$^2$.
(I) $m = NIA = 100\times5\times0.01 = 5$ A$\cdot$m$^2$.
(II) $\tau = mB\sin\theta = 5\times2.0\times\sin30^{\circ} = 5$ N$\cdot$m.

questions.question: (b) (i) Derive an expression for the force $\vec{F}$ acting on a conductor of length $L$ and area of cross-section $A$ carrying current $I$ and placed in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$. (ii) A part of a wire carrying $2.0$ A current and bent at $90^{^{\circ}}$ at two points is placed in a region of uniform magnetic field $\vec{B} = -(0.50$ T $) \hat{k}$, as shown in the figure. Calculate the magnitude of the net force acting on the wire.
questions.answer:
(b)(i) Let the conductor have length $L$, area of cross-section $A$, with $n$ free charge carriers of charge $e$ per unit volume moving with drift velocity $\vec{v_d}$ along the conductor. Current $I = nAev_d$.
Force on one charge carrier in field $\vec{B}$ is $e(\vec{v_d}\times\vec{B})$.
Total number of carriers in the conductor is $nAL$, so total force $\vec{F} = nAL\,e(\vec{v_d}\times\vec{B}) = (nAev_d)(\vec{L}\times\vec{B}) = I(\vec{L}\times\vec{B})$, where $\vec{L}$ is the length vector along the current direction.
Thus $\vec{F} = I\vec{L}\times\vec{B}$, magnitude $F = BIL\sin\theta$, direction given by the right-hand (or Fleming's left-hand) rule.
(ii) In a uniform field, the net force on any bent wire equals the force on a straight wire joining its two end points, i.e. $\vec{F} = I\vec{L}_{eff}\times\vec{B}$, where $\vec{L}_{eff}$ is the vector from the starting to the end point of the wire; the bends themselves contribute no extra net force since the forces on the connecting segments cancel appropriately, so only this effective straight-line length and current determine the magnitude $F = BIL_{eff}\sin\theta$.

questions.question: (a) (i) A proton moving with velocity $\vec{V}$ in a non-uniform magnetic field traces a path as shown in the figure. The path followed by the proton is always in the plane of the paper. What is the direction of the magnetic field in the region near points $P$, $Q$ and $R$? What can you say about relative magnitude of magnetic fields at these points? (ii) A current carrying circular loop of area $A$ produces a magnetic field $B$ at its $r$ centre. Show that the magnetic moment of the loop is $\frac{2BA}{\mu_{0}}\frac{A}{\pi}$. OR (b) (i) Derive an expression for the torque acting on a rectangular current loop suspended in a uniform magnetic field. (ii) A charged particle is moving in a circular path with velocity $\vec{V}$ in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$. It is made to pass through a sheet of lead and as a consequence, it loses one half of its kinetic energy without change in its direction. How will (1) the radius of its path (2) its time period of revolution change?
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Since the path lies entirely in the plane of the paper and the magnetic force must always act as the centripetal force (perpendicular to $\vec{v}$, in the plane of the paper), the magnetic field at P, Q and R must be perpendicular to the plane of the paper, i.e. either into or out of the page, its exact sense at each point fixed by $\vec{F}=q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ pointing toward the centre of curvature there. Since $r = \frac{mv}{qB}$, the field is stronger where the path curves more sharply (smaller radius of curvature) and weaker where the path is nearly straight.
(ii) At the centre of a circular loop, $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$, so $I = \frac{2Br}{\mu_0}$. Magnetic moment $m = IA = \frac{2BrA}{\mu_0}$. Since $A = \pi r^2$, $r = \sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}}$, giving $m = \frac{2BA}{\mu_0}\sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}}$.

OR

(b)(i) For a rectangular loop of sides $a,b$ carrying current $I$ in field $B$, with area vector making angle $\theta$ with $B$: the forces on the sides of length $b$ are each $BIb$, oppositely directed, separated by perpendicular distance $a\sin\theta$, forming a couple. Torque $\tau = BIb\times a\sin\theta = BIA\sin\theta$, i.e. $\vec{\tau} = \vec{m}\times\vec{B}$ with $m = IA$.
(ii) Radius $r = \frac{mv}{qB}$ and $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$; when KE halves, $v' = \frac{v}{\sqrt2}$, so the new radius $r' = \frac{r}{\sqrt2}$ (decreases). Period $T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$ is independent of $v$, so the time period remains unchanged.

questions.question: (i) What is the source of force acting on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field? Obtain the expression for force acting between two long straight parallel conductors carrying steady currents and hence define ’ampere’. (ii) A point charge q is moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$. Find the work done by the magnetic force on the charge. (iii) Explain the necessary conditions in which the trajectory of a charged particle is helical in a uniform magnetic field.
questions.answer:
(i) The force on a current-carrying conductor arises from the Lorentz force $\vec F = q\vec v_d \times \vec B$ experienced by the free electrons drifting with drift velocity $v_d$ inside the conductor.
Summing over all charge carriers gives $F = BIL\sin\theta$, direction by Fleming's left-hand rule.
For two long parallel wires carrying currents $I_1, I_2$ separated by $d$: wire A produces $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}$ at wire B, so force per unit length on B is $f = B_1 I_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$ (attractive if currents are parallel, repulsive if antiparallel).
Definition: one ampere is that current which, flowing in each of two infinite parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force of $2\times10^{-7}$ N per metre of length on each.
(ii) $\vec F = q\vec v \times \vec B$ is always perpendicular to $\vec v$, so $dW = \vec F\cdot\vec v\,dt = 0$; the magnetic force does no work on the charge.
(iii) The path is helical when $\vec v$ has both a component $v_\perp$ perpendicular to $\vec B$ (giving circular motion) and a component $v_\parallel$ parallel to $\vec B$ (giving uniform straight-line motion, unaffected by the force); together these produce a helix with pitch $v_\parallel T$.

questions.question: (i) A current carrying loop can be considered as a magnetic dipole placed along its axis. Explain. (ii) Obtain the relation for magnetic dipole moment $\vec{M}$ of current carrying coil. Give the direction of $\vec{M}$. (iii) A current carrying coil is placed in an external uniform magnetic field. The coil is free to turn in the magnetic field. What is the net force acting on the coil? Obtain the orientation of the coil in stable equilibrium. Show that in this orientation the flux of the total field (field produced by the loop + external field) through the coil is maximum.
questions.answer:
(i) At points on its axis far from the loop, the magnetic field of a current loop varies as $B \propto \frac{1}{x^3}$, exactly like the axial field of a short bar magnet; hence a current loop behaves as a magnetic dipole with its dipole moment along the axis.
(ii) For $N$ turns of area $A$ carrying current $I$: $\vec M = NI\vec A$.
Direction of $\vec M$ is given by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers along the current direction, the thumb gives the direction of $\vec M$, perpendicular to the plane of the loop.
(iii) Net force on the coil in a uniform field is zero (forces on opposite sides cancel), but it experiences a torque $\vec\tau = \vec M \times \vec B$.
The coil rotates until $\vec M$ is parallel to $\vec B$; potential energy $U = -MB\cos\theta$ is minimum at $\theta = 0$, giving stable equilibrium with $\vec M \parallel \vec B$.
In this orientation the plane of the coil is perpendicular to $\vec B$, so the external flux through it is maximum, and the coil's own field adds to it, making the total flux linked maximum.

questions.question: (a) (i) With the help of a labelled diagram, explain the principle of working of a moving coil galvanometer. Write the purpose of using (i) radial magnetic field, and (ii) soft iron core, in it. (ii) Define current sensitivity of a galvanometer. "Increasing the current sensitivity may not necessarily increase the voltage sensitivity." Give reason. OR (b) (i) (I) Write Ampere’s circuital law in mathematical form and explain the terms used. (II) As the current carrying solenoid is made longer, the magnetic field produced outside it approaches zero. Why? (III) A flexible loop of irregular shape carrying current when located in an external magnetic field, changes to a circular shape. Give reason. (ii) A galvanometer of resistance $G$ is converted into a voltmeter to measure up to $V$ volts, by connecting a resistance $R_{1}$ in series with the coil. If $R_{1}$ is replaced by $R_{2}$, then it can only measure up to $\frac{V}{2}$ volt. Find the value of the resistance $R_{3}$ (in terms of $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$) needed to convert it into a voltmeter that can read up to $2V$.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Principle: a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a torque $\tau = NIAB\sin\theta$, which deflects the coil against a restoring torsional spring until $NIAB\sin\theta = k\theta$; deflection $\theta$ is thus a measure of current $I$.
Radial field: keeps the plane of the coil always parallel to $\vec B$ (i.e. $\theta = 90^\circ$ always), so $\tau \propto I$ and the scale is linear.
Soft iron core: concentrates the field lines, increasing $B$ and hence sensitivity, and helps make the field radial.
(ii) Current sensitivity $I_s = \frac{\theta}{I} = \frac{NAB}{k}$.
Voltage sensitivity $V_s = \frac{\theta}{V} = \frac{NAB}{kR}$, where $R$ is the coil resistance.
Increasing $I_s$ (say by increasing $N$) also increases $R$ proportionally (more turns of wire), so $V_s = I_s/R$ need not increase — it can remain unchanged or even decrease.

questions.question: (a) (i) A particle of mass m and charge q is moving with a velocity $\vec{v}$ in a magnetic field $B$ as shown in the figure. Show that it follows a helical path.
