(b) The potential energy $U(r)$ is nearly zero for large $r$, falls to a minimum (negative) near $r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm showing attraction, and rises very steeply for $r < r_0$ showing strong repulsion at short separations.

questions.question: A nucleus $^{23}{}_{10}Ne$ undergoes $\beta$-decay and becomes $^{23}{}_{11}Na$. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of electrons emitted assuming that the daughter nucleus and anti-neutrino carry negligible kinetic energy. Mass of $^{23}{}_{10}Ne = 22.994455 u$ Mass of $^{23}{}_{11}Na = 22.989770 u 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c^{2}$
questions.answer:
$Q = [M(^{23}_{10}Ne) - M(^{23}_{11}Na)]c^2$
$\Delta m = 22.994455 - 22.989770 = 0.004685$ u
$Q = 0.004685 \times 931.5 \approx 4.36$ MeV
Since the daughter nucleus and antineutrino carry negligible kinetic energy, this $Q$ value is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron, $\approx 4.36$ MeV.

questions.question: State the law of radioactive decay. If $N_{0}$ is the number of radioactive nuclei in the sample at some initial time $t_{0}$, find out the relation to determine the number $N$ present at a subsequent time. Draw a plot of $N$ as a function of time.
questions.answer:
Law of radioactive decay: the number of nuclei disintegrating per unit time is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present, $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N$, where $\lambda$ is the decay constant.
Integrating from $t_0$ (with $N = N_0$) to $t$ gives $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda(t-t_0)}$.
The plot of $N$ versus $t$ is an exponentially decreasing curve starting at $N_0$ and asymptotically approaching zero, never actually reaching zero.

questions.question: Draw a plot of the binding energy per nucleon as a function of mass number for a large number of nuclei. Explain the energy release in the process of nuclear fission from the above plot. Write a typical nuclear reaction in which a large amount of energy is released in the process of nuclear fission.
questions.answer:
The binding energy per nucleon curve rises sharply for small $A$, peaks near $A = 56$ ($\approx 8.7$ MeV/nucleon), and decreases gradually for heavier nuclei.
Since heavy nuclei (large $A$) have lower BE/nucleon than medium nuclei, splitting a heavy nucleus into two medium fragments increases the total binding energy, and this excess energy is released as the kinetic energy of fragments and neutrons.
A typical fission reaction: $^{1}_{0}n + {}^{235}_{92}U \rightarrow {}^{141}_{56}Ba + {}^{92}_{36}Kr + 3\,^{1}_{0}n + Q$, releasing about $200$ MeV per fission.

questions.question: Draw a plot of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation. What is the significance of negative potential energy in the graph drawn?
questions.answer:
The potential energy $U(r)$ of a pair of nucleons is zero for large separation, decreases sharply to a minimum negative value near $r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm, and rises very steeply to large positive values for $r < r_0$.
The negative potential energy in the range beyond $r_0$ signifies that the nuclear force is attractive in this region, which is what binds the nucleons together to form a stable nucleus.

questions.question: Draw a graph showing the variation of potential energy between a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation. Indicate the regions in which the nuclear force is (i) attractive, (ii) repulsive.
questions.answer:
The graph of potential energy $U(r)$ versus separation $r$ starts at zero for large $r$, falls to a minimum negative value at $r = r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm, and then rises steeply and becomes strongly positive for $r < r_0$.
For $r > r_0$: $U$ is negative, so the nuclear force is attractive.
For $r < r_0$: $U$ rises sharply and becomes positive, so the nuclear force is strongly repulsive, preventing the nucleons from collapsing into each other.

questions.question: Draw the graph showing the variation of binding energy per nucleon with mass number. Give the reason for the decrease of binding energy per nucleon for nuclei with high mass numbers.
questions.answer:
The binding energy per nucleon, $\frac{E_b}{A}$, rises sharply for low mass numbers, reaches a broad maximum of about $8.7$ MeV near $A = 56$ (iron region), and then decreases slowly for higher mass numbers, falling to about $7.6$ MeV for $A \approx 238$.
For heavy nuclei the number of protons is large, so the long-range Coulomb repulsion between them grows faster than the short-range attractive nuclear force, which reduces the net binding energy per nucleon as $A$ increases.

questions.question: Name the reaction which takes place when a slow neutron beam strikes $23592$ U nuclei. Write the nuclear reaction involved.
questions.answer:
This is nuclear fission.
$^{1}_{0}n + {}^{235}_{92}U \rightarrow {}^{236}_{92}U \rightarrow {}^{141}_{56}Ba + {}^{92}_{36}Kr + 3\,^{1}_{0}n + \text{energy}$

questions.question: In the series of radioactive disintegration of $23892$ U, first an alpha-particle and then a betaparticle is emitted. What is the atomic number and mass number of the new nucleus formed by these successive disintegrations?
questions.answer:
Alpha emission: $Z$ decreases by $2$, $A$ decreases by $4$, giving $^{234}_{90}Th$.
Beta emission from this nucleus: $Z$ increases by $1$, $A$ unchanged, giving the final nucleus with atomic number $91$ and mass number $234$ (i.e. $^{234}_{91}Pa$).

questions.question: (a) Consider the following nuclides: $126$ C, $19880$ Hg, $146$ C, $19779$ Au. Group them into isotopes and isotones. (b) How does the size of a nucleus depend on its mass number $A$? Hence prove that the density of nucleus is a constant, independent of $A$, for all nuclei.
questions.answer:
(a) $^{12}_{6}C$ and $^{14}_{6}C$ have the same $Z = 6$, so they are isotopes.
$^{198}_{80}Hg$ (neutrons $= 198-80=118$) and $^{197}_{79}Au$ (neutrons $=197-79=118$) have the same neutron number, so they are isotones.
(b) The nuclear radius varies as $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$, where $R_0 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-15}$ m.
So the nuclear volume $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A$, i.e. $V \propto A$.
Density $\rho = \frac{\text{mass}}{V} = \frac{Am_p}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \frac{m_p}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3}$, which is independent of $A$, showing that nuclear density is constant for all nuclei.

questions.question: Differentiate between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion. Give one example for each with nuclear reaction.
questions.answer:
Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei of comparable mass, usually initiated by bombardment with a slow neutron, releasing a large amount of energy.
Example: $^{1}_{0}n + {}^{235}_{92}U \rightarrow {}^{141}_{56}Ba + {}^{92}_{36}Kr + 3\,^{1}_{0}n$, releasing about $200$ MeV.
Nuclear fusion is the combining of two light nuclei to form a single heavier nucleus, which occurs only at extremely high temperature and pressure.
Example: $4\,^{1}_{1}H \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}He + 2e^{+} + 2\nu + \gamma$, releasing about $26$ MeV.

questions.question: Draw a plot showing the variation of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation $(r)$. Using this plot, show that the nuclear force is (i) attractive for $r > r_{0}$, and (ii) repulsive for $r < r_{0}$.
questions.answer:
The potential energy $U(r)$ of a pair of nucleons is zero at large $r$, decreases to a minimum negative value at $r = r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm, and then rises very steeply and becomes positive for $r < r_0$.
The nuclear force is related to potential energy by $F = -\dfrac{dU}{dr}$.
(i) For $r > r_0$: $U$ increases (becomes less negative) as $r$ increases, so $\dfrac{dU}{dr} > 0$, giving $F < 0$; the negative sign indicates the force acts to decrease $r$, i.e. it is attractive.
(ii) For $r < r_0$: $U$ increases very steeply as $r$ decreases, so $\dfrac{dU}{dr} < 0$, giving $F > 0$; the positive sign indicates the force acts to increase $r$, i.e. it is strongly repulsive.

questions.question: In the nuclear reaction: $^{2}{}_{1}H +^{2}{}_{1}H \rightarrow^{A}{}_{2} X +^{1}{}_{0}n$ (a) Find the value of A. (b) Calculate the amount of energy released in the reaction. Given: $m(^{2}{}_{1}H) = 2$ · $014102$ u, $m(^{A}{}_{2} X) = 3$ · $016049$ u, $m(^{1}{}_{0}n) = 1$ · $008665$ u, 1 u = 931·5 MeV/c $2$
questions.answer:
(a) By conservation of mass number: $2 + 2 = A + 1$, so $A = 3$. The product nucleus is $^{3}_{2}He$.
(b) Mass defect: $\Delta m = 2m(^{2}_{1}H) - [m(^{3}_{2}He) + m(^{1}_{0}n)]$
$\Delta m = 2(2.014102) - (3.016049 + 1.008665) = 4.028204 - 4.024714 = 0.003490$ u
Energy released $= \Delta m \times 931.5$ MeV $= 0.003490 \times 931.5 \approx 3.25$ MeV

questions.question: (a) Distinguish between isotopes and isobars, giving one example for each. (b) Derive the relation between atomic mass unit (u) and electron volt (eV).
questions.answer:
(a) Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same atomic number $Z$) having different mass numbers, e.g. $^{12}_{6}C$ and $^{14}_{6}C$.
Isobars are atoms of different elements having the same mass number $A$ but different atomic numbers, e.g. $^{40}_{18}Ar$ and $^{40}_{20}Ca$.
(b) By Einstein's mass-energy relation, $E = mc^2$.
For $m = 1$ u $= 1.660539 \times 10^{-27}$ kg and $c = 3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s,
$E = 1.660539 \times 10^{-27} \times (3 \times 10^{8})^2 = 1.494 \times 10^{-10}$ J
Converting to eV: $E = \dfrac{1.494 \times 10^{-10}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 9.33 \times 10^{8}$ eV $= 931.5$ MeV
Hence $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV/$c^2$.

questions.question: (a) (i) Write any two features of nuclear forces. (ii) If both the number of protons and the neutrons are conserved in each nuclear reaction, in what way is mass converted into energy (or vice versa) in a nuclear reaction? Explain.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Two features of nuclear forces:
Nuclear force is the strongest force in nature (about $100$ times the electromagnetic force) and is short-ranged, acting only up to about $2$-$3$ fm.
It is charge-independent, i.e. the force between $p$-$p$, $n$-$n$ and $p$-$n$ pairs is nearly the same.
(ii) Although the number of protons and neutrons is conserved, the binding energy per nucleon of the reactant nuclei differs from that of the product nuclei. Since binding energy $BE = \Delta m c^2$, this difference in binding energy corresponds to a difference in mass of the nuclei (mass defect), which appears as the energy released or absorbed, $Q = \Delta m c^2$.

questions.question: (a) Define ’Mass defect’ and ’Binding energy’ of a nucleus. Describe ’Fission process’ on the basis of binding energy per nucleon. (b) A deuteron contains a proton and a neutron and has a mass of $2.013553$ u. Calculate the mass defect for it in u and its energy equivalence in MeV. ($m_{p} = 1.007277$ u, $m_{n} = 1.008665$ u, $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV $/c^{2}$)
questions.answer:
(a) Mass defect $\Delta m = [Zm_p + (A-Z)m_n] - M$, the difference between the sum of masses of free nucleons and the actual nuclear mass.
Binding energy $BE = \Delta m c^2$, the energy required to separate a nucleus into its free nucleons.
Fission: heavy nuclei ($A \approx 240$) have lower $BE/A$ than medium nuclei ($A \approx 100$-$120$); on splitting, $BE/A$ increases, so the excess binding energy is released.
(b) $\Delta m = (m_p+m_n)-m_d = (1.007277+1.008665)-2.013553 = 0.002389$ u
$BE = \Delta m c^2 = 0.002389 \times 931.5 = 2.225$ MeV

questions.question: (a) Show the variation of binding energy per nucleon with mass number. Write the significance of the binding energy curve. (b) Two nuclei with lower binding energy per nucleon form a nuclei with more binding energy per nucleon. (i) What type of nuclear reaction is it? (ii) Whether the total mass of nuclei increases, decreases or remains unchanged? (iii) Does the process require energy or produce energy?
questions.answer:
(a) The $BE/A$ vs $A$ curve rises steeply for low $A$, peaks near $A = 56$ (iron) at about $8.7$-$8.8$ MeV/nucleon, then decreases slowly for heavier nuclei.
Significance: nuclei near the peak are most stable; heavy nuclei (left of peak region on the falling side) can undergo fission and light nuclei (rising part) can undergo fusion, both increasing $BE/A$ and releasing energy.
(b) (i) It is a nuclear fusion reaction.
(ii) The total mass decreases.
(iii) The process produces (releases) energy, since $Q = \Delta m c^2 > 0$.

questions.question: (a) Consider the so-called ’D-T reaction’ (Deuterium-Tritium reaction). In a thermonuclear fusion reactor, the following nuclear reaction occurs: $^{2}{}_{1}H +^{3}{}_{1}H -\rightarrow^{4}{}_{2}He +^{1}{}_{0}n + Q$ Find the amount of energy released in the reaction. Given: $m(^{2}{}_{1}H) = 2$· $014102$ u $m(^{3}{}_{1}H) = 3$· $016049$ u $m(^{4}{}_{2}He) = 4$· $002603$ u $m(^{1}{}_{0}n) = 1$· $008665$ u $1$ u $= 931$ MeV $/c^{2}$ OR (b) Show that the nuclear density is independent of mass number.
questions.answer:
(a) $\Delta m = [m(^2_1H)+m(^3_1H)] - [m(^4_2He)+m(^1_0n)]$
$\Delta m = (2.014102+3.016049)-(4.002603+1.008665) = 5.030151-5.011268 = 0.018883$ u
$Q = \Delta m c^2 = 0.018883 \times 931 = 17.58$ MeV
The reaction releases about $17.58$ MeV of energy.

OR

(b) Nuclear radius $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$, where $R_0 \approx 1.2$ fm.
Nuclear volume $V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A$
Mass of nucleus $\approx A m_N$ ($m_N$ = mass of one nucleon)
Density $\rho = \dfrac{Am_N}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{3m_N}{4\pi R_0^3}$, which is independent of $A$, so nuclear density is the same for all nuclei.

questions.question: Find the $Q$ value of the following nuclear reaction: $^{12}{}_{6} C +^{12}{}_{6} C -\rightarrow^{20}{}_{10}Ne +^{4}{}_{2}He$ Is this reaction exothermic or endothermic? Given: $m(^{12}{}_{6} C) = 12$· $000000$ u $m(^{20}{}_{10}Ne) = 19$· $992439$ u $m(^{4}{}_{2}He) = 4$· $002603$ u $1$ u $= 931$ MeV $/c^{2}$

(a) Differentiate between ’nuclear fission’ and ’nuclear fusion’. Briefly discuss one example of each. (b) Draw a graph of potential energy between a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation.
questions.answer:
(a) Fission: a heavy nucleus splits into two medium-mass nuclei with release of energy, e.g. $^{235}_{92}U + n \rightarrow \, ^{141}_{56}Ba + \,^{92}_{36}Kr + 3n +$ energy, used in nuclear reactors.
Fusion: two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus with release of energy, e.g. $^2_1H + \,^2_1H \rightarrow \,^3_2He + n +$ energy, requiring very high temperature ($\sim 10^7$ K) as in the Sun.
Fission occurs at ordinary temperatures and is easier to control; fusion needs extremely high temperature/pressure and releases more energy per unit mass.
(b) The graph of PE vs separation $r$ shows $U \approx 0$ for large $r$, becomes negative (attractive) with a minimum near $r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm, then rises sharply positive (repulsive) for $r < r_0$.

questions.question: Briefly explain how energy is produced in stars, giving two examples of the nuclear reactions involved.
questions.answer:
Energy in stars is produced by nuclear fusion, in which light nuclei combine to form heavier nuclei with release of energy, since the binding energy per nucleon of the product is greater than that of the reactants.
In Sun-like stars, the proton-proton cycle operates:
$^1_1H + \,^1_1H \rightarrow \,^2_1H + e^+ + \nu$
$^2_1H + \,^1_1H \rightarrow \,^3_2He + \gamma$
$^3_2He + \,^3_2He \rightarrow \,^4_2He + 2\,^1_1H$
The net effect is four protons fusing into a helium nucleus, releasing about $26.7$ MeV. In heavier stars, the carbon-nitrogen (CNO) cycle achieves the same net fusion using carbon as a catalyst.

questions.question: (a) State any two properties of a nucleus. (b) Why is the density of a nucleus much more than that of an atom? (c) Show that the density of the nuclear matter is the same for all nuclei.
questions.answer:
(a) Nuclear radius follows $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$ (with $R_0 \approx 1.2$ fm), and nuclear density is nearly constant ($\approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}$ kg/m$^3$) for all nuclei, independent of mass number.
(b) The entire mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus, whose radius ($\sim 10^{-15}$ m) is about $10^5$ times smaller than the atomic radius ($\sim 10^{-10}$ m), giving a volume about $10^{15}$ times smaller; hence nuclear density is far greater than atomic density.
(c) Volume $V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A$ and mass $\approx A m_N$, so density $\rho = \dfrac{Am_N}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{3m_N}{4\pi R_0^3}$, which is independent of $A$ and hence the same for all nuclei.

questions.question: (a) Write two characteristic properties of nuclear force. (b) Draw a plot of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation. Write two important conclusions that can be drawn from the plot.
questions.answer:
(a) Nuclear force is the strongest known force, about $100$ times the electromagnetic force, and is short-ranged, effective only up to $2$-$3$ fm.
It is charge-independent, being the same for $p$-$p$, $n$-$n$ and $p$-$n$ pairs.
(b) The PE vs separation $r$ graph shows $U \approx 0$ for large $r$, a negative minimum near $r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm, and a sharp positive rise for $r < r_0$.
Conclusions: (1) the force is attractive for $r > r_0$ and strongly repulsive for $r < r_0$, preventing nucleon collapse; (2) $U \rightarrow 0$ beyond about $3$ fm, confirming the short range of the nuclear force.

questions.question: (a) Plot a graph depicting potential energy of a pair of nucleons in a nucleus as a function of their separation. (b) Identify the regions where the nuclear force is (i) attractive, and (ii) repulsive. Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
(a) The plot of PE, $U$, between a pair of nucleons versus their separation $r$ shows $U \approx 0$ for large $r$, decreasing to a negative minimum near $r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm, then rising steeply to large positive values for $r < r_0$.
(b) (i) Attractive region: for $r$ between about $0.8$ fm and $3$ fm, $U$ is negative and decreasing with $r$, so $F = -\dfrac{dU}{dr}$ is negative (directed to pull nucleons together), i.e. attractive.
(ii) Repulsive region: for $r < r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm, $U$ rises sharply with decreasing $r$, so $F = -\dfrac{dU}{dr}$ is positive (directed to push nucleons apart), i.e. strongly repulsive, preventing the nucleons from collapsing.

questions.question: (a) Briefly discuss three characteristics of the forces between nucleons. (b) Which out of $^{168} O$ and $^{147} N$ nuclei is more stable and why?
questions.answer:
(a) Three characteristics of nuclear force:
(i) It is short-range, effective only up to about $2$-$3$ fm and negligible beyond that.
(ii) It is charge-independent — the force between $p$-$p$, $n$-$n$ and $n$-$p$ is approximately the same.
(iii) It is the strongest force in nature and shows saturation, i.e. a nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours, not all nucleons.
(b) $^{16}_{8}O$ (magic number, both $Z=8$ and $N=8$) has binding energy per nucleon $\approx 7.97$ MeV, greater than that of $^{14}_{7}N$ ($\approx 7.48$ MeV).
Hence $^{16}_{8}O$ is more stable.

questions.question: (a) Define atomic mass unit (u). (b) Calculate the energy required to separate a deuteron into its constituent parts (a proton and a neutron). Given: $m(D) = 2.014102$ u; $m_{p} = 1.007825$ u; $m_{n} = 1.008665$ u.
questions.answer:
(a) One atomic mass unit is defined as $1/12$th the mass of one atom of the carbon-12 isotope: $1u = 1.660539 \times 10^{-27}$ kg.
(b) Mass defect $\Delta m = m_p + m_n - m(D) = 1.007825 + 1.008665 - 2.014102 = 0.002388$ u
Binding (separation) energy $= \Delta m \times 931$ MeV/u $= 0.002388 \times 931 \approx 2.22$ MeV.
This is the energy needed to separate the deuteron into a free proton and neutron.

questions.question: (a) Differentiate between nuclear fission and fusion. (b) The fission properties of $23994$ Pu are very similar to those of $23592$ U. How much energy (in MeV), is released if all the atoms in $1$ g of pure $23994$ Pu undergo fission? The average energy released per fission is $180$ MeV.
questions.answer:
(a) Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter fragments (with release of neutrons and energy), while nuclear fusion is the combining of two light nuclei into a heavier nucleus with release of energy.
Fission can occur at ordinary temperatures on neutron bombardment; fusion requires extremely high temperature and pressure to overcome Coulomb repulsion.
(b) Number of atoms in $1$ g: $N = \frac{1}{239} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 2.52 \times 10^{21}$
Total energy $= N \times 180$ MeV $= 2.52 \times 10^{21} \times 180 \approx 4.53 \times 10^{23}$ MeV.

questions.question: Draw a diagram to show the variation of binding energy per nucleon with mass number for different nuclei and mention its two features. Why do lighter nuclei usually undergo nuclear fusion?
questions.answer:
The graph of binding energy per nucleon ($BE/A$) versus mass number $A$ rises steeply for low $A$, reaches a maximum of about $8.7$ MeV near $A = 56$ (iron), and then decreases slowly for heavier nuclei.
Two features: (i) $BE/A$ is low for both very light and very heavy nuclei, being maximum for medium mass nuclei. (ii) The curve is fairly flat (nearly constant $\approx 8.5$ MeV) for $30 < A < 170$.
Lighter nuclei undergo fusion because combining them increases the binding energy per nucleon (moving up the curve towards the peak), so mass is converted to energy which is released.

questions.question: (i) Distinguish between nuclear fission and fusion giving an example of each. (ii) Explain the release of energy in nuclear fission and fusion on the basis of binding energy per nucleon curve.
questions.answer:
(i) Fission: a heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei of comparable mass with release of energy, e.g. $^{235}_{92}U + n \rightarrow ^{141}_{56}Ba + ^{92}_{36}Kr + 3n$.
Fusion: two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus with release of energy, e.g. $^{2}_{1}H + ^{2}_{1}H \rightarrow ^{3}_{2}He + n$.
(ii) The $BE/A$ vs $A$ curve rises from light nuclei to a peak near $A = 56$ and then falls for heavy nuclei.
In fission, a heavy nucleus (lower $BE/A$) splits into fragments closer to the peak (higher $BE/A$); in fusion, light nuclei (lower $BE/A$) combine to give a nucleus closer to the peak (higher $BE/A$).
In both cases $BE/A$ increases, so mass is converted into energy that is released.

questions.question: (i) How is the size of a nucleus found experimentally? Write the relation between the radius and mass number of a nucleus. (ii) Prove that the density of a nucleus is independent of its mass number.
questions.answer:
(i) The size of a nucleus is found experimentally from high-energy electron scattering or $\alpha$-particle (Rutherford) scattering experiments, using the distance of closest approach or diffraction pattern to estimate the nuclear radius.
The relation is $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$, where $R_0 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-15}$ m is a constant.
(ii) Nuclear density $\rho = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} = \dfrac{A m_u}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3} = \dfrac{A m_u}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{3m_u}{4\pi R_0^3}$
Since $A$ cancels out, $\rho$ depends only on constants $m_u$ and $R_0$, so it is the same for all nuclei, independent of mass number.

questions.question: (a) (i) Prove that the nuclear density is same for all nuclei. (ii) Draw a plot of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation. Draw two inferences from this plot. OR (b) (i) Draw a graph to show the variation of the number of scattered particles detected ($N$) in Geiger-Marsden experiment as a function of scattering angle ($\theta$). (ii) Discuss briefly two conclusions that can be drawn from this graph and how they lead to the discovery of nucleus in an atom.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Nuclear density $\rho = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} = \dfrac{A m_u}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}$, and using $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$, this gives $\rho = \dfrac{A m_u}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{3m_u}{4\pi R_0^3}$
Since $A$ cancels, $\rho$ is independent of $A$, so it is the same for all nuclei.
(ii) The plot of potential energy $U$ versus separation $r$ shows a minimum (negative $U$) at $r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm, rising steeply to positive values for $r < r_0$, and approaching zero for $r$ beyond a few fm.
Inferences: the nuclear force is attractive for $r > r_0$ and strongly repulsive for $r < r_0$; the force has a very short range, becoming negligible beyond a few fm.

questions.question: Draw a plot showing the variation of potential energy of two nucleons as a function of distance between them. Identify the regions in which the force between the nucleons is (i) attractive, and (ii) repulsive. Justify your answers.
questions.answer:
The potential energy $U$ of a pair of nucleons plotted against their separation $r$ shows a deep minimum at $r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm, rises sharply as $r$ decreases further, and gradually approaches zero as $r$ increases beyond a few fm.
(i) For $r > r_0$ (up to about $2$-$3$ fm), $U$ increases with decreasing $r$ (slope negative, force $F = -dU/dr$ positive/attractive), so the force is attractive.
(ii) For $r < r_0$, $U$ rises very steeply as $r$ decreases (force pushes nucleons apart), so the force is strongly repulsive, preventing the nucleons from collapsing into each other.
Beyond a few fm, $U \to 0$, showing the force is short-ranged.

questions.question: (a) Calculate the binding energy of an alpha particle in MeV. Given mass of a proton $= 1.007825 u$ mass of a neutron $= 1.008665 u$ mass of He nucleus $= 4.002800 u 1u = 931$ MeV $/c^{2}$ OR (b) A heavy nucleus P of mass number 240 and binding energy 7.6 MeV per nucleon splits into two nuclei Q and R of mass number 110 and 130 and binding energy per nucleon 8.5 MeV and 8.4 MeV respectively. Calculate the energy released in the fission.

Calculate the energy released in MeV in the following reaction: $21$ H $+^{3}{}_{1}$ H $\rightarrow^{4}{}_{2}$ He $+ n$ Given: $m(^{2}{}_{1}$ H $) = 2.014102$ u $m(^{3}{}_{1}$ H $) = 3.016049$ u $m(^{4}{}_{2}$ He $) = 4.002603$ u $m_{n} = 1.008665$ u
questions.answer:
Mass of reactants $= m(^2_1H) + m(^3_1H) = 2.014102 + 3.016049 = 5.030151$ u
Mass of products $= m(^4_2He) + m_n = 4.002603 + 1.008665 = 5.011268$ u
Mass defect $\Delta m = 5.030151 - 5.011268 = 0.018883$ u
Energy released $= \Delta m \times 931.5$ MeV $= 0.018883 \times 931.5 \approx 17.59$ MeV.

questions.question: (i) Depict the variation of the potential energy of a pair of nucleons with the separation between them. (ii) Imagine the fission of a $5626$ Fe into two equal fragments of $2813$ Al nucleus. Is the fission energetically possible? Justify your answer by working out $Q$ value of the process. Given: $m(^{56}{}_{26}$ Fe $) = 55.93494$ u, $m(^{28}{}_{13}$ Al $) = 27.98191$ u.
questions.answer:
(i) As the separation $r$ between two nucleons decreases from large values, the potential energy first becomes negative (attractive), reaching a minimum of about $-40$ MeV near $r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm; for $r < r_0$ it rises very steeply to large positive values (strong repulsion), while for $r$ beyond a few fm the PE tends to zero, showing the short range of the nuclear force.
(ii) $Q = [m(^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}) - 2m(^{28}_{13}\text{Al})]c^2$
$Q = [55.93494 - 2(27.98191)] \times 931.5$ MeV
$Q = (55.93494 - 55.96382) \times 931.5 = -0.02888 \times 931.5$
$Q \approx -26.9$ MeV
Since $Q$ is negative, energy must be supplied rather than released, so this fission is not energetically possible.

questions.question: (a) James Chadwick, in 1932, studied the emission of neutral radiations when Beryllium nuclei were bombarded with alpha particles. He concluded that emitted radiations were neutrons and not photons. Explain. (b) Two nuclei may have the same radius, even though they contain different number of protons and neutrons. Explain.
questions.answer:
(a) When Be nuclei were bombarded with $\alpha$-particles, the emitted neutral radiation ejected protons from paraffin with kinetic energies as high as $5.7$ MeV.
If this radiation were $\gamma$-photons, applying energy-momentum conservation (Compton-type collision with a proton) would require the photon energy to be about $55$ MeV, far exceeding the energy available in the Be$+\alpha$ reaction.
Treating the radiation instead as neutral particles of mass nearly equal to the proton (neutrons) undergoing elastic collisions correctly explained the observed proton recoil energies, so Chadwick concluded the radiation was neutrons, not photons.
(b) Nuclear radius $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$ depends only on the mass number $A$, not separately on the number of protons or neutrons, so two isobaric nuclei (same $A$, different $Z$ and $N$) can have the same radius.

questions.question: (a) Differentiate between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion. (b) Deuterium undergoes fusion as per the reaction: $^{2}{}_{1}H +^{2}{}_{1}H \rightarrow^{3}{}_{2}He +^{1}{}_{0}n + 3.27 MeV$. Find the duration for which an electric bulb of 500 W can be kept glowing by the fusion of 100 g of deuterium.
questions.answer:
(a) Fission: a heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei of comparable mass, usually initiated by slow neutron capture, releasing about $200$ MeV per event; used in reactors/bombs and produces radioactive waste.
Fusion: two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, requiring extremely high temperature/pressure to overcome Coulomb repulsion; releases more energy per unit mass and produces little radioactive waste.
(b) Number of deuterium nuclei, $N = \frac{100}{2} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.011 \times 10^{25}$
Each reaction uses $2$ deuterons, so number of reactions $= 1.5055 \times 10^{25}$
Energy released $= 1.5055 \times 10^{25} \times 3.27 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13}$ J $= 7.88 \times 10^{12}$ J
Time $= \frac{7.88 \times 10^{12}}{500} = 1.575 \times 10^{10}$ s $\approx 500$ years

questions.question: In a fission event of $23892$ U by fast moving neutrons, no neutrons are emitted and final products, after the beta decay of the primary fragments, are $14058$ Ce and $9944$ Ru. Calculate $Q$ for this process. Neglect the masses of electrons/positrons emitted during the intermediate steps. Given: $m (^{238}{}_{92}$ U $) = 238.05079$ u; $m (^{140}{}_{58}$ Ce $) = 139.90543$ u; $m (^{99}{}_{44}$ Ru $) = 98.90594$ u; $m (^{1}{}_{0}$ n $) = 1.008665$ u.

The nucleus $23592$ U initially at rest, decays into $23190$ X by emitting an $\alpha$-particle $23592$ U $-\rightarrow 23190$ X $+^{4}{}_{2}$ He $+$ energy. The binding energies per nucleon of the parent nucleus, the daughter nucleus and $\alpha$-particle are $7$· $8$ MeV, $7$· $835$ MeV and $7$· $07$ MeV, respectively. Assuming the daughter nucleus to be formed in the unexcited state and neglecting its share in the energy of the reaction, find the speed of the emitted $\alpha$-particle. (Mass of $\alpha$-particle $= 6$· $68 \times 10^{-27}$ kg)
questions.answer:
Total BE of $^{235}_{92}$U $= 235 \times 7.8 = 1833$ MeV
Total BE of $^{231}_{90}$X $= 231 \times 7.835 = 1809.9$ MeV
Total BE of $\alpha$-particle $= 4 \times 7.07 = 28.28$ MeV
$Q = \text{BE(daughter)} + \text{BE}(\alpha) - \text{BE(parent)} = 1809.9 + 28.28 - 1833 = 5.165$ MeV
Neglecting the daughter's share, this energy appears entirely as KE of the $\alpha$-particle:
$\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 5.165 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13}$ J $= 8.264 \times 10^{-13}$ J
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 8.264 \times 10^{-13}}{6.68 \times 10^{-27}}} \approx 1.57 \times 10^{7}$ m/s

questions.question: (a) Differentiate between half-life and average life of a radioactive substance. (b) A radioactive substance decays for an interval of time equal to its mean life. Find the fraction of the amount of the substance which is left undecayed after this time interval.
questions.answer:
(a) Half-life $T_{1/2}$ is the time in which half the initial number of radioactive nuclei decay, $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$.
Average (mean) life $\tau$ is the average time for which a nucleus exists before decaying, $\tau = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{T_{1/2}}{\ln 2} \approx 1.44\, T_{1/2}$, so mean life is always greater than half-life.
(b) After $t = \tau = 1/\lambda$: $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda \tau} = N_0 e^{-1}$
Fraction undecayed $= \dfrac{N}{N_0} = \dfrac{1}{e} \approx 0.368$, i.e. about $36.8\%$ remains.

questions.question: (a) The density of the nuclear matter is tremendously larger than the physical density of the material. Explain. (b) The nuclear forces are not coulomb forces between nucleons. Explain. (c) Draw a plot of the potential energy between a pair of nucleons as a function of distance between them inside a nucleus.
questions.answer:
(a) Nuclear density $\rho = \dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3}$, independent of $A$ since $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$; it is enormous ($\sim 2.3 \times 10^{17}$ kg/m$^3$) because nearly the entire mass of the atom is concentrated in the tiny nuclear volume ($\sim$ fm scale), while the atom itself is mostly empty space occupied by electrons.
(b) Nuclear force is short-range ($\sim 2$–$3$ fm) and charge-independent, acting equally between $p$-$p$, $n$-$n$ and $p$-$n$ pairs, and is attractive and much stronger than the Coulomb force at nuclear separations; Coulomb force is long-range, acts only between charges, and is repulsive between protons — hence the two forces are fundamentally different.
(c) The PE vs. $r$ curve is strongly negative with a minimum around $r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm, rises steeply to large positive values for $r < r_0$, and falls to nearly zero for $r$ greater than a few fm.

questions.question: (a) Define the term decay constant of a radioactive substance. (b) The half life of $^{238}U$ undergoing $\alpha$ decay is $4.5 \times 10^{9}$ years. Calculate the activity of $10 ^{92}$ g sample of $^{23892} U$.
questions.answer:
(a) Decay constant $\lambda$ is the probability of decay per unit time of a nucleus, defined by $\lambda = -\dfrac{1}{N}\dfrac{dN}{dt}$; it is characteristic of the radioactive species.
(b) $T_{1/2} = 4.5 \times 10^{9}$ yr $= 1.42 \times 10^{17}$ s, so $\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{1.42 \times 10^{17}} = 4.88 \times 10^{-18}$ s$^{-1}$
$N = \dfrac{10}{238} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 2.53 \times 10^{22}$ atoms
Activity $A = \lambda N = 4.88 \times 10^{-18} \times 2.53 \times 10^{22} \approx 1.23 \times 10^{5}$ decays/s

questions.question: Draw the curve showing the variation of binding energy per nucleon with the mass number of nuclei. Using it explain the fusion of nuclei lying on ascending part and fission of nuclei lying on descending part of this curve.
questions.answer:
The curve of binding energy per nucleon ($BE/A$) versus mass number $A$ rises steeply for light nuclei, reaches a broad maximum of about $8.7$–$8.8$ MeV near $A = 56$ (iron region), and then decreases slowly for heavier nuclei.
On the ascending (low-$A$) part, light nuclei have low $BE/A$; when they fuse to form a nucleus closer to the peak, the $BE/A$ increases, so energy is released — this is nuclear fusion.
On the descending (high-$A$) part, heavy nuclei have lower $BE/A$ than medium-mass nuclei; when such a heavy nucleus splits into two fragments nearer the peak, the total $BE/A$ increases and energy is released — this is nuclear fission.
In both processes, mass is converted to energy because the products are more tightly bound than the reactants.

questions.question: Define the term ’decay constant’ of a radioactive sample. The rate of disintegration of a given radioactive nucleus is $10000$ disintegrations/s and $5000$ disintegrations/s after $20$ hr and $30$ hr respectively from start. Calculate the half life and initial number of nuclei at $t = 0$.
questions.answer:
Decay constant $\lambda$ is the fraction of the total number of nuclei that decay per unit time, $\lambda = -\dfrac{1}{N}\dfrac{dN}{dt}$.
Since $R = R_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, $\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = e^{\lambda(t_2 - t_1)}$
$\dfrac{10000}{5000} = 2 = e^{\lambda \times 10}$ (hr), so $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{10} = 0.0693$ hr$^{-1}$
Half-life $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = 10$ hr
$R_0 = R_1 e^{\lambda \times 20} = 10000 \times 4 = 40000$ dis/s
$\lambda = 1.925 \times 10^{-5}$ s$^{-1}$, so $N_0 = \dfrac{R_0}{\lambda} = \dfrac{40000}{1.925 \times 10^{-5}} \approx 2.08 \times 10^{9}$ nuclei

questions.question: Write the relation between half life and average life of a radioactive nucleus.
questions.answer:
The decay constant $\lambda$ is the probability of decay per unit time of a nucleus.
Half life is defined by $N_0/2 = N_0 e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}}$, giving $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$.
Average (mean) life is $\tau = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$.
Dividing the two expressions, $T_{1/2} = 0.693\,\tau$, so the half life is $0.693$ times the mean life, or equivalently $\tau = 1.44\,T_{1/2}$.

questions.question: In a given sample two isotopes $A$ and $B$ are initially present in the ratio of $1: 2$. Their half lives are $60$ years and $30$ years respectively. How long will it take so that the sample has these isotopes in the ratio of $2: 1$?
Show that density of nucleus is independent of its mass number $A$.
questions.answer:
Nuclear radius: $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$, where $R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15}$ m.
Nuclear volume: $V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A$.
Nuclear mass $\approx A m_p$ (each nucleon has mass $\approx m_p$).
Density $\rho = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} = \dfrac{A m_p}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{m_p}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3}$.
Since $A$ cancels out, $\rho$ is a constant, independent of mass number $A$, and comes out to be about $2.3 \times 10^{17}$ kg/m$^3$ for all nuclei.

questions.question: Why is it difficult to detect the presence of an anti-neutrino during $\beta$-decay? Define the term decay constant of a radioactive nucleus and derive the expression for its mean life in terms of the decay constant. OR (a) State two distinguishing features of nuclear force. (b) Draw a plot showing the variation of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation. Mark the regions on the graph where the force is (i) attractive, and (ii) repulsive.
questions.answer:
An antineutrino has no charge and negligible (nearly zero) rest mass, so it does not ionise matter and interacts extremely weakly with matter (very small interaction cross-section).
It can pass through large thicknesses of matter, even the entire Earth, without interacting, making its direct detection extremely difficult; it is inferred only from momentum and energy conservation in $\beta$-decay.
Decay constant $\lambda$ is the reciprocal of the time in which the number of undecayed nuclei reduces to $1/e$ of its initial value, i.e., the probability of decay per unit time of a nucleus.
For $N_0$ nuclei at $t=0$, number decaying between $t$ and $t+dt$ is $dN = \lambda N_0 e^{-\lambda t}\,dt$.
Mean life $\tau = \dfrac{1}{N_0}\int_0^{\infty} t\,\lambda N_0 e^{-\lambda t}\,dt = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$.

questions.question: Draw a graph showing the variation of binding energy per nucleon with mass number of different nuclei. Write any two salient features of the curve. How does this curve explain the release of energy both in the processes of nuclear fission and fusion?
questions.answer:
The graph of binding energy per nucleon ($BE/A$) versus mass number $A$ rises sharply for light nuclei, reaches a broad maximum of about $8.7$ MeV near $A = 56$ (iron region), and then decreases slowly for heavy nuclei.
Salient features: (i) $BE/A$ is low for both very light and very heavy nuclei, and maximum for medium mass nuclei ($A \approx 30$ to $120$); (ii) beyond $A \approx 120$, $BE/A$ decreases gradually, showing heavy nuclei are less tightly bound.
In fission, a heavy nucleus (low $BE/A$) splits into two medium nuclei of higher $BE/A$; in fusion, light nuclei (low $BE/A$) combine into a heavier nucleus of higher $BE/A$. In both cases the final $BE/A$ is greater, so energy is released.

questions.question: (a) Plot a graph showing the variation of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation. Also indicate the regions where the force is (i) attractive and (ii) repulsive. (b) Write two characteristic properties of nuclear force.
questions.answer:
(a) The potential energy of a pair of nucleons is plotted against their separation $r$. It is large and positive (repulsive) for $r$ less than about $0.8$ fm, falls steeply and becomes negative, reaching a minimum (equilibrium, most attractive) near $r_0 \approx 0.8$ fm, then rises asymptotically to zero for large $r$ (a few fm), beyond which the force is negligible.
Region of attraction: from the minimum outward to a few fm; region of repulsion: separations less than about $0.8$ fm.
(b) Two characteristic properties of nuclear force: (i) it is a short-range force, effective only up to about $2$–$3$ fm and negligible beyond; (ii) it is charge-independent, i.e., the $n$–$n$, $p$–$p$ and $n$–$p$ forces are approximately equal, and it is much stronger than the electrostatic or gravitational force.

questions.question: Plot a graph showing the variation of number of undecayed nuclei in a radioisotope as a function of time. Hence define half life of a nucleus and obtain its relation with average life.
questions.answer:
The graph of number of undecayed nuclei $N$ versus time $t$ is an exponential decay curve, $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, starting at $N_0$ and asymptotically approaching zero as $t \to \infty$, never actually reaching zero.
Half life $T_{1/2}$ is the time in which the number of undecayed nuclei reduces to half of its initial value, i.e., $N_0/2 = N_0 e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}}$, giving $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$.
Since mean life $\tau = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$, we get $T_{1/2} = 0.693\,\tau$.

questions.question: (a) Distinguish between isotopes and isobars, giving one example for each. (b) Why is the mass of a nucleus always less than the sum of the masses of its constituents? Write one example to justify your answer. OR (a) Classify the following six nuclides into (i) isotones, (ii) isotopes, and (iii) isobars: $^{126} C$, $^{3}{}_{2}He$, $^{19880} Hg$, $^{3}{}_{1}H$, $^{19779} Au$, $^{146} C$. (b) How does the size of a nucleus depend on its mass number? Hence explain why the density of nuclear matter should be independent of the size of the nucleus.
questions.answer:
(a) Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number $Z$ but different mass number $A$, e.g., $^{1}_{1}H$ and $^{2}_{1}H$.
Isobars are atoms of different elements having the same mass number $A$ but different atomic number $Z$, e.g., $^{3}_{1}H$ and $^{3}_{2}He$.
(b) The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of masses of its constituent nucleons because some mass is converted into binding energy (mass defect $\Delta m$) released when the nucleons combine, as per $E = \Delta m\, c^2$.
Example: mass of a deuteron ($m_p + m_n \approx 2.0165$ u) is less than the sum $m_p + m_n$, the difference $\Delta m \approx 0.0024$ u accounting for its binding energy of about $2.2$ MeV.

questions.question: (a) Explain the processes of nuclear fission and nuclear fusion by using the plot of binding energy per nucleon $(BE/A)$ versus the mass number $A$. (b) A radioactive isotope has a half-life of $10$ years. How long will it take for the activity to reduce to $3.125\%$? $-$
questions.answer:
(a) In nuclear fission, a heavy nucleus (low $BE/A$, near $A \approx 240$) splits into two medium mass nuclei with higher $BE/A$ (near $A \approx 56$–$120$); since the products are more tightly bound, the difference in binding energy is released as energy.
In nuclear fusion, two light nuclei (low $BE/A$, small $A$) combine to form a heavier nucleus with higher $BE/A$; again the increase in binding energy per nucleon appears as released energy.
(b) $3.125\% = \dfrac{1}{32} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^5$, so number of half lives $n = 5$.
Time taken $t = n \times T_{1/2} = 5 \times 10 = 50$ years.

questions.question: (i) A radioactive nucleus ’A’ undergoes a series of decays as given below: $A-\rightarrow^{\alpha}A_{1}-\rightarrow^{\beta} A_{2}-\rightarrow^{\alpha}A_{3}-\rightarrow^{\gamma}A_{4}$ The mass number and atomic number of $A_{2}$ are 176 and 71 respectively. Determine the mass and atomic numbers of $A_{4}$ and $A$. (ii) Write the basic nuclear processes underlying $\beta^{+}$ and $\beta^{-}$ decays.
questions.answer:
(i) Beta decay increases atomic number by 1 (mass unchanged); alpha decay decreases mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2; gamma decay changes neither.
Given $A_2$: mass $=176$, atomic number $=71$.
$A_1 \xrightarrow{\beta} A_2$: so $A_1$ has mass $=176$, atomic number $=70$.
$A \xrightarrow{\alpha} A_1$: so $A$ has mass $=176+4=180$, atomic number $=70+2=72$.
$A_2 \xrightarrow{\alpha} A_3$: so $A_3$ has mass $=176-4=172$, atomic number $=71-2=69$.
$A_3 \xrightarrow{\gamma} A_4$: mass and atomic number unchanged, so $A_4$: mass $=172$, atomic number $=69$.
Thus $A$: mass number $180$, atomic number $72$; $A_4$: mass number $172$, atomic number $69$.
(ii) $\beta^-$ decay: $n \rightarrow p + e^- + \bar{\nu}$ (a neutron converts to a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino).
$\beta^+$ decay: $p \rightarrow n + e^+ + \nu$ (a proton converts to a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino).

questions.question: (a) State the law of radioactive decay. Write the SI unit of ’activity’. (b) There are $4\sqrt{2} \times 10^{6}$ radioactive nuclei in a given radioactive sample. If the half life of the sample is $20$ s, how many nuclei will decay in $10$ s?
questions.answer:
(a) The law of radioactive decay states that the number of nuclei disintegrating per unit time is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present, i.e. $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N$, giving $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$.
The SI unit of activity is the becquerel ($Bq$), equal to one disintegration per second.
(b) $N(t) = N_0 (1/2)^{t/T}$
$N(10) = 4\sqrt{2}\times10^{6}\times(1/2)^{10/20} = 4\sqrt{2}\times10^{6}/\sqrt{2} = 4\times10^{6}$
Nuclei decayed $= 4\sqrt{2}\times10^{6} - 4\times10^{6} = 4\times10^{6}(\sqrt{2}-1) \approx 1.66\times10^{6}$

questions.question: (a) Write the process of $\beta$-decay. How can radioactive nuclei emit $\beta$-particles even though they do not contain them? Why do all electrons emitted during $\beta$-decay not have the same energy? (b) A heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei. Which one of the two – parent nucleus or the daughter nuclei has more binding energy per nucleon?
questions.answer:
(a) In $\beta^{-}$-decay, a neutron inside the nucleus transforms as $n \rightarrow p + e^{-} + \bar{\nu}$; the electron is created at the instant of decay, not pre-existing in the nucleus, so nuclei can emit $\beta$-particles without containing them.
The energy released in each decay is shared randomly between the electron and the antineutrino, so the electrons carry a continuous range of energies rather than a fixed value.
(b) The daughter nuclei formed after fission have greater binding energy per nucleon than the parent nucleus, since this increase is the source of the energy released.

questions.question: (a) Derive the relation between the decay constant and half life of a radioactive substance. (b) A radioactive element reduces to $25\%$ of its initial mass in $1000$ years. Find its half life.
questions.answer:
(a) Number of undecayed nuclei $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$.
At $t = T$ (half life), $N = N_0/2$, so $N_0/2 = N_0 e^{-\lambda T}$, giving $e^{\lambda T} = 2$.
Taking log: $\lambda T = \ln 2$, so $T = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$.
(b) $N/N_0 = 0.25 = (1/2)^2$, so $1000$ years $= 2T$.
$T = 500$ years.

questions.question: (a) Write the basic nuclear process involved in the emission of $\beta^{+}$ in a symbolic form, by a radioactive nucleus. (b) In the reactions given below: (i) $116$ C $\rightarrow^{y}{}_{z}$ B $+ x + \nu$ (ii) $126$ C $+^{12}{}_{6}$ C $\rightarrow^{20}{}_{a}$ Ne $+^{b}{}_{c}$ He Find the values of $x$, $y$, and $z$ and $a$, $b$ and $c$.
questions.answer:
(a) $ eta^{+}$ decay arises from the basic process $p ightarrow n + e^{+} + 
u$ occurring inside the nucleus.
(b) (i) $^{11}_{6}C ightarrow\ ^{y}_{z}B + x + 
u$: charge and mass number conservation give $z = 5$, $y = 11$, and $x = e^{+}$ (positron), i.e. $^{11}_{6}C ightarrow\ ^{11}_{5}B + e^{+} + 
u$.
(ii) $^{12}_{6}C + ^{12}_{6}C ightarrow\ ^{20}_{a}Ne + ^{b}_{c}He$: mass number balance ($24 = 20+b$) gives $b = 4$, charge balance ($12 = a+c$) with $a=10$ gives $c = 2$, so it is an $\alpha$-particle, $^{4}_{2}He$.

questions.question: Half life of $^{238}U$ against $\alpha$-decay is $4.5 \times 10^{9}$ years. Calculate the activity of $1$ g sample of $^{92}{}^{238}U$. Given Avogadro’s number $= 6 \times 10^{26}$ atoms/kmol. $^{92}$
questions.answer:
Number of atoms in $1$ g of $^{238}U$:
$N = \dfrac{1\times10^{-3}}{238}\times6\times10^{26} = 2.52\times10^{21}$ atoms
Decay constant: $\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{4.5\times10^{9}\times3.156\times10^{7}\ \text{s}} = 4.88\times10^{-18}\ \text{s}^{-1}$
Activity: $A = \lambda N = 4.88\times10^{-18}\times2.52\times10^{21} \approx 1.23\times10^{4}\ \text{Bq}$

questions.question: (a) Derive the mathematical expression for law of radioactive decay for a sample of a radioactive nucleus. (b) How is the mean life of a given radioactive nucleus related to the decay constant?
questions.answer:
(a) Let $N$ be the number of undecayed nuclei at time $t$. The rate of decay is proportional to $N$: $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N$, where $\lambda$ is the decay constant.
Separating variables and integrating from $N_0$ at $t=0$ to $N$ at $t$: $\int_{N_0}^{N}\dfrac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\int_0^t dt$, giving $\ln(N/N_0) = -\lambda t$.
Hence $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$.
(b) Mean life is the reciprocal of the decay constant: $\tau = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$.

questions.question: Plot a graph showing the variation of binding energy per nucleon as a function of mass number. Which property of nuclear force explains the approximate constancy of binding energy in the range $30 < A < 170$? How does one explain the release of energy in both the processes of nuclear fission and fusion from the graph?
questions.answer:
The graph of binding energy per nucleon versus mass number $A$ rises steeply for small $A$, peaks around $A = 56$ (near iron), and then decreases slowly for large $A$, remaining nearly flat between $A = 30$ and $A = 170$.
This near-constancy is explained by the saturation property of nuclear forces: each nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours (short range), so binding energy per nucleon does not keep increasing with $A$.
Since the curve rises on both sides of the peak, both fission of a heavy nucleus (low BE/A, right side) into medium nuclei (higher BE/A) and fusion of light nuclei (low BE/A, left side) into a medium nucleus (higher BE/A) move the products to a higher binding energy per nucleon, releasing energy.

questions.question: Obtain the relation between the decay constant and half life of a radioactive sample. The half life of a certain radioactive material against $\alpha$-decay is 100 days. After how much time, will the undecayed fraction of the material be $6.25\%$?
questions.answer:
Number of undecayed nuclei follows $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$.
At $t = T$ (half life), $N_0/2 = N_0 e^{-\lambda T}$, so $\lambda T = \ln 2$, giving $T = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$.
Given $6.25\% = \dfrac{1}{16} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^4$, so the time elapsed is $4$ half lives.
$t = 4T = 4\times100 = 400$ days.

questions.question: Distinguish between nuclear fission and fusion. Show how in both these processes energy is released. Calculate the energy release in MeV in the deuterium-tritium fusion reaction: $^{2}{}_{1}H +^{3}{}_{1} H \rightarrow^{4}{}_{2} He + n$ Using the data: $m(^{2}{}_{1}H) = 2.014102$ u $m(^{3}{}_{1}H) = 3.016049$ u $m(^{4}{}_{2}He) = 4.002603$ u $m_{n} = 1.008665$ u $1u = 931.5$ MeV/ $c^{2}$
questions.answer:
Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei of comparable mass, usually triggered by neutron bombardment, whereas nuclear fusion is the combining of two light nuclei into a heavier nucleus, requiring very high temperature to overcome Coulomb repulsion.
In both processes the binding energy per nucleon of the products is greater than that of the reactants; the corresponding decrease in total mass appears as energy release, $E = \Delta m c^2$.
For the given reaction:
Mass of reactants $= 2.014102 + 3.016049 = 5.030151$ u
Mass of products $= 4.002603 + 1.008665 = 5.011268$ u
$\Delta m = 0.018883$ u
$Q = 0.018883\times931.5 \approx 17.59$ MeV

questions.question: (a) Deduce the expression, $N = N_{0}e^{-\lambda t}$, for the law of radioactive decay. (b) (i) Write symbolically the process expressing the $\beta^{+}$ decay of $^{22}{}_{11}Na$. Also write the basic nuclear process underlying this decay. (ii) Is the nucleus formed in the decay of the nucleus $^{22}{}_{11}Na$, an isotope or isobar?
questions.answer:
(a) The rate of decay of a radioactive sample is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei: $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N$.
Integrating, $\int_{N_0}^{N}\dfrac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\int_0^t dt$, which gives $\ln(N/N_0) = -\lambda t$, so $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$.
(b) (i) $^{22}_{11}Na \rightarrow\ ^{22}_{10}Ne + e^{+} + \nu$; the underlying basic process is $p \rightarrow n + e^{+} + \nu$.
(ii) $^{22}_{10}Ne$ has the same mass number as $^{22}_{11}Na$ but a different atomic number, so it is an isobar of $^{22}_{11}Na$, not an isotope.

questions.question: For the past some time, Aarti had been observing some erratic body movement, unsteadiness and lack of coordination in the activities of her sister Radha, who also used to complain of severe headache occasionally. Aarti suggested to her parents to get a medical check-up of Radha. The doctor thoroughly examined Radha and diagnosed that she has a brain tumour. (a) What, according to you, are the values displayed by Aarti? (b) How can radioisotopes help a doctor to diagnose brain tumour?
questions.answer:
(a) Aarti displayed the values of observant care, concern, alertness and responsibility towards her sister's well-being, and prompt, rational decision-making by advising a timely medical check-up.
(b) A radioisotope (e.g. technetium-99m) tagged to a suitable carrier compound is injected into the patient; it accumulates preferentially in the diseased tissue.
The gamma radiation emitted is detected by a gamma camera/scanner, producing an image that shows the location, size and shape of the tumour, since diseased cells absorb the tracer differently from healthy cells.

questions.question: (a) In a typical nuclear reaction, e.g. _ $\{1\}^{2\}}${$H\} + \{$_ $\{1\}^{2\}}${$H\}\} -\rightarrow\{$_ $\{2\}^{3\}}${$He\}\} + n + 3.27${$MeV \},$ although number of nucleons is conserved, yet energy is released. How? Explain. (b) Show that nuclear density in a given nucleus is independent of mass number $A$.
questions.answer:
(a) The rest mass of the two deuterium nuclei (reactants) is slightly greater than the total rest mass of the products ($_2^3He$ and neutron); this difference is the mass defect $\Delta m$.
By Einstein's mass-energy relation, this mass defect is converted into energy, $\Delta E = \Delta m c^2$, which appears as the $3.27$ MeV released, even though the total number of nucleons before and after the reaction remains the same.
(b) Nuclear radius $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$, so nuclear volume $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A$.
Since nuclear mass $\approx A \times m_p$ (mass of one nucleon), density $\rho = \frac{mass}{volume} = \frac{A m_p}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \frac{3m_p}{4\pi R_0^3}$, which is independent of $A$.

questions.question: (a) Write symbolically the $\beta^{-}$ decay process of $3215$ P. (b) Derive an expression for the average life of a radionuclide. Give its relationship with the half-life.
questions.answer:
(a) $_{15}^{32}P \rightarrow {}_{16}^{32}S + {}_{-1}^{0}e + \bar{\nu}$
(b) Number of nuclei decaying in time $dt$ is $dN = \lambda N\, dt$, each having lived time $t$.
Average life $\tau = \frac{\int_0^\infty t\,\lambda N\, dt}{\int_0^\infty \lambda N\, dt}$, and using $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, this integral gives $\tau = \frac{1}{\lambda}$.
Since half-life $T_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{\lambda}$, relation with average life is $T_{1/2} = 0.693\,\tau$.

questions.question: Draw a plot of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separations. Mark the regions where the nuclear force is (i) attractive and (ii) repulsive. Write any two characteristic features of nuclear forces.
questions.answer:
The potential energy $U(r)$ of a pair of nucleons is plotted against their separation $r$: for large $r$, $U$ is nearly zero; as $r$ decreases, $U$ falls to a minimum (negative) around $r \approx 0.8$ fm, indicating the attractive region, and then rises sharply to large positive values for $r < 0.8$ fm, indicating the strongly repulsive core.
(i) Attractive region: roughly $0.8$ fm $< r < $ a few fm.
(ii) Repulsive region: $r < 0.8$ fm.
Two characteristic features: nuclear force is short-range (negligible beyond $\sim 3-4$ fm) and charge-independent (same between p-p, n-n and n-p), and it is much stronger than gravitational or electrostatic force.

questions.question: (i) What characteristic property of nuclear force explains the constancy of binding energy per nucleon $(BE/A)$ in the range of mass number ’ $A$’ lying $30 < A < 170$? (ii) Show that the density of nucleus over a wide range of nuclei is constant — independent of mass number $A$.
questions.answer:
(i) The short-range and saturation property of nuclear force means each nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours, not with all nucleons in the nucleus.
Hence, beyond a certain $A$, adding more nucleons does not increase the binding energy per nucleon proportionally, so $BE/A$ remains nearly constant ($\approx 8.5$ MeV) for $30 < A < 170$.
(ii) Nuclear radius $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$, so volume $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A$.
Since nuclear mass $\propto A$, density $\rho = \frac{mass}{volume} = \frac{A m_p}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \frac{3m_p}{4\pi R_0^3}$, independent of $A$, confirming nuclear density is constant for all nuclei.

questions.question: State the law of radioactive decay. Plot a graph showing the number $(N)$ of undecayed nuclei as a function of time $(t)$ for a given radioactive sample having half life $T_{1/2}$. Depict in the plot the number of undecayed nuclei at (i) $t = 3T_{1/2}$ and (ii) $t = 5T_{1/2}$.
questions.answer:
Law of radioactive decay: the number of nuclei disintegrating per unit time is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present, $\frac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N$, giving $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, where $\lambda$ is the decay constant.
The $N$ vs $t$ graph is an exponentially decreasing curve starting at $N_0$ and asymptotically approaching zero.
(i) At $t = 3T_{1/2}$: $N = N_0/8$, marked on the curve.
(ii) At $t = 5T_{1/2}$: $N = N_0/32$, marked further along the curve, closer to the time axis.

questions.question: (i) Define ’activity’ of a radioactive material and write its S.I. unit. (ii) Plot a graph showing variation of activity of a given radioactive sample with time. $-$ (iii) The sequence of stepwise decay of a radioactive nucleus is $D-\rightarrow^{\alpha}D_{1}-\rightarrow^{\beta}D_{2}$ If the atomic number and mass number of $D_{2}$ are 71 and 176 respectively, what are their corresponding values for D?
questions.answer:
(i) Activity is the rate of disintegration of nuclei in a radioactive sample, $R = -\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$. Its SI unit is becquerel (Bq), equal to one disintegration per second.
(ii) The activity $R = R_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ vs $t$ graph is an exponentially decreasing curve, similar in shape to the $N$ vs $t$ curve, starting at $R_0$ and falling towards zero.
(iii) $\alpha$-decay: $Z$ decreases by 2, $A$ decreases by 4; $\beta$-decay: $Z$ increases by 1, $A$ unchanged.
For $D_2$: $Z=71$, $A=176$. Working backwards through $\beta$-decay, $D_1$ has $Z=70$, $A=176$; working backwards through $\alpha$-decay, $D$ has $Z=72$, $A=180$.

questions.question: Draw a plot showing the variation of binding energy per nucleon versus the mass number $A$. Explain with the help of this plot the release of energy in the processes of nuclear fission and fusion.
questions.answer:
The graph of binding energy per nucleon $(BE/A)$ vs mass number $A$ rises steeply for low $A$, peaks around $A \approx 56$ (iron, $BE/A \approx 8.7$ MeV), then decreases slowly for heavier nuclei.
Fission: a heavy nucleus (large $A$, lower $BE/A$) splits into two medium nuclei (higher $BE/A$), so binding energy per nucleon increases, and this difference is released as energy.
Fusion: two very light nuclei (small $A$, low $BE/A$) combine to form a heavier nucleus (higher $BE/A$) nearer the peak, so the increase in binding energy per nucleon is released as energy.
In both processes, the system moves towards the peak of the curve, converting mass defect into energy as per $E = \Delta m c^2$.

questions.question: Distinguish between isotopes and isobars. Give one example for each species. A radioactive isotope has a half-life of $5$ years. How long will it take the activity to reduce to $3.125\%$?
questions.answer:
Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number $Z$ but different mass number $A$ (different number of neutrons), e.g. $_1^1H$ and $_1^2H$.
Isobars are atoms of different elements having the same mass number $A$ but different atomic number $Z$, e.g. $_6^{14}C$ and $_7^{14}N$.
Given $3.125\% = \frac{1}{32} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^5$, so 5 half-lives have elapsed: $t = 5 \times T_{1/2} = 5 \times 5 = 25$ years.

questions.question: Calculate the energy released during the $\alpha$-decay of $^{238}{}_{92} U \rightarrow^{234}{}_{90} Th+^{4}{}_{2}He$. Given: 1. atomic mass of $^{23892} U$ = 238.05079 u 2. atomic mass of $^{23490} Th$ = 234.04363 u 3. atomic mass of $^{4}{}_{2}He$ = 4.00260 u $1 u = 931.5 MeV/c^{2}$. Is this decay spontaneous? Give reason.
questions.answer:
Mass defect $\Delta m = m(^{238}U) - [m(^{234}Th) + m(^4He)]$
$\Delta m = 238.05079 - (234.04363 + 4.00260) = 238.05079 - 238.04623 = 0.00456$ u
Energy released $Q = \Delta m \times 931.5$ MeV $= 0.00456 \times 931.5 \approx 4.25$ MeV.
Since $Q > 0$ (positive energy is released without any external energy input), the decay is spontaneous.

questions.question: Draw the graph to show variation of binding energy per nucleon with mass number of different atomic nuclei. Calculate binding energy/nucleon of $^{40}{}_{20}Ca$ nucleus. Given: mass of $^{40}{}_{20}Ca$ = 39.962589 u mass of proton = 1.007825 u mass of neutron = 1.008665 u and $1 u = 931 MeV/c^{2}$
questions.answer:
The graph of binding energy per nucleon versus mass number $A$ rises sharply for light nuclei, reaches a maximum of about $8.7$ MeV near $A = 56$ (iron), and then decreases slowly for heavy nuclei.
Mass defect: $\Delta m = 20 m_p + 20 m_n - m_{Ca} = 20(1.007825) + 20(1.008665) - 39.962589$
$\Delta m = 40.32980 - 39.962589 = 0.367211$ u
Binding energy $= \Delta m \times 931 = 0.367211 \times 931 = 341.87$ MeV
Binding energy per nucleon $= 341.87/40 = 8.55$ MeV

questions.question: Explain, with the help of a nuclear reaction in each of the following cases, how the neutron to proton ratio changes during (i) alpha-decay (ii) beta-decay.
questions.answer:
(i) Alpha-decay: An alpha particle (2 protons, 2 neutrons) is emitted, e.g. $^{238}_{92}U \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}Th + {}^{4}_{2}He$.
Since heavy nuclei have $N > Z$, removing equal numbers of neutrons and protons increases the neutron-to-proton ratio.
(ii) Beta-decay: A neutron converts to a proton, e.g. $^{234}_{90}Th \rightarrow {}^{234}_{91}Pa + e^{-} + \bar{\nu}$.
Since $N$ decreases by 1 and $Z$ increases by 1, the neutron-to-proton ratio decreases.

questions.question: Why is the mass of a nucleus always less than the sum of the masses of its constituents, neutrons and protons? If the total number of neutrons and protons in a nuclear reaction is conserved, how then is the energy absorbed or evolved in the reaction? Explain.
questions.answer:
The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its constituent nucleons because some mass is converted into binding energy, $\Delta E = \Delta m c^{2}$, released when the nucleons come together to form the nucleus; this mass defect $\Delta m$ accounts for the difference.
Although the number of nucleons (protons + neutrons) is conserved in a nuclear reaction, the total binding energy of the products can differ from that of the reactants, since binding energy per nucleon varies with mass number.
This difference in binding energy appears as the mass difference $\Delta m$ between reactants and products, and by $E = \Delta m c^{2}$, energy is released (if products are more tightly bound) or absorbed (if less tightly bound).

questions.question: Draw a graph showing the variation of binding energy per nucleon with mass number for different nuclei. Explain, with the help of this graph, the release of energy by the process of nuclear fusion.
questions.answer:
The graph of binding energy per nucleon versus mass number $A$ rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks at about $8.7$ MeV near $A = 56$, and falls slowly for heavy nuclei.
In nuclear fusion, two light nuclei (small $A$, low BE/nucleon) combine to form a heavier nucleus (larger $A$, higher BE/nucleon), moving up the graph towards the peak.
Since the product nucleus has greater binding energy per nucleon than the reactants, mass is converted to energy, $E = \Delta m c^{2}$, and energy is released, e.g. $^{2}_{1}H + {}^{2}_{1}H \rightarrow {}^{3}_{2}He + n + \text{energy}$.

questions.question: (a) Draw a graph showing the variation of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation. Indicate the regions in which nuclear force is (i) attractive, and (ii) repulsive. (b) Write two characteristic features of nuclear force which distinguish it from the coulomb force.
questions.answer:
(a) The potential energy $V(r)$ of a pair of nucleons is large and positive (repulsive) for very small separations ($r < 0.8$ fm), falls to a minimum negative value near $r \approx 0.8$ fm, and rises towards zero for larger separations (beyond about $3$ fm the force vanishes).
Attractive region: $r$ between about $0.8$ fm and $3$ fm.
Repulsive region: $r < 0.8$ fm.
(b) Nuclear force is short-range (acts only up to a few fm, unlike Coulomb force which is long-range) and is charge-independent (same between p-p, n-n, p-n, unlike Coulomb force which acts only between charges).

questions.question: (a) Show that the decay rate ’ $R$’ of a sample of a radionuclide is related to the number of radioactive nuclei ’ $N$’ at the same instant by the expression $R = \lambda N$. (b) The half-life of $238$ U against $\alpha$-decay is $1.5 \times 10^{17}$ s. What is the activity of a sample of $238$ U having $25 \times 10^{20}$ atoms?
questions.answer:
(a) Let $N$ be the number of radioactive nuclei at time $t$. The decay probability per nucleus per unit time is constant, $\lambda$ (decay constant).
Number of nuclei decaying in time $dt$: $dN = -\lambda N \, dt$
Decay rate $R = -\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$, showing $R$ is proportional to $N$ at that instant.
(b) $\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{1.5 \times 10^{17}} = 4.62 \times 10^{-18}$ s$^{-1}$
$R = \lambda N = 4.62 \times 10^{-18} \times 25 \times 10^{20} = 1.16 \times 10^{4}$ disintegrations/s

questions.question: Give the mass number and atomic number of elements on the right-hand side of the decay process. The graph shows how the activity of a sample of radon-220 changes with time. Use the graph to determine its half-life. Calculate the value of decay constant of radon-220.
questions.answer:
Radon-220 undergoes alpha-decay: $^{220}_{86}Rn \rightarrow {}^{216}_{84}Po + {}^{4}_{2}He$, so the daughter nucleus on the right has mass number $216$ and atomic number $84$ (with the alpha particle having mass number $4$, atomic number $2$).
From the graph, the activity falls to half its initial value in a time of about $55$ s, so the half-life $T_{1/2} \approx 55$ s.
Decay constant $\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{55} \approx 1.26 \times 10^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$

questions.question: Asha’s mother read an article in the newspaper about a disaster that took place at Chernobyl. She could not understand much from the article and asked a few questions from Asha regarding the article. Asha tried to answer her mother’s questions based on what she learnt in Class XII Physics. (a) What was the installation at Chernobyl where the disaster took place? What, according to you, was the cause of this disaster? (b) Explain the process of release of energy in the installation at Chernobyl. (c) What, according to you, were the values displayed by Asha and her mother?
questions.answer:
(i) The installation was a nuclear power plant (nuclear reactor) using controlled nuclear fission of $^{235}_{92}U$ to generate electricity. The disaster was caused by a flawed reactor design combined with operator error during a safety test, leading to an uncontrolled increase in the fission chain reaction, a power surge, and explosion.
(ii) In the reactor, slow neutrons cause $^{235}_{92}U$ nuclei to undergo fission, splitting into lighter nuclei and releasing 2-3 fast neutrons plus energy; a moderator slows these neutrons so they can sustain a controlled chain reaction, and the heat released is used to produce steam that drives turbines to generate electricity.
(iii) The values shown were Asha's scientific temperament, awareness and eagerness to apply classroom learning to real-world events, and her mother's inquisitiveness and willingness to learn from her child.

questions.question: (a) Derive the law of radioactive decay $N = N_{0}e^{-\lambda t}$. (b) The half life of $238$ U undergoing $\alpha$-decay is $4.5 \times 10^{9}$ years. Find its mean life. (c) What fraction of the initial mass of a radioactive substance will decay in five half-life periods? OR (a) State the postulates of Bohr’s model of hydrogen atom and derive the expression for Bohr radius. (b) Find the ratio of the longest and the shortest wavelengths amongst the spectral lines of Balmer series in the spectrum of hydrogen atom.
questions.answer:
(a) Let $N_0$ be the number of nuclei at $t=0$. The number of nuclei decaying in time $dt$ is proportional to $N$: $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N$.
Rearranging: $\dfrac{dN}{N} = -\lambda \, dt$. Integrating from $0$ to $t$: $\ln N - \ln N_0 = -\lambda t$, so $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$.
(b) Mean life $\tau = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{T_{1/2}}{0.693} = \dfrac{4.5 \times 10^{9}}{0.693} = 6.49 \times 10^{9}$ years.
(c) After 5 half-lives, fraction remaining $= (1/2)^5 = 1/32$, so fraction decayed $= 1 - 1/32 = 31/32$ of the initial mass.

OR

(a) Bohr's postulates: electrons revolve in stable circular orbits without radiating energy; angular momentum is quantized, $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$; radiation is emitted/absorbed only when an electron jumps between orbits, $h\nu = E_i - E_f$.
For a hydrogen atom, Coulomb force provides centripetal force: $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}$
Using $v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi m r}$ and substituting gives $r_n = \dfrac{n^2 h^2 \epsilon_0}{\pi m e^2}$, the Bohr radius (for $n=1$, $r_1 = 0.53$ Å).
(b) $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)$; longest wavelength ($n=3$): $\lambda_{max} = 36/5R$; shortest wavelength ($n=\infty$): $\lambda_{min} = 4/R$.
Ratio $\lambda_{max}/\lambda_{min} = 9/5 = 1.8$

questions.question: Distinguish between ’nuclear fission’ and ’nuclear fusion’. Which one of them is used for release of energy in a nuclear reactor? Name one fuel used in a nuclear reactor.
questions.answer:
Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus (like $^{235}_{92}U$) into two lighter nuclei of comparable mass, along with release of neutrons and energy, when bombarded by a slow neutron.
Nuclear fusion is the combining of two light nuclei (like isotopes of hydrogen) to form a heavier nucleus, with release of energy; it requires very high temperatures (about $10^7$ K) to overcome Coulomb repulsion.
Fission can be controlled using moderators and control rods, while fusion (as achieved so far) is uncontrolled (as in a hydrogen bomb).
Nuclear fission is used for the release of energy in a nuclear reactor.
A commonly used fuel in a nuclear reactor is enriched uranium ($^{235}_{92}U$).

questions.question: What are radiation hazards? Mention four safety measures which should be taken against radioactive radiation.
questions.answer:
Radiation hazards are the harmful biological effects produced when living tissue absorbs ionizing radiation ($\alpha, \beta, \gamma$) from radioactive sources.
Such radiation can damage cell structure and DNA, causing genetic mutations, radiation sickness, burns, and cancer (e.g. leukaemia); the damage depends on the type, energy and dose of radiation absorbed.
Safety measures:
(i) Radioactive sources should be handled with long tongs and stored in thick lead containers to shield the radiation.
(ii) Workers should keep the maximum possible distance from the source, since intensity falls as $1/r^2$.
(iii) Exposure time near a source should be kept to a minimum.
(iv) Protective lead aprons, gloves and radiation-monitoring (dosimeter) badges should always be worn, and radioactive waste disposed of safely.

questions.question: What are radio isotopes? Write their any four uses.
questions.answer:
Radioisotopes are unstable (radioactive) isotopes of an element; they have the same atomic number as the stable isotope but a different mass number, and they decay by emitting $\alpha$, $\beta$ or $\gamma$ radiation.
Uses:
(i) Medical diagnosis and therapy: Iodine-131 is used to study/treat thyroid disorders, and Cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy for treating cancer.
(ii) Agriculture: Phosphorus-32 is used as a tracer to study the uptake of fertilizers by plants and to develop improved crop varieties through induced mutation.
(iii) Archaeology and geology: Carbon-14 is used for radiocarbon dating of fossils and archaeological samples.
(iv) Industry: Radioisotopes are used to detect leaks in pipelines and to check the thickness of materials in industrial gauging.

questions.question: A concave lens of focal length 10 cm is cut into two identical plano-concave lenses. The focal length of each lens will be: (A) 20 cm (B) 30 cm (C) 40 cm (D) 5 cm
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
For the original biconcave lens, $\frac{1}{10} = \frac{1}{f'} + \frac{1}{f'}$ (two identical plano-concave halves in contact), giving $f' = 20$ cm.

questions.question: A concave lens of focal length 40 cm is coaxially in contact with two convex lenses, each of focal length 20 cm, on each side. The focal length of the combination is: (A) zero (B) $\frac{40}{3}$ cm (C) $-\frac{20}{3}$ cm (D) $\frac{40}{3}$ cm
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
Using $P = P_1 + P_2 + P_3 = \frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{20} - \frac{1}{40} = \frac{3}{40}$ per cm, the combination is converging with $f = \frac{40}{3}$ cm.

questions.question: Light from a small object in air falls on a spherical glass surface $(n = 1.5)$ of radius of curvature $R$. A real image of the object will be formed if the object distance $u$ is related to $R$ as: (A) $u < \frac{R}{2}$ (B) $\frac{R}{2}< u < R$ (C) $R < u < 2R$ (D) $u > 2R$
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
Using $\frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2-n_1}{R}$ with $n_1=1, n_2=1.5$, a real image ($v>0$) is obtained only when the object distance exceeds $2R$.

questions.question: Case Study: In an experiment with convex lens of focal length $f$, the screen is fixed at a distance $D$ from the object. A student slowly moves the lens away from the object towards the screen and finds that she is able to form sharp image of the object for two positions of the lens. The distance between these two positions of the lens is $d$. The value of $d$ is: (A) $p \frac{D(D -4f)}{D(D -2f)}$ (B) $p$ (C) $2 \frac{\sqrt{Df}}{D(D -f)}$ (D) $p$
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
In the displacement method, the two lens positions are separated by $d = \sqrt{D(D-4f)}$, obtained from $u_1 + v_1 = D$ and the lens formula, showing the object-screen distance and displacement determine $f$.

questions.question: Compared to the size of the object, the images formed in the two positions of the lens are respectively: (A) reduced, enlarged (B) reduced, reduced (C) enlarged, enlarged (D) enlarged, reduced
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
By the principle of reversibility of light, the two positions of the lens simply interchange the values of $u$ and $v$, so if one position gives a magnified image ($u<v$) the other must give a diminished image ($u>v$); since the lens is first moved from near the object, it gives the enlarged image first, then the reduced image.

questions.question: If the distance between object and screen is $80$· $00$ cm and the lens forms sharp images at two positions separated by $20$· $00$ cm, the focal length of convex lens is: (A) $15$· $50$ cm (B) $18$· $75$ cm (C) $20$· $50$ cm (D) $22$· $75$ cm
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Using $f = \frac{D^2 - d^2}{4D} = \frac{(80)^2 - (20)^2}{4 \times 80} = \frac{6400 - 400}{320} = 18.75$ cm.

questions.question: Consider a convex lens of focal length $15$ cm. For which of the following values of object-screen distance, two positions of the object can be found to obtain sharp image on the screen? (A) $45$ cm (B) $50$ cm (C) $55$ cm (D) $65$ cm
questions.answer:
Option (D) is correct.
Two positions of the lens (and hence two sharp images) exist only when the object-screen distance exceeds $4f = 4 \times 15 = 60$ cm, which is satisfied only by $65$ cm.

questions.question: A thin convex lens of focal length $10$ cm and another thin lens of focal length $f$ are placed coaxially in contact. If the power of their combination is $2$ D, the value of $f$ is: (A) $-15$ cm (B) $-10$ cm (C) $-20$ cm (D) $-30$ cm
questions.answer:
Option (C) is correct.
Using $P = P_1 + P_2$: $P_1 = \frac{100}{10} = 10$ D, so $P_2 = 2 - 10 = -8$ D, giving $f_2 = \frac{100}{-8} \approx -20$ cm, showing the second lens is diverging.

questions.question: A thin plano-convex lens and a thin equi-concave lens are kept coaxially in contact as shown in the figure. Assuming both the lenses are made of glass of refractive index $\mu$, and $R$ is the radius of curvature of each curved surface, the focal length of the combination is: (A) $\frac{R}{\mu -1}$ (B) $-\frac{R}{\mu -1}$ (C) $\frac{2R}{\mu -1}$ (D) $-\frac{2R}{\mu -1}$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct.
Power of plano-convex lens $= (\mu-1)/R$ and power of equi-concave lens $= -2(\mu-1)/R$, so combined power $P = -(\mu-1)/R$, giving $f = -R/(\mu-1)$.

questions.question: A telescope has an objective lens of focal length $144$ cm and an eyepiece of focal length $6$· $0$ cm. The magnifying power and the length of the telescope tube will be respectively: (A) $24, 150$ cm (B) $42, 138$ cm (C) $24, 138$ cm (D) $42, 150$ cm
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
$M = f_o/f_e = 144/6 = 24$ and tube length $= f_o + f_e = 144 + 6 = 150$ cm.

questions.question: In which of the following, total internal reflection does not occur? (A) Twinkling of stars (B) Brilliance of diamonds (C) Optical fibre (D) Reflecting prism
questions.answer:
Option (A) is correct.
Twinkling of stars is caused by atmospheric refraction due to varying air density, not total internal reflection.

questions.question: A plano-convex lens, made of glass $(n = 1$· $5)$ has a curved surface whose radius is $40$ cm. The image formed of an object is of the same size as that of the object. The distance of the object from the lens is: (A) $40$ cm (B) $80$ cm (C) $160$ cm (D) $200$ cm
questions.answer:
