A P-type crystal is electrically neutral because each acceptor atom that contributes a hole becomes a fixed negative ion, and the number of such immobile negative ions equals the number of holes created, so the total positive and negative charges balance.

questions.question: The given inputs A, B are fed to a 2-input NOR gate. Draw the output wave form of the gate.
questions.answer:
For a 2-input NOR gate, $Y = \overline{A+B}$, so the output is high only during the time intervals when both $A$ and $B$ are simultaneously low.
The output waveform is therefore drawn as a pulse that is high only in those regions where both input waveforms are at logic $0$ together, and low (logic $0$) whenever either $A$ or $B$ (or both) is high, following the same time axis as the given inputs.

questions.question: The output of an OR gate is connected to both the inputs of a NAND gate. Draw the logic circuit of this combination of gates and write its truth table.
questions.answer:
Logic circuit: inputs $A$ and $B$ are fed to an OR gate whose output $C = A+B$ is connected to both inputs of a NAND gate, giving final output $Y = \overline{C \cdot C} = \overline{C} = \overline{A+B}$.
This combination behaves as a NOR gate.
Truth table: $A=0,B=0,Y=1$; $A=0,B=1,Y=0$; $A=1,B=0,Y=0$; $A=1,B=1,Y=0$.

questions.question: Two semiconductor materials $X$ and $Y$ shown in the given figure, are made by doping germanium crystal with indium and arsenic respectively. The two are joined end to end and connected to a battery as shown. (i) Will the junction be forward biased or reverse biased? (ii) Sketch a V-I graph for this arrangement.
questions.answer:
(i) $X$ (doped with indium, a trivalent impurity) is a P-type semiconductor, and $Y$ (doped with arsenic, a pentavalent impurity) is an N-type semiconductor; since the P-side is connected to the positive terminal and the N-side to the negative terminal of the battery, the junction is forward biased.
(ii) The V-I graph shows negligible current up to a threshold (knee) voltage, after which current rises sharply and almost linearly with increasing forward voltage, characteristic of a forward-biased p-n junction diode.

questions.question: Draw and explain the output waveform across the load resistor $R$, if the input waveform is as shown in the given figure.
questions.answer:
For an AC input applied to a single diode in series with load $R$ (half-wave rectifier configuration), the diode conducts only during the half cycle for which it is forward biased, allowing current to flow through $R$, and blocks the other half cycle when it is reverse biased.
Hence the output waveform across $R$ consists of only the positive (or negative, depending on diode orientation) half cycles of the input, appearing as a series of one-directional pulses separated by zero-output intervals, unlike the continuous alternating input.

questions.question: Explain how the width of depletion layer in a p-n junction diode changes when the junction is (i) forward biased (ii) reverse biased.
questions.answer:
(i) Forward bias: the applied voltage opposes the internal barrier field, pushing majority carriers toward the junction, so the depletion layer becomes narrower and the barrier potential decreases.
(ii) Reverse bias: the applied voltage adds to the internal barrier field, pulling majority carriers away from the junction, so the depletion layer becomes wider and the barrier potential increases.

questions.question: With the help of a diagram, show the biasing of a light emitting diode (LED). Give its two advantages over conventional incandescent lamps.
questions.answer:
In forward bias, an LED is connected with the p-side to the positive terminal and the n-side to the negative terminal of the battery through a current-limiting resistor $R$, so that the junction current stays below the rated value.
Circuit: Battery (+) $\rightarrow$ resistor $R$ $\rightarrow$ p-side of LED $\rightarrow$ n-side $\rightarrow$ Battery ($-$).
On forward biasing, electrons and holes recombine at the junction and release energy as light (electroluminescence).
Advantages over incandescent lamps: (i) Low operating voltage, low power consumption and high efficiency (little heat loss). (ii) Fast switching (no warm-up time), longer life and more robust construction.

questions.question: In the figure below, circuit symbol of a logic gate and input wave form is shown. (i) Name the logic gate, (ii) write its truth table and (iii) give the output wave form.
questions.answer:
(i) The gate is an AND gate (output goes high only when both inputs are simultaneously high, as seen from the waveform).
(ii) Truth table:
$A=0,B=0 \Rightarrow Y=0$
$A=0,B=1 \Rightarrow Y=0$
$A=1,B=0 \Rightarrow Y=0$
$A=1,B=1 \Rightarrow Y=1$
(iii) Output waveform: $Y$ stays at logic 0 (low) throughout, except during the time intervals where both input waveforms $A$ and $B$ are simultaneously high, when $Y$ rises to logic 1 (high), following the same duration as the overlap of the two high pulses.

questions.question: An ac voltage $V_{i} = 12 \sin(100\pi t)$ V is applied between points A and B in a network of two ideal diodes and three resistors as shown in figure. During the positive half-cycle of the input voltage $V_{i}$ supplied to the network: (a) Identify which of the two diodes will conduct and why? (b) Redraw an equivalent circuit diagram to show the flow of current. (c) Calculate the output voltage drops $V_{o}$ across the three resistors when the input voltage attains its peak value.
questions.answer:
(a) During the positive half-cycle, terminal A is at higher potential than B. The diode whose anode faces A (say $D_1$) gets forward biased and conducts, since current can flow easily through it; the other diode $D_2$, with its anode facing B, gets reverse biased and does not conduct (acts as open circuit).
(b) Equivalent circuit: replace $D_1$ by a plain connecting wire (zero resistance) and remove the branch containing $D_2$ (open circuit); the source $V_i$ then drives current only through the resistors in the remaining path.
(c) At peak, $V_i = 12$ V. Since diodes are ideal, this entire 12 V appears across the resistors in the conducting branch; using the potential-divider rule for resistors in series, $V_o = V_i \left(\dfrac{R}{R_1+R_2+R_3}\right)$ for the resistor concerned, giving output voltage drops that together sum to $12$ V across the conducting branch.

questions.question: Briefly explain the two important processes that occur during the formation of a p-n junction.
questions.answer:
Diffusion: Due to concentration gradient across the junction, electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side and holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side, constituting a diffusion current.
Drift: The diffusion of charge carriers leaves behind uncompensated ions, creating a depletion region and an internal electric field directed from n-side to p-side. This field drives minority carriers (electrons on p-side, holes on n-side) across the junction, constituting a drift current opposite to the diffusion current.
In equilibrium, diffusion current equals drift current, and a potential barrier (barrier potential) is established across the junction.

questions.question: A semiconductor has equal electron and hole concentration of $3 \times 10^{6}$ m $-3$. On doping with a certain impurity, the hole concentration increases to $6 \times 10^{10}$ m $-3$. (a) What type of semiconductor is obtained on doping? (b) Calculate the new electron concentration of the semiconductor. (c) How does the energy gap of semiconductor change with doping? Draw the energy band diagram for it.
questions.answer:
(a) Since hole concentration increases while electron concentration is expected to fall (as $n_e n_h = n_i^2$), the majority carriers are holes, so it is a p-type semiconductor.
(b) $n_i^2 = n_e n_h$ for the intrinsic case: $n_i = 3 \times 10^{6}$ m$^{-3}$, so $n_i^2 = 9 \times 10^{12}$ m$^{-6}$.
For the doped semiconductor, $n_e = \dfrac{n_i^2}{n_h} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{12}}{6 \times 10^{10}} = 1.5 \times 10^{2}$ m$^{-3}$.
(c) The energy gap $E_g$ of the semiconductor does not change on doping; only new, discrete energy levels are introduced. For p-type doping, an acceptor energy level is created just above the top of the valence band, close to $E_v$, from which electrons are easily excited to create holes in the valence band.

questions.question: (a) Draw the V-I characteristics of silicon diode. (b) Explain the following terms: (i) minority carrier injection in forward bias (ii) breakdown voltage in reverse bias
questions.answer:
(a) Forward-bias branch: current $I$ rises slowly near $V=0$, then increases exponentially and steeply after a threshold (knee) voltage (about $0.7$ V for silicon).
Reverse-bias branch: only a small, almost constant reverse saturation current flows until the reverse voltage reaches the breakdown voltage, beyond which current increases sharply.
(b) (i) Minority carrier injection: In forward bias, the barrier is lowered and majority carriers cross the junction in large numbers; on entering the other region they become minority carriers there, so the minority carrier concentration near the junction rises well above its equilibrium value — this is minority carrier injection.
(ii) Breakdown voltage: The reverse voltage at which the reverse current increases abruptly and sharply (due to avalanche or Zener effect), causing the junction to lose its blocking property.

questions.question: With the help of circuit diagrams, briefly explain the forward biasing and the reverse biasing of a p-n junction diode.
questions.answer:
Forward biasing: The p-side of the junction diode is connected to the positive terminal and the n-side to the negative terminal of the battery (through a resistor). This reduces the width of the depletion layer and the potential barrier, allowing majority carriers to diffuse across the junction easily, so a large current flows.
Reverse biasing: The p-side is connected to the negative terminal and the n-side to the positive terminal. This increases the depletion layer width and the potential barrier, so majority carriers cannot cross the junction; only a small current due to minority carriers flows (until breakdown).
Circuit diagrams: In both cases, the diode is connected in series with a battery and a milliammeter/microammeter (and a resistor), with the battery polarity reversed between the forward and reverse cases as described above.

questions.question: With the help of a circuit diagram, explain the working of a full wave rectifier. Depict the input and output waveforms.
questions.answer:
A center-tapped transformer secondary is connected to two diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$, whose cathodes are joined together and connected through a load resistor $R_L$ back to the center tap.
During one half-cycle, the upper end of the secondary is positive, forward biasing $D_1$; it conducts and current flows through $R_L$.
During the next half-cycle, the lower end becomes positive, forward biasing $D_2$, which conducts and again sends current through $R_L$ in the same direction.
Thus both half-cycles of the ac input contribute to the output, and the output waveform consists of a series of unidirectional pulses (full-wave rectified, pulsating dc) at twice the frequency of the input sinusoidal waveform.

questions.question: (a) Draw circuit arrangement for studying $V$ - $I$ characteristics of a $p$- $n$ junction diode. (b) Show the shape of the characteristics of a diode. (c) Mention two information that you can get from these characteristics.
questions.answer:
(a) Circuit: A p-n junction diode is connected in series with a battery, a rheostat (to vary voltage), and a milliammeter, with a voltmeter connected across the diode; for forward bias the p-side is joined to the positive terminal, and for reverse bias (with a microammeter instead) the n-side is joined to the positive terminal.
(b) Shape: In forward bias, current stays near zero until a threshold (knee) voltage, then rises steeply and almost linearly. In reverse bias, only a tiny, nearly constant saturation current flows until the breakdown voltage, beyond which current increases sharply.
(c) Information obtainable: (i) the threshold/knee voltage and forward dynamic resistance $r_d = \Delta V/\Delta I$; (ii) the reverse breakdown voltage and reverse saturation current.

questions.question: (a) What are majority and minority charge carriers in an extrinsic semiconductor? (b) A p-n junction is forward biased. Describe the movement of the charge carriers which produce current in it. (c) The graph shows the variation of current with voltage for a p-n junction diode. Estimate the dynamic resistance of diode at V = $-0.6$ volt.
questions.answer:
(a) In a p-type semiconductor, holes are the majority carriers and electrons are the minority carriers; in an n-type semiconductor, electrons are the majority carriers and holes are the minority carriers.
(b) On forward biasing, the barrier potential is reduced. Holes from the p-side move across the junction into the n-side, and electrons from the n-side move across into the p-side; these carriers recombine near and beyond the junction, and the movement of holes and electrons together constitutes the forward current, which flows conventionally from the p-side to the n-side inside the diode.
(c) Dynamic resistance is $r_d = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}$, found from the slope of the reverse characteristic near $V = -0.6$ V. Since this lies in the reverse-biased (saturation current) region where current changes very little with voltage, $\Delta I$ is very small, so the dynamic resistance is very high, of the order of $10^5$–$10^6$ $\Omega$.

questions.question: (a) What are majority and minority charge carriers of p-type and n-type semiconductors? (b) Explain briefly the formation of diffusion current and drift current in a p-n junction diode.
questions.answer:
(a) In an n-type semiconductor, electrons are the majority carriers and holes are the minority carriers.
In a p-type semiconductor, holes are the majority carriers and electrons are the minority carriers.
(b) Due to concentration gradient across the junction, majority carriers move from their region to the other (electrons from n to p, holes from p to n), constituting diffusion current.
This diffusion leaves behind ionized donors and acceptors, creating a depletion region and an electric field directed from n to p.
This field drives the minority carriers (electrons in p, holes in n) across the junction, constituting drift current, which flows opposite to the diffusion current.

questions.question: (a) Draw the energy-band diagrams for conductors, semiconductors and insulators at $T = 0$ K. How is an electron-hole pair formed in a semiconductor at room temperature? (b) Carbon and silicon both, are members of IV group of periodic table and have the same lattice structure. Carbon is an insulator whereas silicon is a semiconductor. Explain.
questions.answer:
For a conductor at $T = 0$ K, the conduction and valence bands overlap, so free electrons are available.
For an insulator, the forbidden energy gap $E_g$ is very large (~ $6$ eV), and the valence band is completely full while the conduction band is empty.
For a semiconductor, $E_g$ is small (~ $1$ eV), the valence band is full and conduction band empty at $0$ K.
At room temperature, some valence electrons gain thermal energy $\geq E_g$ and jump to the conduction band, leaving vacancies (holes) behind in the valence band; thus an electron-hole pair is formed.
Carbon (diamond) has a large $E_g$ (~ $5.4$ eV), so at room temperature no electrons can cross the gap and it behaves as an insulator.
Silicon has a much smaller $E_g$ (~ $1.1$ eV), so thermal energy at room temperature is sufficient to excite some electrons to the conduction band, making it a semiconductor.

questions.question: Differentiate between half-wave and full-wave rectification. With the help of a circuit diagram, explain the working of a full-wave rectifier.
questions.answer:
A half-wave rectifier uses a single diode and conducts only during one half of the input AC cycle, so output is obtained for only half the cycle, giving low ripple frequency (equal to input frequency) and low efficiency.
A full-wave rectifier uses two diodes (with a centre-tapped transformer) or four diodes (bridge) and conducts during both halves of the input cycle, giving continuous pulsating DC output with ripple frequency twice the input frequency and higher efficiency.
Working: the centre-tapped secondary gives voltages in opposite phase to the two diode anodes; during one half-cycle diode $D_1$ conducts and $D_2$ is reverse biased, during the other half $D_2$ conducts and $D_1$ is reverse biased.
Current through the load $R_L$ flows in the same direction in both halves, so a unidirectional pulsating output appears across $R_L$ in every half-cycle.

questions.question: Explain the process of formation of ’depletion layer’ and ’potential barrier’ in a p-n junction region of a diode, with the help of a suitable diagram. Which feature of junction diode makes it suitable for its use as a rectifier?
questions.answer:
When a p-n junction is formed, holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side and electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side due to the concentration gradient.
This leaves behind uncompensated negative acceptor ions near the junction on the p-side and positive donor ions on the n-side, creating a region depleted of mobile charge carriers, called the depletion layer.
The immobile ions set up an electric field directed from n to p across the junction, which opposes further diffusion of majority carriers; the corresponding potential difference is the potential barrier ($\approx 0.3$ V for Ge, $0.7$ V for Si).
The junction diode conducts significantly only when forward biased (barrier lowered) and offers very high resistance when reverse biased (barrier raised), i.e., it conducts current in only one direction; this asymmetric conduction property makes it suitable as a rectifier.

questions.question: Draw the circuit diagrams for obtaining the $V -I$ characteristics of a $p$- $n$ junction diode. Explain briefly the salient features of the $V -I$ characteristics in (i) forward biasing, and (ii) reverse biasing.
questions.answer:
Circuit: for forward bias, the p-side of the diode is connected to the positive terminal of a battery through a milliammeter and rheostat, with a voltmeter across the diode; for reverse bias, the battery polarity is reversed and a microammeter is used instead.
(i) Forward biasing: initially current is very small until the applied voltage exceeds the threshold/knee voltage, after which current increases rapidly and almost linearly with voltage, since the barrier potential is overcome and majority carriers flow easily.
(ii) Reverse biasing: current is very small (of the order of microamperes) and almost independent of applied voltage, called reverse saturation current, since it is due to minority carriers only; beyond a certain reverse voltage, breakdown occurs and current increases sharply.

questions.question: On the basis of energy band diagrams, distinguish between (i) an insulator, (ii) a semiconductor, and (iii) a conductor.
questions.answer:
(i) Insulator: the valence band is completely filled and the conduction band is empty, separated by a very large energy gap $E_g \approx 6$ eV or more, so electrons cannot be excited into the conduction band under normal conditions.
(ii) Semiconductor: valence band is full and conduction band empty at $0$ K, but $E_g$ is small ($\approx 1$ eV), so at room temperature some electrons acquire enough thermal energy to jump to the conduction band, giving small conductivity.
(iii) Conductor: the conduction and valence bands overlap (or the conduction band is partially filled), so $E_g = 0$ and electrons are freely available for conduction even at $0$ K.

questions.question: (a) Explain the characteristics of a p-n junction diode that makes it suitable for its use as a rectifier. (b) With the help of a circuit diagram, explain the working of a full wave rectifier.
questions.answer:
(a) A p-n junction diode offers very low resistance and conducts appreciable current when forward biased, but offers very high resistance and allows only a negligible current when reverse biased.
This property of conducting current in essentially one direction only allows it to convert AC (which reverses direction periodically) into a unidirectional pulsating output, making it suitable as a rectifier.
(b) In a full-wave rectifier, a centre-tapped transformer feeds two diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$ whose cathodes are joined at the load $R_L$, with the centre tap grounded.
During one half-cycle $D_1$ is forward biased and conducts while $D_2$ is reverse biased; during the next half-cycle $D_2$ conducts while $D_1$ is cut off.
Since current flows through $R_L$ in the same direction in both halves, a continuous pulsating unidirectional output is obtained across $R_L$ for the entire input cycle.

questions.question: Explain the following, giving reasons: (a) A doped semiconductor is electrically neutral. (b) In a p-n junction under equilibrium, there is no net current. (c) In a diode, the reverse current is practically not dependent on the applied voltage.
questions.answer:
(a) Doping only replaces some host atoms with impurity atoms of different valency; the number of protons and electrons introduced are equal, so the crystal as a whole carries no net charge and remains electrically neutral.
(b) At equilibrium, the diffusion current (majority carriers moving down the concentration gradient) is exactly balanced by the drift current (minority carriers moved by the junction field) in the opposite direction, so the two cancel and the net current across the junction is zero.
(c) The reverse current is due to minority carriers, whose number depends only on the rate of thermal generation of electron-hole pairs (i.e., on temperature), not on the applied voltage; hence it quickly saturates and remains practically constant with increasing reverse voltage until breakdown occurs.

questions.question: State the working principle of an LED. Write any two important advantages and two disadvantages of LED.
questions.answer:
An LED is a forward-biased p-n junction made of a suitable direct-bandgap semiconductor which emits light (spontaneous emission) when electrons recombine with holes at or near the junction, the photon energy released being approximately equal to the band gap $E_g$ (i.e., $h\nu \approx E_g$).
Advantages: (i) low operating voltage and power consumption, (ii) fast switching action with no warm-up time, and long life with high reliability.
Disadvantages: (i) performance degrades with rise in temperature, (ii) available only for a limited range of colours/wavelengths determined by the material's band gap.

questions.question: With the help of a circuit diagram, explain the working of a $p$- $n$ junction diode as a full-wave rectifier. Also draw its input and output waveforms.
questions.answer:
Circuit: the secondary of a transformer is centre-tapped, with its two ends connected to the anodes of diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$, whose cathodes are joined together and connected through load $R_L$ back to the centre tap.
During one half-cycle, the upper end of the secondary is positive, so $D_1$ is forward biased and conducts, sending current through $R_L$, while $D_2$ (reverse biased) is cut off.
During the next half-cycle, the polarity reverses, so $D_2$ conducts through $R_L$ while $D_1$ is cut off.
In both halves, current flows through $R_L$ in the same direction, so the output is a series of unidirectional pulses at twice the input frequency.
Waveform: the input is a sinusoidal AC wave (both positive and negative half-cycles), while the output consists of only positive humps (pulsating DC) for every half-cycle, with no negative portion.

questions.question: Briefly explain how emf is generated in a solar cell. Draw its I-V characteristics.
questions.answer:
A solar cell is a p-n junction that generates emf when solar radiation falls on it, without any external bias.
When photons of energy greater than the band gap fall near the junction, electron-hole pairs are generated on both sides.
The built-in field of the depletion region sweeps electrons to the n-side and holes to the p-side, so the n-side becomes negative and p-side positive, giving an open-circuit voltage $V_{OC}$.
On connecting a load, a short-circuit current $I_{SC}$ flows in the reverse direction of a normal diode.
I-V characteristic: the curve lies entirely in the fourth quadrant, starting at $I_{SC}$ on the current axis and meeting the voltage axis at $V_{OC}$, showing power is delivered by the cell (not consumed).

questions.question: Draw the energy band diagrams for conductors, semiconductors and insulators. Which band determines the electrical conductivity of a solid? How is the electrical conductivity of a semiconductor affected with rise in its temperature? Explain.
questions.answer:
Conductors: the conduction band and valence band overlap, so no energy gap exists and electrons move freely.
Insulators: a large energy gap ($E_g > 3$ eV) separates a completely filled valence band from an empty conduction band, so electrons cannot cross it.
Semiconductors: a small energy gap ($E_g \approx 1$ eV, e.g. $1.1$ eV for Si) separates the filled valence band from the empty conduction band.
It is the conduction band (and the gap $E_g$ between it and the valence band) that determines electrical conductivity, since only electrons in the conduction band can carry current.
With rise in temperature, more valence electrons acquire enough thermal energy to cross $E_g$ into the conduction band, increasing the number of free electrons and holes; hence the conductivity of a semiconductor increases (resistance decreases) with temperature.

questions.question: Answer the following, giving reason: (a) The resistance of a p-n junction is low when it is forward biased and is high when it is reverse biased. (b) Doping of intrinsic semiconductors is a necessity for making electronic devices. (c) Photodiodes are operated in reverse bias.
questions.answer:
(a) In forward bias the applied voltage opposes the built-in potential, narrowing the depletion region and lowering the barrier, so majority carriers cross easily giving low resistance; in reverse bias the depletion region widens and the barrier increases, allowing only a negligible minority-carrier current, giving high resistance.
(b) An intrinsic semiconductor has very few free carriers (only thermally generated pairs), so its conductivity is too low and uncontrollable for devices; doping introduces a controlled, fixed number of majority carriers (electrons in n-type, holes in p-type), giving a predictable, enhanced conductivity needed to fabricate diodes, transistors, etc.
(c) In reverse bias the reverse saturation current is negligible in the dark and changes almost linearly with the light intensity through generation of extra electron-hole pairs; this makes the change in current easily measurable and proportional to illumination, which is not the case in forward bias.

questions.question: (i) Draw V-I characteristics of a p-n junction diode. (ii) Differentiate between the threshold voltage and the breakdown voltage for a diode. (iii) Write the property of a junction diode which makes it suitable for rectification of ac voltages.
questions.answer:
(i) The V-I characteristic has two branches: in forward bias, current remains nearly zero until the threshold voltage is reached, after which it rises sharply (exponentially) with voltage; in reverse bias, only a small, almost constant reverse saturation current flows until the breakdown voltage, beyond which current increases abruptly.
(ii) Threshold (or cut-in) voltage is the forward voltage above which the forward current through the diode increases rapidly (about $0.7$ V for Si, $0.3$ V for Ge); breakdown voltage is the reverse voltage at which the reverse current increases sharply due to avalanche/zener breakdown, and it is much larger in magnitude than the threshold voltage.
(iii) A junction diode conducts current in only one direction (offers low resistance in forward bias and high resistance in reverse bias); this unidirectional conduction property makes it suitable for rectification of ac voltages.

questions.question: Draw circuit diagram and explain the working of a zener diode as a dc voltage regulator with the help of its I-V characteristic.
questions.answer:
Circuit: An unregulated dc input $V_i$ is connected through a series resistor $R_s$ to a zener diode connected in reverse bias, with the load $R_L$ connected in parallel with the zener; output voltage $V_o$ is taken across the load/zener.
Working: The zener is chosen so that its breakdown voltage equals the desired regulated output. As long as the input voltage stays above $V_Z$, the zener operates in its breakdown region, where its I-V characteristic is almost vertical, meaning current through it can change over a wide range while the voltage across it (hence $V_o$) stays essentially constant at $V_Z$.
If $V_i$ increases, the extra voltage drops across $R_s$ (extra current flows through the zener), and if $V_i$ decreases (or load current changes), the zener current adjusts accordingly, keeping $V_o$ constant.
Thus the sharp breakdown characteristic of the zener maintains a constant output voltage despite fluctuations in input voltage or load current.

questions.question: What is the purpose of heavy doping of p- and n-sides of a zener diode?
questions.answer:
Heavy doping makes the depletion region of the zener diode very thin, so a strong electric field ($\approx 10^7$ V/m) is set up across it even for a small reverse voltage.
This thin, highly-doped junction allows breakdown (zener/avalanche) to occur at a low, precisely defined reverse voltage $V_Z$, which is essential for the diode to be used reliably as a voltage regulator.

questions.question: With the help of a simple diagram, explain the working of a silicon solar cell, giving all three basic processes involved. Draw its I-V characteristic.
questions.answer:
A solar cell is basically a p-n junction with a thin, transparent p-layer on top so that light can reach the depletion region, with metal contacts on the front (grid) and back for collecting current.
Three basic processes:
1. Generation: photons with energy greater than the band gap are absorbed near the junction, creating electron-hole pairs.
2. Separation: the built-in electric field of the depletion region separates these pairs before they recombine, sweeping electrons to the n-side and holes to the p-side.
3. Collection: the accumulated electrons and holes are collected at the front and back metal contacts, driving current through the external circuit, so the cell acts as a source of emf.
I-V characteristic: the curve lies in the fourth quadrant, starting from the short-circuit current $I_{SC}$ on the current axis and reaching the open-circuit voltage $V_{OC}$ on the voltage axis, indicating that the cell delivers power to the external circuit.

questions.question: Draw the circuit diagram of a full wave rectifier using two p-n junction diodes. Explain its working and show input and output voltage variations.
questions.answer:
Circuit: The secondary of a transformer with a centre tap is connected to two diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$; the p-side of each diode is connected to the two ends of the secondary, their n-sides are joined together and connected through the load $R_L$ back to the centre tap.
Working: During one half cycle of the ac input, the upper end of the secondary is positive, so $D_1$ is forward biased and conducts, sending current through $R_L$; $D_2$ is reverse biased and does not conduct.
During the next half cycle, the lower end becomes positive, so $D_2$ conducts through $R_L$ while $D_1$ is reverse biased.
Thus current flows through $R_L$ in the same direction during both halves of the input cycle, so the output across $R_L$ consists of a series of positive pulses (rectified but pulsating dc) at twice the frequency of the ac input, unlike the sinusoidal (both positive and negative) input voltage waveform.

questions.question: What is the function of a solar cell? Briefly explain its working and draw its I-V characteristic curve.
questions.answer:
Function: A solar cell converts solar (light) energy directly into electrical energy (emf) without any external bias, using the photovoltaic effect at a p-n junction.
Working: When sunlight falls on the thin p-layer and reaches the depletion region, photons of energy greater than the band gap generate electron-hole pairs; the junction's built-in field separates them, sending electrons to the n-side and holes to the p-side, making the n-side negative and p-side positive; these charges are collected by metal contacts and drive current through the external circuit.
I-V characteristic: the graph is plotted in the fourth quadrant, with the curve starting at the short-circuit current $I_{SC}$ on the current axis and ending at the open-circuit voltage $V_{OC}$ on the voltage axis, showing that the cell supplies power rather than consuming it.

questions.question: (a) Plot V-I characteristics for an illuminated photodiode under reverse bias for three different illumination intensities $I_{1} > I_{2} > I_{3}$. (b) In a zener regulated power supply, a zener diode with $V_{Z} = 6$ V is used for regulation. The load current should be $4.0$ mA and zener current is five times the load current for unregulated input of $10$ V. Find the series resistor $R_{s}$ used in the power supply.
questions.answer:
(a) For each illumination intensity, the reverse-bias V-I curve is nearly flat (a small, almost constant reverse saturation/photocurrent independent of reverse voltage), but the curves are shifted so that the reverse current is largest for $I_1$, less for $I_2$, and least for $I_3$, i.e., the three horizontal lines lie in the order $I_1 > I_2 > I_3$ on the current axis, all parallel to the voltage axis.
(b) Given $V_Z = 6$ V, $I_L = 4.0$ mA, $I_Z = 5I_L = 20$ mA, $V_i = 10$ V.
Total current through $R_s$: $I = I_L + I_Z = 24$ mA.
$R_s = \dfrac{V_i - V_Z}{I} = \dfrac{10 - 6}{24 \times 10^{-3}}$
$R_s = 166.7\ \Omega$

questions.question: Name the diode which can act as a voltage regulator. Explain its working with the help of its labelled circuit diagram. Draw its V-I characteristic.
questions.answer:
The Zener diode acts as a voltage regulator.
Circuit: An unregulated dc input $V_i$ is connected through a series resistance $R_s$ to a Zener diode connected in reverse bias, with the load $R_L$ connected in parallel with the Zener diode; output $V_o$ is taken across the Zener diode.
Working: As long as input voltage is greater than the Zener breakdown voltage $V_z$, the Zener conducts and maintains the output voltage constant at $V_z$ across $R_L$; any increase in input voltage or load current is absorbed by change in current through $R_s$, keeping $V_o = V_z$ constant.
$V$-$I$ characteristic: In forward bias it behaves like an ordinary diode; in reverse bias, current is negligible until $V_z$ is reached, after which current increases sharply at almost constant voltage $V_z$ (a steep nearly vertical line in the reverse quadrant).

questions.question: (a) Why is an intrinsic semiconductor deliberately converted into an extrinsic semiconductor by adding impurity atoms? (b) Explain briefly the two processes that occur in p-n junction region to create a potential barrier.
questions.answer:
(a) An intrinsic semiconductor has very low conductivity at room temperature since only a few electron-hole pairs are thermally generated.
Doping with impurity atoms increases the number of free charge carriers (electrons or holes), thereby increasing conductivity and making the material useful for practical devices.
(b) Diffusion: due to concentration gradient across the junction, electrons diffuse from n-side to p-side and holes diffuse from p-side to n-side, leaving behind ionised donor and acceptor atoms near the junction.
Drift: the immobile ions create an electric field directed from n-side to p-side, which drives minority carriers (electrons from p to n, holes from n to p) in the opposite direction; equilibrium between diffusion and drift currents establishes the potential barrier.

questions.question: With the help of a circuit diagram, explain how two p-n junction diodes along with a centre tapped transformer can be used as a full wave rectifier.
questions.answer:
Circuit: A centre-tapped transformer's secondary has its two ends connected to the p-side of two diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$, whose n-sides are joined together and connected to one end of the load $R_L$; the other end of $R_L$ is connected to the centre tap of the secondary (taken as ground).
Working: During one half cycle of the ac input, the upper end of the secondary is positive, so $D_1$ is forward biased and conducts, while $D_2$ is reverse biased.
During the next half cycle, polarity reverses, so $D_2$ conducts while $D_1$ is reverse biased.
Thus current flows through $R_L$ in the same direction during both halves of the input cycle, giving a pulsating unidirectional (full wave rectified) output across $R_L$.

questions.question: (a) How are energy bands formed in a crystalline solid? (b) Draw the energy band diagrams for p-type and n-type semiconductors. Depict the donor/acceptor energy levels in these diagrams and write their significance.
questions.answer:
(a) In an isolated atom, electrons occupy discrete energy levels. When atoms come together to form a crystal, due to the interatomic interactions and Pauli's exclusion principle, each discrete level splits into a large number of closely spaced levels, forming continuous energy bands (valence band and conduction band) separated by a forbidden energy gap.
(b) For a p-type semiconductor: the energy band diagram shows the acceptor energy level $E_A$ located just above the top of the valence band $E_V$; electrons from the valence band easily jump to $E_A$, leaving holes in the valence band as majority carriers.
For an n-type semiconductor: the donor energy level $E_D$ lies just below the bottom of the conduction band $E_C$; electrons from $E_D$ easily jump into the conduction band, becoming majority carriers (electrons).
Significance: these shallow levels show that only a small ionisation energy is needed to release the extra carriers introduced by doping, explaining the high conductivity of extrinsic semiconductors.

questions.question: What is a solar cell? Draw its $V$ - $I$ characteristics. Explain the three processes involved in its working. OR Draw the circuit diagram of a full wave rectifier. Explain its working showing its input and output waveforms.
questions.answer:
A solar cell is a p-n junction diode that converts solar (light) energy directly into electrical energy based on the photovoltaic effect, without any external bias.
$V$-$I$ characteristic: It lies in the fourth quadrant of the $I$-$V$ plane, showing that the cell delivers power; the curve gives the open-circuit voltage $V_{oc}$ (at $I=0$) and short-circuit current $I_{sc}$ (at $V=0$).
Three processes: (1) Generation of electron-hole pairs due to absorption of photons of energy greater than the band gap, near or within the depletion region.
(2) Separation of electrons and holes due to the junction's electric field, electrons driven towards the n-side and holes towards the p-side.
(3) Collection of these charge carriers at the respective electrodes, causing a photovoltage and a current to flow through an external load, generating electric power.

questions.question: Explain the formation of potential barrier and depletion region in a p-n junction diode. What is effect of applying forward bias on the width of depletion region? OR What is photo diode? Briefly explain its working and draw its $V$ - $I$ characteristics.
questions.answer:
When a p-n junction is formed, electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side and holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side across the junction.
This diffusion leaves behind uncompensated positive ions on the n-side and negative ions on the p-side near the junction, creating a region depleted of mobile charge carriers, called the depletion region.
The immobile ions set up an internal electric field directed from n-side to p-side, which opposes further diffusion of majority carriers; this field corresponds to a potential difference called the potential barrier.
Effect of forward bias: the applied field opposes the internal field, so the effective barrier field decreases, causing the depletion region width to decrease and allowing majority carriers to diffuse across the junction easily.

questions.question: Three photo diodes $D_{1}$, $D_{2}$ and $D_{3}$ are made of semiconductors having band gaps of $2.5$ eV, $2$ eV and $3$ eV respectively. Which of them will not be able to detect light of wavelength $600$ nm?
questions.answer:
Photon energy corresponding to $\lambda = 600$ nm is $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1242 \text{ eV nm}}{600 \text{ nm}} \approx 2.07$ eV.
A photodiode can detect a given wavelength of light only if its band gap $E_g$ is less than or equal to the photon energy, i.e., $E_g \leq E$.
Here $D_1$ ($E_g = 2.5$ eV) and $D_3$ ($E_g = 3$ eV) have band gaps greater than $2.07$ eV, so they will not be able to detect light of wavelength $600$ nm; only $D_2$ ($E_g = 2$ eV) can detect it.

questions.question: Why photodiodes are required to operate in reverse bias? Explain.
questions.answer:
Photodiodes are operated in reverse bias because the reverse saturation current, though very small without illumination, changes linearly with the light intensity falling on the junction, giving a measurable and easily distinguishable change with incident light.
In reverse bias, the depletion region is wide and the internal electric field is strong, so photo-generated electron-hole pairs are quickly and efficiently swept across the junction, producing a fast photocurrent response.
Also, since the reverse current in the dark is very small, even a small photocurrent produced by light can be detected with good sensitivity, which would not be possible in forward bias where the current is already large.

questions.question: Describe briefly the functions of the three segments of n-p-n transistor.
questions.answer:
Emitter (n-segment): It is heavily doped and of moderate size; its function is to supply a large number of majority charge carriers (electrons) for current flow through the transistor.
Base (p-segment): It is very thin and lightly doped; its function is to allow most of the electrons injected from the emitter to pass through to the collector, with only a small fraction recombining with holes to constitute the base current.
Collector (n-segment): It is moderately doped and larger in size than the emitter; its function is to collect the majority charge carriers that pass through the base, constituting the collector current, and to dissipate the heat generated at the junction.

questions.question: Draw the circuit arrangement for studying the output characteristics of n-p-n transistor in CE configuration. Explain how the output characteristics is obtained.
questions.answer:
Circuit: The n-p-n transistor is connected in CE configuration with the emitter common to both input and output circuits, base-emitter junction forward biased through $V_{BB}$ and a variable resistance, and collector-emitter junction reverse biased through $V_{CC}$; a milliammeter measures collector current $I_C$ and voltmeter measures $V_{CE}$.
Procedure: For a fixed value of base current $I_B$, the collector-emitter voltage $V_{CE}$ is varied in steps by adjusting $V_{CC}$, and the corresponding collector current $I_C$ is noted at each step.
A graph is plotted between $I_C$ (y-axis) and $V_{CE}$ (x-axis) for this fixed $I_B$, giving one output characteristic curve.
This is repeated for several different fixed values of $I_B$ to obtain a family of output characteristic curves, each showing that $I_C$ rises sharply for small $V_{CE}$ and then becomes nearly constant (saturation followed by active region).

questions.question: Draw the circuit diagram of a full wave rectifier and explain its working. Also, give the input and output waveforms.
questions.answer:
Circuit: a centre-tapped transformer secondary feeds two diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$, whose free ends are joined and connected through a load resistance $R_L$ back to the centre tap, which is earthed.
Working: during one half cycle end A of secondary is positive, so $D_1$ is forward biased and conducts, sending current through $R_L$; during the next half cycle end B is positive, so $D_2$ conducts, sending current through $R_L$ in the same direction as before.
Since current flows through $R_L$ in the same direction in both half cycles, both halves of the ac input are rectified.
Waveforms: the input is a continuous sine wave, while the output across $R_L$ consists of a series of unidirectional pulses (each a rectified half sine), occurring at twice the input frequency.

questions.question: Give reason to explain why $n$ and $p$ regions of a Zener diode are heavily doped. Find the current through the Zener diode in the circuit given below: (Zener breakdown voltage is $15$ V)
questions.answer:
The $n$ and $p$ regions of a Zener diode are heavily doped so that the depletion region becomes extremely thin (of order $10^{-6}$ m); even a small reverse voltage then produces a very high electric field ($\sim 5\times10^{6}$ V/m) across the junction, causing breakdown (Zener/avalanche) at a well-defined, sharp reverse voltage $V_Z$.
For the circuit, applying Kirchhoff's law to the series resistor $R$ and the parallel combination of Zener and load $R_L$:
Current through $R$: $I = \dfrac{V_i - V_Z}{R}$
Current through load: $I_L = \dfrac{V_Z}{R_L}$
Current through Zener diode: $I_Z = I - I_L$, using $V_Z = 15$ V and the given $V_i$, $R$, $R_L$.

questions.question: Prove that in a common-emitter amplifier, the output and input differ in phase by $180^{^{\circ}}$. In a transistor, the change of base current by $30 \mu$ A produces change of $0.02$ V in the base-emitter voltage and a change of $4$ mA in the collector current. Calculate the current amplification factor and the load resistance used, if the voltage gain of the amplifier is $400$.
questions.answer:
In a CE amplifier, output is taken across $R_C$ as $V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_C R_C$.
When the input signal increases, base current $I_B$ increases, so $I_C = \beta I_B$ also increases, increasing the drop $I_C R_C$; hence $V_{CE}$ decreases.
Thus a rising input corresponds to a falling output, i.e., output is $180^{\circ}$ out of phase with input.
Numerical: $\beta_{ac} = \dfrac{\Delta I_C}{\Delta I_B} = \dfrac{4\times10^{-3}}{30\times10^{-6}} = 133.3$
Input resistance $r_i = \dfrac{\Delta V_{BE}}{\Delta I_B} = \dfrac{0.02}{30\times10^{-6}} = 666.7\ \Omega$
Voltage gain $A_v = \beta_{ac}\dfrac{R_C}{r_i} = 400 \Rightarrow R_C = \dfrac{400\times666.7}{133.3} \approx 2000\ \Omega = 2\ k\Omega$

questions.question: What is the reason to operate photodiodes in reverse bias? A p-n photodiode is fabricated from a semiconductor with a band gap of range of $2.5$ to $2.8$ eV. Calculate the range of wavelengths of the radiation which can be detected by the photodiode.
questions.answer:
A photodiode is operated in reverse bias because the reverse (drift) current due to light-generated minority carriers changes linearly and sensitively with light intensity, giving a fast and easily measurable response, unlike the forward current which is dominated by majority-carrier diffusion and is insensitive to illumination.
Using $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E_g}$ with $hc \approx 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm:
For $E_g = 2.5$ eV: $\lambda = \dfrac{1240}{2.5} \approx 496$ nm
For $E_g = 2.8$ eV: $\lambda = \dfrac{1240}{2.8} \approx 443$ nm
So the photodiode can detect wavelengths in the range $443$ nm to $496$ nm.

questions.question: Draw the circuit diagram of a full wave rectifier. Explain its working principle. Show the input waveforms given to the diodes $D_{1}$ and $D_{2}$ and the corresponding output waveforms obtained at the load connected to the circuit.
questions.answer:
Circuit: the secondary of a centre-tapped transformer is connected to two diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$; their cathodes (or anodes) are joined together and connected through the load $R_L$ to the earthed centre tap.
Working: in one half cycle, one end of the secondary is at higher potential, forward biasing $D_1$, which conducts and drives current through $R_L$; in the next half cycle the other end becomes positive, forward biasing $D_2$, which conducts and drives current through $R_L$ in the same direction as before, while the other diode remains reverse biased.
Input waveform: $D_1$ and $D_2$ receive sinusoidal voltages that are $180^{\circ}$ out of phase with each other (each conducting during alternate half cycles).
Output waveform: the current/voltage across $R_L$ is a series of unidirectional pulses obtained by combining the conducting half cycles of both diodes, giving a ripple at twice the supply frequency.

questions.question: (a) (i) Write the truth tables of the logic gates marked $P$ and $Q$ in the given circuit. (ii) Write the truth table for the circuit. (b) Why are NOR gates considered as universal gates? OR (a) Explain how a potential barrier is developed in a p-n junction diode. (b) Draw the circuit arrangement for studying the V-I characteristics of a p-n junction diode in reverse bias. Plot the V-I characteristics in this case.
questions.answer:
(a) When a p-n junction is formed, electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side and holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side because of the concentration gradient across the junction.
This diffusion leaves behind uncompensated ionized donor ions (positive) on the n-side and ionized acceptor ions (negative) on the p-side near the junction, forming a depletion region.
The exposed ions set up an internal electric field directed from n to p, which opposes further diffusion of majority carriers; equilibrium is reached when the diffusion current equals the drift current, and this internal field corresponds to a potential barrier $V_0$ (about $0.3$ V for Ge, $0.7$ V for Si).
(b) Circuit: the p-side of the diode is connected to the negative terminal and the n-side to the positive terminal of a battery, in series with a milliammeter/microammeter and rheostat, with a voltmeter across the diode.
Characteristics: the reverse current is very small (of the order of $\mu$A) and remains almost constant (saturation current) with increasing reverse voltage, until the breakdown voltage is reached, beyond which the current rises sharply.

questions.question: Draw the energy band diagram of (i) n-type, and (ii) p-type semiconductors at temperature $T > 0$ K. In the case of n-type Si-semiconductor, the donor energy level is slightly below the bottom of conduction band whereas in p-type semiconductor, the acceptor energy level is slightly above the top of valence band. Explain, giving examples, what role do these energy levels play in conduction and valence bands.
questions.answer:
n-type semiconductor: the donor energy level $E_d$ lies just below the bottom of the conduction band, so at $T>0$ K, the small thermal energy is sufficient to ionize donor atoms (e.g., pentavalent P, As in Si), exciting their extra loosely bound electrons into the conduction band; these electrons become the majority charge carriers responsible for conduction.
p-type semiconductor: the acceptor energy level $E_a$ lies just above the top of the valence band, so electrons from the valence band easily jump into these empty acceptor states (e.g., trivalent B, In in Si get an electron from valence band), leaving behind holes in the valence band as majority carriers responsible for conduction.
In both cases, the closeness of the impurity level to the respective band means only a small thermal energy is needed to create free carriers, which greatly increases conductivity compared to the intrinsic semiconductor.

questions.question: With what considerations in view is a photodiode fabricated? Explain its working with the help of a suitable diagram. With the help of V-I characteristics, state how photodiode is used to detect optical signals.
questions.answer:
A photodiode is fabricated using a semiconductor whose band gap is close to the energy of the photons to be detected, so that light is efficiently absorbed near the junction; it is operated in reverse bias to give a fast, sensitive response.
Working: the junction is kept close to the surface with a transparent window so that incident light falls on or near the depletion region; absorbed photons generate electron-hole pairs, and under reverse bias the built-in field sweeps these minority carriers across the junction, adding to the reverse saturation current, which increases with light intensity.
V-I characteristics: for a fixed reverse voltage, the family of I-V curves for different illumination intensities shows the reverse current increasing almost linearly with intensity while remaining nearly independent of the reverse voltage, so the diode current can be used to measure the optical signal.

questions.question: How is a light emitting diode fabricated? Briefly explain the basic processes involved in the emission of spontaneous radiation from it. Write two advantages of LED lamps over the incandescent low power lamps.
questions.answer:
An LED is fabricated using a heavily doped direct band gap semiconductor (such as GaAs, GaAsP or GaP), with the junction kept very close to the surface and encapsulated in a transparent resin so that emitted light can escape without excessive reabsorption.
Basic process: under forward bias, electrons are injected from the n-region and holes from the p-region across the junction; these excess minority carriers recombine radiatively with majority carriers near the junction, releasing energy approximately equal to the band gap $E_g$ as a photon (spontaneous emission), the photon's wavelength being decided by the choice of semiconductor material.
Advantages over incandescent lamps: (1) much lower power consumption and operating voltage for the same light output, and (2) faster switching, no warm-up time, and much longer working life with greater robustness.

questions.question: How is Zener diode fabricated? Draw its I-V characteristic and use this to explain the working of a Zener diode as a voltage regulator.
questions.answer:
A Zener diode is fabricated from heavily doped p and n regions so that the depletion layer is very thin, allowing a high electric field to develop across the junction even at a small reverse voltage, giving a sharp, well-defined breakdown voltage $V_Z$.
I-V characteristic: the forward branch is similar to an ordinary diode; in the reverse direction, current remains very small until the reverse voltage reaches $V_Z$, beyond which the current rises sharply while the voltage across the diode stays almost constant at $V_Z$ (a nearly vertical curve).
Voltage regulator: the Zener diode is connected in reverse bias across the load, in series with a resistor $R$ from the unregulated dc supply; as long as the input voltage stays above $V_Z$ and the Zener current lies between $I_{Z,min}$ and $I_{Z,max}$, any excess current due to changes in input voltage or load current is absorbed by the Zener diode, keeping the load voltage fixed at $V_Z$.

questions.question: The figure shows the V-I characteristic of a semiconductor diode designed to operate under reverse bias. (a) Identify the semiconductor diode used. (b) Draw the circuit diagram to obtain the given characteristics of this device. (c) Briefly explain one use of this device.
questions.answer:
(a) The device is a Zener diode, since it shows a sharp increase in reverse current after a certain reverse voltage $V_z$ (breakdown voltage), the reverse characteristic being nearly flat before breakdown.
(b) Circuit: A battery, rheostat and milliammeter are connected in series with the Zener diode in reverse bias (n-side to positive terminal), with a voltmeter across the diode to note $V$ for corresponding reverse current $I$.
(c) It is used as a voltage regulator: connected in reverse bias across a fluctuating supply through a series resistance, it maintains a constant output voltage $V_z$ across the load irrespective of variations in input voltage or load current.

questions.question: (a) Differentiate between three segments of an n-p-n transistor on the basis of their size and level of doping. (b) Draw a plot of transfer characteristic and show which portion of the characteristic is used in amplification and why.
questions.answer:
(a) Emitter: moderately sized, heavily doped, supplies majority charge carriers.
Base: very thin and lightly doped, allows most carriers from emitter to pass to collector.
Collector: largest in size, moderately doped, collects the charge carriers.
(b) Transfer characteristic is a plot of output voltage $V_{CE}$ versus input current $I_B$; it shows three regions - cut-off, active and saturation.
The active (linear) region, between cut-off and saturation, is used for amplification because here $V_{CE}$ varies linearly with $I_B$, giving faithful (undistorted) amplification of the signal.

questions.question: (a) A student wants to use two p-n junction diodes to convert alternating current into direct current. Draw the labelled circuit diagram she would use and explain how it works. (b) Give the truth table and circuit symbol for NAND gate.
questions.answer:
(a) Circuit: Two diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$ are connected to the two ends of a centre-tapped secondary of a transformer, with the centre tap grounded; the load $R_L$ is connected between the common cathode point and ground, giving a full-wave rectifier.
Working: During one half cycle $D_1$ is forward biased and conducts, while during the next half cycle $D_2$ is forward biased and conducts; thus current flows through $R_L$ in the same direction during both halves of the AC cycle, producing pulsating unidirectional (DC) output.
(b) NAND gate: $Y = \overline{A.B}$
Truth table: $A=0,B=0,Y=1$; $A=0,B=1,Y=1$; $A=1,B=0,Y=1$; $A=1,B=1,Y=0$.
Symbol: an AND gate symbol followed by a small circle (bubble) at the output terminal.

questions.question: Draw the typical input and output characteristics of an n-p-n transistor in CE configuration. Show how these characteristics can be used to determine (a) the input resistance $(r_{i})$, and (b) current amplification factor $(\beta)$.
questions.answer:
Input characteristic: a plot of base current $I_B$ versus base-emitter voltage $V_{BE}$ at constant $V_{CE}$, resembling a forward-biased diode curve.
Output characteristic: a plot of collector current $I_C$ versus collector-emitter voltage $V_{CE}$ for different fixed values of $I_B$, showing active, saturation and cut-off regions.
(a) Input resistance $r_i = \left(\dfrac{\Delta V_{BE}}{\Delta I_B}\right)_{V_{CE}}$, found from the slope of the input characteristic at constant $V_{CE}$.
(b) Current amplification factor $\beta = \left(\dfrac{\Delta I_C}{\Delta I_B}\right)_{V_{CE}}$, found from the output characteristics by taking two curves at constant $V_{CE}$ and dividing the change in $I_C$ by the corresponding change in $I_B$.

questions.question: Write the two processes that take place in the formation of a p-n junction. Explain with the help of a diagram, the formation of depletion region and barrier potential in a p-n junction.
questions.answer:
Two processes: diffusion of majority charge carriers across the junction (electrons from n-side to p-side and holes from p-side to n-side), and drift of minority carriers due to the electric field so set up.
Diagram (described): When p-type and n-type semiconductors are joined, electrons diffuse from n to p and holes diffuse from p to n, leaving behind uncompensated ionized donors (positive) on the n-side and ionized acceptors (negative) on the p-side near the junction.
This region, depleted of mobile charge carriers, is called the depletion region, and the electric field developed across it, directed from n-side to p-side, opposes further diffusion; the resulting potential difference across the depletion region is the barrier potential.

questions.question: For a CE-transistor amplifier, the audio signal voltage across the collector resistance of $2 k\Omega$ is $2 V$. Given the current amplification factor of the transistor is 100, find the input signal voltage and base current, if the base resistance is $1 k\Omega$.
questions.answer:
$I_C = \dfrac{V_C}{R_C} = \dfrac{2\text{ V}}{2\text{ k}\Omega} = 1$ mA
$I_B = \dfrac{I_C}{\beta} = \dfrac{1\text{ mA}}{100} = 0.01$ mA $= 10\ \mu$A
Input signal voltage $V_i = I_B \times R_B = 0.01\text{ mA} \times 1\text{ k}\Omega = 0.01$ V $= 10$ mV

questions.question: A zener diode is fabricated by heavily doping both p- and n- sides of the junction. Explain, why? Briefly explain the use of zener diode as a dc voltage regulator with the help of a circuit diagram.
questions.answer:
Heavy doping on both sides makes the depletion region very thin, so a moderate reverse voltage produces a very high electric field across it (of order $10^7$ V/m), sufficient to break covalent bonds and cause Zener breakdown at a low, precisely defined reverse voltage $V_z$.
Circuit: The unregulated DC input is connected to the Zener diode in reverse bias through a series resistance $R_s$, with the load $R_L$ connected in parallel with the diode.
As long as the input voltage stays above $V_z$, the Zener diode conducts and maintains the voltage across itself (and hence across $R_L$) constant at $V_z$, any excess voltage being dropped across $R_s$, and any change in input voltage or load current is absorbed by a change in the Zener current, keeping the output voltage regulated.

questions.question: Explain briefly with the help of necessary diagrams, the forward and the reverse biasing of a p-n junction diode. Also draw their characteristic curves in the two cases.
questions.answer:
Forward biasing: The p-side is connected to the positive terminal and n-side to the negative terminal of the battery; this reduces the barrier potential and width of the depletion region, allowing majority carriers to diffuse easily, so a large current flows for a small applied voltage after the threshold voltage.
Reverse biasing: The p-side is connected to the negative terminal and n-side to the positive terminal; this increases the barrier potential and depletion width, so only a small reverse saturation current (due to minority carriers) flows, remaining nearly constant with voltage until breakdown occurs.
Characteristic curves: In the forward-bias curve, current $I$ rises slowly at first then increases sharply after a threshold voltage (first quadrant); in the reverse-bias curve, current remains small and nearly constant (a few $\mu$A) until breakdown, when it increases suddenly (third quadrant, on a much smaller current scale).

questions.question: (a) In the following diagram, is the junction diode forward biased or reverse biased? (b) Draw the circuit diagram of a full wave rectifier and state how it works.
questions.answer:
(a) The diode is forward biased if its p-side is connected to the higher potential terminal (current allowed to flow through it in the circuit); it is reverse biased if the p-side is connected to the lower potential terminal (no conventional current path through the diode).
(b) Circuit: Two diodes $D_1$, $D_2$ are joined to the two ends of a centre-tapped transformer secondary, with the centre tap earthed, and the load $R_L$ connected between the common diode terminal and earth.
Working: In each half cycle of the AC input, one of the two diodes is forward biased and conducts, so current flows through $R_L$ in the same direction during both halves, giving a continuous pulsating DC output for the complete cycle.

questions.question: (a) Write the functions of the three segments of a transistor. (b) The figure shows the input waveforms $A$ and $B$ for ’AND’ gate. Draw the output waveform and write the truth table for this logic gate.
questions.answer:
(a) Emitter: heavily doped, emits (supplies) majority charge carriers into the base.
Base: thin and lightly doped, passes most of the injected carriers from emitter to collector with little recombination.
Collector: moderately doped and largest, collects the charge carriers arriving from the base and constitutes the output circuit.
(b) For an AND gate, $Y = A.B$, so output $Y$ is HIGH only when both inputs $A$ and $B$ are HIGH simultaneously; the output waveform is HIGH only during the time intervals where both input waveforms are HIGH together, and LOW otherwise.
Truth table: $A=0,B=0,Y=0$; $A=0,B=1,Y=0$; $A=1,B=0,Y=0$; $A=1,B=1,Y=1$.

questions.question: (a) In the following diagram, which bulb out of $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ will glow and why? (b) Draw a diagram of an illuminated p-n junction solar cell. (c) Explain briefly the three processes due to which generation of emf takes place in a solar cell.
questions.answer:
(a) Bulb $B_2$ will glow, since the solar cell forward-biases the diode-like arm containing $B_2$ and it conducts, while the arm with $B_1$ remains reverse biased/non-conducting depending on circuit polarity; effectively current flows through the path allowed by the p-n junction's forward direction.
(b) A solar cell diagram shows a thin, heavily doped $n$-layer on top of a thicker $p$-layer, with a metal grid (finger electrodes) on the illuminated top surface for current collection and a metal contact covering the back of the $p$-layer, connected to an external load.
(c) Generation of EMF occurs due to: (i) generation of electron-hole pairs by photons of energy greater than the band gap near the junction; (ii) separation of electrons and holes by the built-in electric field of the depletion region, electrons moving to the $n$-side and holes to the $p$-side; (iii) collection of these separated charges by the electrodes, creating a photovoltage across the junction.

questions.question: (a) Draw the circuit diagram for studying the characteristics of a transistor in common emitter configuration. Explain briefly and show how input and output characteristics are drawn. (b) The figure shows input waveforms $A$ and $B$ to a logic gate. Draw the output waveform for an OR gate. Write the truth table for this logic gate and draw its logic symbol.
questions.answer:
(a) The circuit has the base-emitter junction forward biased through battery $V_{BB}$ with a rheostat, and the collector-emitter junction reverse biased through battery $V_{CC}$; a milliammeter measures $I_B$ in the base circuit and another measures $I_C$ in the collector circuit, with voltmeters across $V_{BE}$ and $V_{CE}$.
Input characteristics are drawn by plotting $I_B$ versus $V_{BE}$ at constant $V_{CE}$; output characteristics are drawn by plotting $I_C$ versus $V_{CE}$ at constant $I_B$.
(b) For an OR gate, output $Y = A + B$, so $Y$ is HIGH whenever $A$ or $B$ (or both) is HIGH, and LOW only when both are LOW.
Truth table: $A=0,B=0,Y=0$; $A=0,B=1,Y=1$; $A=1,B=0,Y=1$; $A=1,B=1,Y=1$.
The logic symbol is the curved-back, pointed-front OR gate shape with inputs $A$, $B$ on the left and output $Y$ on the right.

questions.question: (a) Draw the circuit diagram of an n-p-n transistor amplifier in common emitter configuration. (b) Derive an expression for voltage gain of the amplifier and hence show that the output voltage is in opposite phase with the input voltage.
questions.answer:
(a) The circuit shows an $n$-$p$-$n$ transistor in CE configuration with the emitter common to input and output, base-emitter junction forward biased via $V_{BB}$ and input signal $v_i$ in series, collector-emitter junction reverse biased via $V_{CC}$ through load resistance $R_C$, and output taken across $R_C$.
(b) Small change in base current $\Delta I_B$ produces a change in collector current $\Delta I_C = \beta \Delta I_B$, causing change in output voltage $\Delta V_0 = \Delta I_C R_C$, while input voltage change is $\Delta V_i = \Delta I_B R_i$.
Voltage gain $A_v = \dfrac{\Delta V_0}{\Delta V_i} = \dfrac{\beta R_C}{R_i}$.
As $I_C$ increases, $V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_C R_C$ decreases, so an increase in input voltage causes a decrease in output voltage; hence output is $180°$ out of phase with input.

questions.question: (a) In the following diagram ’ $S$’ is a semiconductor. Would you increase or decrease the value of $R$ to keep the reading of the ammeter $A$ constant when $S$ is heated? Give reason for your answer. (b) Draw the circuit diagram of a photodiode and explain its working. Draw its $I -V$ characteristics.
questions.answer:
(a) $R$ should be increased, because heating a semiconductor decreases its resistance (more charge carriers are thermally generated), so $R$ must be increased proportionately to keep the total circuit resistance, and hence the ammeter reading, constant.
(b) The photodiode circuit has the $p$-$n$ junction connected in reverse bias with a battery and microammeter in series, with light allowed to fall on the junction through a window.
When light of energy greater than the band gap falls on the junction, electron-hole pairs are generated; these are swept by the junction field to give a reverse current proportional to the incident light intensity.
The $I$-$V$ characteristics show a family of curves in the third/fourth quadrant, where reverse current increases (becomes more negative) with increasing illumination intensity for the same reverse voltage, and is nearly independent of reverse voltage.

questions.question: (i) Explain with the help of a diagram the formation of depletion region and barrier potential in a $pn$ junction. (ii) Draw the circuit diagram of a half wave rectifier and explain its working.
questions.answer:
(i) When a $p$-$n$ junction is formed, holes diffuse from the $p$-side to the $n$-side and electrons diffuse from the $n$-side to the $p$-side, leaving behind uncompensated ionized acceptors (negative) on the $p$-side and donors (positive) on the $n$-side near the junction.
This region, depleted of mobile charge carriers, is called the depletion region, and the resulting internal electric field opposes further diffusion, creating a barrier potential (about $0.3$ V for Ge, $0.7$ V for Si) that must be overcome for further current flow.
(ii) A half wave rectifier circuit has a transformer secondary connected to a single diode in series with a load resistance $R_L$.
During the positive half cycle of the AC input, the diode is forward biased and conducts, so current flows through $R_L$ and a pulse of output voltage appears; during the negative half cycle, the diode is reverse biased and does not conduct, so output is zero, giving a unidirectional, pulsating output for only half of each cycle.

questions.question: For a CE-transistor amplifier, the audio signal voltage across the collector resistance of $2$ k $\Omega$ is $2$ V. Suppose the current amplification factor of the transistor is $100$, find the input signal voltage and base current, if the base resistance is $1$ k $\Omega$.
questions.answer:
Voltage gain in terms of current gain: $A_v = \beta \dfrac{R_C}{R_i}$
Here $\beta = 100$, $R_C = 2$ k$\Omega$, $R_i = 1$ k$\Omega$, so $A_v = 100 \times \dfrac{2}{1} = 200$
Input signal voltage: $v_i = \dfrac{v_0}{A_v} = \dfrac{2}{200} = 0.01$ V
Base current: $i_B = \dfrac{v_i}{R_i} = \dfrac{0.01}{1000} = 1 \times 10^{-5}$ A $= 10\ \mu$A

questions.question: What is Global Positioning System? Explain its working principle in brief.
questions.answer:
The Global Positioning System (GPS) is a satellite-based navigation system that determines the precise position, velocity and time of a receiver anywhere on or near the Earth's surface.
It consists of a constellation of about $24$ satellites orbiting the Earth, each continuously transmitting signals containing its precise position and the time of transmission.
A GPS receiver on the ground picks up signals from at least four satellites simultaneously and calculates the time delay for each signal to arrive.
Using the known speed of the electromagnetic wave ($c$) and these time delays, the receiver computes its distance from each satellite by trilateration, and by combining these distances, determines its exact latitude, longitude and altitude.

questions.question: Explain briefly, with the help of a circuit diagram, the transistor action of npn transistor in CE configuration. Draw the typical shapes of input and output characteristics.
questions.answer:
In CE configuration, the emitter is common to both input (base-emitter) and output (collector-emitter) circuits; the base-emitter junction is forward biased and the base-collector junction is reverse biased.
A small forward bias at the emitter-base junction causes electrons (majority carriers in the $n$-type emitter) to be injected into the thin, lightly doped base; most of these diffuse across the base and are swept into the collector by the reverse-biased junction, giving $I_C \approx I_E$, while only a small fraction recombines to constitute $I_B$, so $I_E = I_B + I_C$ and small changes in $I_B$ produce large changes in $I_C$ (current amplification, $I_C = \beta I_B$).
Input characteristic ($I_B$ vs $V_{BE}$ at constant $V_{CE}$) resembles a forward-biased diode curve, rising after a threshold voltage.
Output characteristic ($I_C$ vs $V_{CE}$ at constant $I_B$) shows $I_C$ rising steeply for small $V_{CE}$ then nearly saturating (flattening) for larger $V_{CE}$, with a separate curve for each $I_B$ value.

questions.question: (i) Describe the working of photodiode by drawing the circuit diagram. (ii) Draw the characteristics of a photodiode for different illumination intensities. (iii) Why is photodiode operated in reverse bias even though the reverse bias current is much weaker than the current in forward bias?
questions.answer:
(i) A photodiode is a $p$-$n$ junction operated under reverse bias, connected in series with a battery and a microammeter, with the junction exposed to light through a transparent window.
When photons of energy greater than the band gap fall near the junction, electron-hole pairs are generated; the junction's electric field separates them, sweeping electrons to the $n$-side and holes to the $p$-side, producing a reverse (photo) current proportional to the incident light intensity.
(ii) The $I$-$V$ characteristics show a family of nearly horizontal curves below the voltage axis, where the reverse current is almost independent of reverse voltage but increases with increasing illumination intensity.
(iii) A photodiode is operated in reverse bias because, although the current is weaker than in forward bias, the reverse (photo)current changes linearly and significantly with light intensity, whereas in forward bias the diode current is dominated by the large forward diffusion current and is not sensitive to small changes caused by light; reverse bias also gives a faster response.

questions.question: (i) Name two important processes that occur during the formation of a pn junction. (ii) Draw the circuit diagram of a full wave rectifier along with the input and output waveforms. Briefly explain how the output voltage/current is unidirectional.
questions.answer:
(i) The two important processes are diffusion of majority charge carriers (holes from $p$-side, electrons from $n$-side) across the junction, and drift of minority carriers due to the electric field set up in the depletion region.
(ii) A full wave rectifier circuit uses a center-tapped transformer secondary connected to two diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$, with the load resistance $R_L$ connected between the diode outputs (common cathode/anode point) and the center tap.
During one half cycle, $D_1$ is forward biased and conducts while $D_2$ is reverse biased, giving output current through $R_L$ in one direction; during the next half cycle, $D_2$ conducts and $D_1$ is cut off, again giving current through $R_L$ in the same direction.
Thus current flows through $R_L$ in the same direction for both halves of the AC cycle, giving a unidirectional, pulsating output for the complete cycle (unlike half wave rectification where output exists for only half the cycle).

questions.question: (i) Distinguish between a conductor and a semi conductor on the basis of energy band diagram. (ii) The following figure shows the input waveforms ($A$, $B$) and the output waveform ($Y$ ) of a gate. Identify the gate, write its truth table and draw its logic symbol.
questions.answer:
(i) In a conductor the conduction band and valence band overlap, or the conduction band is partially filled, so electrons are freely available for conduction even at very low temperature. In a semiconductor there is a small energy gap $E_g \approx 1$ eV between the valence and conduction bands, so only a few electrons cross to the conduction band at room temperature, giving small but finite conductivity.
(ii) The output $Y$ is high only when both inputs $A$ and $B$ are high simultaneously, so the gate is an AND gate.
Truth table: $A=0,B=0,Y=0$; $A=0,B=1,Y=0$; $A=1,B=0,Y=0$; $A=1,B=1,Y=1$.
Logic symbol: a D-shaped block with inputs $A$, $B$ entering the flat side and output $Y$ leaving the curved side, labelled AND.

questions.question: (i) Explain briefly the process of emission of light by a Light Emitting Diode (LED). (ii) Which semiconductors are preferred to make LEDs and why? (iii) Give two advantages of using LEDs over conventional incandescent lamps.
questions.answer:
(i) In a forward biased LED, electrons from the $n$-side and holes from the $p$-side are injected across the junction and recombine near it; the energy released in this recombination is emitted as light (photons) of energy $\approx E_g$.
(ii) Direct band gap semiconductors such as $GaAs$, $GaAsP$ and $GaP$ are preferred because recombination there releases the energy directly as a photon without the phonon (heat) loss that occurs in indirect band gap materials, giving high light output efficiency.
(iii) Advantages over incandescent lamps: low operating voltage, low power consumption and low heat generation; longer life, faster switching (no warm-up time) and greater robustness/reliability.

questions.question: Draw a circuit diagram of a common emitter amplifier using n-p-n transistor. Derive an expression for the current gain $\beta_{ac}$.
questions.answer:
Circuit: an $n$-$p$-$n$ transistor with emitter grounded (common to input and output); input signal is applied between base and emitter via a coupling capacitor, base bias set by $R_B$ and $V_{BB}$; output is taken across a load resistor $R_C$ connected between collector and $V_{CC}$, coupled out through a capacitor.
Derivation: A small input signal changes the base-emitter voltage, producing a change $\Delta I_B$ in base current, which in turn produces a change $\Delta I_C$ in collector current at constant $V_{CE}$.
The ac current gain is defined as
$\beta_{ac} = \left(\dfrac{\Delta I_C}{\Delta I_B}\right)_{V_{CE} = \text{constant}}$
obtained from the slope of the $I_C$ versus $I_B$ output characteristic at fixed $V_{CE}$.

questions.question: Write two important considerations used while fabricating a Zener diode. Explain, with the help of a circuit diagram, the principle and working of a Zener diode as voltage regulator.
questions.answer:
