By Huygens' principle, as point $A$ touches the surface, secondary wavelets spread out from $A$ and $B$; by the time the wavelet from $B$ reaches $C$ on the surface, the wavelet from $A$ has travelled an equal distance $v\tau$ and spread to a sphere; the common tangent $CD$ gives the new reflected wavefront.
Since $AC = BC$ (both surfaces are drawn common to the two triangles) and $AD = BC = v\tau$, triangles $ABC$ and $DCA$ are congruent, giving $\angle i = \angle r$, so the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.

questions.question: Define the term, "refractive index" of a medium. Verify Snell’s law of refraction when a plane wavefront is propagating from a denser to a rarer medium.
questions.answer:
Refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in that medium, $n = c/v$; equivalently it equals the ratio of sine of angle of incidence to sine of angle of refraction for light entering that medium.
Consider a plane wavefront $AB$ travelling in a denser medium (speed $v_1$) incident on the denser–rarer interface at angle $i$. As the point $A$ reaches the surface, secondary wavelets from $B$ travel to $C$ in time $\tau$, while the wavelet from $A$ travels into the rarer medium (speed $v_2 > v_1$) a distance $AD = v_2\tau$; the tangent $CD$ is the refracted wavefront.
From the geometry, $\sin i = BC/AC = v_1\tau/AC$ and $\sin r = AD/AC = v_2\tau/AC$, so $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$, which is Snell's law, with $\sin r > \sin i$ confirming bending away from the normal on going from denser to rarer medium.

questions.question: (a) Explain how an unpolarised light gets polarised when incident on the interface separating the two transparent media. (b) Green light is incident at the polarising angle on a certain transparent medium. The angle of refraction is $30^{^{\circ}}$. Find (i) polarising angle, and (ii) refractive index of the medium.
questions.answer:
(a) When unpolarised light strikes the interface between two media at a particular angle called the polarising angle $i_p$, the reflected ray is found to be completely plane polarised (with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence), while the refracted ray remains partially polarised; at this angle the reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular, giving Brewster's law $n = \tan i_p$.
(b) Since $i_p + r = 90^{\circ}$, $i_p = 90^{\circ}-30^{\circ} = 60^{\circ}$.
Refractive index $n = \tan i_p = \tan 60^{\circ} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.732$.

questions.question: (a) Define a wavefront. Using Huygens’ geometrical construction, explain with the help of a diagram how the plane wavefront travels from the instant $t_{1}$ to $t_{2}$ in air. (b) A plane wavefront is incident on a convex lens. Explain, with the help of the diagram, the shape of the refracted wavefront formed.
questions.answer:
(a) A wavefront is the locus of all points vibrating in the same phase at a given instant. By Huygens' construction, every point on the wavefront at $t_1$ acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets; drawing these wavelets of radius $v\Delta t$ (where $\Delta t = t_2-t_1$) from each point and constructing their common tangent (envelope) gives the new wavefront at $t_2$, which for a plane wavefront in air remains plane and parallel to the wavefront at $t_1$, displaced forward by $v\Delta t$.
(b) When a plane wavefront falls on a convex lens, the central part of the wavefront passes through a greater thickness of glass than the edges, so it is delayed more (travels slower in glass), while the edges are delayed less; consequently the emerging wavefront becomes spherical, converging towards the focus of the lens.

questions.question: (a) Good quality sunglasses made of polaroids are preferred over ordinary coloured glasses. Explain why. (b) How is plane polarized light defined? (c) A beam of plane polarised light is passed through a polaroid. Show graphically, variation of the intensity of the transmitted light with angle of rotation of the polaroid.
questions.answer:
(a) Ordinary coloured glasses merely reduce the total intensity of light reaching the eye but let both horizontal and vertical vibrations through, so glare (which is largely polarised due to reflection from surfaces like water/roads) still passes; polaroid sunglasses have their transmission axis oriented to absorb the horizontally polarised reflected glare while transmitting the rest, giving much better glare reduction.
(b) Plane polarised light is light in which the electric field vector oscillates only along one fixed direction (in a plane containing the direction of propagation), instead of in all directions perpendicular to propagation as in unpolarised light.
(c) By Malus's law, $I = I_0\cos^2\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the polaroid's axis and the plane of polarisation; the graph of $I$ versus $\theta$ is a $\cos^2\theta$ curve, maximum ($I_0$) at $\theta=0^{\circ},180^{\circ}$ and zero at $\theta=90^{\circ},270^{\circ}$.

questions.question: (a) What do you understand by coherent sources? (b) Derive the expression for the intensity distribution in the interference pattern on the screen when two harmonic waves having same amplitude ($a$) and phase difference ($\phi$) are superposed on each other. Hence obtain the conditions for constructive and destructive interference.
questions.answer:
(a) Coherent sources are two sources that emit light waves of the same frequency (wavelength) having a constant (time-independent) phase difference, so that a stable interference pattern can be observed.
(b) Let the two waves at a point be $y_1 = a\sin\omega t$ and $y_2 = a\sin(\omega t+\phi)$. Their superposition gives $y = y_1+y_2 = A\sin(\omega t+\theta)$, where $A^2 = a^2+a^2+2a^2\cos\phi = 4a^2\cos^2(\phi/2)$.
Since intensity $I \propto A^2$, $I = 4a^2\cos^2(\phi/2) = I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi$.
Constructive interference (maximum intensity $I=4a^2$) occurs when $\phi = 2n\pi$ (path difference $= n\lambda$); destructive interference ($I=0$) occurs when $\phi = (2n+1)\pi$ (path difference $= (2n-1)\lambda/2$).

questions.question: Answer the following questions: (a) In a single slit diffraction experiment, the width of the slit is made double the original width. How does this affect the size and intensity of the central diffraction band? (b) How is the width of the central maximum changed when red light is replaced by blue? (c) In what way is diffraction from each slit related to the interference pattern in a double slit experiment?
questions.answer:
(a) Angular width of central maximum $\theta \propto 1/a$; doubling the slit width $a$ halves the width of the central diffraction band. Since more light passes through the wider slit, the amplitude at the centre doubles, so intensity ($\propto$ amplitude$^2$) becomes four times the original.
(b) Width of central maximum $\propto \lambda$; since blue light has a shorter wavelength than red, replacing red with blue light decreases (narrows) the width of the central maximum.
(c) The diffraction pattern of each individual slit acts as an "envelope" that modulates the intensity of the interference fringes from the double slit; the interference fringes (closely spaced) are visible only within this broader diffraction envelope, and fringes falling at diffraction minima are missing (missing orders).

questions.question: (a) Show using a proper diagram how unpolarised light can be linearly polarised by reflection from a transparent glass surface. (b) The figure shows a ray of light falling normally on the face $AB$ of an equilateral glass prism having refractive index $\frac{3}{2}$, placed in water of refractive index $\frac{4}{3}$. Will this ray suffer total internal reflection on striking the face $AC$? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
(a) When unpolarised light strikes a transparent glass surface at the polarising (Brewster's) angle $i_p$, the reflected ray is completely plane polarised with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence, while the refracted ray is only partially polarised; at this angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other, giving $n = \tan i_p$.
(b) Since the ray falls normally on face $AB$, it travels undeviated and strikes face $AC$ at an angle equal to the prism angle, $i = 60^{\circ}$.
Critical angle for the glass–water interface: $\sin\theta_c = \dfrac{n_{water}}{n_{glass}} = \dfrac{4/3}{3/2} = \dfrac{8}{9}$, so $\theta_c = \sin^{-1}(8/9) \approx 62.7^{\circ}$.
Since the angle of incidence $60^{\circ}$ at $AC$ is less than $\theta_c \approx 62.7^{\circ}$, the ray does not undergo total internal reflection; it refracts and emerges out of face $AC$.

questions.question: (a) If one of two identical slits producing interference in Young’s experiment is covered with glass, so that the light intensity passing through it is reduced to $50\%$, find the ratio of the maximum and minimum intensity of the fringe in the interference pattern. (b) What kind of fringes do you expect to observe if white light is used instead of monochromatic light?
questions.answer:
(a) Let $I_1 = I$ (intensity through open slit) and $I_2 = 0.5I$ (through glass-covered slit).
Amplitude ratio: $\dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_2}{I_1}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
$\dfrac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \dfrac{(a_1+a_2)^2}{(a_1-a_2)^2} = \dfrac{(\sqrt{2}+1)^2}{(\sqrt{2}-1)^2} \approx 34:1$
(b) With white light, only a few coloured fringes are seen on either side of a central white fringe; beyond that the fringes overlap and the pattern becomes a general illumination.

questions.question: A monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident normally on a narrow slit of width ’ $a$’ to produce a diffraction pattern on the screen placed at a distance $D$ from the slit. With the help of a relevant diagram, deduce the conditions for obtaining maxima and minima on the screen. Use these conditions to show that angular width of central maximum is twice the angular width of secondary maximum.
questions.answer:
The slit of width $a$ is divided into secondary wavelets that interfere on the screen at angle $\theta$.
Minima: path difference $a\sin\theta = n\lambda$, $n = 1,2,3,...$
Secondary maxima (approx.): $a\sin\theta = (n+\tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$
For small $\theta$: $\theta_n \approx n\lambda/a$.
Central maximum lies between first minima on either side ($n=\pm1$), so its angular width $= 2\lambda/a$.
Angular width of a secondary maximum (between consecutive minima) $= \lambda/a$.
Hence angular width of central maximum $= 2 \times$ angular width of secondary maximum.

questions.question: Draw the intensity distributions for (i) the fringes produced in interference, and (ii) the diffraction bands produced due to single slit. Write two points of difference between the phenomena of interference and diffraction.
questions.answer:
(i) Interference: a series of equally spaced bright and dark fringes of the same maximum intensity $I_{max} = 4I_0$, varying as $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)$.
(ii) Diffraction: a broad central maximum flanked by weaker, unequally spaced secondary maxima whose intensity falls off rapidly with order.
Differences:
1. In interference all bright fringes have equal intensity; in diffraction the central maximum is much more intense than the secondary maxima.
2. Interference fringes are equally spaced; diffraction fringes are unequally spaced, with the central maximum twice as wide as the others.

questions.question: (i) State law of Malus. (ii) Draw a graph showing the variation of intensity ($I$) of polarised light transmitted by an analyser with angle ($\theta$) between polariser and analyser. (iii) What is the value of refractive index of a medium of polarising angle $60^{^{\circ}}$?
questions.answer:
(i) Malus' law: when a beam of plane polarised light is incident on an analyser, the intensity of light transmitted through the analyser is $I = I_0\cos^2\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the transmission axes of the polariser and analyser.
(ii) The graph of $I$ vs $\theta$ is a $\cos^2\theta$ curve: $I = I_0$ at $\theta = 0^{\circ}$, falling to zero at $\theta = 90^{\circ}$, rising back to $I_0$ at $\theta = 180^{\circ}$.
(iii) By Brewster's law, $\mu = \tan\theta_p = \tan 60^{\circ} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73$.

questions.question: Define the term wave front. State Huygen’s principle. Consider a plane wave front incident on a thin convex lens. Draw a proper diagram to show how the incident wave front traverses through the lens and after refraction focusses on the focal point of the lens, giving the shape of the emergent wave front. OR Explain the following, giving reasons: (i) When monochromatic light is incident on a surface separating two media, the reflected and refracted light both have the same frequency as the incident frequency. (ii) When light travels from a rarer to a denser medium, the speed decreases. Does this decrease in speed imply a reduction in the energy carried by the wave? (iii) In the wave picture of light, intensity of light is determined by the square of the amplitude of the wave. What determines the intensity in the photon picture of light?
questions.answer:
A wavefront is the locus of all points oscillating in the same phase.
Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets spreading out with the speed of light in that medium; the envelope of these wavelets at any later instant gives the new wavefront.
When a plane wavefront falls on a convex lens, the central part travels through more glass (denser medium) and is delayed less in time terms but the wave slows down there over a shorter geometric path than the edges over a longer path in air; the optical path length is the same for all rays, so all secondary wavelets reach the focal point in phase simultaneously.
The emergent wavefront is therefore a spherical wavefront converging to the focal point $F$, with the lens converting the plane wavefront into a converging spherical wavefront.
OR
(i) Frequency is a property of the source; reflection and refraction do not change the source, so the reflected and refracted waves have the same frequency as the incident wave.
(ii) No. Speed $v = f\lambda$ decreases because $\lambda$ decreases while $f$ stays constant; energy of the wave depends on amplitude and frequency, not on speed, so energy is not reduced.
(iii) In the photon picture, intensity is determined by the number of photons crossing unit area per unit time (photon flux), each photon carrying energy $h\nu$.

questions.question: (a) In Young’s double slit experiment, two slits are $1$ mm apart and the screen is placed $1$ m away from the slits. Calculate the fringe width when light of wavelength $500$ nm is used. (b) What should be the width of each slit in order to obtain $10$ maxima of the double slits pattern within the central maximum of the single slit pattern?
questions.answer:
(a) $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{500 \times 10^{-9} \times 1}{1 \times 10^{-3}} = 5 \times 10^{-4}$ m $= 0.5$ mm
(b) Width of central diffraction maximum (linear) $= \dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}$, and double-slit fringe spacing $= \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$.
Number of double-slit maxima within central maximum $= \dfrac{2\lambda D/a}{\lambda D/d} = \dfrac{2d}{a} = 10$
So $a = \dfrac{2d}{10} = \dfrac{2 \times 1\text{ mm}}{10} = 0.2$ mm

questions.question: (i) Derive Snell’s law on the basis of Huygen’s wave theory when light is travelling from a denser to a rarer medium. (ii) Draw the sketches to differentiate between plane wavefront and spherical wavefront.
questions.answer:
(i) Let $XY$ be the interface, $v_1, v_2$ the speeds in denser (medium 1) and rarer (medium 2) media, with $v_2 > v_1$. Let AB be an incident plane wavefront striking the surface, with A reaching the surface before B travels distance $BC = v_1 t$.
In the same time $t$, the secondary wavelet from A travels $AD = v_2 t$ in medium 2.
In triangles ABC and ADC: $\sin i = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{v_1 t}{AC}$, $\sin r = \dfrac{AD}{AC} = \dfrac{v_2 t}{AC}$
$\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$ (since $v \propto 1/n$), which is Snell's law; since $v_2 > v_1$, $r > i$, i.e. the ray bends away from the normal.
(ii) A plane wavefront (from a distant source) is a set of parallel straight lines/planes perpendicular to the rays; a spherical wavefront (from a point source) is a set of concentric circles/spheres with rays radiating outward from the centre.

questions.question: Two harmonic waves of monochromatic light $y_{1} = a \cos \omega t$ and $y_{2} = a \cos(\omega t + \phi)$ are superimposed on each other. Show that maximum intensity in interference pattern is four times the intensity due to each slit. Hence write the conditions for constructive and destructive interference in terms of the phase angle $\phi$.
questions.answer:
Resultant displacement: $y = y_1+y_2 = a\cos\omega t + a\cos(\omega t+\phi) = R\cos(\omega t+\alpha)$, giving $R^2 = a^2+a^2+2a^2\cos\phi = 2a^2(1+\cos\phi) = 4a^2\cos^2(\phi/2)$
Intensity $I \propto R^2$, so $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)$, where $I_0 = a^2$ is the intensity due to each wave alone.
Maximum value occurs when $\cos^2(\phi/2) = 1$, giving $I_{max} = 4I_0$, i.e. four times the intensity due to one slit.
Constructive interference (maximum): $\phi = 2n\pi$, $n = 0, \pm1, \pm2,...$
Destructive interference (minimum): $\phi = (2n+1)\pi$, $n = 0, \pm1, \pm2,...$

questions.question: (a) Write the necessary conditions to obtain sustained interference fringes. (b) In Young’s double slit experiment, plot a graph showing the variation of fringe width versus the distance of the screen from the plane of the slits keeping other parameters same. What information can one obtain from the slope of the curve? (c) What is the effect on the fringe width if the distance between the slits is reduced keeping other parameters same?
questions.answer:
(a) Conditions for sustained interference: the two sources must be coherent (constant phase difference), must emit light of the same frequency/wavelength, preferably same amplitude for good contrast, and be narrow and close together with the screen far away.
(b) $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$, so the graph of $\beta$ vs $D$ is a straight line passing through the origin. The slope of the line equals $\lambda/d$, so if $d$ is known, the wavelength $\lambda$ of light used can be determined from the slope.
(c) Since $\beta = \lambda D/d$, reducing $d$ (keeping $\lambda$ and $D$ same) increases the fringe width $\beta$, i.e. $\beta \propto 1/d$.

questions.question: Answer the following questions: (a) In a double slit experiment using light of wavelength 600 nm, the angular width of the fringe formed on a distant screen is $0.1^{^{\circ}}$. Find the spacing between the two slits. (b) Light of wavelength 5000 propagating in air gets partly reflected from the surface of water. How will the wavelengths and frequencies of the reflected and refracted light be affected?
questions.answer:
(a) Angular fringe width $\theta = \lambda/d$, so $d = \lambda/\theta$.
$\theta = 0.1^{\circ} = 0.1 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = 1.745 \times 10^{-3}$ rad
$d = \dfrac{600 \times 10^{-9}}{1.745 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 3.44 \times 10^{-4}$ m $\approx 0.34$ mm
(b) Reflected light stays in air, so its frequency and wavelength remain unchanged (5000 Å).
Refracted light enters water: frequency remains the same (determined by the source), but speed decreases, so wavelength decreases ($\lambda_{water} = \lambda_{air}/\mu_{water}$).

questions.question: (a) Show, giving a suitable diagram, how unpolarized light can be polarised by reflection. (b) Two polaroids $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are placed with their pass axes perpendicular to each other. Unpolarised light of intensity $I_{0}$ is incident on $P_{1}$. A third polaroid $P_{3}$ is kept in between $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ such that its pass axis makes an angle of 60 $^{\circ}$ with that of $P_{1}$. Determine the intensity of light transmitted through $P_{1}$, $P_{3}$ and $P_{2}$.
questions.answer:
(a) When unpolarised light is incident on a transparent surface (e.g., glass) at a particular angle called the Brewster angle $i_{B}$, the reflected ray is completely plane polarised, with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence. This happens when the reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular, giving $\tan i_{B} = n$ (Brewster's law), $n$ being the refractive index of the medium.
(b) Intensity after $P_{1}$: $I_{1} = \dfrac{I_{0}}{2}$.
After $P_{3}$ (angle $60^{\circ}$ from $P_{1}$): $I_{2} = I_{1}\cos^{2}60^{\circ} = \dfrac{I_{0}}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{I_{0}}{8}$.
After $P_{2}$ (angle between $P_{3}$ and $P_{2}$ is $30^{\circ}$): $I_{3} = I_{2}\cos^{2}30^{\circ} = \dfrac{I_{0}}{8}\times\dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{3I_{0}}{32}$.

questions.question: (a) In what way is diffraction from each slit related to the interference pattern in a double slit experiment? (b) Two wavelengths of sodium light $590$ nm and $596$ nm are used, in turn, to study the diffraction taking place at a single slit of aperture $2 \times 10^{-4}$ m. The distance between the slit and the screen is $1.5$ m. Calculate the separation between the positions of the first maxima of the diffraction pattern obtained in the two cases.
questions.answer:
(a) In a double slit, each slit itself produces a single-slit diffraction pattern. The double-slit interference fringes are formed within, and modulated by, this diffraction envelope, so the interference pattern has decreasing intensity fringes and some orders may be missing where the interference maxima fall on diffraction minima.
(b) Position of first secondary maximum: $y = \dfrac{3}{2}\dfrac{\lambda D}{a}$.
Separation: $\Delta y = \dfrac{3D}{2a}(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}) = \dfrac{3\times1.5}{2\times2\times10^{-4}}\times(596-590)\times10^{-9}$
$\Delta y = 11250\times6\times10^{-9} = 6.75\times10^{-5}$ m $= 0.0675$ mm.

questions.question: In Young’s double slit experiment, the two slits $0.15$ mm apart are illuminated by monochromatic light of wavelength $450$ nm. The screen is $1.0$ m away from the slits. (a) Find the distance of the second (i) bright fringe, (ii) dark fringe from the central maximum. (b) How will the fringe pattern change if the screen is moved away from the slits?
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Second bright fringe: $y_{2} = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{2\times450\times10^{-9}\times1.0}{0.15\times10^{-3}} = 6\times10^{-3}$ m $= 6$ mm.
(ii) Second dark fringe: $y = \left(2-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{1.5\times450\times10^{-9}\times1.0}{0.15\times10^{-3}} = 4.5\times10^{-3}$ m $= 4.5$ mm.
(b) Fringe width $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$, so as $D$ increases, $\beta$ increases: fringes become wider and less intense, though their number and spacing pattern remain uniform.

questions.question: How does an unpolarised light get polarised when passed through a polaroid? Two polaroids are set in crossed positions. A third polaroid is placed between the two making an angle $\theta$ with the pass axis of the first polaroid. Write the expression for the intensity of light transmitted from the second polaroid. In what orientations will the transmitted intensity be (i) minimum and (ii) maximum?
questions.answer:
An unpolarised light wave has vibrations in all directions perpendicular to its propagation direction. A polaroid has molecules aligned along a particular direction (pass axis); it absorbs the component of the electric field perpendicular to this axis and transmits only the component parallel to it, so the transmitted light becomes plane polarised, with intensity reduced to half.
For the given arrangement, intensity transmitted from $P_{2}$: $I = \dfrac{I_{0}}{8}\sin^{2}2\theta$.
(i) Minimum (zero) when $\theta = 0^{\circ}$ or $90^{\circ}$.
(ii) Maximum (equal to $\dfrac{I_{0}}{8}$) when $\theta = 45^{\circ}$.

questions.question: (a) Why are coherent sources necessary to produce a sustained interference pattern? (b) In Young’s double slit experiment using monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$, the intensity of light at a point on the screen where path difference is $\lambda$, is $K$ units. Find out the intensity of light at a point where path difference is $\lambda/3$.
questions.answer:
(a) Coherent sources maintain a constant phase difference at every point on the screen. Without this, the phase difference would change randomly with time, so the interference pattern would shift continuously and the eye would perceive only a uniform average intensity, not a stationary fringe pattern.
(b) $I = 4I_{1}\cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{\delta}{2}\right)$, where $\delta = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times(\text{path difference})$.
At path difference $\lambda$: $\delta = 2\pi$, so $I = 4I_{1} = K$, giving $I_{1} = K/4$.
At path difference $\lambda/3$: $\delta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so $I = 4I_{1}\cos^{2}60^{\circ} = 4I_{1}\times\dfrac{1}{4} = I_{1} = \dfrac{K}{4}$.

questions.question: Define a wavefront. Use Huygens’ geometrical construction to show the propagation of a plane wavefront from a rarer medium (1) to a denser medium (2) undergoing refraction. Hence derive Snell’s law of refraction. OR (a) Use Huygens’ geometrical construction to show the behaviour of a plane wavefront (i) passing through a biconvex lens; (ii) reflecting by a concave mirror. (b) When monochromatic light is incident on a surface separating two media, why does the refracted light have the same frequency as that of the incident light?
questions.answer:
A wavefront is the locus of all points in a medium vibrating in the same phase at a given instant.
Let $AB$ be a plane wavefront in medium 1 incident on the interface at angle $i$. By Huygens' principle, each point on $AB$ becomes a source of secondary wavelets. Let $\tau$ be the time for a wavelet from $B$ to reach $C$ on the interface: $BC = v_{1}\tau$. In the same time, the wavelet from $A$ travels a distance $v_{2}\tau$ in medium 2, forming the refracted wavefront $CD$ with $AD = v_{2}\tau$.
From right triangles $ABC$ and $ACD$: $\sin i = \dfrac{v_{1}\tau}{AC}$, $\sin r = \dfrac{v_{2}\tau}{AC}$.
So $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_{1}}{v_{2}} = {}_{1}n_{2}$, which is Snell's law.

OR
(a)(i) A plane wavefront incident on a biconvex lens emerges as a converging spherical wavefront, converging towards the focus, since the central part is delayed less than the edges (thicker at centre for a convex lens gives more optical path there, but net effect is convergence).
(ii) A plane wavefront reflected from a concave mirror also becomes a converging spherical wavefront, converging at the focus of the mirror.
(b) Frequency is determined by the source; the number of wavefronts crossing the boundary per second must remain the same on both sides for the wave to be continuous, so frequency stays unchanged (only wavelength and speed change) on refraction.

questions.question: Describe Young’s double slit experiment to produce interference pattern due to a monochromatic source of light. Deduce the expression for the fringe width.
questions.answer:
Two narrow, coherent slits $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$, separated by distance $d$, are illuminated by a monochromatic source and act as coherent sources. Light from them overlaps on a screen placed at distance $D$, producing alternate bright and dark fringes due to constructive and destructive interference.
At point $P$ on the screen, path difference $= \dfrac{yd}{D}$, where $y$ is the distance of $P$ from the central point $O$.
For bright fringes: $\dfrac{yd}{D} = n\lambda \Rightarrow y_{n} = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}$.
For dark fringes: $\dfrac{yd}{D} = \left(n-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda$.
Fringe width (spacing between consecutive bright or dark fringes): $\beta = y_{n+1} - y_{n} = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$.

questions.question: Use Huygen’s principle to verify the laws of refraction.
questions.answer:
Let $AB$ be an incident plane wavefront in a rarer medium (speed $v_{1}$) meeting the interface at angle $i$. According to Huygens' principle, every point on $AB$ acts as a source of secondary wavelets.
While the wavelet from $B$ travels distance $BC = v_{1}\tau$ to reach the interface at $C$, the wavelet from $A$ travels $AD = v_{2}\tau$ into the denser medium (speed $v_{2}$), and $CD$ is the new refracted wavefront.
From triangle $ABC$: $\sin i = \dfrac{v_{1}\tau}{AC}$; from triangle $ACD$: $\sin r = \dfrac{v_{2}\tau}{AC}$.
So $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_{1}}{v_{2}} = n_{21}$ = constant, verifying Snell's law.
Since incident ray, normal, and refracted wavefront all lie in the plane of the diagram, the incident ray, refracted ray, and normal lie in the same plane, verifying the second law of refraction.

questions.question: (a) Describe briefly, with the help of suitable diagram, how the transverse nature of light can be demonstrated by the phenomenon of polarization. (b) When unpolarized light passes from air to a transparent medium, under what condition does the reflected light get polarized?
questions.answer:
(a) Light from a source is passed through a polaroid $P_{1}$, which transmits only the component of the vibration along its pass axis, giving plane polarised light. When a second polaroid $P_{2}$ is placed after $P_{1}$ and rotated, the transmitted intensity varies as $I = I_{0}\cos^{2}\theta$ (Malus' law) and becomes zero when $P_{2}$ is perpendicular to $P_{1}$. Since a longitudinal wave cannot be blocked this way (it has no transverse vibration direction to select), this behaviour proves that light is a transverse wave.
(b) The reflected light is completely polarised when the angle of incidence equals the Brewster angle $i_{B}$, given by $\tan i_{B} = n$, i.e., when the reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular.

questions.question: The intensity at the central maxima (O) in a Young’s double slit experiment is $I_{0}$. If the distance OP equals one-third of the fringe width of the pattern, show that the intensity at point P would be $\frac{I_{0}}{4}$.
questions.answer:
Intensity at any point: $I = 4I_{1}\cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{\delta}{2}\right)$, where at $O$ ($\delta=0$), $I = 4I_{1} = I_{0}$.
Fringe width $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$, so $OP = \dfrac{\beta}{3} = \dfrac{\lambda D}{3d}$.
Path difference at $P$: $\Delta = \dfrac{d\cdot OP}{D} = \dfrac{\lambda}{3}$.
Phase difference: $\delta = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\dfrac{\lambda}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.
Intensity at $P$: $I_{P} = I_{0}\cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = I_{0}\times\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{I_{0}}{4}$, as required.

questions.question: In the experiment on diffraction due to a single slit, show that (i) the intensity of diffraction fringes decreases as the order (n) increases. (ii) angular width of the central maximum is twice that of the first order secondary maximum.
questions.answer:
$(i)$ In the phasor (vector addition) treatment of a single slit, the central maximum is formed when all secondary wavelets from the slit add in phase, giving maximum resultant amplitude.
For the $n$th secondary maximum, the slit is effectively divided into $(2n+1)$ parts of which only one part contributes constructively, the rest cancelling in pairs; so the resultant amplitude falls off roughly as $1/(2n+1)$, giving intensity $I_n \approx \dfrac{I_0}{(2n+1)^2\pi^2/2}$, which decreases rapidly as $n$ increases.
$(ii)$ Minima occur at $a\sin\theta_n = n\lambda$.
Central maximum lies between $n=-1$ and $n=+1$, so its angular width $= 2\theta_1 = \dfrac{2\lambda}{a}$.
The first secondary maximum lies between $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, so its angular width $=\theta_2-\theta_1=\dfrac{\lambda}{a}$.
Hence angular width of central maximum $=2\times$ angular width of first secondary maximum.

questions.question: (i) Light passes through two polaroids $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ with pass axis of $P_{2}$ making an angle $\theta$ with the pass axis of $P_{1}$. For what value of $\theta$ is the intensity of emergent light zero? (ii) A third polaroid is placed between $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ with its pass axis making an angle $\beta$ with the pass axis of $P_{1}$. Find a value of $\beta$ for which the intensity of light emerging from $P$ is $\frac{I_{0}}{8}$, where $I$ is the intensity of light on the polaroid $P$. $2 0 1$
questions.answer:
$(i)$ By Malus' law, $I=I_0\cos^2\theta$. Emergent intensity is zero when $\cos\theta=0$, i.e. $\theta=90^\circ$.
$(ii)$ Let intensity incident on $P_1$ be $I_0$, so intensity after $P_1$ is $\dfrac{I_0}{2}$.
With $P_3$ at angle $\beta$ to $P_1$ and $P_2$ at $90^\circ$ to $P_1$, intensity after $P_2$ is $I=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2\beta\cos^2(90^\circ-\beta)=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2\beta\sin^2\beta=\dfrac{I_0}{8}\sin^2 2\beta$.
Setting $I=\dfrac{I_0}{8}$ gives $\sin^2 2\beta=1$, so $2\beta=90^\circ$, i.e. $\beta=45^\circ$.

questions.question: What is an unpolarized light? Explain with the help of suitable ray diagram how an unpolarized light can be polarized by reflection from a transparent medium. Write the expression for Brewster angle in terms of the refractive index of denser medium.
questions.answer:
Unpolarized light is light whose electric field vector vibrates randomly in all directions perpendicular to the direction of propagation, with no preferred direction.
When unpolarized light is incident on a transparent medium (e.g. glass), the reflected ray is partially polarized, and at one particular angle of incidence, called the Brewster angle $\theta_B$, the reflected ray is completely plane polarized with its vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence, while the refracted ray remains partially polarized.
At this angle, the reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular ($\theta_B + r = 90^\circ$).
Brewster's law: $n=\tan\theta_B$, where $n$ is the refractive index of the denser medium with respect to the rarer medium.

questions.question: In a single slit diffraction experiment, when a tiny circular obstacle is placed in the path of light from a distant source, a bright spot is seen at the centre of the shadow of the obstacle. Explain why? State two points of difference between the interference pattern obtained in Young’s double slit experiment and the diffraction pattern due to a single slit.
questions.answer:
When light from a distant source falls on a small circular obstacle, the waves diffract around its edge (by Huygens' principle every point on the edge acts as a source of secondary wavelets).
Since all points on the edge are equidistant from the centre of the shadow, the secondary wavelets reaching the centre travel equal path lengths and arrive in phase, interfering constructively to produce a bright spot (Poisson's spot) at the centre of the geometrical shadow.
Differences: $(1)$ In YDSE all bright fringes have nearly equal intensity and are equally spaced, whereas in single-slit diffraction the central maximum is much brighter and wider, and intensity of successive secondary maxima falls off rapidly.
$(2)$ YDSE fringes arise from superposition of waves from two coherent point sources, while diffraction fringes arise from superposition of infinite secondary wavelets from different parts of the same wavefront.

questions.question: In Young’s double slit experiment, monochromatic light of wavelength $630 nm$ illuminates the pair of slits and produces an interference pattern in which two consecutive bright fringes are separated by $8.1 mm$. Another source of monochromatic light produces the interference pattern in which the two consecutive bright fringes are separated by $7.2 mm$. Find the wavelength of light from the second source. What is the effect on the interference fringes if the monochromatic source is replaced by a source of white light?
questions.answer:
Fringe width $\beta=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$, so $\lambda \propto \beta$ for the same setup ($D,d$ unchanged).
$\lambda_2=\lambda_1\times\dfrac{\beta_2}{\beta_1}=630\text{ nm}\times\dfrac{7.2}{8.1}=560$ nm.
If the monochromatic source is replaced by white light, the central fringe remains white (zero path difference for all wavelengths), while fringes on either side become coloured (different wavelengths giving maxima at different positions), and beyond a few fringes the pattern overlaps into general illumination, so no clear fringe pattern is visible.

questions.question: State two conditions to obtain sustained interference of light. In Young’s double slit experiment, using light of wavelength 400 nm, interference fringes of width $X$ are obtained. The wavelength of light is increased to 600 nm and the separation between the slits is halved. If one wants the observed fringe width on the screen to be the same in the two cases, find the ratio of the distance between the screen and the plane of the interfering sources in the two arrangements.
questions.answer:
Two conditions for sustained interference: $(1)$ The two sources must be coherent, i.e. emit light of the same frequency/wavelength with a constant phase difference. $(2)$ The sources should be narrow, close together, and preferably of equal or nearly equal amplitude.
Fringe width: $\beta=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$.
Case 1: $\beta_1=\dfrac{\lambda_1 D_1}{d_1}$ with $\lambda_1=400$ nm.
Case 2: $\beta_2=\dfrac{\lambda_2 D_2}{d_2}$ with $\lambda_2=600$ nm, $d_2=d_1/2$.
For $\beta_1=\beta_2$: $\dfrac{400 D_1}{d_1}=\dfrac{600 D_2}{d_1/2}=\dfrac{1200 D_2}{d_1}$, giving $\dfrac{D_1}{D_2}=\dfrac{1200}{400}=3$.
So $D_1:D_2=3:1$.

questions.question: State Huygens’ principle. For reflection of a plane wave front at a plane reflecting surface, construct the corresponding reflected wave front. Using this diagram, prove that angle of incidence is equal to angle of reflection.
questions.answer:
Huygens' principle states that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets spreading out in all directions with the speed of the wave, and the new wavefront at any later instant is the surface tangent (envelope) to all these secondary wavelets.
Construction: Let $AB$ be a plane wavefront incident on reflecting surface $MN$ at angle $i$. When end $A$ strikes the surface, secondary wavelets from $B$ still travel a distance $BC=vt$ to reach the surface. Meanwhile, the wavelet from $A$ spreads out as a hemisphere of radius $AD=vt$ in the same time. The tangent plane $CD$ from $C$ to this hemisphere gives the reflected wavefront.
Proof: In triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$, $AC$ is common, $BC=AD=vt$, and $\angle ABC=\angle ADC=90^\circ$. Hence the triangles are congruent, so $\angle BAC=\angle DCA$.
Since $\angle BAC$ is the angle of incidence $i$ and $\angle DCA$ is the angle of reflection $r$ (angles between the wavefronts and the reflecting surface equal the angles between the rays and the normal), we get $i=r$.

questions.question: What is meant by interference of light? In a double slit experiment with monochromatic light, fringes are obtained on a screen placed at some distance from the slits. If the screen is moved by $5 \times 10^{-2}$ m towards the slits, the change in fringe width is $3 \times 10^{-5}$ m. If the distance between slits is $10^{-3}$ m, calculate the wavelength of light used.
questions.answer:
Interference of light is the phenomenon of redistribution of light energy due to superposition of light waves from two coherent sources, producing regions of maximum intensity (constructive interference) and minimum intensity (destructive interference) alternately.
Fringe width $\beta=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$, so $\Delta\beta=\dfrac{\lambda}{d}\Delta D$.
Given $\Delta D=5\times10^{-2}$ m, $\Delta\beta=3\times10^{-5}$ m, $d=10^{-3}$ m.
$\lambda=\dfrac{\Delta\beta \cdot d}{\Delta D}=\dfrac{3\times10^{-5}\times10^{-3}}{5\times10^{-2}}=6\times10^{-7}$ m $=600$ nm.

questions.question: In a Young’s double-slit experiment, the two slits behave as coherent sources. When coherent light waves superpose over each other they create an interference pattern of successive bright and dark regions due to constructive and destructive interference. Two slits $2$ mm apart are illuminated by a source of monochromatic light and the interference pattern is observed on a screen $5.0$ m away from the slits as shown in the figure.
questions.answer:
$(i)$ Fringe width is given by $\beta=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength of light, $D$ the slit-to-screen distance and $d$ the slit separation; here $d=2\times10^{-3}$ m and $D=5.0$ m.
$(ii)$ For a sustained interference pattern, the two slits must act as coherent sources, i.e. emit waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference, obtained here by illuminating both slits from the same monochromatic source.
$(iii)$ If the slit separation $d$ is decreased (slits brought closer), the fringe width $\beta$ increases since $\beta \propto \dfrac{1}{d}$; similarly, increasing $D$ also increases $\beta$.
$(iv)$ If white light is used instead of monochromatic light, the central fringe is white, while fringes on either side are coloured and the pattern becomes indistinct after a few fringes due to overlapping of different wavelengths.

questions.question: Diffraction of light is bending of light around the corners of an object whose size is comparable with the wavelength of light. Diffraction actually defines the limits of ray optics. This limit for optical instruments is set by the wavelength of light. An experimental arrangement is set up to observe the diffraction pattern due to a single slit. Answer the following questions based on the above: (a) How will the width of central maximum be affected if the wavelength of light is increased? (b) Under what condition is the first minimum obtained? (c) Write two points of difference between interference and diffraction patterns. OR (c) Two students are separated by a $7$ m partition wall in a room $10$ m high. If both light and sound waves can bend around obstacles, how is it that the students are unable to see each other even though they can converse easily?
questions.answer:
(a) Width of central maximum $=\dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}$, so it is directly proportional to $\lambda$; increasing the wavelength increases the width of the central maximum.
(b) The first minimum is obtained when the path difference between wavelets from the two edges of the slit equals one wavelength, i.e. $a\sin\theta=\lambda$.
(c) $(1)$ In interference all bright fringes are of the same intensity, whereas in diffraction the central maximum is much brighter and the intensity of successive secondary maxima falls off rapidly.
$(2)$ Interference fringes are equally spaced (uniform fringe width), while diffraction fringes are unequally spaced, with the central maximum twice as wide as the secondary maxima.
OR
(c) Appreciable diffraction (bending around an obstacle) occurs only when the size of the obstacle/opening is comparable to the wavelength of the wave. Sound waves have wavelengths of the order of centimetres to metres, comparable to the size of the partition wall, so sound bends around it easily and reaches the other student. Light waves have wavelengths of the order of $10^{-7}$ m, far smaller than the wall's dimensions, so light does not bend appreciably around it and travels essentially in straight lines, preventing the students from seeing each other.

questions.question: (a) What are coherent sources? Why are they necessary for observing stable interference pattern? Draw a graph showing the variation of intensity of light with the position on the screen in Young’s double-slit experiment.
questions.answer:
Coherent sources are two sources that emit light waves of the same frequency (wavelength) and in phase or having a constant phase difference that does not change with time.
They are necessary for a stable interference pattern because if the phase difference between the two sources varies randomly with time (as for two independent sources), the positions of maxima and minima keep shifting rapidly; the eye/detector then records only the time-averaged uniform intensity and no fixed pattern is seen.
With coherent sources the phase difference at any point on the screen remains fixed, so the positions of constructive and destructive interference are fixed, giving a stable, observable pattern.
Intensity distribution graph: $I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi x d}{\lambda D}\right)$, plotted against position $x$ on the screen, gives a series of equally spaced bright fringes of maximum intensity $4I_0$ separated by dark points of zero intensity, symmetric about the central maximum, all bright fringes having equal intensity.

questions.question: (b) Find the intensity of light at a point on the screen when two interfering waves of the same intensity $(I_{0})$ have a path difference of: (i) $\frac{\lambda}{4}$ and (ii) $\frac{\lambda}{3}$.
questions.answer:
For two waves of equal intensity $I_0$ superposing with phase difference $\phi$, the resultant intensity is $I = I_0 + I_0 + 2\sqrt{I_0 I_0}\cos\phi = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)$, where $\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x$.
(i) For $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}$: $\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 4I_0 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 2I_0$.
(ii) For $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{3}$: $\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so $I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 4I_0 \times \dfrac{1}{4} = I_0$.

questions.question: (ii) A beam of coherent light of wavelength $550$ nm is incident normal to the plane of a pair of two slits $S$ and $S$ each of width $1$· $2 \times 10^{-6}$ m separated by $1$· $1$ mm. Dark $1 2$ and bright fringes are observed on a screen $2$· $2$ m away from the plane of the slits. Calculate: (I) fringe width. (II) distance of the second dark fringe from the central maximum. (III) what will happen when the entire apparatus is immersed in water.
questions.answer:
(I) Fringe width: $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{550 \times 10^{-9} \times 2.2}{1.1 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.1 \times 10^{-3}$ m $= 1.1$ mm.
(II) Position of $n$th dark fringe: $x_n = (n - \tfrac{1}{2})\beta$; for $n = 2$, $x_2 = 1.5\beta = 1.5 \times 1.1 = 1.65$ mm from the central maximum.
(III) On immersing in water (refractive index $\mu \approx 1.33$), the wavelength decreases to $\lambda' = \dfrac{\lambda}{\mu}$, so the fringe width decreases to $\beta' = \dfrac{\beta}{\mu} \approx 0.83$ mm; the fringe pattern becomes narrower but its nature remains unchanged.

questions.question: (a) (i) A parallel beam of monochromatic light falls normally on a single slit of width $^{'}a^{'}$ and a diffraction pattern is observed on a screen placed at distance $D$ from the slits. Explain: (I) the formation of maxima and minima in the diffraction pattern, and (II) why the maxima go on becoming weaker and weaker with its increasing number $(n)$. (ii) Write any two points of difference between interference pattern due to double-slit and diffraction pattern due to single-slit.
questions.answer:
(a)(i)(I) Each point on the unblocked wavefront within the slit acts as a source of secondary wavelets (Huygens' principle). Wavelets from different parts of the slit travelling at angle $\theta$ to the screen interfere.
Minima occur when the path difference between wavelets from the two edges of the slit is $a\sin\theta = n\lambda$ ($n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$), since the slit can then be divided into an even number of equal parts whose contributions cancel pairwise.
Maxima (secondary) occur approximately midway between successive minima, i.e. $a\sin\theta \approx (n + \tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$, where the slit can be divided into an odd number of parts, leaving one part's contribution uncancelled.
(II) As $n$ increases, the slit is divided into more parts of which only one part remains effectively uncancelled; this uncancelled fraction of the total slit width becomes smaller for higher $n$, so successive secondary maxima have rapidly decreasing intensity.
(ii) In double-slit interference all bright fringes have equal intensity and are equally spaced; in single-slit diffraction, fringes are of unequal width and unequal, rapidly decreasing intensity, with the central maximum twice as wide and much brighter than the secondary maxima.

questions.question: (a) (i) (1) What are coherent sources? Why are they necessary for observing a sustained interference pattern? (2) Lights from two independent sources are not coherent. Explain. (ii) Two slits $0.1$ mm apart are arranged $1.20$ m from a screen. Light of wavelength $600$ nm from a distant source is incident on the slits. (1) How far apart will adjacent bright interference fringes be on the screen? (2) Find the angular width (in degree) of the first bright fringe. OR (b) (i) Define a wavefront. An incident plane wave falls on a convex lens and gets refracted through it. Draw a diagram to show the incident and refracted wavefront. (ii) A beam of light coming from a distant source is refracted by a spherical glass ball (refractive index $1.5$) of radius $15$ cm. Draw the ray diagram and obtain the position of the final image formed.
questions.answer:
(a)(i)(1) Coherent sources are sources emitting waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference. They are necessary because only then do the positions of maxima and minima on the screen remain fixed with time, giving a stable, observable interference pattern; otherwise the pattern shifts rapidly and only a uniform average intensity is seen.
(2) Light from independent sources is emitted by different atoms in random, uncorrelated bursts (each lasting about $10^{-8}$ s), so the phase difference between the two sources changes randomly and rapidly; hence they cannot be coherent.
(ii) $d = 0.1$ mm $= 1 \times 10^{-4}$ m, $D = 1.20$ m, $\lambda = 600$ nm $= 6 \times 10^{-7}$ m.
(1) $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{6 \times 10^{-7} \times 1.20}{1 \times 10^{-4}} = 7.2 \times 10^{-3}$ m $= 7.2$ mm.
(2) Angular width $= \dfrac{\lambda}{d} = 6 \times 10^{-3}$ rad $= 6 \times 10^{-3} \times \dfrac{180}{\pi} \approx 0.34^\circ$.

questions.question: (i) Light consisting of two wavelengths 600 nm and 480 nm is used to obtain interference fringes in a double slit experiment. The screen is placed 1.0 m away from slits which are 1.0 nm apart. (1) Calculate the distance of the third bright fringe on the screen from the central maximum for wavelength 600 nm. (2) Find the least distance from the central maximum where the bright fringes due to both the wavelengths coincide. (ii) (1) Draw the variation of intensity with angle of diffraction in single slit diffraction pattern. Write the expression for value of angle corresponding to zero intensity locations. (2) In what way diffraction of light waves differs from diffraction of sound waves?
questions.answer:
(i)(1) Third bright fringe for $\lambda = 600$ nm: $x_3 = \dfrac{3\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{3 \times 600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.0}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.8 \times 10^{-3}$ m $= 1.8$ mm.
(2) Bright fringes coincide when $n_1\lambda_1 = n_2\lambda_2$, i.e. $600n_1 = 480n_2 \Rightarrow 5n_1 = 4n_2$; smallest integers $n_1 = 4$, $n_2 = 5$.
Least distance $= \dfrac{n_1\lambda_1 D}{d} = \dfrac{4 \times 600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.0}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 2.4 \times 10^{-3}$ m $= 2.4$ mm.
(ii)(1) The intensity vs diffraction angle graph shows a tall central maximum flanked symmetrically by much weaker, rapidly decreasing secondary maxima. Zero intensity (minima) occur at $a\sin\theta = n\lambda$, $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$.
(2) Sound waves have wavelengths (cm range) comparable to everyday obstacles/openings, so their diffraction is easily observed; light waves have very small wavelengths ($\sim 10^{-7}$ m), so diffraction is noticeable only through very narrow slits or small obstacles.

questions.question: (a) (i) Give any two differences between the interference pattern obtained in Young’s double-slit experiment and a diffraction pattern due to a single slit. (ii) Draw an intensity distribution graph in case of a double-slit interference pattern. (iii) In Young’s double-slit experiment using monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$, the intensity of light at a point on the screen, where path difference is $\lambda$, is K units. Find the intensity of light at a point on the screen where the path difference is $\frac{\lambda}{3}$. OR (b) (i) Draw a labelled ray diagram of a compound microscope showing image formation at least distance of distinct vision. Derive an expression for its magnifying power. (ii) A telescope consists of two lenses of focal length 100 cm and 5 cm. Find the magnifying power when the final image is formed at infinity.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) In YDSE all bright fringes are equally spaced and of equal intensity; in single-slit diffraction, fringes are unequally spaced (central maximum is twice as wide as others) and intensity decreases rapidly for higher-order maxima.
(ii) The intensity distribution for double-slit interference follows $I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi x d}{\lambda D}\right)$ - equally spaced peaks of equal height $4I_0$ separated by zero-intensity points, symmetric about the central maximum.
(iii) Path difference $\lambda$ corresponds to phase difference $2\pi$, giving maximum (constructive) intensity: $K = 4I_0$, so $I_0 = K/4$.
For path difference $\lambda/3$: phase difference $\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so $I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 4I_0 \times \dfrac{1}{4} = I_0 = \dfrac{K}{4}$.

questions.question: (i) The displacement of two light waves, each of amplitude ’ $a$’ and frequency $\omega$, emanating from two coherent sources of light, are given by $y_{1} = a \cos \omega t$ and $y_{2} = a \cos(\omega t + \phi)$. $\phi$ is the phase difference between the two waves. These light waves superpose at a point. Obtain the expression for the resultant intensity at that point. (ii) In Young’s double slit experiment, find the ratio of intensities at two points on a screen when waves emanating from two slits reaching these points have path differences (i) $\frac{\lambda}{6}$ and (ii) $\frac{\lambda}{4}$.
questions.answer:
(i) $y_1 = a\cos\omega t$, $y_2 = a\cos(\omega t + \phi)$; resultant displacement $y = y_1 + y_2 = R\cos(\omega t + \theta)$, where $R^2 = a^2 + a^2 + 2a^2\cos\phi = 2a^2(1 + \cos\phi) = 4a^2\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)$.
Since intensity $I \propto (\text{amplitude})^2$, and $I_0 \propto a^2$ for each wave, $I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)$.
(ii) $\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x$. For $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{6}$: $\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, $I_1 = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 4I_0 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 3I_0$.
For $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}$: $\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $I_2 = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 4I_0 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 2I_0$.
Ratio $I_1 : I_2 = 3 : 2$.

questions.question: (i) Differentiate between a wavefront and a ray. (ii) State Huygen’s principle and verify laws of reflection using suitable diagram. (iii) In Young’s double slit experiment, the slits $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ are $3$ mm apart and the screen is placed $1.0$ m away from the slits. It is observed that the fourth bright fringe is at a distance of $5$ mm from the second dark fringe. Find the wavelength of light used.
questions.answer:
(i) A wavefront is the locus of all points vibrating in the same phase (a surface), whereas a ray is the direction of propagation of the wave, always perpendicular to the wavefront at every point (a line).
(ii) Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets that spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave; the new wavefront at any later instant is the envelope (common tangent) of these secondary wavelets.
Using a plane wavefront $AB$ incident on a reflecting surface, taking equal time $\tau$ for wavelets from $B$ to reach the surface at $C$ while a secondary wavelet from $A$ spreads to radius $v\tau$, the triangles $ABC$ and $AEC$ (with $AE = BC = v\tau$) are congruent, giving $\angle i = \angle r$, verifying the law of reflection.
(iii) $d = 3 \times 10^{-3}$ m, $D = 1.0$ m. Fourth bright fringe: $x_4 = 4\beta$; second dark fringe: $x_2' = 1.5\beta$ (where $\beta = \lambda D/d$).
Given $x_4 - x_2' = 2.5\beta = 5 \times 10^{-3}$ m, so $\beta = 2 \times 10^{-3}$ m.
$\lambda = \dfrac{\beta d}{D} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-3} \times 3 \times 10^{-3}}{1.0} = 6 \times 10^{-6}$ m.

questions.question: (i) A plane light wave propagating from a rarer into a denser medium, is incident at an angle $i$ on the surface separating two media. Using Huygen’s principle, draw the refracted wave and hence verify Snell’s law of refraction. (ii) In a Young’s double slit experiment, the slits are separated by $0.30$ mm and the screen is kept $1.5$ m away. The wavelength of light used is $600$ nm. Calculate the distance between the central bright fringe and the $4$ th dark fringe.
questions.answer:
(i) Let $AB$ be a plane wavefront in the rarer medium (speed $v_1$) incident at angle $i$ on the surface $XY$. When the wavelet from $A$ reaches $C$ on the surface after time $\tau$, the wavelet from $B$ has travelled into the denser medium (speed $v_2 < v_1$) up to radius $v_2\tau$, forming the refracted wavefront $CE$.
From geometry, $\sin i = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{v_1\tau}{AC}$ and $\sin r = \dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{v_2\tau}{AC}$.
Dividing, $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = {}^1n_2$ (a constant for the two media), which is Snell's law of refraction.
(ii) $d = 0.30$ mm $= 3 \times 10^{-4}$ m, $D = 1.5$ m, $\lambda = 600$ nm $= 6 \times 10^{-7}$ m.
Position of $n$th dark fringe: $x_n = (2n-1)\dfrac{\lambda D}{2d}$; for $n = 4$:
$x_4 = 7 \times \dfrac{6 \times 10^{-7} \times 1.5}{2 \times 3 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.05 \times 10^{-2}$ m $= 10.5$ mm.

questions.question: (i) Discuss briefly diffraction of light from a single slit and draw the shape of the diffraction pattern. (ii) An object is placed between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror. Using mirror formula, prove mathematically that it produces a virtual and an enlarged image.
questions.answer:
(i) By Huygens' principle each point of the wavefront inside a narrow slit acts as a source of secondary wavelets; these wavelets interfere on the screen to give a diffraction pattern consisting of a broad, intense central maximum flanked symmetrically by weaker secondary maxima and minima, the intensity of the secondary maxima falling off rapidly with order. The central band is twice as wide as any secondary band.
(ii) Let the object lie between pole and focus, so $u=-x$ with $0<x<f$ (f = magnitude of focal length; actual focal length $=-f$ for concave mirror).
Mirror formula: $\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f}\Rightarrow \frac{1}{v}=-\frac{1}{f}+\frac{1}{x}=\frac{f-x}{fx}$
Since $x<f$, $(f-x)>0$, so $v>0$: the image forms behind the mirror, i.e. it is virtual.
$v=\dfrac{fx}{f-x}$, and since $f-x<f$, $v>x$, so the image distance exceeds the object distance.
Magnification $m=-\dfrac{v}{u}=\dfrac{v}{x}>1$ and positive, so the image is erect and enlarged.
Thus a concave mirror forms a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object lies between the pole and focus.

questions.question: (i) (1) Write two points of difference between an interference pattern and a diffraction pattern. (2) Name any two factors on which the fringe width in a Young’s double-slit experiment depends. (ii) In Young’s double-slit experiment, the two slits are separated by a distance equal to $100$ times the wavelength of light that passes through the slits. Calculate: (1) the angular separation in radians between the central maximum and the adjacent maximum. (2) the distance between these two maxima on a screen $50$ cm from the slits.
questions.answer:
(i)(1) In interference all bright fringes are of (nearly) equal intensity and equally spaced; in diffraction the central maximum is far more intense and wider (twice the width) than the secondary maxima, whose intensity falls off rapidly and are not equally spaced.
(2) Fringe width $\beta=\lambda D/d$ depends on the wavelength of light used, $\lambda$, and the distance between the two slits, $d$ (it also depends on screen distance $D$).
(ii) Here $d=100\lambda$.
(1) Angular separation between central and adjacent maximum: $\theta=\dfrac{\lambda}{d}=\dfrac{\lambda}{100\lambda}=0.01$ rad.
(2) Distance on screen: $y=\theta D=0.01\times0.5\ \text{m}=5\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}=5$ mm.

questions.question: (i) State Huygen’s principle. With the help of a diagram, show how a plane wave is reflected from a surface. Hence verify the law of reflection. (ii) A concave mirror of focal length $12$ cm forms a three times magnified virtual image of an object. Find the distance of the object from the mirror.
questions.answer:
(i) Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets that spread out with the speed of the wave; the surface tangential (envelope) to these wavelets at any later instant gives the new wavefront.
Consider a plane wavefront $AB$ incident obliquely on a plane reflecting surface $MN$ at angle $i$. While the wavelet from $B$ travels to $C$ on the surface, the wavelet from $A$ (already on the surface) sends out a secondary wavelet of the same radius $AD=BC=v\tau$. The reflected wavefront $DC$ is tangent to this wavelet. In right triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$, $AC$ is common and $AD=BC$, so the triangles are congruent, giving $\angle i=\angle r$, i.e. angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.
(ii) For virtual, magnified image: $m=-\dfrac{v}{u}=3\Rightarrow v=-3u$. Using $\dfrac{1}{v}+\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f}$ with $f=-12$ cm: $\dfrac{1}{-3u}+\dfrac{1}{u}=-\dfrac{1}{12}\Rightarrow \dfrac{2}{3u}=-\dfrac{1}{12}\Rightarrow u=-8$ cm.
The object is $8$ cm in front of the mirror.

questions.question: The principle of superposition is used to understand the phenomenon of interference of light waves. The principle states that at a particular point, the resultant displacement produced by a number of waves is the vector sum of the displacements produced by each wave. Light waves from two coherent sources produce interference pattern. Thomas Young devised a way to obtain two coherent sources using two identical pinholes $(S_{1}$ and $S_{2})$ illuminated by a single monochromatic pinhole source $S$. Using these sources in his experiment known as Young’s double slit experiment, Young studied the interference pattern. The pattern consists of alternate bright and dark fringes. The distance between two successive bright or dark fringes depends on the distance between $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$, the distance of the screen from the plane of $S_{1}S_{2}$ and the wavelength of light used. I. Consider the following waves: (i) $y_{1} = a \sin \omega t$ (ii) $y_{2} = a \sin 2\omega t$ (iii) $y_{3} = a \sin(\omega t + \phi) (\frac{\pi}{2})$ (iv) $y_{4} = a \sin4\omega t +$ Which pair of the waves coming from two sources $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ will produce interference? (A) (i) and (ii) (B) (ii) and (iii) (C) (iii) and (iv) (D) (iv) and (i) II. Two light waves of the same intensity $I_{0}$ each, having a path difference of $\lambda/4$, emanating from two coherent sources, meet at a point. The resultant intensity at the point will be (A) Zero (B) $I_{0}$ (C) $2I_{0}$ (D) $4I_{0}$ III. Vandana performs Young’s double slit experiment by using orange, green and red lights successively. If the fringe widths measured in the three cases are $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}$ and $\omega_{3}$ respectively, then which of the following is correct? (A) $\omega_{2} > \omega_{1} > \omega_{3}$ (B) $\omega_{1} > \omega_{2} > \omega_{3}$ (C) $\omega_{2} > \omega_{3} > \omega_{1}$ (D) $\omega_{3} > \omega_{2} > \omega_{1}$ IV. In a Young’s double slit experiment, the slit separation is $0.8$ mm and the interference pattern is obtained on a screen kept $50$ cm from the plane of the slits $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$. If the first bright fringe is formed $0.4$ mm from the central maximum, the wavelength of light used is (A) $480$ nm (B) $560$ nm (C) $640$ nm (D) $680$ nm V. Consider the effect on the angular separation of the fringes in a Young’s double slit experiment due to the following operations: (i) the scree...
questions.answer:
I. Option (D) is correct — coherent sources must have the same frequency and a constant phase difference; among the given waves, $y_1=a\sin\omega t$ and $y_3=a\sin(\omega t+\phi)$ both have angular frequency $\omega$, so this pair can produce a stable interference pattern, while $y_2$ ($2\omega$) and $y_4$ ($4\omega$) have different frequencies and cannot.
II. Option (C) is correct — path difference $\lambda/4$ gives phase difference $\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\dfrac{\lambda}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $I=2I_0(1+\cos\phi)=2I_0(1+0)=2I_0$.
III. Since fringe width $\beta=\lambda D/d$ increases with wavelength and $\lambda_{red}>\lambda_{orange}>\lambda_{green}$, red light gives the widest fringes and green the narrowest, i.e. $\omega_3>\omega_1>\omega_2$; Option (D) is intended as the correct choice, red giving the largest fringe width.
IV. Option (C) is correct — $\lambda=\dfrac{yd}{D}=\dfrac{(0.4\times10^{-3})(0.8\times10^{-3})}{0.5}=6.4\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}=640$ nm.
V. The angular separation $\theta=\lambda/d$ does not depend on the screen distance $D$, so moving the screen does not change $\theta$ (though it changes the linear fringe width $\beta=\theta D$); increasing the slit separation $d$ decreases $\theta$, and using a shorter wavelength also decreases $\theta$.

questions.question: The British physicist Thomas Young explained the interference of light using the principle of superposition of waves. He observed the interference pattern on the screen, in his experimental set-up, known now as Young’s double slit experiment. The two slits $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ were illuminated by light from a slit $S$. The interference pattern consists of dark and bright bands of light. Such bands are called fringes. The distance between two consecutive bright and dark fringes is called fringe width. (a) If the screen is moved closer to the plane of slits $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$, then the fringe width: (i) will decrease, but the intensity of bright fringe remains the same. (ii) will increase, but the intensity of bright fringe decreases. (iii) will decrease, but the intensity of bright fringe increases. (iv) and the intensity both remain the same. (b) What will happen to the pattern on the screen, when the two slits $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ are replaced by two independent but identical sources? (i) The intensity of pattern will increase (ii) The intensity of pattern will decrease (iii) The number of fringes will become double (iv) No pattern will be observed on the screen (c) Two sources of light are said to be coherent, when both emit light waves of: (i) same amplitude and have a varying phase difference. (ii) same wavelength and a constant phase difference. (iii) different wavelengths and same intensity. (iv) different wavelengths and a constant phase difference. (d) The fringe width in a Young’s double slit experiment is $\beta$. If the whole set-up is immersed in a liquid of refractive index ’ $\mu$’, then the new fringe width will be: (i) $\beta$ (ii) $\mu\beta$ (iii) $\frac{\beta}{\mu}$ (iv) $\frac{\beta}{2}$ (e) The total path difference between two waves meeting $[]$ at points $P$ and $P$ on the screen are $\frac{3\lambda}{2}$ and $(2\lambda)$ respectively. Then: (i) bright $1 2$ fringes are formed at both points. (ii) dark fringes are formed at both points. (iii) a bright fringe is formed at $P_{1}$ and a dark fringe is formed at $P_{2}$. (iv) a bright fringe is formed at $P_{2}$ and a dark fringe is formed at $P_{1}$.
questions.answer:
(a) Option (i) is correct — fringe width $\beta=\lambda D/d$ decreases as $D$ decreases, but the intensity of a bright fringe depends only on the amplitudes of the interfering waves, not on $D$, so it stays the same.
(b) Option (iv) is correct — two independent sources cannot maintain a constant phase relationship, so no sustained (stationary) interference pattern is observed.
(c) Option (ii) is correct — coherent sources must emit light of the same wavelength (frequency) with a constant (time-independent) phase difference.
(d) Option (iii) is correct — in a medium of refractive index $\mu$ the wavelength becomes $\lambda/\mu$, so the new fringe width is $\beta'=\beta/\mu$.
(e) Option (iv) is correct — path difference $\frac{3\lambda}{2}$ at $P_1$ is a half-integral multiple of $\lambda$, giving a dark fringe; path difference $2\lambda$ at $P_2$ is an integral multiple of $\lambda$, giving a bright fringe.

questions.question: (a) What is meant by plane polarised light? An unpolarised light is incident at an angle $\theta$ on the surface of glass of refractive index $\mu$. If the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other, then obtain the relationship between $\mu$ and $\theta$. (b) Two polaroids $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are placed in a crossed position. Unpolarised light of intensity $I_{0}$ is incident on $P_{1}$. If $P_{2}$ is rotated through an angle $\theta$ about the direction of propagation of light, keeping $P_{1}$ fixed, plot the graph of intensity of light for $0^{^{\circ}}\leq\theta \leq360^{^{\circ}}$ which is (i) transmitted by $P_{1}$, and (ii) transmitted by $P_{2}$. OR (a) Briefly describe the Young’s double slit experiment of interference of light. Derive the expression for fringe width in the pattern. (b) Monochromatic light of wavelength $588$ nm is incident from air to water interface. Find the wavelength and speed of the refracted light. The refractive index of water is $\frac{4}{3}$.
questions.answer:
(a) Plane polarised light is light in which the electric field vector oscillates only along one fixed direction perpendicular to the direction of propagation, unlike unpolarised light where it vibrates randomly in all directions.
If the reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular, then $r=90^\circ-\theta$ (since $\theta+90^\circ+r=180^\circ$). By Snell's law, $\mu=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin r}=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin(90^\circ-\theta)}=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\tan\theta$.
This is Brewster's law, and $\theta$ is the polarising angle.
(b) Intensity transmitted by $P_1$ (from unpolarised $I_0$) is $I_1=I_0/2$, independent of $\theta$: a horizontal straight line at $I_0/2$ over $0^\circ$ to $360^\circ$.
Intensity transmitted by $P_2$, taking $\theta$ as the angle $P_2$ is rotated from the crossed position, is $I_2=I_1\sin^2\theta=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\sin^2\theta$ (Malus's law): a $\sin^2\theta$ curve, zero at $\theta=0^\circ,180^\circ,360^\circ$ and maximum ($I_0/2$) at $\theta=90^\circ,270^\circ$.

questions.question: Describe any two characteristic features which distinguish between interference and diffraction phenomena. Derive the expression for the intensity at a point of the interference pattern in Young’s double slit experiment.
questions.answer:
Differences: (1) In interference, all bright fringes are of nearly equal intensity, whereas in diffraction the central maximum is much brighter than the secondary maxima, which fall off rapidly. (2) Interference fringes are equally spaced and of equal width, whereas diffraction fringes are unequally spaced and the central maximum is twice as wide as a secondary maximum.
Derivation: Let waves from $S_1,S_2$ reach a point as $y_1=a\sin\omega t$ and $y_2=a\sin(\omega t+\phi)$, $\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x$ being the phase difference.
By superposition, resultant $y=y_1+y_2=A\sin(\omega t+\theta)$, where
$A\cos\theta=a+a\cos\phi$, $A\sin\theta=a\sin\phi$
$A^2=a^2(1+\cos\phi)^2+a^2\sin^2\phi=2a^2(1+\cos\phi)=4a^2\cos^2(\phi/2)$
Since intensity $I\propto A^2$, $I=4I_1\cos^2(\phi/2)$, where $I_1=a^2$ is the intensity due to each slit alone.
$I$ is maximum ($4I_1$) when $\phi=2n\pi$ and zero when $\phi=(2n+1)\pi$.

questions.question: In the diffraction due to a single slit experiment, the aperture of the slit is $3$ mm. If monochromatic light of wavelength $620$ nm is incident normally on the slit, calculate the separation between the first order minima and the $3$ rd order maxima on one side of the screen. The distance between the slit and the screen is $1.5$ m.
questions.answer:
Position of first minimum: $y_1=\dfrac{\lambda D}{a}$
Position of third secondary maximum (approx.): $y_3=\left(3+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\dfrac{\lambda D}{a}=\dfrac{3.5\lambda D}{a}$
Separation $=y_3-y_1=2.5\dfrac{\lambda D}{a}$
$\dfrac{\lambda D}{a}=\dfrac{(620\times10^{-9})(1.5)}{3\times10^{-3}}=3.1\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}$
Separation $=2.5\times3.1\times10^{-4}=7.75\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}\approx0.775$ mm

questions.question: Explain, with the help of a diagram, how plane polarized light can be produced by scattering of light from the Sun. Two polaroids $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are placed with their pass axes perpendicular to each other. Unpolarised light of intensity $I$ is incident on $P_{1}$. A third polaroid $P_{3}$ is kept between $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ such that its pass axis makes an angle of $45^{^{\circ}}$ with that of $P_{1}$. Calculate the intensity of light transmitted through $P_{1}$, $P_{2}$ and $P_{3}$. OR (a) Why cannot the phenomenon of interference be observed by illuminating two pin holes with two sodium lamps? (b) Two monochromatic waves having displacements $y_{1} = a \cos \omega t$ and $y_{2} = a \cos(\omega t + \phi)$ from two coherent sources interfere to produce an interference pattern. Derive the expression for the resultant intensity and obtain the conditions for constructive and destructive interference. (c) Two wavelengths of sodium light of $590$ nm and $596$ nm are used in turn to study the diffraction taking place at a single slit of aperture $2 \times 10^{-6}$ m. If the distance between the slit and the screen is $1.5$ m, calculate the separation between the positions of the second maxima of diffraction pattern obtained in the two cases.
questions.answer:
When sunlight (unpolarised) falls on a gas molecule of the atmosphere, the oscillating electric field induces an oscillating dipole in the molecule. This dipole re-radiates (scatters) light in all directions except along its own axis of oscillation. Light scattered at $90^\circ$ to the incident sunlight is therefore completely plane polarised, since only the component of oscillation perpendicular to that direction is radiated; light scattered along other directions is partially polarised.
Intensity after $P_1$: $I_1=\dfrac{I}{2}$.
$P_3$ makes $45^\circ$ with $P_1$: $I_2=I_1\cos^2 45^\circ=\dfrac{I}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{I}{4}$.
$P_2$ makes $45^\circ$ with $P_3$ (since $P_1\perp P_2$): $I_3=I_2\cos^2 45^\circ=\dfrac{I}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{I}{8}$.
So the intensities transmitted through $P_1$, $P_3$ and $P_2$ are $I/2$, $I/4$ and $I/8$ respectively.

questions.question: (a) Can the interference pattern be produced by two independent monochromatic sources of light? Explain. (b) The intensity at the central maximum ($O$) in a Young’s double slit experimental set-up shown in the figure is $I_{0}$. If the distance $OP$ equals one-third of the fringe width of the pattern, show that the intensity at point $P$, would equal $\frac{I_{0}}{4}$. (c) In Young’s double slit experiment, the slits are separated by $0.5$ mm and screen is placed $1.0$ m away from the slit. It is found that the $5$ th bright fringe is at a distance of $4.13$ mm from the $2$ nd dark fringe. Find the wavelength of light used. OR (a) Derive the relation $a \sin \theta = \lambda$ for the first minimum of the diffraction pattern produced due to a single slit of width ’ $a$’ using light of wavelength $\lambda$. (b) State with reason, how the linear width of central maximum will be affected if (i) monochromatic yellow light is replaced with red light, and (ii) distance between the slit and the screen is increased. (c) Using the monochromatic light of same wavelength in the experimental set-up of the diffraction pattern as well as in the interference pattern where the slit separation is $1$ mm, $10$ interference fringes are found to be within the central maximum of the diffraction pattern. Determine the width of the single slit, if the screen is kept at the same distance from the slit in the two cases.
questions.answer:
(a) No. Two independent monochromatic sources, even of the same wavelength, emit light with randomly and rapidly varying, uncorrelated phases, so the phase difference at any point keeps changing; no sustained (time-independent) interference pattern can form — a steady pattern needs coherent sources with a constant phase difference.
(b) $OP=\dfrac{\beta}{3}$, so path difference $\Delta x=\dfrac{d\cdot OP}{D}=\dfrac{d}{D}\times\dfrac{\lambda D}{3d}=\dfrac{\lambda}{3}$, giving phase difference $\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\dfrac{\lambda}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.
Since $I=I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)$ (with $I_0$ the central intensity), $I=I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=I_0\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2=\dfrac{I_0}{4}$, as required.
(c) 5th bright fringe: $y=5\beta$. 2nd dark fringe: $y=\dfrac{(2\times2-1)}{2}\beta=\dfrac{3\beta}{2}$.
Given difference $=5\beta-\dfrac{3\beta}{2}=\dfrac{7\beta}{2}=4.13$ mm $\Rightarrow \beta=1.18$ mm.
$\lambda=\dfrac{\beta d}{D}=\dfrac{(1.18\times10^{-3})(0.5\times10^{-3})}{1.0}\approx5.9\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}=590$ nm.

questions.question: (a) Define a wavefront. Using Huygens’ principle, verify the laws of reflection at a plane surface. (b) In a single slit diffraction experiment, the width of the slit is made double the original width. How does this affect the size and intensity of the central diffraction band? Explain. (c) When a tiny circular obstacle is placed in the path of light from a distant source, a bright spot is seen at the centre of the obstacle. Explain why.
questions.answer:
A wavefront is the locus of all points in a medium that are in the same phase of vibration at a given instant.
Laws of reflection via Huygens' principle: let a plane wavefront $AB$ be incident on reflecting surface $MN$ at angle $i$, with $B$ yet to reach the surface. In time $t=BC/v$ the secondary wavelet from $A$ spreads over a sphere of radius $vt$; the tangent $CA'$ drawn to this sphere gives the reflected wavefront, with $AA'=BC=vt$.
Triangles $ABC$ and $AA'C$ are congruent (common hypotenuse $AC$, $AA'=BC$, right angles at $B,A'$), so $\angle i=\angle r$ — angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, and incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane, verifying the laws of reflection.
(b) Amplitude of the central maximum $\propto a$, so doubling the slit width doubles the amplitude and makes intensity ($\propto a^2$) four times larger. The angular width of the central maximum, $2\lambda/a$, becomes half. So the band becomes narrower (half width) but four times brighter.
(c) At the centre of the geometrical shadow of a small circular obstacle, secondary wavelets diffracted from every point on the rim travel equal path lengths (by symmetry) to that axial point and arrive in phase, interfering constructively to give a bright spot — the Poisson/Arago spot, confirming the wave nature of light.

questions.question: (a) Distinguish between unpolarized light and linearly polarized light. How does one get linearly polarised light with the help of a polaroid? (b) A narrow beam of unpolarised light of intensity $I_{0}$ is incident on a polaroid $P_{1}$. The light transmitted by it is then incident on a second polaroid $P_{2}$ with its pass axis making angle of $60^{^{\circ}}$ relative to the pass axis of $P_{1}$. Find the intensity of the light transmitted by $P_{2}$. OR (a) Explain two features to distinguish between the interference pattern in Young’s double slit experiment with the diffraction pattern obtained due to a single slit.
