(b) A monochromatic light of wavelength $500 nm$ is incident normally on a single slit of width $0.2 mm$ to produce a diffraction pattern. Find the angular width of the central maximum obtained on the screen. Estimate the number of fringes obtained in Young’s double slit experiment with fringe width $0.5 mm$, which can be accommodated within the region of total angular spread of the central maximum due to single slit.
questions.answer:
(a) Unpolarised light has its electric field vibrating randomly in all directions perpendicular to the direction of propagation, with no preferred direction; linearly polarised light has vibrations confined to one fixed direction.
A polaroid contains long-chain molecules aligned along one direction; it absorbs the electric field component along the chains and transmits only the component along its pass axis, so unpolarised light emerging from it is linearly polarised along that axis.
(b) After $P_1$: $I_1=I_0/2$ (unpolarised light, only half the intensity passes any polaroid), now polarised along $P_1$'s axis.
By Malus's law, after $P_2$ (at $60^{\circ}$ to $P_1$): $I_2=I_1\cos^2 60^{\circ}=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{I_0}{8}$.

questions.question: (a) Define wavefront. Use Huygens’ principle to verify the laws of refraction. (b) How is linearly polarised light obtained by the process of scattering of light? Find the Brewster angle for air - glass interface, when the refractive index of glass $= 1.5$.
questions.answer:
A wavefront is the locus of points vibrating in the same phase at a given instant.
Let plane wavefront $AB$ in medium 1 (speed $v_1$) be incident on the interface at angle $i$. While the wavelet from $B$ travels $BC=v_1t$ to reach the surface, the secondary wavelet from $A$ in medium 2 (speed $v_2$) spreads to radius $AA'=v_2t$; the tangent $CA'$ gives the refracted wavefront at angle $r$.
Since $AC$ is common, $\sin i=v_1t/AC$, $\sin r=v_2t/AC$, so $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}={}_1n_2=$ constant — Snell's law is verified, with incident ray, refracted ray and normal in one plane.
(b) When unpolarised sunlight strikes an air molecule, electrons oscillate along the incident $E$-field; an oscillating charge does not radiate along its own axis of oscillation, so light scattered at $90^{\circ}$ to the incident beam contains only the perpendicular component and is completely plane polarised.
Brewster angle: $\tan i_B=\mu=1.5\Rightarrow i_B=\tan^{-1}(1.5)\approx 56.3^{\circ}$.

questions.question: (a) Define wavefront. Use Huygens’ principle to verify the laws of refraction. (b) How is linearly polarised light obtained by the process of scattering of light? Find the Brewster angle for air-glass interface, when the refractive index of glass $= 1.5$. OR (a) Draw a ray diagram to show the image formation by a combination of two thin convex lenses in contact. Obtain the expression for the power of this combination in terms of the focal lengths of the lenses. (b) A ray of light passing from air through an equilateral glass prism undergoes minimum deviation when the angle of incidence is $\frac{3}{4}$ th of the angle of prism. Calculate the speed of light in the prism.
questions.answer:
A wavefront is the locus of points vibrating in the same phase at a given instant.
Consider a plane wavefront $AB$ in medium 1 (speed $v_1$) incident on the boundary at angle $i$. While the disturbance from $B$ reaches the surface at $C$ in time $t=BC/v_1$, the secondary wavelet from $A$ in medium 2 (speed $v_2$) spreads to radius $AA'=v_2t$. Tangent $CA'$ is the refracted wavefront, making angle $r$ with the surface.
Since $AC$ is common, $\sin i=v_1t/AC$ and $\sin r=v_2t/AC$, giving $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}={}_1n_2=$ constant — Snell's law is verified, and incident ray, refracted ray, normal lie in one plane.
(b) Scattering polarises light because electrons of air molecules oscillate along the incident $E$-field and do not radiate along their own oscillation axis; light scattered at $90^{\circ}$ to the incident beam is therefore completely plane polarised.
Brewster angle for air-glass: $\tan i_B=\mu=1.5\Rightarrow i_B=\tan^{-1}(1.5)\approx 56.3^{\circ}$.

questions.question: (a) Explain why the intensity of light coming out of a polaroid does not change irrespective of the orientation of the pass axis of the polaroid. (b) State, using a proper diagram, the condition when unpolarized light incident on the boundary between two transparent media produces polarised light. Explain briefly. Hence show that the angle of incidence $i_{B}$ is related to the refractive index $\mu$ by the relation, $\mu = \tan i_{B}$. OR (a) A point object $O$ on the principal axis of a spherical surface of radius of curvature $R$ separating two media of refractive indices $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ forms an image $I$ as shown in the figure. Prove that $\frac{n_{2}}{v}-\frac{n_{1}}{u}= \frac{n_{2} -n_{1}}{R}$. Use this expression to derive lens maker’s formula. Draw the necessary diagram. (b) A convex lens is placed over a plane mirror. A pin is now positioned so that there is no parallax between the pin and its image formed by this lens-mirror combination. How will you use this observation to find focal length of the lens? Explain briefly.
questions.answer:
(a) Unpolarised light has, on average, equal intensity components along every direction perpendicular to its propagation direction — there is no preferred direction. When passed through a polaroid, the transmitted intensity is always $I_0/2$ whatever the orientation of the pass axis, because the average of $\cos^2\theta$ over all randomly oriented components is always $\tfrac{1}{2}$; hence intensity does not change on rotating the polaroid, unlike for already polarised light, which follows Malus's law and shows maxima and minima on rotation.
(b) When unpolarised light is incident on the interface between two transparent media at the polarising angle $i_B$, the reflected ray is completely plane polarised (vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence), and the reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular.
Since $i_B+90^{\circ}+r=180^{\circ}$, $r=90^{\circ}-i_B$. By Snell's law, $\mu=\dfrac{\sin i_B}{\sin r}=\dfrac{\sin i_B}{\sin(90^{\circ}-i_B)}=\dfrac{\sin i_B}{\cos i_B}=\tan i_B$.

questions.question: (a) Why does unpolarised light from a source show a variation in intensity when viewed through a polaroid which is rotated? Show with the help of a diagram, how unpolarised light from sun gets linearly polarised by scattering. (b) Three identical polaroid sheets $P_{1}$, $P_{2}$ and $P_{3}$ are oriented so that the pass axis of $P_{2}$ and $P_{3}$ are inclined at angles of $60^{^{\circ}}$ and $90^{^{\circ}}$ respectively with the pass axis of $P_{1}$. A monochromatic source $S$ of unpolarized light of intensity $I_{0}$ is kept in front of the polaroid sheet $P_{1}$ as shown in the figure. Determine the intensities of light as observed by the observer at $O$, when polaroid $P_{2}$ is rotated with respect to $P_{1}$ at angles $\theta = 30^{^{\circ}}$ and $60^{^{\circ}}$.
questions.answer:
(a) A polaroid transmits only the field component along its pass axis (Malus's law, $I=I_0\cos^2\theta$). For genuinely unpolarised light the vibrations are distributed equally in all transverse directions, so the average transmitted intensity stays fixed at $I_0/2$ however the polaroid is rotated — a steady, non-varying intensity is the signature of unpolarised light, unlike polarised light, which shows maxima and minima on rotation.
When unpolarised sunlight strikes an air molecule, its electrons oscillate along the incident $E$-field and do not radiate along their own oscillation axis; light scattered at $90^{\circ}$ to the incident beam therefore contains only the component perpendicular to the scattering plane and is completely plane polarised.
(b) $I(P_1)=I_0/2$. With $P_2$ at angle $\theta$ to $P_1$: $I(P_2)=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2\theta$. $P_3$ is fixed at $90^{\circ}$ to $P_1$, so the angle between $P_2$ and $P_3$ is $(90^{\circ}-\theta)$: $I(P_3)=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta=\dfrac{I_0}{8}\sin^2 2\theta$.
At $\theta=30^{\circ}$: $\sin^2 60^{\circ}=3/4$, so $I=\dfrac{3I_0}{32}$.
At $\theta=60^{\circ}$: $\sin^2 120^{\circ}=3/4$, so $I=\dfrac{3I_0}{32}$ again.

questions.question: (a) Derive an expression for path difference in Young’s double slit experiment and obtain the conditions for constructive and destructive interference at a point on the screen. (b) The intensity at the central maxima in Young’s double slit experiment is $I_{0}$. Find out the intensity at a point where the path difference is $\frac{\lambda}{6}$, $\frac{\lambda}{4}$ and $\frac{\lambda}{3}$.
questions.answer:
(a) Let $S_1,S_2$ be coherent sources separated by $d$, screen at distance $D$. For point $P$ on the screen at distance $y$ from the centre, path difference $\Delta=S_2P-S_1P\approx\dfrac{yd}{D}$ (since $D\gg d$).
Constructive interference (bright fringe): $\Delta=n\lambda$, $n=0,\pm1,\pm2,\dots$
Destructive interference (dark fringe): $\Delta=(n+\tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$.
(b) Resultant intensity: $I=I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi\Delta}{\lambda}\right)$, $I_0$ being the central maximum intensity.
For $\Delta=\lambda/6$: $I=I_0\cos^2(30^{\circ})=\dfrac{3I_0}{4}$.
For $\Delta=\lambda/4$: $I=I_0\cos^2(45^{\circ})=\dfrac{I_0}{2}$.
For $\Delta=\lambda/3$: $I=I_0\cos^2(60^{\circ})=\dfrac{I_0}{4}$.

questions.question: When a parallel beam of monochromatic source of light of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident on a single slit of width $a$, show how the diffraction pattern is formed at the screen by the interference of the wavelets from the slit. Show that, besides the central maximum at $[] \theta = 0$, secondary maxima are observed at $\theta =n + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\lambda}{a}$ and the minima at $\theta = \frac{n\lambda}{a}$. Why do secondary maxima get weaker in intensity with increasing $n$? Explain. OR (i) Draw a ray diagram showing the geometry of formation of image of a point object situated on the principal axis and on the convex side of a spherical surface of radius of curvature $R$. Taking the rays as incident from a rarer medium of refractive index $n$ to a denser medium of refractive index $n$, derive the relation $\frac{n_{2}}{v}-\frac{n_{1}}{u}= \frac{n_{2} -n_{1}}{R}$, $1 2$ where symbols have their usual meaning. (ii) Explain briefly how the focal length of a convex lens changes with increase in wavelength of incident light. (iii) What happens to the focal length of convex lens when it is immersed in water? Refractive index of the material of lens is greater than that of water.
questions.answer:
Divide the slit of width $a$ into a large number of equally spaced coherent secondary (Huygens) sources. At angle $\theta$ to the normal, wavelets from the two edges of the slit have path difference $a\sin\theta$.
At $\theta=0$, all wavelets travel equal paths and arrive in phase, giving the most intense central maximum.
Minima: if $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$, the slit can be divided into $2n$ equal strips such that corresponding wavelets from each half differ in path by $\lambda/2$ and cancel pairwise, giving zero intensity at $\theta=n\lambda/a$.
Secondary maxima: occur approximately midway between successive minima, where the slit can be divided into an odd number $(2n+1)$ of parts so that only one unpaired part contributes, at $\theta\approx(n+\tfrac{1}{2})\lambda/a$.
As $n$ increases, the effective contributing width (one out of $2n+1$ parts) becomes a smaller fraction of the slit, so the secondary maxima become progressively weaker.

questions.question: (a) Use Huygens’ principle to show the propagation of a plane wavefront from a denser medium to a rarer medium. Hence find the ratio of the speeds of wavefronts in the two media. (b) (i) Why does an unpolarised light incident on a polaroid get linearly polarised? (ii) Derive the expression of Brewster’s law when unpolarised light passing from a rarer to a denser medium gets polarised on reflection at the interface.
questions.answer:
(a) Let plane wavefront $AB$ in the denser medium (speed $v_1$) be incident on the boundary at angle $i$. While the wavelet from $B$ travels $BC=v_1t$ to reach the surface, the wavelet from $A$ in the rarer medium (speed $v_2$) spreads to radius $AA'=v_2t$; tangent $CA'$ gives the refracted wavefront. Since $AC$ is common, $\sin i=v_1t/AC$, $\sin r=v_2t/AC$, so $\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}=\dfrac{\sin r}{\sin i}$. As the ray bends away from the normal on entering the rarer medium ($r>i$), $v_2>v_1$ — light travels faster in the rarer medium.
(b)(i) A polaroid contains long-chain molecules aligned along one direction; it absorbs the field component perpendicular to its pass axis and transmits only the component along the axis, so the transmitted light has vibrations confined to one direction and is linearly polarised.
(ii) At the Brewster angle $i_B$, the reflected ray is completely polarised and the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular: $i_B+90^{\circ}+r=180^{\circ}\Rightarrow r=90^{\circ}-i_B$. By Snell's law, $\mu=\dfrac{\sin i_B}{\sin r}=\dfrac{\sin i_B}{\cos i_B}=\tan i_B$.

questions.question: (a) Using Huygens’s construction of secondary wavelets explain how a diffraction pattern is obtained on a screen due to a narrow slit on which a monochromatic beam of light is incident normally. (b) Show that the angular width of the first diffraction fringe is half that of the central fringe. $[]$ (c) Explain why the maxima at $\theta =n + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\lambda}{a}$ become weaker and weaker with increasing $n$.
questions.answer:
(a) The slit of width $a$ is treated as a continuous array of coherent secondary (Huygens) sources. Wavelets travelling at angle $\theta$ to the incident direction are brought together on a screen; those from the two edges of the slit have path difference $a\sin\theta$. Their superposition gives a bright central maximum at $\theta=0$, alternating minima at $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$, and weaker secondary maxima at $a\sin\theta\approx(n+\tfrac12)\lambda$ on either side.
(b) The first minima occur at $\theta=\pm\lambda/a$, so the central maximum has full angular width $2\lambda/a$. The first secondary maximum lies between the first minimum ($\theta=\lambda/a$) and second minimum ($\theta=2\lambda/a$), so its angular width is $2\lambda/a-\lambda/a=\lambda/a$ — exactly half that of the central maximum.
(c) At the $n$-th secondary maximum the slit can be divided into $(2n+1)$ equal parts; wavelets from $2n$ of these cancel pairwise (out of phase by $\pi$), leaving only one part's contribution. As $n$ increases, this fraction $1/(2n+1)$ of the slit decreases, so the intensity of successive secondary maxima falls off rapidly.

questions.question: (a) (i) ’Two independent monochromatic sources of light cannot produce a sustained interference pattern’. Give reason. (ii) Light waves each of amplitude "a" and frequency " $\omega$", emanating from two coherent light sources superpose at a point. If the displacements due to these waves is given by $y_{1} = a \cos \omega t$ and $y_{2} = a \cos(\omega t + \phi)$ where $\phi$ is the phase difference between the two, obtain the expression for the resultant intensity at the point. (b) In Young’s double slit experiment, using monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$, the intensity of light at a point on the screen where path difference is $\lambda$, is K units. Find out the intensity of light at a point where path difference is $\lambda/3$. OR (a) How does one demonstrate, using a suitable diagram, that unpolarised light when passed through a Polaroid gets polarised? (b) A beam of unpolarised light is incident on a glass-air interface.Show, using a suitable ray diagram, that light reflected from the interface is totally polarised, when $\mu = \tan i_{B}$, where $\mu$ is the refractive index of glass with respect to air and $i_{B}$ is the Brewster’s angle.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) In two independent sources, atoms emit light randomly and independently of each other, so the phase difference $\phi$ between the two waves changes randomly and very rapidly with time. Since a sustained pattern requires $\phi$ to remain constant, no stationary interference pattern is observed.
(ii) Resultant displacement: $y = y_1+y_2 = a\cos\omega t + a\cos(\omega t+\phi)$.
Using phasor addition, resultant amplitude $R$ satisfies $R^2 = a^2+a^2+2a^2\cos\phi = 2a^2(1+\cos\phi) = 4a^2\cos^2(\phi/2)$.
Since intensity $\propto$ (amplitude)$^2$, $I = 4a^2\cos^2(\phi/2) = I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)$, where $I_0 = 4a^2$ is the intensity when $\phi=0$.
(b) At path difference $\lambda$: $\phi=2\pi$, so $I_0\cos^2\pi = I_0 = K$.
At path difference $\lambda/3$: $\phi = 2\pi/3$, so $I = I_0\cos^2(\pi/3) = I_0(1/2)^2 = I_0/4 = K/4$.
The intensity at that point is $K/4$.

OR
(a) Unpolarised light has its electric field vibrating in all directions perpendicular to the direction of propagation. A polaroid consists of long chain molecules aligned along a fixed direction; it absorbs the component of $E$ parallel to the chains and transmits only the component along its transmission axis. The emergent light has vibrations confined to one plane, i.e. it is plane polarised. This can be verified by placing an analyser polaroid after it and rotating it: the transmitted intensity varies as $I=I_0\cos^2\theta$ (Malus's law), becoming zero when the analyser is crossed at $90^\circ$.
(b) When unpolarised light strikes a glass surface, both reflected and refracted rays are partially polarised. At the Brewster angle $i_B$, the reflected ray is totally plane polarised (vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence), and the reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular, so $i_B+r=90^\circ$.
By Snell's law, $\mu = \dfrac{\sin i_B}{\sin r} = \dfrac{\sin i_B}{\sin(90^\circ-i_B)} = \dfrac{\sin i_B}{\cos i_B} = \tan i_B$.

questions.question: (a) In Young’s double slit experiment, describe briefly how bright and dark fringes are obtained on the screen kept in front of a double slit. Hence obtain the expression for the fringe width. (b) The ratio of the intensities at minima to the maxima in the Young’s double slit experiment is 9: 25. Find the ratio of the widths of the two slits. OR (a) Describe briefly how a diffraction pattern is obtained on a screen due to a single narrow slit illuminated by a monochromatic source of light. Hence obtain the conditions for the angular width of secondary maxima and secondary minima. (b) Two wavelengths of sodium light of 590 nm and 596 nm are used in turn to study the diffraction taking place at a single slit of aperture $2 \times 10^{-6}$ m. The distance between the slit and the screen is 1.5 m. Calculate the separation between the positions of first maxima of the diffraction pattern obtained in the two cases.
questions.answer:
(a) Light from a monochromatic source falls on two narrow, closely spaced coherent slits $S_1,S_2$, which act as secondary coherent sources. The waves from them overlap on the screen; at points where the path difference is an integral multiple of $\lambda$, they interfere constructively giving bright fringes, and where it is $(n+\tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$, they interfere destructively giving dark fringes.
For slit separation $d$ and screen distance $D$, path difference $=\dfrac{yd}{D}$. Bright fringes: $y_n=\dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}$. Fringe width $\beta = y_{n+1}-y_n = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$.
(b) $\dfrac{I_{min}}{I_{max}}=\dfrac{9}{25}\Rightarrow \dfrac{a_1+a_2}{a_1-a_2}=\dfrac{5}{3}$, giving $a_1=4a_2$.
Since intensity/slit-width ratio equals $a^2$ ratio, width ratio $=\dfrac{a_1^2}{a_2^2}=16:1$.

OR
(a) Each point of the slit acts as a source of secondary wavelets (Huygens' principle). Wavelets travelling straight ahead ($\theta=0$) reinforce to give a strong central maximum. For other angles $\theta$, the slit is divided into pairs/parts whose wavelets interfere; minima occur when the path difference between extreme rays $a\sin\theta = n\lambda$ ($n=1,2,3,\dots$), giving angular width condition $\sin\theta = n\lambda/a$. Secondary maxima occur approximately midway, at $a\sin\theta \approx (n+\tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$.
(b) Position of first secondary maximum: $y=\dfrac{3\lambda D}{2a}$.
For $\lambda_1=590$ nm: $y_1=\dfrac{3\times590\times10^{-9}\times1.5}{2\times2\times10^{-6}}=0.664$ m.
For $\lambda_2=596$ nm: $y_2=\dfrac{3\times596\times10^{-9}\times1.5}{2\times2\times10^{-6}}=0.671$ m.
Separation $=y_2-y_1\approx6.75\times10^{-3}$ m $=6.75$ mm.

questions.question: (a) In Young’s double slit experiment, derive the condition for (i) constructive interference and (ii) destructive interference at a point on the screen. (b) A beam of light consisting of two wavelengths, $800$ nm and $600$ nm is used to obtain the interference fringes in a Young’s double slit experiment on a screen placed $1.4$ m away. If the two slits are separated by $0.28$ mm, calculate the least distance from the central bright maximum where the bright fringes of the two wavelengths coincide. OR (a) How does an unpolarized light incident on a polaroid get polarized? Describe briefly, with the help of a necessary diagram, the polarization of light by reflection from a transparent medium. (b) Two polaroids ’A’ and ’B’ are kept in crossed position. How should a third polaroid ’C’ be placed between them so that the intensity of polarized light transmitted by polaroid B reduces to $\frac{1}{8}$ th of the intensity of unpolarized light incident on A?
questions.answer:
(a) Let $S_1,S_2$ be coherent slits separated by $d$, screen at distance $D$. At a point P on screen at height $y$ from the centre, path difference $\Delta = S_2P-S_1P \approx \dfrac{yd}{D}$.
Constructive interference (bright fringe) occurs when $\Delta = n\lambda$, $n=0,\pm1,\pm2,\dots$
Destructive interference (dark fringe) occurs when $\Delta = (n+\tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$, $n=0,\pm1,\pm2,\dots$
(b) Bright fringes coincide when $n_1\lambda_1=n_2\lambda_2 \Rightarrow n_1(800)=n_2(600) \Rightarrow n_1=3,\ n_2=4$ (smallest integers).
$y=\dfrac{n_1\lambda_1D}{d}=\dfrac{3\times800\times10^{-9}\times1.4}{0.28\times10^{-3}}=0.012$ m $=12$ mm.
Least distance from central maximum $=12$ mm.

OR
(a) Unpolarised light passed through a polaroid has only the component of $E$ along the polaroid's transmission axis transmitted, producing plane polarised light. When unpolarised light strikes a transparent medium (glass), the reflected and refracted rays are partially polarised; at the Brewster angle $i_B$, reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other and the reflected ray is completely plane polarised, with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence.
(b) Intensity after A: $I_0/2$. If C is at angle $\theta$ to A, intensity after C $=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2\theta$; angle between C and B (crossed with A) is $(90^\circ-\theta)$, so intensity after B $=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta=\dfrac{I_0}{8}\sin^2(2\theta)$.
For this to equal $I_0/8$: $\sin^2(2\theta)=1\Rightarrow\theta=45^\circ$. So C must be placed with its axis at $45^\circ$ to both A and B.

questions.question: Use Huygens’s principle to explain the formation of diffraction pattern due to a single slit illuminated by a monochromatic source of light. When the width of the slit is made double the original width, how would this affect the size and intensity of the central diffraction band?
questions.answer:
Each point on the slit AB acts as a source of secondary wavelets (Huygens' principle). Wavelets travelling undeviated ($\theta=0$) meet in phase at the centre of the screen, giving the central maximum. For a general angle $\theta$, the slit can be divided into two halves; if the path difference between corresponding wavelets from the two halves is $\lambda/2$, they cancel pairwise, giving minima at $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$. Between successive minima lie weaker secondary maxima, obtained approximately at $a\sin\theta=(n+\tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$.
When the slit width $a$ is doubled: the angular half-width of the central maximum, $\theta=\lambda/a$, is halved, so the central band becomes half as wide.
Since twice as much light now passes through and is concentrated in half the angular width, the amplitude at the centre doubles, so the intensity of the central maximum becomes four times the original.

questions.question: (a) What is the effect on the interference fringes in a Young’s double slit experiment when (i) the separation between the two slits is decreased? (ii) the width of the source slit is increased? (iii) the monochromatic source is replaced by a source of white light? Justify your answer in each case. (b) The intensity at the central maxima in Young’s double slit experimental set-up is $I_{0}$. Show that the intensity at a point where the path difference is $\lambda/3$ is $I_{0}/4$. OR (a) Obtain the conditions for the bright and dark fringes in diffraction pattern due to a single narrow slit illuminated by a monochromatic source. Explain clearly why the secondary maxima go on becoming weaker with increasing $n$. (b) When the width of the slit is made double, how would this affect the size and intensity of the central diffraction band? Justify.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Decreasing slit separation $d$ increases fringe width, since $\beta=\lambda D/d$ is inversely proportional to $d$; fringes become wider and farther apart.
(ii) Increasing the source-slit width reduces the coherence of light reaching $S_1,S_2$; overlapping fringe patterns from different points of the source shift the pattern, reducing fringe contrast/visibility until fringes disappear if the slit is too wide.
(iii) With white light, only the central fringe (zero path difference for all $\lambda$) remains white; fringes of different colours (different $\lambda$) form at slightly different positions on either side, giving a few coloured fringes before they overlap into general illumination.
(b) $I=I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)$, with $\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\dfrac{\lambda}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.
$I=I_0\cos^2(\pi/3)=I_0(1/2)^2=I_0/4$. Hence proved.

OR
(a) Minima: $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$; secondary maxima (approx): $a\sin\theta=(n+\tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$. The slit can be divided into $(2n+1)$ equal parts for the $n$th secondary maximum; contributions from all but one part cancel in pairs, leaving only a small fraction of the amplitude uncancelled. As $n$ increases, a smaller fraction of the slit contributes, so successive secondary maxima become progressively weaker.
(b) Doubling the slit width halves the angular (and linear) width of the central diffraction band, and since the amplitude at the centre doubles, the intensity of the central maximum becomes four times the original.

questions.question: State the importance of coherent sources in the phenomenon of interference. In Young’s double slit experiment to produce interference pattern, obtain the conditions for constructive and destructive interference. Hence deduce the expression for the fringe width. How does the fringe width get affected, if the entire experimental apparatus of Young is immersed in water?
questions.answer:
Coherent sources (constant phase difference) are essential for interference because only then does the phase difference $\phi$, and hence the resultant intensity, remain fixed at every point, giving a stationary (sustained) fringe pattern; with incoherent sources $\phi$ fluctuates randomly and the pattern washes out.
In YDSE, for slits $S_1,S_2$ separated by $d$ and screen at distance $D$, path difference at a point $y$ on screen is $\Delta=\dfrac{yd}{D}$.
Constructive interference (bright fringe): $\Delta=n\lambda$.
Destructive interference (dark fringe): $\Delta=(n+\tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$.
Position of $n$th bright fringe: $y_n=\dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}$; fringe width $\beta=y_{n+1}-y_n=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$.
If the apparatus is immersed in water (refractive index $\mu$), the wavelength decreases to $\lambda'=\lambda/\mu$, so fringe width becomes $\beta'=\dfrac{\lambda D}{\mu d}=\dfrac{\beta}{\mu}$, i.e. the fringe width decreases by a factor $\mu$.

questions.question: (a) State Huygens’ principle. Using this principle explain how a diffraction pattern is obtained on a screen due to a narrow slit on which a narrow beam coming from a monochromatic source of light is incident normally. (b) Show that the angular width of the first diffraction fringe is half of that of the central fringe. (c) If a monochromatic source of light is replaced by white light, what change would you observe in the diffraction pattern?
questions.answer:
(a) Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets, spreading out with the speed of light in the medium; the tangential surface to these wavelets at a later instant gives the new wavefront. For a single slit, secondary wavelets from all points across the slit width $a$ reach the screen. Along the direction $\theta=0$ they arrive in phase, producing the central maximum. For angle $\theta$, wavelets from different parts have different path lengths; when the slit is divided into pairs with path difference $\lambda/2$, they cancel, giving minima at $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$.
(b) The first minimum on either side occurs at $\sin\theta=\lambda/a$, so the central maximum has angular width $2\lambda/a$. The first secondary maximum lies between the first and second minima, i.e. between $\sin\theta=\lambda/a$ and $\sin\theta=2\lambda/a$, giving it an angular width $\lambda/a$ — exactly half that of the central maximum.
(c) With white light, the central maximum remains white (zero path difference for all $\lambda$), but the secondary maxima become coloured patterns, violet nearest the centre and red farthest, since their positions depend on $\lambda$.

questions.question: (i) A plane wavefront approaches a plane surface separating two media. If medium ’one’ is optically denser and medium ’two’ is optically rarer, using Huygens’ principle, explain and show how a refracted wavefront is constructed. (ii) Hence verify Snell’s law. (iii) When a light wave travels from a rarer to a denser medium, the speed decreases. Does it imply reduction in its energy? Explain.
questions.answer:
(i) Let the plane wavefront AB be incident on the interface with medium 1 (denser, speed $v_1$) above and medium 2 (rarer, speed $v_2>v_1$) below. When the wavefront reaches the interface at A, secondary wavelets are generated at successive points along the interface as the wavefront advances; since medium 2 is rarer, wavelets there travel faster and spread out to larger radii ($v_2t$) than those still in medium 1. The tangent (envelope) to these secondary wavelets gives the refracted wavefront, which is tilted away from the normal compared to the incident wavefront, since $v_2>v_1$.
(ii) In triangle formed by incident and refracted wavefronts sharing the interface segment BC: $\sin i=\dfrac{v_1t}{BC}$ and $\sin r=\dfrac{v_2t}{BC}$, so $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}=$ constant $=n_{21}$, which is Snell's law.
(iii) No. The speed decreases because the medium is denser, but the frequency (fixed by the source) remains unchanged. Energy of a wave depends on its frequency and amplitude, not on its speed; since there is no absorption, the energy carried by the wave is conserved as it enters the denser medium.

questions.question: State Huygens’s principle. Show, with the help of a suitable diagram, how this principle is used to obtain the diffraction pattern by a single slit. Draw a plot of intensity distribution and explain clearly why the secondary maxima become weaker with increasing order (n) of the secondary maxima.
questions.answer:
Huygens' principle: every point of a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets spreading out with the wave speed in that medium, and the envelope (tangent surface) of these wavelets at a later time gives the new wavefront.
For a single slit of width $a$, each point of the slit acts as a secondary source. Wavelets travelling straight through ($\theta=0$) arrive in phase at the centre of the screen, producing the central maximum. For a general angle $\theta$, imagine the slit divided into two halves; if the path difference between corresponding wavelets from the two halves is $\lambda/2$, they cancel pairwise, giving a minimum when $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$. Between successive minima lie weaker secondary maxima at approximately $a\sin\theta=(n+\tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$.
Intensity distribution: a broad, intense central maximum flanked by much weaker secondary maxima that decrease in intensity with increasing order.
For the $n$th secondary maximum, the slit can be divided into $(2n+1)$ parts; contributions from all but one part cancel in pairs, leaving a progressively smaller uncancelled fraction of amplitude as $n$ increases — hence secondary maxima become weaker with increasing $n$.

questions.question: (a) What is plane polarised light? Two polaroids are placed at $90^{^{\circ}}$ to each other and the transmitted intensity is zero. What happens when one more polaroid is placed between these two, bisecting the angle between them? How will the intensity of transmitted light vary on further rotating the third polaroid? (b) If a light beam shows no intensity variation when transmitted through a polaroid which is rotated, does it mean that the light is unpolarised? Explain briefly.
questions.answer:
(a) Plane polarised light is light in which the electric field vector vibrates only along one fixed direction (a single plane containing the direction of propagation), unlike unpolarised light where it vibrates randomly in all perpendicular directions.
With two crossed polaroids A and B, transmitted intensity is zero. Inserting a third polaroid C between them, bisecting the angle (i.e. at $45^\circ$ to both A and B), gives non-zero transmitted intensity: after A, $I=I_0/2$; after C, $I=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2 45^\circ=\dfrac{I_0}{4}$; after B (at $45^\circ$ to C), $I=\dfrac{I_0}{4}\cos^2 45^\circ=\dfrac{I_0}{8}$.
On further rotating C by angle $\theta$ from A, intensity transmitted by B varies as $I=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2\theta\cos^2(90^\circ-\theta)=\dfrac{I_0}{8}\sin^2(2\theta)$, which is maximum ($I_0/8$) at $\theta=45^\circ$ and zero at $\theta=0^\circ$ or $90^\circ$.
(b) Not necessarily. Besides unpolarised light, circularly polarised light also shows no variation in intensity when passed through a rotating polaroid, since its electric field has equal components in all directions in the plane perpendicular to propagation. A further test (e.g. using a quarter-wave plate before the polaroid) is needed to distinguish between the two.

questions.question: What are coherent sources? Why are coherent sources required to produce interference of light? Give an example of interference of light in everyday life. In Young’s double slit experiment, the two slits are 0.03 cm apart and the screen is placed at a distance of 1.5 m away from the slits. The distance between the central bright fringe and fourth bright fringe is 1 cm. Calculate the wavelength of light used.
questions.answer:
Coherent sources are two sources that emit light waves of the same frequency (wavelength) having either a zero or a constant phase difference between them, so that the phase difference does not change with time.
Coherent sources are essential for interference because only when the phase difference is constant do the positions of maxima (constructive superposition) and minima (destructive superposition) remain fixed on the screen; with incoherent sources the phase difference changes randomly and rapidly, so the pattern keeps shifting and the eye/detector observes only a uniform average intensity — no sustained fringes are seen.
Example: the colours seen in a thin soap bubble or an oil film on water are due to interference of light.
Numerical: $d=0.03\ \text{cm}=3\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}$, $D=1.5\ \text{m}$, distance to 4th bright fringe $x_4=1\ \text{cm}$.
Fringe width $\beta=\dfrac{x_4}{4}=0.25\ \text{cm}=2.5\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}$
$\beta=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\Rightarrow \lambda=\dfrac{\beta d}{D}=\dfrac{2.5\times10^{-3}\times3\times10^{-4}}{1.5}=5\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}=5000\ \text{Å}$

questions.question: State the condition under which the phenomenon of diffraction of light takes place. Derive an expression for the width of central maximum due to diffraction of light at a single slit. A slit of width ’ $a$’ is illuminated by a monochromatic light of wavelength 700 nm at normal incidence. Calculate the value of ’ $a$’ for position of (i) first minimum at an angle of diffraction of $30^{^{\circ}}$. (ii) first maximum at an angle of diffraction of $30^{^{\circ}}$.
questions.answer:
Diffraction occurs appreciably when the size of the obstacle or aperture is comparable to the wavelength of light.
Derivation: Consider a slit of width $a$ illuminated normally by monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$, with a screen at distance $D$. By Huygens' principle, every point of the wavefront in the slit acts as a source of secondary wavelets.
For diffraction at angle $\theta$, the path difference between wavelets from the two edges of the slit is $a\sin\theta$.
Dividing the slit into two halves, wavelets from corresponding points differ in path by $\dfrac{a}{2}\sin\theta$; the first minimum occurs when this equals $\lambda/2$, i.e. $a\sin\theta=\lambda$.
For small $\theta$, $\sin\theta\approx\theta\approx x/D$, so $x_1=\dfrac{D\lambda}{a}$.
Width of central maximum $=2x_1=\dfrac{2D\lambda}{a}$.
Numerical ($\lambda=700\ \text{nm}$, $\theta=30^{\circ}$):
(i) First minimum: $a\sin\theta=\lambda\Rightarrow a=\dfrac{700\times10^{-9}}{\sin30^{\circ}}=1.4\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}$
(ii) First (secondary) maximum: $a\sin\theta=\dfrac{3\lambda}{2}\Rightarrow a=\dfrac{1.5\times700\times10^{-9}}{0.5}=2.1\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}$

questions.question: State the essential condition for diffraction of light to take place. Use Huygen’s principle to explain diffraction of light due to a narrow single slit and the formation of a pattern of fringes obtained on the screen. Sketch the pattern of fringes formed due to diffraction at a single slit showing variation of intensity with angle $\theta$.
questions.answer:
Diffraction takes place only when the size of the slit (or obstacle) is comparable to the wavelength of the light used.
Huygens' explanation: when a plane wavefront falls on a narrow slit $AB$ of width $a$, every point of the wavefront within the slit becomes a source of secondary wavelets spreading in all directions.
Wavelets travelling straight ahead ($\theta=0$) reinforce to give the strong central maximum.
Wavelets travelling at angle $\theta$ have a path difference $a\sin\theta$ between the edges of the slit; dividing the slit into pairs of strips, when $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$ ($n=1,2,3,...$) the wavelets from corresponding strips cancel in pairs, giving minima; between successive minima weaker secondary maxima occur where $a\sin\theta=(n+\tfrac12)\lambda$.
Pattern sketch (intensity $I$ vs $\theta$): a tall, broad central maximum at $\theta=0$ extending up to the first minima at $\sin\theta=\pm\lambda/a$, flanked symmetrically by much weaker secondary maxima of rapidly decreasing intensity separated by minima at $\sin\theta=\pm n\lambda/a$.

questions.question: What are coherent sources of light? Why are coherent sources required to obtain sustained interference pattern? State three characteristic features which distinguish the interference pattern due to two coherently illuminated sources as compared to that observed in a diffraction pattern due to a single slit.
questions.answer:
Coherent sources are two sources emitting light waves of the same frequency with a constant (time-independent) phase difference.
They are required to obtain a sustained interference pattern because only a constant phase difference keeps the positions of bright and dark fringes fixed in space; with incoherent sources the phase difference varies randomly with time, so the pattern shifts continuously and only an average uniform intensity is observed.
Three distinguishing features:
(i) In interference all bright fringes have (nearly) equal intensity and equal width $\beta=\lambda D/d$; in diffraction the central maximum is much brighter and twice as wide as the secondary maxima, whose intensity falls off rapidly.
(ii) Interference results from superposition of waves from two separate coherent sources, whereas diffraction results from superposition of secondary wavelets from different parts of the same wavefront.
(iii) In interference all fringes are equally spaced; in diffraction the fringe (maxima) width is not uniform — it decreases with increasing order.

questions.question: What is interference of light? Write two essential conditions for sustained interference pattern to be produced on the screen. Draw a graph showing the variation of intensity versus the position on the screen in Young’s experiment when (a) both the slits are opened and (b) one of the slits is closed. What is the effect on the interference pattern in Young’s double slit experiment when: (i) screen is moved closer to the plane of slits? (ii) separation between two slits is increased. Explain your answer in each case.
questions.answer:
Interference of light is the phenomenon of redistribution of light intensity due to superposition of two coherent light waves, producing regions of maximum intensity (constructive interference) and minimum intensity (destructive interference).
Two essential conditions:
(i) The two sources must be coherent, i.e. emit waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference.
(ii) The amplitudes of the two waves should be equal or nearly equal, so that dark fringes are almost completely dark and contrast is good.
Graph: (a) With both slits open, intensity varies periodically with position $x$ on the screen following $I=4I_0\cos^2(\pi d x/\lambda D)$, giving equally spaced bright and dark fringes.
(b) With one slit closed, only the diffraction pattern of the single open slit is seen — a broad, nearly uniform (slowly varying) intensity distribution with no fine interference fringes.
Effects:
(i) Screen moved closer ($D$ decreases): fringe width $\beta=\lambda D/d$ decreases, so fringes become closer/narrower.
(ii) Slit separation $d$ increased: since $\beta\propto1/d$, fringe width decreases and fringes come closer together (may eventually become indistinguishable).

questions.question: What is diffraction of light? Draw a graph showing the variation of intensity with angle in a single slit diffraction experiment. Write one feature which distinguishes the observed pattern from the double slit interference pattern. How would the diffraction pattern of a single slit be affected when: (i) the width of the slit is decreased? (ii) the monochromatic source of light is replaced by a source of white light?
questions.answer:
Diffraction of light is the bending of light waves around the edges of an obstacle or aperture and their spreading into the region of geometrical shadow, occurring appreciably when the obstacle/aperture size is comparable to the wavelength.
Graph: intensity $I$ vs angle $\theta$ shows a very high, broad central maximum at $\theta=0$, with much weaker secondary maxima on either side whose intensity decreases rapidly with order, separated by minima at $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$.
Distinguishing feature: unlike interference fringes, which are all of equal width and nearly equal intensity, the diffraction central maximum is twice as wide and far more intense than the secondary maxima, whose intensities fall off quickly.
(i) If slit width $a$ is decreased, the central maximum becomes wider, since its angular width $\propto 1/a$.
(ii) If monochromatic light is replaced by white light, the central maximum remains white (all colours coincide at $\theta=0$), but the secondary maxima become coloured, with violet nearer the centre and red farther away, since fringe positions depend on $\lambda$.

questions.question: (a) How is a wavefront different from a ray? Draw the geometrical shape of the wavefronts when (i) light diverges from a point source, and (ii) light emerges out of a convex lens when a point source is placed at its focus. (b) State Huygens’ principle. With the help of a suitable diagram, prove Snell’s law of refraction using Huygens’ principle.
questions.answer:
(a) A wavefront is the locus of all points vibrating in the same phase, whereas a ray is a line drawn perpendicular to the wavefront indicating the direction of propagation of light energy.
(i) For light diverging from a point source, the wavefronts are concentric spheres centred on the source.
(ii) When a point source is placed at the focus of a convex lens, the emergent wavefronts are plane (parallel rays emerge from the lens).
(b) Huygens' principle states that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets which spread out in all directions with the speed of light in that medium, and the new (forward) wavefront at any later instant is the envelope (common tangent surface) of these secondary wavelets.
Derivation of Snell's law: Let a plane wavefront $AB$ be incident on a plane interface separating medium 1 (speed $v_1$) and medium 2 (speed $v_2$) at angle of incidence $i$. While the wavelet from $B$ travels distance $v_1t$ to reach the interface, the secondary wavelet from $A$ travels $v_2t$ into medium 2. From the geometry of the resulting triangles, $\sin i=\dfrac{v_1t}{AC}$ and $\sin r=\dfrac{v_2t}{AC}$, giving $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}=n_{21}$, which on writing $v=c/n$ gives $n_1\sin i=n_2\sin r$, i.e. Snell's law.

questions.question: (a) In Young’s double slit experiment, deduce the conditions for (i) constructive, and (ii) destructive interference at a point on the screen. Draw a graph showing variation of the resultant intensity in the interference pattern against position $x$ on the screen. (b) Compare and contrast the pattern which is seen with two coherently illuminated narrow slits in Young’s experiment with that seen for a coherently illuminated single slit producing diffraction.
questions.answer:
(a) In YDSE, path difference at a point on the screen is $\Delta=d\sin\theta\approx\dfrac{dx}{D}$.
Constructive interference (bright fringe): $\Delta=n\lambda$, $n=0,\pm1,\pm2,...$, giving $x_n=\dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}$.
Destructive interference (dark fringe): $\Delta=(n+\tfrac12)\lambda$, giving $x_n=(n+\tfrac12)\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$.
Graph: resultant intensity $I=4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi d x}{\lambda D}\right)$ versus $x$ is a periodic curve with equally spaced maxima of value $4I_0$ and minima of zero intensity, all maxima being of equal height.
(b) Comparison: in the double-slit interference pattern all bright fringes are equally spaced and have (nearly) equal intensity, since they arise from superposition of waves from two coherent point sources.
In single-slit diffraction, the central maximum is much wider and brighter than the secondary maxima, whose intensity decreases rapidly with order, since they arise from superposition of secondary wavelets from different parts of the same wavefront; also the widths of successive diffraction maxima are unequal, unlike the uniform fringe width of interference.

questions.question: The power factor of a series LCR circuit at resonance will be: (a) 1 (b) 0 (c) $\frac{1}{2}$ (d) $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
questions.answer:
Option (a) is correct.
At resonance $X_L=X_C$, so impedance $Z=R$ (purely resistive) and power factor $\cos\phi=R/Z=1$.

questions.question: An ac source of voltage $V$ = $V_{m}$ sin $\omega t$ is connected to a series combination of LCR circuit. Draw the phasor diagram. Using it obtain an expression for the impedance of the circuit and the phase difference between applied voltage and the current.
questions.answer:
In the phasor diagram, current $I$ is taken along the reference (x-axis) direction.
$V_R=IR$ is in phase with $I$; $V_L=IX_L$ leads $I$ by $90^{\circ}$; $V_C=IX_C$ lags $I$ by $90^{\circ}$, so $V_L$ and $V_C$ are antiparallel and their resultant is $(V_L-V_C)$ perpendicular to $V_R$.
The applied voltage $V$ is the vector sum of $V_R$ and $(V_L-V_C)$:
$V=\sqrt{V_R^2+(V_L-V_C)^2}=I\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$
So impedance $Z=\dfrac{V}{I}=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$
Phase difference: $\tan\phi=\dfrac{X_L-X_C}{R}$, i.e. $\phi=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{X_L-X_C}{R}\right)$, current lagging or leading the voltage depending on the sign of $(X_L-X_C)$.

questions.question: Find the wavelength of the electron orbiting in the first excited state in hydrogen atom.
questions.answer:
For the first excited state, $n = 2$.
Radius $r_2 = n^2 a_0 = 4 \times 0.529 \times 10^{-10}$ m $= 2.116 \times 10^{-10}$ m.
By Bohr's postulate, $n\lambda = 2\pi r_n$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi r_2}{2} = \pi r_2$.
$\lambda = 3.14 \times 2.116 \times 10^{-10} = 6.65 \times 10^{-10}$ m.

questions.question: Two cells of emfs 1.5 V and 2.0 V having internal resistances 0.2 Ω and 0.3 Ω respectively are connected in parallel. Calculate the emf and internal resistance of the equivalent cell.
questions.answer:
For two cells in parallel, the equivalent emf is $E_{eq} = \dfrac{E_1/r_1 + E_2/r_2}{1/r_1 + 1/r_2}$ and equivalent internal resistance $r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1 r_2}{r_1+r_2}$.
Substituting $E_1=1.5$ V, $r_1=0.2$ Ω, $E_2=2.0$ V, $r_2=0.3$ Ω:
$E_{eq} = \dfrac{7.5+6.67}{5+3.33} = 1.7$ V.
$r_{eq} = \dfrac{0.2\times0.3}{0.5} = 0.12$ Ω.

questions.question: Two sources of equal emf are connected in series. This combination is, in turn connected to an external resistance R. The internal resistance of two sources are $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ ($r_{2}$ > $r_{1}$). If the potential difference across the source of internal resistance r is zero, then R equals to: (a) $\frac{r+r}{r-r}^{1}{}^{2}$ (b) $_{2}{}_{1}r_{2}$– $r_{1}$ (c) $\frac{r r}{r-r}^{1}{}^{2}$ (d) $\frac{r+r}{r r}^{1}{}^{2}$ 2112
questions.answer:
Option (b) is correct, $R = r_2 - r_1$.
Current in the circuit is $I = \dfrac{2\varepsilon}{R+r_1+r_2}$; for zero potential difference across the source of internal resistance $r_2$, $\varepsilon = I r_2$, giving $I = \varepsilon/r_2$.
Equating the two expressions for $I$ gives $R + r_1 + r_2 = 2r_2$, so $R = r_2 - r_1$.

questions.question: A steady current of 8 mA flows through a wire. The number of electrons passing through a cross-section of the wire in 10 s is (A) $4.0 \times 10^{16}$ (B) $5.0 \times 10^{17}$ (C) $1.6 \times 10^{16}$ (D) $1.0 \times 10^{17}$
questions.answer:
Option (B) is correct, $5.0 \times 10^{17}$.
Charge $Q = It = 8\times10^{-3}\times10 = 0.08$ C, and number of electrons $n = Q/e = 0.08/(1.6\times10^{-19}) = 5.0\times10^{17}$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Define intensity of radiation on the basis of photon picture of light. Write its S.I. unit.
questions.answer:
Intensity of radiation is the energy incident per unit area per unit time on a surface, equal to $n \times h\nu$, where $n$ is the number of photons falling per unit area per second.
Its SI unit is $\text{W/m}^2$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An $\alpha$-particle and a proton are accelerated through the same potential difference. Find the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths.
questions.answer:
De Broglie wavelength after acceleration through potential $V$ is $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$.
$\dfrac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_p q_p}{m_\alpha q_\alpha}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_p \cdot e}{4m_p \cdot 2e}} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$.
So $\lambda_\alpha : \lambda_p = 1 : 2\sqrt{2}$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Photons of frequency v are incident on the surface of two metal A and B of threshold frequencies 3 v/4 and 2 v/3, respectively. The ratio of maximum kinetic energy of electrons emitted from A to that from B is (a) 2: 3 (b) 4: 3 (c) 3: 4 (d) 3: 2

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: $The threshold frequency for a metal is 3.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz. $A beam of frequency 9.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz is incident on the metal. Calculate (i) the work function (in eV) of the metal and (ii) the maximum speed of photoelectrons.

Maximum kinetic energy: $KE_{max} = h(
